### Even positive definite unimodular lattices need dimension divisible by 8

**Remember:** Even norms make the theta series modular for everything, which forces eight.

*Rules out counterexamples. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11H06 (Lattices and convex bodies (number-theoretic aspects)), 11E12. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A lattice in ℝⁿ is unimodular when its Gram matrix, the matrix of dot products of a basis, has integer entries and determinant ±1. It is even when every vector x has even norm x·x, and odd otherwise.

**Problem.** A positive definite even unimodular lattice exists only when the dimension n is divisible by 8. Odd unimodular lattices exist in every dimension, for example ℤⁿ. The E₈ and Leech lattices are even, of dimensions 8 and 24.

**How the definition helps.** Evenness makes the theta series invariant under z ↦ z + 1, and that leads to the 8 (our own). The theta series is Σ q to the power x·x/2 over lattice vectors x, with q = e to the 2πiz. Evenness makes the exponents integers, so the series has period 1 (our own). Unimodularity gives the law for z ↦ −1/z, with a factor (z/i) to the power n/2 (our own). Combining the two laws in the modular group forces n ≡ 0 mod 8 (our own). The lattice ℤⁿ is odd, and the page says its theta series is modular only for Γ₀(4). Serre's book proves the mod 8 result by another route (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Unimodular lattice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unimodular_lattice). It says: “If the lattice is even, the form has level 1, and if the lattice is odd the form has Γ₀(4) structure (i.e., it is a modular form of level 4).”

**Sources:**

- [J.-P. Serre, A Course in Arithmetic, Graduate Texts in Mathematics 7, Springer, 1973](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4684-9884-4)
- [J. Milnor and D. Husemoller, Symmetric Bilinear Forms, Springer, 1973](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-642-88330-9)

### Equidistribution makes normal numbers a consequence of ergodicity

**Remember:** A normal number visits intervals at the right frequencies under multiplication by its base.

*True by definition.* MSC 11K16 (Normal numbers, radix expansions, Pisot numbers, Salem numbers, good lattice points, etc.), 37A44. arXiv math.NT, math.DS. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A real number x is normal in integer base b ≥ 2 if every length-k block of its digits has frequency 1/bᵏ. Equivalently, the fractional parts of bᵏx are equidistributed. This means their visits to each interval in \[0, 1) have frequency equal to the length of that interval.

**Problem.** For each integer base b ≥ 2, Lebesgue-almost every real number is normal in base b.

**How the definition helps.** The orbit definition makes normality an instance of the ergodic theorem for interval visits (our own). Multiplication by b modulo 1 preserves Lebesgue measure and is ergodic, meaning every invariant event has measure zero or one. Birkhoff’s theorem makes the frequency of visits to each interval with rational endpoints equal its length for almost every starting point. There are countably many such intervals, and they approximate arbitrary intervals. The digit definition instead asks for frequencies of overlapping digit blocks. The work goes into proving ergodicity and showing that each digit block corresponds to an interval with endpoints of the form j/bᵏ.

**Wikipedia:** [Normal number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Normal_number). It says: “A number x is normal in base b if and only if the sequence {\\left( b<sup>k</sup> x \\right) }<sub>k=0</sub><sup>\\infty</sup> is equidistributed modulo 1”

**Sources:**

- [É. Borel, Les probabilités dénombrables et leurs applications arithmétiques, Rend. Circ. Mat. Palermo 27 (1909) 247–271](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF03019651)

### The Gauss map turns continued fraction digits into ergodic averages

**Remember:** Read each digit as the first digit of the next state.

*True by definition.* MSC 11K50 (Metric theory of continued fractions), 37A44. arXiv math.NT, math.DS. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For an irrational x in (0, 1), let a₁, a₂, … be its continued fraction digits, obtained by repeatedly taking reciprocals and removing integer parts. The Gauss map T takes x to the fractional part of 1/x. Thus aₙ is the integer part of the reciprocal after n − 1 applications of T.

**Problem.** Khinchin’s theorem says that for Lebesgue-almost every x in (0, 1), the geometric mean of its first n digits tends to the same constant. The constant is about 2.685.

**How the definition helps.** Defining the digits through the Gauss map makes their mean logarithm a time average of just one function. The Gauss measure has density 1/((1 + x) log 2) and has the same null sets as Lebesgue measure. The hard part is that T preserves this measure and is ergodic, meaning every invariant event has probability zero or one. Birkhoff’s ergodic theorem then makes the time average of the integrable function log a₁ equal its integral almost everywhere. Exponentiating gives the limit of the geometric means. Khinchin’s original proof did not use this ergodic reformulation.

**Wikipedia:** [Khinchin's constant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Khinchin%27s_constant). It says: “Moreover, it can be proved that T is an ergodic transformation of the measurable space I endowed with the probability measure μ (this is the hard part of the proof).”

**Sources:**

- [C. Ryll-Nardzewski, On the ergodic theorems (II) (Ergodic theory of continued fractions), Studia Math. 12 (1951) 74–79](https://doi.org/10.4064/sm-12-1-74-79)

### Primitive characters give Dirichlet L-functions a clean functional equation

**Remember:** Strip a character down to its true period before you reflect its L-function.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11M06 (\\(\\zeta (s)\\) and \\(L(s, \\chi)\\)), 11L05. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A Dirichlet character modulo q is a completely multiplicative function χ with period q, zero exactly on numbers sharing a factor with q. Its L-function is L(s,χ) = Σ χ(n) n⁻ˢ. Its conductor is the smallest d with χ(m) = χ(n) whenever m, n are coprime to q and m ≡ n mod d. It is primitive when its conductor equals q.

**Problem.** Let χ be a primitive character modulo q &gt; 1, with δ = 0 if χ(−1) = 1 and δ = 1 otherwise. Put Λ(s,χ) = (q/π) to the power (s+δ)/2, times Γ((s+δ)/2) L(s,χ). Then Λ is entire and Λ(s,χ) = W(χ) Λ(1−s, χ̄) with \|W(χ)\| = 1.

**How the definition helps.** Every character comes from exactly one primitive character, so the clean equation for primitive ones is enough. The L-function of an imprimitive character is the primitive L-function times finitely many extra factors. There is one factor 1 − χ\*(p)p⁻ˢ for each prime p that divides q but not the conductor. Each such factor has infinitely many zeros on the line Re s = 0, as the Selberg class page notes. Nothing matches them on the line Re s = 1, so no reflection formula of this shape holds (our own). For primitive characters the proof uses Poisson summation, a formula that turns a sum over the integers into a sum of Fourier transforms (our own). The constant W(χ) is a Gauss sum divided by √q, and for complex χ it has no known closed form (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Dirichlet character](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dirichlet_character), [Dirichlet L-function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dirichlet_L-function), [Selberg class](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Selberg_class). It says: “Primitive characters often simplify (or make possible) formulas in the theories of L-functions and modular forms.”

**Sources:**

- [H. Davenport, Multiplicative Number Theory, 2nd ed., Graduate Texts in Mathematics 74, Springer, 1980](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4757-5927-3)
- [H. L. Montgomery and R. C. Vaughan, Multiplicative Number Theory I: Classical Theory, Cambridge University Press, 2006](https://doi.org/10.1017/CBO9780511618314)

### Riemann’s Hankel integral extends zeta to the whole plane

**Remember:** A fixed contour gives a formula even where the original series diverges.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11M06 (\\(\\zeta (s)\\) and \\(L(s, \\chi)\\)), 30B40. arXiv math.NT, math.CV. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** The usual zeta series sums n⁻ˢ over positive integers when the real part of s exceeds 1. The contour definition uses the integral of (−x)ˢ⁻¹/(eˣ − 1), multiplied by i/(2 sin(πs)Γ(s)), with a branch cut along the positive real axis. Here Γ is the gamma function, which extends the factorial after shifting its argument by one. The Hankel contour runs inward above the cut, circles 0 without touching it, and returns below the cut.

**Problem.** The zeta function extends to the whole complex plane with only a simple pole at s = 1.

**How the definition helps.** The contour definition extends zeta because the integral is holomorphic for every s, with exponential decay along the two rays (our own). The gamma reflection formula rewrites the prefactor as iΓ(1 − s)/(2π), so only positive integers can be poles (our own). The work moves into proving agreement with the series for Re(s) &gt; 1 by collapsing the contour onto the cut (our own). Agreement removes the apparent poles at integers above 1. The integral test shows that the series diverges like 1/(s − 1) as real s decreases to 1, confirming the simple pole (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Riemann zeta function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemann_zeta_function). It says: “2\\sin(\\pi s)\\Gamma(s)\\zeta(s) =i\\oint<sub>H</sub> \\frac{(-x)<sup>s-1</sup>}{e<sup>x-1}\\</sup>,\\mathrm{d}x”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### The Riemann xi function is built to be entire and symmetric

**Remember:** Multiply zeta by its missing factors, and it becomes symmetric and entire.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11M06 (\\(\\zeta (s)\\) and \\(L(s, \\chi)\\)), 11M26. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Landau's xi function is ξ(s) = ½ s(s−1) π to the power −s/2, times Γ(s/2) ζ(s). The factor with π and Γ is the part of the Euler product that belongs to the real numbers (our own). The factor s(s−1) cancels the two poles, at s = 0 and s = 1.

**Problem.** The function ξ is entire, real on the real line, and satisfies ξ(1−s) = ξ(s). Its zeros are exactly the nontrivial zeros ρ of ζ. It has the product ξ(s) = ½ ∏ (1 − s/ρ) over these zeros.

**How the definition helps.** The extra factors are chosen so that every unwanted feature of ζ cancels. The poles of Γ(s/2) at s = −2, −4, … cancel the trivial zeros of ζ (our own). The factor s(s−1) cancels the pole of ζ at 1 and the pole of Γ(s/2) at 0 (our own). What is left has no poles, and its only zeros are the interesting ones. The functional equation then becomes plain symmetry about the line Re s = ½. The product over zeros follows from Hadamard's theorem on entire functions of finite order (our own). The hard part stays: proving the functional equation, which Riemann did with a theta function (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Riemann xi function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemann_xi_function). It says: “In mathematics, the Riemann xi function is a variant of the Riemann zeta function, and is defined so as to have a particularly simple functional equation.”

**Sources:**

- [B. Riemann, Ueber die Anzahl der Primzahlen unter einer gegebenen Grösse, Monatsberichte der Berliner Akademie, 1859](https://www.maths.tcd.ie/pub/HistMath/People/Riemann/Zeta/)

### The stuffle product makes multiple zeta values an algebra

**Remember:** Define word multiplication to copy series multiplication, and the algebra comes free.

*True by definition.* MSC 11M32 (Multiple Dirichlet series and zeta functions and multizeta values), 16T30. arXiv math.NT, math.QA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A multiple zeta value ζ(k₁, …, kᵣ), with k₁ ≥ 2 for convergence, is a sum over n₁ &gt; ⋯ &gt; nᵣ ≥ 1. Each term multiplies the numbers 1/nᵢ raised to the powers kᵢ. Hoffman writes the arguments as words, and the quasi-shuffle product ∗, also called the stuffle, combines two words the way that two such sums multiply. For example, ζ(a)ζ(b) = ζ(a, b) + ζ(b, a) + ζ(a + b), for integers a, b ≥ 2.

**Problem.** The product of two multiple zeta values is a sum of multiple zeta values. So their ℚ-span 𝒵 is a ring.

**How the definition helps.** Our own reason: the stuffle copies the rule for multiplying two nested sums, so the product formula holds nearly by definition. Our own example: the product of two single sums, over m and over n, splits into three cases. In our own example, the cases are m &gt; n, m &lt; n and m = n, and they give the three terms of ζ(a)ζ(b). Our own note: 𝒵 is then a ring at once, because it sits inside the real numbers. The remaining work is in the word algebra: Hoffman shows that ∗ is commutative and associative, and that ζ is a ring homomorphism. The paper cites Hoffman for the formula and gives a criterion for associativity of a wider class of products.

**Paper or page:** [Generalized quasi-shuffle products](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.12386). It says: “For v,w ∈ ℌ⁰ we have ζ(v)ζ(w)=ζ(v∗w). In particular, the space 𝒵 is a ℚ-algebra.”

**Sources:**

- [Masataka Satoh, Generalized quasi-shuffle products, arXiv:2303.12386 (2023)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.12386)
- [Michael E. Hoffman, The Algebra of Multiple Harmonic Series, Journal of Algebra (1997)](https://doi.org/10.1006/jabr.1997.7127)

### Taking the halfway value at jumps makes Riemann's explicit formula exact

**Remember:** At a jump, an inverse transform lands halfway, so define the function there.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11N05 (Distribution of primes), 11M26. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Riemann's prime-power counting function Π₀(x) adds 1/n for each prime power pⁿ below x. At a prime power itself, it takes the average of its values just before and just after the jump. In the same way, π₀(x) equals π(x) − ½ when x is a prime.

**Problem.** For every x &gt; 1, Π₀(x) = li(x) − Σ li(x to the power ρ) − log 2 + I(x). Here li is the logarithmic integral, and ρ runs over the zeros of ζ with 0 &lt; Re s &lt; 1. The last term I(x) is the integral of 1/(t(t²−1) log t) from x to ∞, and Möbius inversion then gives π₀(x).

**How the definition helps.** The formula comes from an inverse Mellin transform, and such transforms take the average value at a jump. The transform is a contour integral of log ζ(s) times xˢ/s (our own). Like a Fourier series, it converges to the mean of the two one-sided limits at a jump (our own). So with a right-continuous counting function the formula would be false at every prime power (our own). With the halfway value it holds at every x &gt; 1. The hard part is the convergence of the sum over zeros, which von Mangoldt proved in 1895.

**Wikipedia:** [Prime-counting function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime-counting_function). It says: “it takes a value halfway between the two sides at the discontinuities of π(x). That added detail is used because the function may then be defined by an inverse Mellin transform.”

**Sources:**

- [B. Riemann, Ueber die Anzahl der Primzahlen unter einer gegebenen Grösse, Monatsberichte der Berliner Akademie, 1859](https://www.maths.tcd.ie/pub/HistMath/People/Riemann/Zeta/)
- [H. von Mangoldt, Zu Riemanns Abhandlung 'Ueber die Anzahl der Primzahlen unter einer gegebenen Grösse', J. reine angew. Math. 114 (1895) 255–305](https://doi.org/10.1515/crll.1895.114.255)

### Dirichlet density makes primes in progressions easy to measure

**Remember:** Measure prime sets by their pole at s = 1, not by counting.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11N13 (Primes in congruence classes), 11R45. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** The Dirichlet density of a set A of primes is a limit as s decreases to 1. One divides Σ p⁻ˢ over p in A by Σ p⁻ˢ over all primes. If A has a natural density among the primes, the two densities agree.

**Problem.** For coprime a and q, the primes p ≡ a mod q have Dirichlet density 1/φ(q). Here φ is Euler's totient function.

**How the definition helps.** Dirichlet density is built from the same sums Σ p⁻ˢ that logarithms of L-functions produce (our own). Each character χ modulo q has an L-function L(s,χ) = Σ χ(n) n⁻ˢ (our own). The sum over p ≡ a mod q is (1/φ(q)) Σ χ̄(a) log L(s,χ) plus a bounded term (our own). Only the principal character has a pole at s = 1 (our own). So the ratio tends to 1/φ(q), once L(1,χ) ≠ 0 is known for the others (our own). Natural density needs much more: no L(s,χ) may vanish on the line Re s = 1 (our own). Then a Tauberian theorem, which turns analytic facts about a series into facts about partial sums, finishes the proof (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Dirichlet density](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dirichlet_density). It says: “the Dirichlet density (or analytic density) of a set of primes, named after Peter Gustav Lejeune Dirichlet, is a measure of the size of the set that is easier to use than the natural density.”

**Sources:**

- [P. G. L. Dirichlet, Beweis des Satzes, dass jede unbegrenzte arithmetische Progression ... unendlich viele Primzahlen enthält (1837), reprinted by Cambridge University Press](https://doi.org/10.1017/CBO9781139237321.012)

### Ignoring finitely many exceptions gives Waring's problem its true constant G(k)

**Remember:** Small stubborn numbers fix g(k); only large numbers fix G(k).

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11P05 (Waring's problem and variants). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For each k, g(k) is the least s such that every positive integer is a sum of at most s k-th powers. The related number G(k) asks this only for every sufficiently large integer.

**Problem.** Hardy and Littlewood's circle method, a way to count representations with Fourier analysis, gives upper bounds for G(k). Vinogradov's refinements gave G(k) ≤ k(3 log k + 11) in 1947. In contrast, g(k) ≥ 2ᵏ + ⌊(3/2)ᵏ⌋ − 2, because of a few small numbers.

**How the definition helps.** G(k) ignores the few small numbers that need many terms, so it measures the real difficulty for large numbers. The lower bound for g(k) comes from one number below 3ᵏ, which can use only the powers 1 and 2ᵏ (our own). For cubes, 23 and 239 need 9 cubes, so g(3) = 9, while G(3) is at most 7 (our own). The circle method counts representations asymptotically, so it can only see large numbers (our own). So G(k) is the quantity that the method can bound. The exact value of G(k) is known only for k = 1, 2 and 4 (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Waring's problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waring%27s_problem). It says: “G(k) is defined to be the least positive integer s such that every sufficiently large integer (i.e. every integer greater than some constant) can be represented as a sum of at most s positive integers to the power of k.”

**Sources:**

- [G. H. Hardy and J. E. Littlewood, Some problems of 'Partitio Numerorum' IV: The singular series in Waring's problem and the value of the number G(k), Math. Z. 12 (1922) 161–188](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01482074)

### Defining ideal norms by prime factorizations makes them multiply

**Remember:** The exponents of prime ideals add when the ideals multiply.

*True by definition.* MSC 11R04 (Algebraic numbers; rings of algebraic integers), 11R27. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** In the ring of integers of a number field, each nonzero ideal factors uniquely into prime ideals. Define its norm as a product over these prime ideals 𝔭. Each factor is the size of the residue field, the ring modulo 𝔭, raised to the exponent of 𝔭. The usual definition counts the elements of the quotient ring by the ideal.

**Problem.** The norm of a product of nonzero integral ideals equals the product of their norms.

**How the definition helps.** With the factorization definition, the norm is multiplicative because exponents add when ideals multiply (our own). The work moves to unique factorization into prime ideals (our own). It also moves to showing that the ring modulo 𝔭ᵉ has N(𝔭)ᵉ elements (our own). The Chinese remainder theorem then gives agreement with the usual definition (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Lemma 8.4. (Properties of the absolute norm)](https://venhance.github.io/napkin/Napkin.pdf). It says: “For any other nonzero ideal 𝔟, Norm(𝔞𝔟) = Norm(𝔞)Norm(𝔟).”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Determinant field norms of algebraic integers are integers

**Remember:** An integer matrix has an integer determinant.

*True by definition.* MSC 11R04 (Algebraic numbers; rings of algebraic integers). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let K be a number field, meaning a finite extension of ℚ. Define N(α), the field norm of α in K, as the determinant of the ℚ-linear map x ↦ αx on K. Another definition multiplies the images of α under all field embeddings of K into ℂ that fix ℚ.

**Problem.** If α satisfies a monic polynomial with integer coefficients, then N(α) is an integer. Such an α is called an algebraic integer.

**How the definition helps.** The determinant definition reduces integrality to finding an integer matrix for multiplication by α (our own). The monic minimal polynomial of α has integer coefficients, by Gauss’s lemma (our own). Its coefficients express the highest power in terms of lower powers, so the power basis gives an integer matrix on ℚ(α) (our own). A basis of K over ℚ(α) repeats that matrix in separate blocks, so the determinant is an integer (our own). The work moves into the minimal polynomial step and the theorem that identifies the determinant with the product of the images. The product proof instead shows the norm is both rational and an algebraic integer (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Field norm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Field_norm). It says: “is defined as the determinant of this linear transformation.”

**Paper or page:** [An Infinitely Large Napkin: Alg Nt: Norm Trace](https://venhance.github.io/napkin/Napkin.pdf), [An Infinitely Large Napkin: Alg Nt: Norm Trace](https://venhance.github.io/napkin/Napkin.pdf). It says: “If α is an algebraic integer, its norm and trace are rational integers.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Lattice-index ideal norms make principal ideal norms absolute field norms

**Remember:** Multiplication scales the lattice by the absolute value of its determinant.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11R04 (Algebraic numbers; rings of algebraic integers), 11R27. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let O be the ring of integers of a number field of degree n. As an additive group, O is isomorphic to ℤⁿ. Define the norm of a nonzero ideal as its index in O, the number of elements of the quotient. Another definition multiplies residue field sizes over the prime factors of the ideal.

**Problem.** The norm of a nonzero principal ideal equals the absolute value of the field norm of its generator.

**How the definition helps.** With the index definition, the theorem reduces to a fact about lattices (our own). The ideal (a) is the image of O under multiplication by a, a linear map of ℤⁿ (our own). The image of such a map has index equal to the absolute value of its determinant (our own). That determinant is the field norm of a, by Napkin Theorem 2.8. The work moves to this fact about lattices, which uses the Smith normal form (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Lemma 8.4. (Properties of the absolute norm)](https://venhance.github.io/napkin/Napkin.pdf). It says: “If 𝔞 = (a) is principal, then Norm(𝔞) = \|Normₖ/ℚ(a)\|.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Requiring monic polynomials gives the right ring of algebraic integers

**Remember:** Algebraic integers are roots of integer polynomials with leading coefficient 1.

*Rules out counterexamples. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11R04 (Algebraic numbers; rings of algebraic integers), 13F05. arXiv math.NT, math.AC. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** An algebraic integer is a complex number that is a root of a monic polynomial with integer coefficients. A monic polynomial is one whose leading coefficient is 1.

**Problem.** The ring of integers of a number field is a Dedekind domain, so its ideals factor uniquely into prime ideals. A Dedekind domain is an integral domain in which every nonzero proper ideal is a product of prime ideals.

**How the definition helps.** The monic definition makes the ring of integers integrally closed, and that is one of the conditions in the definition of a Dedekind domain. A ring is integrally closed when it contains every element of its field of fractions that is a root of a monic polynomial with coefficients in the ring. For example, (1+√−3)/2 is a root of x² − x + 1, so it is an algebraic integer of ℚ(√−3). So the ring of integers of ℚ(√−3) is ℤ\[(1+√−3)/2\], the Eisenstein integers, and not ℤ\[√−3\]. The smaller ring ℤ\[√−3\] is not integrally closed, and it is not even a Dedekind domain; the Wikipedia page on quadratic integers gives it as this example. Unique factorization of elements, rather than ideals, depends on the class number (a number that measures how far ideals are from being principal), and it stays hard.

**Wikipedia:** [Algebraic integer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_integer), [Quadratic integer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quadratic_integer). It says: “In contrast, Z\[√−3\] is not even a Dedekind domain.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Regular primes are the primes where Kummer's proof of Fermat works

**Remember:** For regular p, an ideal with principal pth power is principal already.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11R18 (Cyclotomic extensions), 11R29, 11D41. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** An odd prime p is regular if p does not divide the class number of the cyclotomic field ℚ(ζₚ). Here ζₚ is a primitive pth root of unity, and the class number measures how far ideals are from being principal (generated by one element). Kummer's criterion gives an equivalent test: p divides none of the numerators of the Bernoulli numbers B₂, B₄, …, B₍ₚ₋₃₎.

**Problem.** Fermat's Last Theorem for a prime exponent p says that xᵖ + yᵖ = zᵖ has no solution in positive integers.

**How the definition helps.** The definition marks exactly the primes where Kummer's argument works. The argument factors xᵖ + yᵖ in the ring ℤ\[ζₚ\]. A direct argument with factors fails, because unique factorization of elements fails in that ring. In our own summary of Kummer's argument: if p does not divide the class number, an ideal whose pth power is principal is itself principal. With this fact, Kummer's argument goes through. Irregular primes such as 37 remain, and the full theorem needed Wiles (our own remark).

**Wikipedia:** [Regular prime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regular_prime). It says: “In 1850, Kummer proved that Fermat's Last Theorem is true for a prime exponent p if p is regular.”

**Sources:**

Kummer, Allgemeiner Beweis des Fermatschen Satzes, daß die Gleichung xλ+yλ=zλ durch ganze Zahlen unlösbar ist, für alle diejenigen Potenz-Exponenten λ welche ungerade Primzahlen sind und in den Zählern der ersten 1/2(λ) Bernoullischen zahlen als Factoren nicht vorkommen, J. reine angew. Math. 40 (1850), 130–138](https://doi.org/10.1515/crll.1850.40.130)

### Ignoring finite modules gives a structure theorem for Iwasawa modules

**Remember:** Up to finite error, Iwasawa modules are sums of cyclic pieces.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11R23 (Iwasawa theory), 13J05. arXiv math.NT, math.AC. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** The Iwasawa algebra of the p-adic integers is the power series ring ℤₚ\[\[T\]\]. A quasi-isomorphism of modules over it is a map with finite kernel and finite cokernel.

**Problem.** Every finitely generated torsion module over ℤₚ\[\[T\]\] is quasi-isomorphic to a finite sum of modules ℤₚ\[\[T\]\]/(fⁿ) with f prime. The characteristic power series and the μ and λ invariants are then well defined.

**How the definition helps.** Working up to finite error allows the structure theorem of a principal ideal domain in a ring that is not one. The ring ℤₚ\[\[T\]\] is local of dimension 2, and its maximal ideal (p, T) is not principal (our own). The module ℤₚ\[\[T\]\]/(p, T) is finite, and it is quasi-isomorphic to 0 (our own). So modules need not split exactly into pieces of the form ℤₚ\[\[T\]\]/(fⁿ), but they do up to quasi-isomorphism (our own). The page explains how the μ and λ invariants come from the characteristic power series. Iwasawa built this theory for towers of cyclotomic fields (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Iwasawa algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iwasawa_algebra). It says: “A quasi-isomorphism of modules is a homomorphism whose kernel and cokernel are both finite groups”

**Sources:**

- [Kenkichi Iwasawa, On Γ-extensions of algebraic number fields, Bulletin of the American Mathematical Society 65 (1959)](https://doi.org/10.1090/s0002-9904-1959-10317-7)

### Counting infinite places makes the unit rank places minus one

**Remember:** Unit rank equals the number of infinite places, minus one.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11R27 (Units and factorization). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** An infinite place of a number field is a real embedding, or a pair of complex conjugate embeddings, into ℂ. There are r₁ real places and r₂ complex places.

**Problem.** The unit group of the ring of integers is finitely generated with rank r₁ + r₂ − 1. So the rank is the number of infinite places minus one.

**How the definition helps.** Counting each complex pair once makes the rank a plain count of places, minus one. The log map sends a unit u to the vector of N·log\|u\| at each place. Here N is 1 at a real place and 2 at a complex one. The image lies in the hyperplane where the coordinates sum to zero, because a unit has norm ±1. In the S-unit form, the rank is the size of S minus one, where S contains all infinite places (our own). Counting complex embeddings separately would break this count. The image is a discrete subgroup, and what stays hard is to show that it spans the hyperplane.

**Wikipedia:** [Dirichlet's unit theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dirichlet%27s_unit_theorem). It says: “There will be r + 1 Archimedean places of K, either real or complex.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### The different ideal shows exactly which primes ramify

**Remember:** The different's prime factors are exactly the ramified primes upstairs.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11R29 (Class numbers, class groups, discriminants), 11R32. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let L be a number field with ring of integers O. The inverse different is the set of x in L such that the trace of xy is in ℤ for every y in O. The different is the inverse of this fractional ideal. It measures how far the trace pairing (x, y) ↦ Tr(xy) is from identifying O with its dual.

**Problem.** A prime ideal of L is ramified when it appears to a power above 1 in the factorization of the prime below. This happens exactly when it divides the different.

**How the definition helps.** The different is an ideal upstairs in L, so it can name the ramified primes of L one by one. The discriminant lives in the base field. It only says which primes below have some ramified prime above them. The page gives Dedekind's original definition and cites his 1882 paper. The page also says that the exact exponent is e − 1 for tame ramification and at least e for wild ramification. What stays hard is the local computation of that exponent in the wild case.

**Wikipedia:** [Different ideal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Different_ideal). It says: “Pi divides the relative different δL / K if and only if Pi is ramified, that is, if and only if the ramification index e(i) is greater than 1.”

**Sources:**

- [Richard Dedekind, Über die Discriminanten endlicher Körper, Abhandlungen der Königlichen Gesellschaft der Wissenschaften zu Göttingen 29 (1882)](http://gdz.sub.uni-goettingen.de/en/dms/load/img/?IDDOC=39145)

### The narrow class group decides which primes a norm form represents

**Remember:** Signs matter for norm forms, so count ideals with positive generators.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11R29 (Class numbers, class groups, discriminants), 11R11, 11E16. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** An element of a number field is totally positive when it is positive under every embedding into the real numbers. The narrow class group is the group of fractional ideals modulo principal ideals with a totally positive generator. The ordinary class group allows any generator.

**Problem.** Let K = ℚ(√d) have trivial narrow class group and discriminant D, and let q be the norm form of an integral basis. A prime p equals q(x,y) for some integers exactly in three cases. Either p divides D, or p = 2 and D ≡ 1 mod 8, or p is odd and (D/p) = 1.

**How the definition helps.** The narrow class group tracks the sign of a norm, and the ordinary class group does not. A prime that splits gives a principal ideal (α), and then p = ±N(α), where N is the norm (our own). The ordinary class group cannot tell N(α) = p from N(α) = −p, so it only controls ±p. The field ℚ(√6) shows the difference: its class group is trivial, but its narrow class group has order 2. Here −2 = 2² − 6·1², but 2 is not of the form x² − 6y², since squares are never 2 mod 3 (our own). The hard part is computing the narrow class group of a given field (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Narrow class group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Narrow_class_group). It says: “However, this statement is false if we focus only on p and not −p (and is in fact even false for p = 2), because the narrow class group is nontrivial.”

**Sources:**

- [A. Fröhlich and M. J. Taylor, Algebraic Number Theory, Cambridge University Press, 1991](https://doi.org/10.1017/CBO9781139172165)

### Decomposition groups turn counting prime factors into orbit counting

**Remember:** Primes above p form one orbit; the stabilizer is the decomposition group.

*True by definition.* MSC 11R32 (Galois theory). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let L over K be Galois with group G and P a prime of L above p. The decomposition group of P is the set of elements of G that send P to itself. The inertia group is the part that acts trivially on the residue field.

**Problem.** In a Galois extension, all primes above p have the same ramification index e and residue degree f. With g primes above p, the degree is e·f·g, and g is \|G\| divided by \|D\|.

**How the definition helps.** Once G acts on the primes above p, their number is an orbit size, so the orbit-stabilizer formula gives it. The page uses this formula. The work moves into the fact that G acts transitively on these primes. Transitivity also makes e and f the same for every prime above p. Then D maps onto the Galois group of the residue field extension, with kernel the inertia group. Hilbert set up this theory in his Zahlbericht (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Splitting of prime ideals in Galois extensions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Splitting_of_prime_ideals_in_Galois_extensions). It says: “the decomposition group of Pj, is the subgroup of elements of G sending a given Pj to itself.”

**Sources:**

- [David Hilbert, Die Theorie der algebraischen Zahlkörper, Jahresbericht der Deutschen Mathematiker-Vereinigung 4 (1897)](http://resolver.sub.uni-goettingen.de/purl?GDZPPN002115344)

### Frobenius as a conjugacy class makes Chebotarev's theorem statable

**Remember:** Each prime picks a conjugacy class; classes are hit in proportion to size.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11R32 (Galois theory), 11R45. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let p be a prime number that does not ramify in a Galois extension of ℚ. Its Frobenius element acts as x ↦ xᵖ on the residue field of a prime above p. Different primes above p give conjugate elements, so p gives a conjugacy class.

**Problem.** For a conjugacy class C in G, the primes whose Frobenius class is C have density \|C\| divided by \|G\|.

**How the definition helps.** A prime only fixes its Frobenius up to conjugation, so a conjugacy class is the invariant of p that the theorem can count. The Frobenius element of one prime above p depends on that choice. Taking the class removes the choice. For cyclotomic fields the theorem gives Dirichlet's theorem on primes in progressions (our own). The page says that Frobenius proved an earlier, weaker form about the splitting types of a polynomial. What stays hard is the analytic proof.

**Wikipedia:** [Chebotarev density theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chebotarev_density_theorem). It says: “The statement of the more general Chebotarev density theorem is in terms of the Frobenius element of a prime (ideal), which is in fact an associated conjugacy class C of elements of the Galois group G.”

- [Nikolai Tschebotareff, Die Bestimmung der Dichtigkeit einer Menge von Primzahlen, welche zu einer gegebenen Substitutionsklasse gehören, Mathematische Annalen 95 (1926)](https://doi.org/10.1007/bf01206606)

### Frobenius defined by a pth-power congruence restricts to Frobenius below

**Remember:** Restrict the same power map to the smaller residue field.

*True by definition.* MSC 11R32 (Galois theory). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let L be a Galois number field and 𝔓 a prime ideal of its integers above the prime p. Suppose 𝔓 is unramified, so it appears with exponent one when the ideal generated by p is factored. Define the Frobenius of 𝔓 as the unique automorphism σ of L with σ(x) ≡ xᵖ modulo 𝔓 for every algebraic integer x in L. Another definition lifts the map x ↦ xᵖ, which generates the Galois group of the residue field.

**Problem.** Let L ⊃ K be number fields, both Galois over ℚ, and let 𝔓 in L lie over 𝔭 in K, both unramified. The Frobenius of 𝔓 restricts on K to the Frobenius of 𝔭.

**How the definition helps.** With the congruence definition, the restricted automorphism already passes the test that defines the Frobenius of 𝔭 (our own). For an algebraic integer x of K, σ(x) ≡ xᵖ modulo 𝔓, and both sides lie in the integers of K (our own). So the congruence holds modulo 𝔭, which is 𝔓 intersected with the integers of K (our own). Uniqueness of the Frobenius of 𝔭 then gives equality (our own). The work moves to proving that such a unique automorphism exists at an unramified prime (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Theorem 6.1. (Restrictions of Frobenius elements)](https://venhance.github.io/napkin/Napkin.pdf). It says: “Assume L/ℚ and K/ℚ are both Galois. Let 𝔓 and 𝔭 be unramified as above.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Moduli with real places let conductors tell real abelian fields apart

**Remember:** Put the real place in the modulus to record whether signs matter.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11R37 (Class field theory), 11R20. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A modulus of a number field is a formal product of finite primes with powers and of some real places. Congruence modulo a real place means that the quotient a/b is positive there.

**Problem.** Every abelian extension of a number field has a conductor, the smallest modulus whose ray class field contains it. Over ℚ, let n be the smallest number with K inside the n-th cyclotomic field. The conductor of K is n if K is real and n times ∞ otherwise.

**How the definition helps.** A real place in the modulus records a sign condition, and that is exactly the ramification at infinity. The page says that a modulus encodes ramification data for abelian extensions. For a modulus of 1, the ray class group is the class group. For example, ℚ(ζ₅) has conductor 5 times ∞, and its real subfield ℚ(√5) has conductor 5 (our own). Without real places, every ray class field over ℚ would be real, so ℚ(ζ₅) would have no conductor (our own). What stays hard is the existence theorem of class field theory.

**Wikipedia:** [Modulus (algebraic number theory)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modulus_%28algebraic_number_theory%29), [Conductor (class field theory)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conductor_%28class_field_theory%29). It says: “the conductor of K is then n if K is fixed by complex conjugation and n ∞ otherwise.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Unramified at real places, the Hilbert class field matches the class group

**Remember:** Unramified everywhere, including at infinity, gives exactly the class group.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11R37 (Class field theory), 11R29. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** The Hilbert class field of a number field K is its largest abelian extension that is unramified at every place. Unramified at a real place means that the real embedding stays real in the larger field.

**Problem.** The Galois group of the Hilbert class field over K is isomorphic to the ideal class group of K. Its degree is the class number.

**How the definition helps.** Counting real places as places that can ramify makes the extension match the ordinary class group. The page gives the bad case K = ℚ(√3), which has class number 1. Its extension K(i) is unramified at every finite prime, but the real embeddings become complex. So K(i) must be ruled out, or the extension would be larger than the class group predicts. If ramification at real places is allowed, one gets the narrow class field instead, and K(i) is the narrow class field of ℚ(√3). Furtwängler proved that the Hilbert class field exists.

**Wikipedia:** [Hilbert class field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert_class_field). It says: “That is, every real embedding of K extends to a real embedding of E, rather than to a complex embedding of E.”

**Sources:**

- [Philipp Furtwängler, Allgemeiner Existenzbeweis für den Klassenkörper eines beliebigen algebraischen Zahlkörpers, Mathematische Annalen 63 (1906)](https://doi.org/10.1007/bf01448421)

### Integrating over ideles proves Hecke's functional equation by Poisson summation

**Remember:** One Poisson summation on the adeles gives every Hecke functional equation.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11R42 (Zeta functions and \\(L\\)-functions of number fields), 11R56. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** The adeles of a number field are a restricted product of all its completions, and the ideles are their units. Tate's zeta integral is the integral over the ideles of a test function times a character times a power of the absolute value. The ideles carry a Haar measure, a measure that does not change under translation. For a test function that is a product of local functions, the integral splits into one factor per place.

**Problem.** Every Hecke L-function of a number field extends to a meromorphic function on the whole complex plane. It satisfies a functional equation that relates s and 1 − s. It has poles only when the character is a power of the idele norm (our own).

**How the definition helps.** The zeta integral turns the L-function into an integral over a group, and there Poisson summation applies directly. Inside the adeles, the number field is a discrete subgroup with compact quotient (our own). The local factor at each place, including the Gamma factor at infinite places, comes from one local integral (our own). The page calls Tate's work an elegant and powerful reformulation of Hecke's work. Hecke had used theta series for a lattice in the ring of integers. Iwasawa found the same method independently. What stays hard is computing the local integrals at ramified places (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Tate's thesis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tate%27s_thesis). It says: “Using harmonic analysis, more precisely the Poisson summation formula, he proved the functional equation and meromorphic continuation of the zeta integral and the Hecke L-function.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Summing over ideals gives the Dedekind zeta function an Euler product

**Remember:** Sum over ideals, factor over prime ideals.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11R42 (Zeta functions and \\(L\\)-functions of number fields). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** The Dedekind zeta function of a number field sums N(a)⁻ˢ over all nonzero ideals a of the ring of integers. Here N(a) is the number of elements of the quotient ring. The sum converges when the real part of s is greater than 1.

**Problem.** The Dedekind zeta function is a product over all nonzero prime ideals P of 1/(1 − N(P)⁻ˢ).

**How the definition helps.** Ideals factor uniquely into prime ideals and the norm is multiplicative, so the Euler product follows as for the Riemann zeta function. The page says this directly. A sum over elements up to units would have no such product when unique factorization of elements fails (our own). So the zeta function sees prime ideals, not prime elements. What stays hard is the analytic continuation and the class number formula at s = 1.

**Wikipedia:** [Dedekind zeta function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dedekind_zeta_function). It says: “The norm function is multiplicative with respect to multiplication of ideals, which implies that the Dedekind zeta function has an Euler product over all non-zero prime ideals”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Using inertia-fixed vectors makes the Artin local factor independent of Frobenius lift

**Remember:** Two lifts differ by inertia, which acts as the identity on fixed vectors.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11R42 (Zeta functions and \\(L\\)-functions of number fields), 11F80. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let ρ be a Galois representation with finite image on a vector space V, and p a prime whose residue field has N(p) elements. Inertia is the subgroup acting trivially on the residue field, and a Frobenius lift Frob acts on it by raising to the power N(p). The local Artin factor is the inverse of det(1 − Frob·N(p)⁻ˢ) on the inertia-fixed part of V. Using a Frobenius lift on all of V would depend on the lift.

**Problem.** The local Artin factor does not depend on the chosen lift of Frobenius, even at a ramified prime.

**How the definition helps.** Restricting to inertia-fixed vectors removes the choice, because two lifts of Frobenius differ by an inertia element. That element acts as the identity on the fixed part, so both lifts act the same there (our own). The fixed part is stable under the decomposition group, the subgroup that keeps the prime above p, since inertia is normal in it (our own). On all of V the choice matters. For a ramified quadratic character, inertia acts by −1, so two lifts give opposite values (our own). A different prime above p gives a conjugate operator, so the determinant does not change (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Artin L-function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artin_L-function). It says: “determinant is taken on a linear map restricted to”

**Sources:**

- [Jürgen Neukirch, Algebraic Number Theory, Chapter VII, §10 (1999)](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-662-03983-0)

### Adeles turn two classical theorems of number theory into one compactness statement

**Remember:** Adeles look at a number field at all places at once, real and p-adic.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11R56 (Adèle rings and groups), 11R29, 11R27. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let K be a global field (a number field, or a function field over a finite field). Each place v of K gives a completion Kᵥ, such as ℝ, ℂ or a p-adic field. The ring of adeles 𝔸 of K is the restricted product of all the completions Kᵥ: in each element, all but finitely many components lie in the ring of integers 𝒪ᵥ of Kᵥ. The ideles are the group of units of the adeles, 𝕀 = GL₁(𝔸).

**Problem.** State two classical theorems in one clean form. The first says that the ideal class group is finite. The second is Dirichlet's unit theorem.

**How the definition helps.** The adeles turn both theorems into one statement about compactness. Chevalley and Weil saw that it helps to embed a number field K into the product of its completions at all places, not only the archimedean ones (the real and complex places). K then sits in its adeles as a discrete subgroup with compact quotient, like a lattice in a vector space. With this definition, the two classical theorems together are equivalent to one topological statement: the quotient of the norm-one ideles by K× (the nonzero elements of K) is compact. The proof of this compactness still needs a geometry-of-numbers argument such as Minkowski's theorem. So the definition reorganizes the work rather than removing it.

**nLab:** [ring of adeles](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/ring+of+adeles), [group of ideles](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/group+of+ideles), [ideal class group](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/ideal+class+group). It says: “the finiteness of the ideal class group and the Dirichlet unit theorem are equivalent to a certain quotient of the ideles being compact and discrete.”

**Sources:**

- [Tom Weston, The idelic approach to number theory, lecture notes (undated)](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1PK0lPR7yq-1s1aooX4ZLr_zY4s2Ej36z/view)

### Ideles with almost all unit coordinates have unique normalized representatives over ℚ

**Remember:** One rational factor cancels every finite valuation and fixes the real sign.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11R56 (Adèle rings and groups). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A rational idele is a tuple of a nonzero real number and a nonzero p-adic number for each prime p. All but finitely many p-adic entries must be units of ℤₚ, that is, have valuation zero. An equivalent definition takes the units of the adele ring. Two ideles are in the same class when they differ by a nonzero rational factor.

**Problem.** Each class contains exactly one idele whose p-adic entries are all units and whose real entry is positive.

**How the definition helps.** With the restricted-product definition, only finitely many entries have nonzero valuation, so one rational can clear them all (our own). Divide by the product of the primes raised to these valuations, with the sign that makes the real entry positive (our own). A positive rational that is a unit at every prime is 1, which gives uniqueness (our own). The nLab states the resulting form of the idele class group, (0, ∞) × ∏ ℤₚ×. The work moves to proving that the two definitions of ideles agree (our own).

**nLab:** [group of ideles](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/group+of+ideles). It says: “The idele class group may be expressed as ℚ× ∖ 𝔸ℚ× ≃ (0,∞) × ∏ₚ ℤₚ×.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### The idele class group states Artin reciprocity as one theorem

**Remember:** One group built from K, the idele class group, sees all abelian extensions at once.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11R56 (Adèle rings and groups), 11R37. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** The idele class group of a global field K is the quotient of the ideles 𝕀 by the diagonal copy of K×, the nonzero elements of K. The Artin map goes from the ideles to Gal(Kᵃᵇ/K), the Galois group of the largest abelian extension of K. Take a finite abelian extension L of K and a place v that does not ramify in L. At v, the Artin map sends the component aᵥ to Frobᵥ raised to the power ordᵥ(aᵥ) in Gal(L/K), where Frobᵥ is the Frobenius element and ordᵥ is the valuation at v. At the other places it uses the local Artin maps.

**Problem.** State the main theorem of class field theory in one statement. This theorem describes all abelian extensions of a number field. The classical form needs one statement for each modulus.

**How the definition helps.** The idele class group handles all moduli at once, so reciprocity needs only one statement. Classical class field theory used ray class groups, one for each modulus, and described each finite abelian extension separately (this history is our own framing, not the nLab's). With ideles, Artin reciprocity is one statement. For a number field, the Artin map is surjective and factors through the idele class group. It gives an isomorphism to Gal(Kᵃᵇ/K) from the quotient of the idele class group by the connected component of 1. For function fields the map is instead injective with dense image, and its cokernel is Ẑ/ℤ. The proof of reciprocity is still hard (by cohomology of groups or by L-functions), and the definition only gives it its clean form.

**nLab:** [Artin reciprocity law](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Artin+reciprocity+law), [class field theory](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/class+field+theory), [group of ideles](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/group+of+ideles). It says: “says that this map is surjective, that it factors through the idele class group”

**Sources:**

- [Serge Lang, Algebraic Number Theory, 2nd edition, Graduate Texts in Mathematics 110, Springer (1994)](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4612-0853-2)
- [Jürgen Neukirch, Alexander Schmidt, Kay Wingberg, Cohomology of Number Fields, 2nd edition, Springer (2008)](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-540-37889-1)

### The idele topology is finer than the subspace topology from the adeles

**Remember:** Give the ideles the topology that makes x ↦ x⁻¹ continuous.

*Rules out counterexamples. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11R56 (Adèle rings and groups). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** The ideles 𝕀 are the units of the adeles 𝔸, the ring that combines all completions of a global field. The ideles get the topology of the subset {(x, x⁻¹)} of 𝔸 × 𝔸, not the subspace topology from 𝔸. Equivalently, this is the restricted-product topology with respect to the unit groups 𝒪ᵥ× of the local rings of integers.

**Problem.** Make the group of ideles a topological group, so that inversion is continuous. Then the idele class group and its characters can be used in class field theory.

**How the definition helps.** The new topology makes inversion continuous, and the subspace topology does not. In the subspace topology from the adeles, the map x ↦ x⁻¹ is not continuous, so 𝕀 would not be a topological group. The embedding x ↦ (x, x⁻¹) of 𝕀 into 𝔸 × 𝔸 forces inversion to be continuous. In this topology, the set ℝ× × ∏ₚ ℤₚ× (the nonzero reals times the p-adic units for each prime p) is an open neighbourhood of 1. But this set is not open in the subspace topology. This is a standard device for the units of a topological ring, and it does not by itself prove any theorem of class field theory.

**nLab:** [group of ideles](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/group+of+ideles), [ring of adeles](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/ring+of+adeles). It says: “Note: multiplicative inversion is not continuous in the subspace topology.”

**Sources:**

- [Tom Weston, The idelic approach to number theory, lecture notes](https://web.archive.org/web/20221205214531/https://people.math.umass.edu/~weston/oldpapers/idele.pdf)
- [Pete L. Clark, Adeles and Ideles, lecture notes](https://web.archive.org/web/20240508060418/http://alpha.math.uga.edu/~pete/8410Chapter6.pdf)

### The restricted product topology makes the adele ring locally compact

**Remember:** Keep compact integer rings in all but finitely many coordinates.

*True by definition.* MSC 11R56 (Adèle rings and groups). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A place of a global field is an absolute value up to equivalence, and Kᵥ is the completion at v. The adeles are tuples with an entry in each Kᵥ, lying in the local integer ring Oᵥ at all but finitely many places. Fix a finite set S of places that contains the archimedean ones. The product of the Kᵥ for v in S and the Oᵥ for v outside S, with its product topology, is declared open.

**Problem.** The adele ring of a global field is locally compact. A global field is a number field or a function field of a curve over a finite field.

**How the definition helps.** With the restricted product topology, every adele lies in an open set built from finitely many fields and compact rings. Such a set is locally compact by Tychonoff’s theorem (our own). The nLab notes that the adeles are a union of these open subrings, so they are locally compact. In the topology from the full product of the Kᵥ, the adeles are not locally compact (our own). The work moves to proving that each local integer ring is compact (our own).

**nLab:** [ring of adeles](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/ring+of+adeles). It says: “The restricted product is a filtered colimit of a system of open inclusions between locally compact Hausdorff rings, and is therefore itself locally compact Hausdorff.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### The restricted product topology makes the rationals discrete in their adeles

**Remember:** Integral at every prime and smaller than one forces zero.

*True by definition.* MSC 11R56 (Adèle rings and groups). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** The adeles of ℚ are tuples of a real number and a p-adic number for each prime p. All but finitely many p-adic entries lie in ℤₚ. In the restricted product topology, the set (−1, 1) × ∏ ℤₚ is open, though it constrains every coordinate. In the full product topology, an open set may constrain only finitely many coordinates.

**Problem.** The rational numbers, placed diagonally in the adeles of ℚ, form a discrete subgroup.

**How the definition helps.** With the restricted product topology, one open set around 0 constrains every prime at once (our own). A rational in every ℤₚ has no prime in its denominator, so it is an integer (our own). An integer with absolute value less than 1 is 0 (our own). The work moves to setting up the restricted product topology.

**Wikipedia:** [Adele ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adele_ring). It says: “The field K embeds diagonally in 𝔸ₖ as a discrete subring”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Defining ramification index as a group index makes ramification indices multiply

**Remember:** Indices of nested groups multiply.

*True by definition.* MSC 11S15 (Ramification and extension theory), 13F30. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let A ⊂ B be discrete valuation rings, and normalize the valuation of B to take all values in ℤ. On the fraction field of A it takes only values in a subgroup eℤ. Define the ramification index of B over A as e, the index of this subgroup. Another definition asks that the maximal ideal of A generate the eth power of the maximal ideal of B.

**Problem.** Take discrete valuation rings A ⊂ B ⊂ C. The ramification index of C over A is the product of those of C over B and B over A.

**How the definition helps.** With the group-index definition, the theorem is the tower law for indices of subgroups (our own). The values taken on A, B and C form a chain of subgroups of ℤ under the valuation of C (our own). The work moves to proving that the index definition agrees with the ideal definition (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Lemma 15.112.3.](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0BRL). It says: “Then the ramification indices of B/A and C/B multiply to give the ramification index of C/A.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Defining unramified as finite étale makes composita of unramified extensions unramified

**Remember:** Tensor the integer rings, then select the factor for the compositum.

*True by definition.* MSC 11S15 (Ramification and extension theory), 13B40. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let A be a discrete valuation ring with fraction field K. Call a finite separable extension L of K unramified when the integral closure B of A in L is finite étale over A. Here finite étale means that B is free of finite rank over A, and B modulo the maximal ideal is a product of separable fields. The other test asks for ramification index one and separable residue field extensions.

**Problem.** If L₁ and L₂ are finite separable unramified extensions of K inside one algebraic closure, then their compositum is unramified. The compositum is the smallest field that contains both.

**How the definition helps.** With the finite étale definition, the property passes to tensor products, and composita come from tensor products (our own). The tensor product of the two integral closures over A is finite étale, so it is a product of normal domains (our own). Each factor is the integral closure of A in a field factor of L₁ ⊗ L₂, and the compositum is one such factor (our own). Stacks Lemma 15.112.8 proves that some unramified extension contains both fields, and its part (1) then makes the compositum unramified. The work moves to the agreement of the two tests and to normality of étale algebras (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Lemma 15.112.8.](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0EXR). It says: “there exists a a finite separable extension L/K which is unramified with respect to A containing L₁ and L₂.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### In upper numbering, abelian ramification jumps are integers

**Remember:** Abelian extensions only jump at whole numbers in upper numbering.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11S15 (Ramification and extension theory), 11S31. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A jump of the upper ramification filtration is an index t where the group Gᵗ changes. The lower index s is turned into the upper index η(s), the integral from 0 to s of 1/\|G₀ : Gₓ\|. Here G₀ is the inertia group.

**Problem.** For a finite abelian extension of local fields, every jump of the upper ramification filtration is an integer.

**How the definition helps.** The upper numbering matches the unit groups under the Artin map, and those come in integer steps, so the theorem has a natural form there. The page says that upper numbering matches the filtration of K× modulo norms by the unit groups 1 + mⁿ. In the lower numbering the claim would be empty, because lower jumps are always integers. The conductor page gives the conductor as η(s) + 1, where s is the last lower jump. Hasse–Arf explains why this number is an integer (our own). Hasse proved the case of finite residue fields, and Arf proved the general case. For non-abelian extensions, upper jumps can be fractions, and the page gives Serre's example with a jump at 3/2.

**Wikipedia:** [Hasse–Arf theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hasse%E2%80%93Arf_theorem), [Ramification group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramification_group), [Conductor (class field theory)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conductor_%28class_field_theory%29). It says: “With the above set up of an abelian extension L/K, the theorem states that the jumps of the filtration {Gᵗ(L/K) : t ≥ −1} are all rational integers.”

**Sources:**

- [Cahit Arf, Untersuchungen über reinverzweigte Erweiterungen diskret bewerteter perfekter Körper, Journal für die reine und angewandte Mathematik 181 (1940)](https://doi.org/10.1515/crll.1940.181.1)

### Tame ramification is exactly what a projective ring of integers needs

**Remember:** No wild ramification, and the integers form a projective Galois module.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11S15 (Ramification and extension theory), 11R33. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let L be a Galois extension of ℚ. Its ring of integers factors each prime p into distinct primes, each to the same power e. The number e is the ramification index of p. The prime p is tamely ramified when p does not divide e, and L is tamely ramified when every prime is.

**Problem.** For a finite Galois extension L of ℚ with group G, the ring of integers is a projective ℤ\[G\]-module exactly when L is tamely ramified. A projective module is a direct summand of a free module.

**How the definition helps.** Tame ramification is the condition that makes the local trace map onto, and that gives a local normal basis at each prime (our own). The page gives the Gaussian field ℚ(i) as a field with no normal integral basis. There 2 is not tamely ramified, since its ramification index is 2 (our own). Noether's condition is necessary for a normal integral basis, which is a free module. The page says that the gap between free and projective has its own large theory. An earlier result based on Hilbert's work gives a normal integral basis for every tame abelian field.

**Wikipedia:** [Galois representation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galois_representation). It says: “Then Noether's theorem states that tame ramification is necessary and sufficient for OL to be a projective module over Z\[G\].”

**Sources:**

- [Emmy Noether, Normalbasis bei Körpern ohne höhere Verzweigung, Journal für die reine und angewandte Mathematik 167 (1932)](https://doi.org/10.1515/crll.1932.167.147)

### Upper numbering makes ramification groups pass to quotients

**Remember:** Lower numbering suits subgroups; upper numbering suits quotients.

*True by definition.* MSC 11S15 (Ramification and extension theory), 11S20. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Take a Galois extension of local fields with group G, and let w be the valuation of the larger field. The lower group Gᵤ is the set of σ with w(σ(a) − a) ≥ u + 1 for every integer a of the larger field. The Herbrand function φ is an increasing piecewise linear rescaling of u. The upper groups are Gᵗ = Gᵤ with t = φ(u).

**Problem.** For a normal subgroup H of G, the image of Gᵗ in G/H is (G/H)ᵗ. This is Herbrand's theorem in upper numbering.

**How the definition helps.** The page says that the upper numbering is defined so that quotients behave well. The work moves into Herbrand's theorem for the lower numbering, which needs the Herbrand function. The lower numbering is compatible only with subgroups. Because of compatibility with quotients, upper ramification groups are defined for infinite Galois extensions as limits (our own). This lets one filter the absolute Galois group of a local field. The cost is that upper jumps can be fractions (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Ramification group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramification_group). It says: “The upper numbering is defined so as to be compatible with passage to quotients:”

**Sources:**

- [Jean-Pierre Serre, Local Fields, Graduate Texts in Mathematics 67, Springer (1979)](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4757-5673-9)

### The Weil group makes the reciprocity map an isomorphism

**Remember:** Allow only integer powers of Frobenius, and K× matches exactly.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11S37 (Langlands-Weil conjectures, nonabelian class field theory), 11S31. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For a p-adic field, the Weil group is part of the absolute Galois group. Its elements act on the residue field by an integer power of Frobenius. It is a dense subgroup with its own topology.

**Problem.** For a non-archimedean local field K, the reciprocity map gives an isomorphism from K× to the abelianized Weil group.

**How the definition helps.** K× contains ℤ as the powers of a uniformizer, a generator of the maximal ideal of the integers. Also the Weil group contains ℤ as the powers of Frobenius, so the two match. The Galois group has the profinite integers in that place. So the map from K× into the abelianized Galois group is injective with dense image, not onto (our own). The page says that for finite fields the Weil group is infinite cyclic. Weil introduced the group in 1951. It is also the group used in the local Langlands correspondence.

**Wikipedia:** [Weil group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weil_group). It says: “The reciprocity map of the class formation (G,A) induces an isomorphism from Aᴳ to the abelianization of the Weil group.”

**Sources:**

- [André Weil, Sur la théorie du corps de classes, Journal of the Mathematical Society of Japan 3 (1951)](https://doi.org/10.2969/jmsj/00310001)

### Limits of powers make the Teichmüller lift multiplicative

**Remember:** Limits preserve products, and one more power shifts the sequence.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11S85 (Other nonanalytic theory), 12J25. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let p be prime and let a be a p-adic integer with residue x modulo p. Define the Teichmüller lift ω(x) as the limit of a raised to pⁿ as n grows. The limit uses the p-adic metric, in which multiples of high powers of p are small. Another definition chooses the unique root of Tᵖ = T with residue x, using Hensel’s lemma to lift a simple root.

**Problem.** For residues x and y modulo p, ω(xy) = ω(x)ω(y). Also, ω(x) has residue x and satisfies ω(x)ᵖ = ω(x).

**How the definition helps.** With the limit definition, multiplicativity follows by taking limits of products of the powers. Taking the pth power shifts the sequence by one term, which proves the root equation (our own). The work moves into proving that congruence modulo pᵏ implies congruence of pth powers modulo pᵏ⁺¹ for k ≥ 1 (our own). Successive powers agree modulo increasing powers of p, so they converge, and the same estimate proves independence from a (our own). The root definition instead uses uniqueness to compare the lift of xy with the product of the lifts (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Teichmüller character](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teichm%C3%BCller_character). It says: “If x is an integer mod p, then ω(x) is the unique solution of ω(x)ᵖ = ω(x) that is congruent to x mod p.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Diophantine sets with parameters let Hilbert's tenth problem meet computability

**Remember:** Parameters in, solvability out: that is a computably enumerable set.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11U05 (Decidability (number-theoretic aspects)), 03D25. arXiv math.NT, math.LO. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A set S of tuples of natural numbers is Diophantine if one polynomial p(a, x) with integer coefficients describes it. Namely, a is in S exactly when p(a, x) = 0 has a solution x in natural numbers.

**Problem.** Hilbert's tenth problem asks for an algorithm that decides whether a Diophantine equation has an integer solution. The answer is no.

**How the definition helps.** A single equation has a yes-or-no answer, but a family indexed by parameters defines a set, which can be compared with computably enumerable sets. Then the MRDP theorem says that every computably enumerable set is Diophantine. A noncomputable computably enumerable set then gives a family of equations with no decision method. The hard part is the MRDP theorem itself, in particular Matiyasevich's proof that exponentiation is Diophantine.

**Wikipedia:** [Hilbert's tenth problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert%27s_tenth_problem). It says: “In a Diophantine equation, there are two kinds of variables: the parameters and the unknowns. The Diophantine set consists of the parameter assignments for which the Diophantine equation is solvable.”

**Sources:**

- [Davis, M. (1973). Hilbert's tenth problem is unsolvable. American Mathematical Monthly 80, 233–269.](https://doi.org/10.1080/00029890.1973.11993265)

### Continued fractions with minus signs make the half-line a terminal coalgebra

**Remember:** Always round strictly up, so every number has only one expansion.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11A55 (Continued fractions), 18C40. arXiv math.NT, math.CT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Write a real number x ≥ 1 as a continued fraction with minus signs: x = a₀ − 1/(a₁ − 1/(a₂ − ⋯)). At each step, let β(x) be the smallest integer strictly greater than x. Take β(x) as the next digit, and continue with the number −1/(x − β(x)). This gives a map ξ : ℝ≥1 → ℕ≥2 × ℝ≥1, which sends a number to its first digit and the rest.

**Problem.** We want the real numbers to be the terminal coalgebra of a simple functor. (A coalgebra of a functor F is a set X with a map X → F(X), and the terminal coalgebra is the universal one.) Then a real number is the same thing as its infinite stream of digits.

**How the definition helps.** Rounding strictly up removes the double expansions that stop ordinary continued fractions from working. With the usual continued fractions, the map from ℝ to its digit data is not an isomorphism. Rational numbers have two expansions, and the standard expansion of 2 is just 2, never 1 + 1/1, so no element maps to (1, 1, ∞). That is why ordinary continued fractions make only the irrationals a terminal coalgebra. Pavlović and Pratt use the lexicographic order on ℕ≥2 × X, and they prove that (ℝ≥1, ξ) is the terminal coalgebra on linear orders. In the other direction, the rationals greater than 1, together with ∞, form the initial algebra of the functor X ↦ (ℕ≥2 × X) + 1.

**nLab:** [continued fraction](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/continued+fraction). It says: “It may be tempting to believe that this F-coalgebra structure makes 𝐑 the terminal coalgebra. That is unfortunately not correct because the coalgebra structure ξ: 𝐑 → F(𝐑) is not an isomorphism”

**Sources:**

- [Dusko Pavlović, Vaughan Pratt, On coalgebra of real numbers, Electron. Notes Theor. Comput. Sci. 19 (1999) 103–117](https://doi.org/10.1016/S1571-0661(05)80272-5)

**Problem.** For a subset of the positive integers with positive upper Banach density, take finitely many consecutive backward shifts. The union can have upper Banach density as close to one as desired.

In our own example, take intervals from N to 2N with each N much larger than the last. Any fixed number of shifts leaves ordinary upper density at one half. ### Entropic doubling contracts under homomorphisms

**Remember:** Measure doubling with entropy, and homomorphisms can only shrink it.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11B30 (Arithmetic combinatorics; higher degree uniformity), 11B13, 94A17. arXiv math.NT, math.CO. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** The doubling constant of a finite set A in an abelian group is \|A + A\| divided by \|A\|. Entropic doubling replaces sets by random variables. In our own gloss, it is exp(H(X₁ + X₂) − H(X)) for two independent copies X₁, X₂ of X, where H is Shannon entropy. A related entropic distance between two random variables plays the role of a sumset comparison.

**Problem.** Show that entropic doubling does not grow under a group homomorphism π. Proposition 1.4 proves more: the distance of X₁ and X₂ is at least that of their images plus a fibre average. The paper uses this to give new proofs of known results on subsets of ℤᴰ with small doubling.

**How the definition helps.** Our own reading: entropy splits along a homomorphism into an image part and a fibre part, and sets have no such clean rule. The abstract names contraction under homomorphisms as one of the better properties. Proposition 1.4 states this split as an inequality, and it derives the contraction from it. So an argument can pass to a quotient group and to its fibres without losing control (our own reading). Our own note: results with entropy must still be turned back into results about sets, and that is the remaining work.

**Paper or page:** [Sumsets and entropy revisited](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.13403), [Sumsets and entropy revisited](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.13403). It says: “it enjoys somewhat better properties; for instance, it contracts upon applying a homomorphism.”

### Unique square completion turns a 1-step nilspace into an abelian group

**Remember:** Fix an origin, then the fourth corner of a square is the sum.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11B30 (Arithmetic combinatorics; higher degree uniformity). arXiv math.CO, math.DS. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A nilspace is a set X with chosen maps from the vertices of each cube {0,1}ⁿ into X, called cubes. Cubes stay cubes under the maps between discrete cubes, and every pair of points is a 1-cube. Every corner, a cube with one vertex missing, extends to a full cube. A nilspace is 1-step when every corner of a square, three of its vertices, has exactly one completion.

**Problem.** Every 1-step nilspace X has an abelian group A that acts on X freely and transitively. The cubes of X are exactly the maps ω ↦ x + ω₁h₁ + … + ωₙhₙ, for x in X and h₁, …, hₙ in A.

**How the definition helps.** Unique completion lets one define addition directly. In our own explanation, fix an origin o, complete the square with corners o, x and y, and call the fourth corner x + y. The hard part, done in the paper, is proving the group laws and showing that this one group describes the cubes of every dimension.

**Paper or page:** [Notes on nilspaces: algebraic aspects](https://arxiv.org/abs/1601.03693v3). It says: “Then there is an abelian group A such that 𝒩 is a principal homogeneous space of A and the cubes on 𝒩 are the projections of the degree-1 cubes on A.”

**Sources:**

- [Pablo Candela, Notes on nilspaces: algebraic aspects, arXiv:1601.03693 (2017). Discrete Analysis, 2017:15, 59pp](https://arxiv.org/abs/1601.03693v3)

**Remember:** Orient the algebra first, then the form classes give its ideal classes.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11E16 (General binary quadratic forms), 11R65, 14F06. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A quadratic algebra over a scheme S is an algebra that is locally free of rank two. A line bundle on S is a module that is locally free of rank one. The Picard group is the group of invertible modules under tensor product. For a line bundle N, an N-orientation is an isomorphism from the quotient of the algebra by the scalars to the dual of N.

**Problem.** Let S be a scheme on which 2 is not a zero divisor, and fix a line bundle N, a discriminant and a parity. Classes of primitive N-twisted binary quadratic forms with these invariants match the Picard group of the N-oriented algebra with them.

**How the definition helps.** The orientation keeps track of the algebra when the quotient by scalars has no global basis. The paper shows that the discriminant and the parity classify the oriented algebras. The paper says that Wood's earlier bijection needs this refinement to give Picard groups.

**Paper or page:** [Recovering the Picard group of quadratic algebras from Wood's binary quadratic forms](https://arxiv.org/abs/2111.13422v5). It says: “Extending the notion of orientation of quadratic algebras to the non-free case is another key step, eventually leading us to the desired parametrization.”

**Remember:** Integer matrix means even cross terms.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11E25 (Sums of squares and representations by other particular quadratic forms), 11E12. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A quadratic form has integer matrix if its symmetric matrix has integer entries. Then every cross term 2aᵢⱼxᵢxⱼ has an even coefficient. A form is integral, or integer-valued, if it takes only integer values. For example, x² + xy + y² is integer-valued but does not have integer matrix.
