**nLab:** [regular action](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/regular+action). It says: “Transitivity ensures that all the points in the homotopy quotient are connected by equivalences, while freeness means that the space of equivalences between two points is itself contractible.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Represented cohomology turns coefficient fibers into long exact sequences

**Remember:** Mapping into a fiber gives a fiber of mapping spaces.

*True by definition.* MSC 18N60 (\\((\\infty,1)\\)-categories (quasi-categories, Segal spaces, etc.); \\(\\infty\\)-topoi, stable \\(\\infty\\)-categories), 55U35, 18F20. arXiv math.CT, math.AT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Work in an ∞-category with finite limits, and choose a coefficient object A with a base point. Represented cohomology of X with coefficients in A is the set of path components of the space of maps X → A. Its degree −n version, for n ≥ 0, uses the n-fold loop object of A instead.

**Problem.** A fiber sequence of pointed coefficient objects gives a long exact sequence in nonpositive degrees. Here the fiber is the pullback of the target’s base point along the map. The terms in degree zero are pointed sets, not necessarily groups.

**How the definition helps.** The mapping-space definition gives the exact sequence because mapping into a fiber produces a fiber sequence of spaces. It also turns maps into iterated loop objects into loops on the original mapping space. Taking components therefore gives the homotopy groups in negative degrees and the pointed sets in degree zero. The usual long exact homotopy sequence gives the result. Compared with a cochain definition, the work lies in proving that the mapping spaces recover the cohomology in question. Brown’s work on sheaf cohomology gives one such comparison (our own summary).

**nLab:** [cohomology](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/cohomology), [fiber sequence](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/fiber+sequence). It says: “By projecting everything to connected components with Π₀ this then yields an ordinary long exact sequence of pointed sets”

**Sources:**

- [K. S. Brown, Abstract homotopy theory and generalized sheaf cohomology, Transactions of the American Mathematical Society 186 (1973) 419–458](https://doi.org/10.1090/S0002-9947-1973-0341469-9)

### Stable ∞-categories make finite-limit preservation equivalent to finite-colimit preservation

**Remember:** The same squares test preservation of finite limits and finite colimits.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 18N60 (\\((\\infty,1)\\)-categories (quasi-categories, Segal spaces, etc.); \\(\\infty\\)-topoi, stable \\(\\infty\\)-categories), 18G80. arXiv math.CT, math.AT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** An ∞-category has spaces of maps and keeps track of their higher homotopies. It is stable if it has a zero object and finite limits and colimits, and its pullback squares are exactly its pushout squares. A zero object is both initial and terminal.

**Problem.** A functor between stable ∞-categories preserves finite limits exactly when it preserves finite colimits.

**How the definition helps.** The square-based definition makes finite limits and finite colimits use the same tests. A functor preserving finite limits keeps the zero object and pullbacks, so it keeps the initial object and pushouts. These generate finite colimits. The reverse argument exchanges limits and colimits. The alternative definition compares only fiber and cofiber sequences, the pullback and pushout squares with a zero corner. Showing that the two definitions agree is where the work lies (our own summary).

**nLab:** [stable (infinity,1)-category](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/stable+%28infinity%2C1%29-category). It says: “every exact triangle is coexact and vice versa, i.e. every morphism is the cokernel of its kernel and the kernel of its cokernel.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Terminal-cone limits in ∞-categories are unique up to contractible choice

**Remember:** All terminal cones form a space equivalent to a point.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 18N60 (\\((\\infty,1)\\)-categories (quasi-categories, Segal spaces, etc.); \\(\\infty\\)-topoi, stable \\(\\infty\\)-categories), 18A30. arXiv math.CT, math.AT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A cone connects an object to every entry of a diagram, with compatible maps and higher homotopies. In an ∞-category, an object is terminal if every space of maps into it is contractible, meaning equivalent to a point. A limit is a terminal object in the ∞-category of cones.

**Problem.** If a limit exists, the full subcategory of limit cones is a contractible space.

**How the definition helps.** The terminal-cone definition reduces uniqueness to the map spaces between terminal objects (our own explanation). Each is contractible, and all its maps are equivalences because the reverse maps and the identity composites exist up to homotopy. Thus the terminal objects form a space equivalent to a point if there is at least one. The equivalent slice definition instead uses a trivial fibration, a map that lifts against every simplex boundary. The work in that presentation is proving the slice test and the map-space test agree.

**nLab:** [terminal object in an (infinity,1)-category](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/terminal+object+in+an+%28infinity%2C1%29-category). It says: “instead of demanding that from any other object there is a unique morphism into the terminal object, in a quasi-category there is a contractible infinity-groupoid of such morphisms”

**Sources:**

- [J. Lurie, Higher Topos Theory, Annals of Mathematics Studies 170, Princeton University Press, 2009](https://doi.org/10.1515/9781400830558)

### Axioms for (∞,n)-categories make all the models give one theory

**Remember:** (∞,n)-categories come from freely gluing strict n-categorical shapes, with nothing extra.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 18N65 (\\((\\infty, n)\\)-categories and \\((\\infty,\\infty)\\)-categories). arXiv math.CT, math.AT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** The Barwick–Schommer-Pries axioms describe an (∞,1)-category of (∞,n)-categories. It must be presentable, that is, generated under colimits by a small set of objects. It must be strongly generated by a set of strict n-categories, such as globes and their pastings. It must also respect certain basic pushouts, have certain base-change adjoints, and be universal with these properties.

**Problem.** There are many models of (∞,n)-categories, such as complete Segal Θₙ-spaces and iterated complete Segal spaces. Show that they all give the same homotopy theory. Also compute the automorphisms of that theory.

**How the definition helps.** With the axioms, uniqueness is almost immediate, so comparing models reduces to checking axioms. Under the Barwick–Schommer-Pries axioms, the (∞,1)-category of (∞,n)-categories is unique up to equivalence almost by the first axiom. Its automorphism ∞-group can be computed from the axioms. To compare two models, one then only checks that each model satisfies the axioms. That check is the remaining hard work for each model.

**nLab:** [(infinity,n)-category](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/%28infinity%2Cn%29-category). It says: “By the first axiom, the localization demanded in the universal property is essentially unique.”

**Sources:**

- [Clark Barwick, Christopher Schommer-Pries, On the Unicity of the Homotopy Theory of Higher Categories, J. Amer. Math. Soc. 34 (2021) 1011–1058, arXiv:1112.0040](https://arxiv.org/abs/1112.0040)

### Defining monoidal n-categories as degenerate higher categories makes delooping true by definition

**Remember:** A k-tuply monoidal n-category is an (n+k)-category squashed to one point below level k.

*True by definition.* MSC 18N65 (\\((\\infty, n)\\)-categories and \\((\\infty,\\infty)\\)-categories), 18N70. arXiv math.CT, math.AT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A k-tuply monoidal n-category is a pointed (n+k)-category (one with a chosen object) in which any two parallel j-morphisms are equivalent for j &lt; k. Parallel means that they have the same source and the same target. Its j-morphisms are then renamed as (j−k)-morphisms.

**Problem.** The delooping hypothesis says that k-tuply monoidal n-categories are the same as pointed (k−1)-connected (n+k)-categories.

**How the definition helps.** If you take these degenerate (n+k)-categories as the definition, then the delooping hypothesis holds by definition. The content then moves to another question. Does this definition agree with hand-made ones, such as monoidal or braided monoidal categories? The nLab checks this in low dimensions. For (∞,n)-categories defined by iterated enrichment, Gepner and Haugseng proved the hypothesis as a theorem.

**nLab:** [delooping hypothesis](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/delooping+hypothesis), [k-tuply monoidal n-category](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/k-tuply+monoidal+n-category). It says: “Not infrequently the delooping hypothesis is used to supply a definition of”

**Sources:**

- [John C. Baez, James Dolan, Higher-dimensional algebra and topological quantum field theory, J. Math. Phys. 36 (1995) 6073–6105, arXiv:q-alg/9503002](https://arxiv.org/abs/q-alg/9503002)
- [David Gepner, Rune Haugseng, Enriched ∞-categories via non-symmetric ∞-operads, Adv. Math. (2015), arXiv:1312.3178](https://arxiv.org/abs/1312.3178)

### Defining monoidal structure by little cubes turns stabilization into a theorem

**Remember:** k monoidal structures are k directions in which little cubes can sit side by side.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 18N65 (\\((\\infty, n)\\)-categories and \\((\\infty,\\infty)\\)-categories), 18N70. arXiv math.CT, math.AT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A k-tuply monoidal n-category is defined as an n-category with an action of the little k-cubes operad. In other words, it is an Eₖ-algebra in n-categories. An operad records the ways to combine several inputs into one output. The little k-cubes operad records the ways to put several small cubes side by side inside one k-dimensional cube.

**Problem.** The Baez–Dolan stabilization hypothesis says this: for k ≥ n+2, a k-tuply monoidal n-category is already maximally monoidal, that is, symmetric monoidal. More monoidal structures beyond that point add nothing new.

**How the definition helps.** The little-cubes definition gives the hypothesis an exact meaning, so it can be proved. Before a definition of k-tuply monoidal n-category existed, nobody could state the hypothesis exactly. With the little-cubes definition, the hypothesis becomes a theorem for (n,1)-categories (n-categories in which every morphism above the first level is invertible). The first full proof in print comes from Lurie's work on Eₖ-algebras. Gepner and Haugseng proved a strong general form for (∞,n)-categories, which they define by iterated enrichment.

**nLab:** [stabilization hypothesis](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/stabilization+hypothesis), [k-tuply monoidal n-category](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/k-tuply+monoidal+n-category). It says: “makes good sense, as discussed further below. With this definition the stabilization hypothesis is a theorem at least for (n,1)-categories”

**Sources:**

- [Jacob Lurie, Derived Algebraic Geometry VI: E<sub>k</sub> Algebras, arXiv:0911.0018](https://arxiv.org/abs/0911.0018)
- [David Gepner, Rune Haugseng, Enriched ∞-categories via non-symmetric ∞-operads, Adv. Math. (2015), arXiv:1312.3178](https://arxiv.org/abs/1312.3178)
- [John C. Baez, James Dolan, Higher-dimensional algebra and topological quantum field theory, J. Math. Phys. 36 (1995) 6073–6105, arXiv:q-alg/9503002](https://arxiv.org/abs/q-alg/9503002)

### Fully dualizable objects make the cobordism hypothesis a precise statement

**Remember:** A fully dualizable object bends back on itself in every dimension, like a point.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 18N65 (\\((\\infty, n)\\)-categories and \\((\\infty,\\infty)\\)-categories), 57R56, 18M10. arXiv math.CT, math.AT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** An (∞,n)-category is a higher category with morphisms in all levels, in which the morphisms above level n are invertible. An object of a symmetric monoidal (∞,n)-category is fully dualizable if it has a dual, and the unit and counit of the duality have adjoints, which have adjoints in turn, and so on up to level n−1. The framed bordism (∞,n)-category Bordₙᶠʳ has framed points as objects, cobordisms between them as morphisms, and higher cobordisms as higher morphisms.

**Problem.** The cobordism hypothesis says that Bordₙᶠʳ is the free symmetric monoidal (∞,n)-category with duals on one object. So a framed fully extended TQFT Z (topological quantum field theory, here a symmetric monoidal functor out of the bordism category) is determined by its value Z(point). Also, every fully dualizable object gives such a TQFT.

**How the definition helps.** Full dualizability gives the hypothesis an exact meaning, but it does not prove it. Baez and Dolan stated the hypothesis in 1995, before definitions of the needed higher categories existed. With (∞,n)-categories and full dualizability, the statement becomes precise. Evaluation at the point is an equivalence from symmetric monoidal functors Bordₙᶠʳ → C to the ∞-groupoid (a higher category in which all morphisms are invertible) of fully dualizable objects of C. The proof is hard, and the nLab calls Lurie's account a detailed but incomplete sketch. Other tangential structures, such as orientation or spin, follow from the framed case. The fully dualizable objects carry an O(n)-action, and theories with a G-structure are classified by the homotopy fixed points of the induced G-action.

**nLab:** [cobordism hypothesis](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/cobordism+hypothesis), [fully dualizable object](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/fully+dualizable+object), [functorial field theory](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/functorial+field+theory). It says: “before definitions of these higher category theoretical notions were available.”

**Sources:**

- [Jacob Lurie, On the Classification of Topological Field Theories, Current Developments in Mathematics 2008 (2009) 129–280, arXiv:0905.0465](https://arxiv.org/abs/0905.0465)
- [John C. Baez, James Dolan, Higher-dimensional algebra and topological quantum field theory, J. Math. Phys. 36 (1995) 6073–6105, arXiv:q-alg/9503002](https://arxiv.org/abs/q-alg/9503002)

### Keeping the basepoint makes the periodic table of higher categories hold

**Remember:** Keep the basepoint, or extra transformations creep in.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 18N65 (\\((\\infty, n)\\)-categories and \\((\\infty,\\infty)\\)-categories), 18N70. arXiv math.CT, math.AT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A k-tuply monoidal n-category is a pointed (k−1)-connected (n+k)-category. Here (k−1)-connected means that any two parallel j-morphisms are equivalent for every j less than k. The basepoint is extra data. Functors and transformations must respect the basepoint.

**Problem.** The claim is that the entries of the Baez–Dolan periodic table hold as equivalences of higher categories. For example, 1-tuply monoidal 0-categories are monoids, and 2-tuply monoidal 0-categories are commutative monoids.

**How the definition helps.** The basepoint removes extra transformations, so the expected equivalences hold. Without the basepoint, take two functors f and g between one-object categories. A natural transformation from f to g is then an element y with f(x)y = y g(x) for all x. So the 2-category of connected 1-categories is not the 1-category of monoids. In the same way, for doubly degenerate bicategories, the modifications that are not identities stop the tricategory from being the category of commutative monoids (Cheng and Gurski). Pointed functors and pointed transformations remove these extra cells, and then the expected equivalences hold. The Eckmann–Hilton argument still does the work of making the monoid commutative.

**nLab:** [k-tuply monoidal n-category](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/k-tuply+monoidal+n-category), [periodic table](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/periodic+table). It says: “However, the nonidentity modifications do screw things up, so the tricategory of 1-connected bicategories is not equivalent to the 1-category of commutative monoids.”

**Sources:**

- [Eugenia Cheng, Nick Gurski, The periodic table of n-categories for low dimensions I: degenerate categories and degenerate bicategories, arXiv:0708.1178](https://arxiv.org/abs/0708.1178)
- [John C. Baez, James Dolan, Higher-dimensional algebra and topological quantum field theory, J. Math. Phys. 36 (1995) 6073–6105, arXiv:q-alg/9503002](https://arxiv.org/abs/q-alg/9503002)

### Simpson conjectures that only the unit laws need to be weak

**Remember:** Keep everything strict except the identities.

*Rules out counterexamples. Confidence: medium.* MSC 18N65 (\\((\\infty, n)\\)-categories and \\((\\infty,\\infty)\\)-categories), 18N20. arXiv math.CT, math.AT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A semi-strict ∞-category in Simpson's sense has strictly associative composition and strict interchange laws (the rule that composing horizontally then vertically gives the same result as the other order). Only its unit laws hold weakly, that is, up to equivalence.

**Problem.** Simpson's conjecture says that every weak ∞-category is equivalent to one in which only the unit laws are weak. In particular, such structures model all homotopy types.

**How the definition helps.** Making only the units weak is Simpson's proposed way around a known obstruction. Kapranov and Voevodsky claimed that ∞-groupoids that are strict except for inverses model all homotopy types. Simpson proved that no strict n-groupoid, for n ≥ 3, realizes the n-type of the 2-sphere, for any realization functor that is compatible with homotopy groups. The nLab says this makes the claim seem wrong. Simpson suggested that weakening only the units would avoid the problem. Joyal and Kock proved a version in dimension 3: one-object 3-groupoids that are strict except for weak identity arrows model all connected, simply connected homotopy 3-types. The general case is open, so this definition is a proposed fix, not a finished theorem.

**nLab:** [Simpson's conjecture](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Simpson%27s+conjecture), [semi-strict infinity-category](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/semi-strict+infinity-category). It says: “Simpson's conjecture is proven up to the case of 3-categories with a single object.”

**Sources:**

- [Carlos Simpson, Homotopy types of strict 3-groupoids, arXiv:math/9810059 (1998)](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/9810059)
- [André Joyal, Joachim Kock, Weak units and homotopy 3-types, in: Categories in Algebra, Geometry and Mathematical Physics, Contemp. Math. 431 (2007) 257–276; arXiv:math/0602084](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0602084)

### Trimble n-categories build the fundamental n-groupoid into the definition

**Remember:** T says how to glue paths, and the same T defines composition and fundamental n-groupoids.

*True by definition.* MSC 18N65 (\\((\\infty, n)\\)-categories and \\((\\infty,\\infty)\\)-categories), 18M75, 55P15. arXiv math.CT, math.AT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** An operad is a family of spaces of k-input operations together with a way to compose them. Let T be the operad of ways to cut the unit interval into k pieces: Tₖ is the space of continuous maps \[0,1\] → \[0,k\] that send 0 to 0 and 1 to k. A Trimble 0-category is a set. A Trimble (n+1)-category is a set of objects with an n-category of morphisms between each pair, which together form an algebra over the operad ΠₙT; here Πₙ is the fundamental n-groupoid functor, applied to T.

**Problem.** Give an algebraic definition of weak n-category such that every space X has a fundamental n-groupoid ΠₙX that is functorial in X. The fundamental n-groupoid records the points, the paths, the homotopies between paths, and so on up to dimension n.

**How the definition helps.** Paths in X glue in the ways that T allows, so the fundamental n-groupoid of X fits the definition with no extra work. The paths in X form a T-algebra in an obvious way, and applying Πₙ to it gives a ΠₙT-algebra. By definition, this is a Trimble (n+1)-category, namely Πₙ₊₁X. For n = 0, Π₀T is the associative operad, so this gives the usual fundamental groupoid. The induction needs one real theorem: Πₙ₊₁ preserves finite products and coproducts. The definition does not prove the homotopy hypothesis, which says that ∞-groupoids are the same as spaces up to homotopy. The nLab page on that hypothesis says that, even with the fundamental ∞-groupoid built in, it is unclear how to prove it for Trimble ∞-groupoids.

**nLab:** [Trimble n-category](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Trimble+n-category), [homotopy hypothesis](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/homotopy+hypothesis). It says: “This definition was introduced in order to give an algebraic notion of fundamental n-groupoid”

**Sources:**

- [Tom Leinster, A Survey of Definitions of n-Category, arXiv:math/0107188 (2001)](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0107188)

## 19 \\(K\\)-theory

### Marks defined as hom-set sizes make the mark map a ring homomorphism

**Remember:** A pair is fixed exactly when both entries are fixed.

*True by definition.* MSC 19A22 (Frobenius induction, Burnside and representation rings), 20C15. arXiv math.RT, math.GR. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For a finite group G, the Burnside ring is built from finite G-sets, with disjoint union as sum and Cartesian product as product. The H-mark of a G-set X is the number of points that the subgroup H fixes. Write it as the number of G-maps from G/H to X.

**Problem.** For each subgroup H, the H-mark gives a ring homomorphism from the Burnside ring to ℤ.

**How the definition helps.** As a count of maps out of G/H, the mark sends products to products at once. A G-map from G/H into a disjoint union lands in one part, because G/H is a single orbit, so sums go to sums. The nLab says that the hom-set description makes the ring homomorphism manifest. Formal differences then extend the map from the semiring to the ring. A description by product coefficients on orbits would need those coefficients first; this comparison is our own.

**nLab:** [table of marks](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/table+of+marks). It says: “all other steps use that the mark homomorphism is a ring homomorphism, which we made manifest by expressing the marks via hom-sets”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Finitely generated projectives keep K₀ from collapsing under the Eilenberg swindle

**Remember:** An infinite sum absorbs one more copy of its summand.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 19A99 (Grothendieck groups and \\(K<sub>0</sub>\\)), 18F25. arXiv math.KT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Define K₀ of a ring from finitely generated projective modules under direct sum, and then adjoin inverses. A projective module is a direct summand of a free module. If all projective modules were allowed, including infinitely generated ones, the group would be zero.

**Problem.** Let an additive category have countable direct sums. Then its Grothendieck group, built from direct sums alone, is zero. An additive category is one where maps can be added and finite direct sums exist.

**How the definition helps.** The restriction to finitely generated modules removes the infinite sums that the swindle needs. For any object A, let S be the sum of countably many copies of A. Then A ⊕ S ≅ S, so \[A\] + \[S\] = \[S\] and \[A\] = 0. The nLab gives this argument as the reason to restrict to finitely generated projective modules. With that restriction, K₀(ℤ) = ℤ, since rank is additive (our own).

**nLab:** [Eilenberg swindle](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Eilenberg+swindle). It says: “This is the reason that, for instance, one has to restrict oneself to categories of finitely generated (projective) modules (which lack infinite direct sums)”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Defining K₁ as an abelianization makes every homomorphism to abelian groups factor

**Remember:** Any abelian-valued homomorphism of matrix groups factors through K₁.

*True by definition.* MSC 19B99 (Whitehead groups and \\(K<sub>1</sub>\\)). arXiv math.KT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let GL(R) be the union of the groups GLₙ(R), where A is identified with the block matrix diag(A, 1). Define K₁(R) as the abelianization of GL(R), its quotient by the commutator subgroup. The older definition divides GL(R) by the subgroup E(R) generated by elementary matrices. An elementary matrix is the identity plus one off-diagonal entry.

**Problem.** Every group homomorphism from GL(R) to an abelian group factors uniquely through K₁(R). The determinant over a commutative ring is one example.

**How the definition helps.** A homomorphism to an abelian group kills all commutators, so it factors through the abelianization (our own). With the quotient by E(R), one must first know that E(R) is the commutator subgroup. That fact is Whitehead's lemma, which Wikipedia states, and the work goes there.

**Wikipedia:** [Algebraic K-theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_K-theory). It says: “K₁(A) is the abelianization of the infinite general linear group”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### The plus construction defines all higher K-groups as homotopy groups

**Remember:** Make π₁ of BGL(R) abelian, keep the homology, and read off K-groups.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 19D06 (\\(Q\\)- and plus-constructions). arXiv math.KT, math.AT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For a ring R, let GL(R) be the union of the groups GLₙ(R), and let BGL(R) be its classifying space. The K-theory space is BGL(R)⁺, where ⁺ is Quillen's plus construction. This construction kills the subgroup E(R) of elementary matrices in the fundamental group without changing homology; E(R) is perfect, which means that it equals its own commutator subgroup. Then Kₙ(R) is defined as πₙ(BGL(R)⁺) for n ≥ 1.

**Problem.** Define higher K-groups Kₙ(R) for all n that come from one space. They should agree with the classical K₁(R) = GL(R)/E(R) and with Milnor's K₂.

**How the definition helps.** The plus construction is built to give the right fundamental group, so K₁ is correct by construction. The construction kills exactly the perfect normal subgroup E(R) of π₁ and keeps the homology. By Whitehead's lemma, E(R) is the commutator subgroup of GL(R), so π₁(BGL(R)⁺) = GL(R)/E(R) = K₁(R). The group π₂(BGL(R)⁺) agrees with Milnor's K₂(R), which is a short theorem, so all K-groups are homotopy groups of one space. Long exact sequences of K-groups are hard to get from this definition. They come more easily from Quillen's Q-construction. The real content is then Quillen's theorem that the two definitions agree.

**nLab:** [Quillen plus construction](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Quillen+plus+construction), [algebraic K-theory](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/algebraic+K-theory), [Steinberg group](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Steinberg+group). It says: “The plus construction doesn't change the homology of the space but 'kills' a perfect normal subgroup of G within the classifying space BG.”

**Sources:**

- [Charles Weibel, The K-book: An introduction to algebraic K-theory, Graduate Studies in Mathematics 145, AMS (2013), Section IV.1](https://sites.math.rutgers.edu/~weibel/Kbook.html)
- [Marc Hoyois, On Quillen's plus construction (2019)](https://hoyois.app.uni-regensburg.de/papers/acyclic.pdf)

### Milnor K-theory's Steinberg relation is exactly what the Galois symbol needs

**Remember:** Once the Steinberg relation holds, cup products give a map on symbols.

*True by definition.* MSC 19D45 (Higher symbols, Milnor \\(K\\)-theory), 12G05. arXiv math.KT, math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For a field F, the Milnor K-group Kₙᴹ(F) is generated by symbols {a₁, …, aₙ} of nonzero elements. Symbols are multiplicative in each entry. A symbol is zero when two adjacent entries are a and 1 − a, which is the Steinberg relation. Quillen's K-groups, defined from the homotopy groups of a space, agree with these only up to degree two.

**Problem.** Let m be invertible in F, and let μₘ be the group of m-th roots of unity. Cup products of Kummer classes give a homomorphism from Kₙᴹ(F)/m to Galois cohomology with coefficients in the n-fold tensor power of μₘ. The Kummer class of a records how the Galois group moves the m-th roots of a.

**How the definition helps.** The cup product is multilinear, so only the Steinberg relation needs checking. That check is that the cup product of the Kummer classes of a and 1 − a is zero (our own). It follows from writing 1 − a as a norm from the field generated by an m-th root of a (our own). Wikipedia states that the map satisfies the defining relations of the Milnor K-group. For Quillen's groups there is no such presentation by symbols beyond degree two (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Algebraic K-theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_K-theory). It says: “satisfying the defining relations of the Milnor K-group”

**Sources:**

- [John Milnor, Algebraic K-theory and quadratic forms (1970).](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01425486)

### Defining relative K-theory as a homotopy fiber builds in exactness

**Remember:** A homotopy fiber remembers how a class becomes zero.

*True by definition.* MSC 19D99 (Higher algebraic \\(K\\)-theory), 19D06. arXiv math.KT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let R be a ring with an ideal I. Quillen's K-theory gives a space K(R) whose homotopy groups are the K-groups of R. Define relative K-theory K(R, I) as the homotopy fiber of K(R) → K(R/I). Its points are points of K(R) together with a path from their image to the base point.

**Problem.** The relative K-groups fit into a long exact sequence ⋯ → Kₙ(R, I) → Kₙ(R) → Kₙ(R/I) → Kₙ₋₁(R, I) → ⋯.

**How the definition helps.** Every map of spaces gives a long exact sequence of homotopy groups for its homotopy fiber, so this sequence holds by definition. Wikipedia states that the program sought definitions for which the sequence arises in this way. Older algebraic definitions of relative K₀ and K₁ gave only the low-degree part, checked by hand (our own). The work moves to constructing K(R) as a space and comparing the fiber with those older groups (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Algebraic K-theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_K-theory). It says: “the long exact sequence for relative K-groups arises as the long exact homotopy sequence of a fibration”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Defining G₀ pushforward by derived direct images makes pushforwards compose

**Remember:** Compose the derived maps before taking their classes.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 19E08 (\\(K\\)-theory of schemes), 14F06. arXiv math.AG, math.KT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let G₀ of a Noetherian scheme be the Grothendieck group of coherent sheaves. For a proper map f, define pushforward by the class of the derived direct image Rf∗, a single complex with coherent cohomology. The sheaf definition sends a sheaf F to the alternating sum of its higher direct images Rⁱf∗F.

**Problem.** Let f : X → Y and g : Y → Z be proper maps of Noetherian schemes. On G₀, pushing forward along g ∘ f equals pushing forward along f and then along g.

**How the definition helps.** Derived direct images compose, Rg∗ ∘ Rf∗ = R(g ∘ f)∗, as the Stacks Project states, so the classes agree. In the sheaf definition, one would need the Leray spectral sequence to compare the alternating sums (our own). The work moves to two facts (our own). For a proper map, Rf∗ keeps cohomology bounded and coherent. The class of a complex equals the alternating sum of its cohomology classes.

**Paper or page:** [Cohomology](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0D5T). It says: “Then Rg∗ ∘ Rf∗ = R(g ∘ f)∗ as functors”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Dividing K₁ by group elements makes Whitehead torsion independent of cell lifts

**Remember:** Changing a cell lift multiplies by a group element that the quotient kills.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 19J10 (Whitehead (and related) torsion), 57Q10. arXiv math.GT, math.KT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let G be the fundamental group and ℤ\[G\] its integral group ring. The Whitehead group Wh(G) is K₁(ℤ\[G\]) modulo the classes of ±g for g in G. Torsion starts as a matrix over ℤ\[G\], computed from the cells of the universal cover. That matrix depends on a choice of ordered, oriented lift of each cell.

**Problem.** Whitehead torsion of a homotopy equivalence of finite connected CW complexes does not depend on the choices of cell lifts and orientations.

**How the definition helps.** Changing one lift or orientation multiplies a basis vector by ±g, and the quotient kills that factor (our own). Wikipedia gives the quotient by elementary matrices, elements of G and ±1. The remaining work is to show independence from the other choices in the construction (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Whitehead torsion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whitehead_torsion). It says: “the quotient of GL(ℤ\[G\]) by the subgroup generated by elementary matrices, elements of G and ±1”

**Sources:**

- [John Milnor, Whitehead torsion (1966).](https://doi.org/10.1090/S0002-9904-1966-11484-2)

### Defining the Fredholm index by a K-theory boundary map makes indices add

**Remember:** The boundary map sends multiplication of invertible classes to addition of indices.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 19K56 (Index theory), 47A53, 46L80. arXiv math.OA, math.FA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A Fredholm operator on a separable infinite-dimensional Hilbert space has finite-dimensional kernel and cokernel. It is invertible in the Calkin algebra, the bounded operators modulo the compact operators. Define its index as the image of its K₁ class under the boundary map to K₀ of the compact operators, which is ℤ. The direct definition is dim ker T − dim coker T.

**Problem.** For Fredholm operators S and T, the index of ST is the index of S plus the index of T.

**How the definition helps.** In K₁ the class of a product is the sum of the classes, and the boundary map is a homomorphism (our own). Wikipedia notes that the index map appears in the six-term exact sequence of the Calkin algebra. With the dimension formula, one must instead track kernels and cokernels through the product (our own). The work moves to matching the boundary map with the dimension formula (our own). It also uses Atkinson's theorem: Fredholm operators are those invertible modulo compact operators.

**Wikipedia:** [Operator K-theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operator_K-theory). It says: “The Fredholm index map appears in the 6-term exact sequence given by the Calkin algebra.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Characterizing Adams operations by line bundles makes them compose multiplicatively

**Remember:** An m-th tensor power of an n-th power is an mn-th power.

*True by definition.* MSC 19L20 (\\(J\\)-homomorphism, Adams operations), 55S25. arXiv math.AT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** On complex K-theory, the Adams operation ψᵏ is the unique natural ring map with ψᵏ\[L\] = \[L⊗ᵏ\] for every line bundle L. Adams's explicit definition writes ψᵏ as a Newton polynomial in exterior powers of a bundle. Uniqueness uses the splitting principle: a suitable pullback splits any bundle into line bundles and is injective on K-theory.

**Problem.** On complex K-theory of finite CW complexes, ψᵐ ∘ ψⁿ = ψᵐⁿ.

**How the definition helps.** The composite ψᵐ ∘ ψⁿ is a natural ring map that sends \[L\] to \[L⊗ᵐⁿ\], so uniqueness makes it ψᵐⁿ (our own). With Newton polynomials, one would have to compose two polynomials in exterior powers (our own). The nLab states the line-bundle property and the uniqueness of the operation. The work moves to existence, given by the Newton formulas, and to the splitting principle behind uniqueness (our own).

**nLab:** [Adams operation](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Adams+operation). It says: “applied to a class x ≔ \[L\] represented by a line bundle L, ψᵏ is the kth tensor power”

**Sources:**

- [J. F. Adams, Vector Fields on Spheres (1962).](https://doi.org/10.2307/1970213)

### Defining equivariant K-theory by G-bundles gives the representation ring at a point

**Remember:** A bundle with a group action over one point is a representation.

*True by definition.* MSC 19L47 (Equivariant \\(K\\)-theory), 19A22. arXiv math.AT, math.KT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let G be a compact Lie group. A G-vector bundle is a complex vector bundle with a G-action that is linear on fibers. Define equivariant K-theory by formal differences of G-bundles, with direct sum as addition and tensor product as multiplication. The operator model uses K-theory of a crossed product algebra, which encodes the action.

**Problem.** For a compact Lie group G, equivariant K-theory of a point is the complex representation ring R(G). R(G) consists of formal differences of finite-dimensional complex representations.

**How the definition helps.** Over one point a G-bundle is a single vector space with a linear G-action, that is, a representation. The nLab says that this isomorphism follows immediately from the elementary definition. In the operator model, the same group is K₀ of the group C\*-algebra of G (our own). Identifying that with R(G) needs the Green–Julg theorem or the Peter–Weyl decomposition (our own).

**nLab:** [equivariant K-theory](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/equivariant+K-theory). It says: “a G-equivariant vector bundle over the point is manifestly just a linear representation of G on a complex vector space”

**Sources:**

- [Graeme Segal, Equivariant K-theory (1968).](https://www.numdam.org/item/PMIHES%5F1968%5F%5F34%5F%5F129%5F0/)

### An acyclic map to an E₁-group is a plus construction

**Remember:** Into a group-like space, any acyclic map is already the plus construction.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 19D06 (\\(Q\\)- and plus-constructions), 55P48. arXiv math.AT, math.KT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A map is acyclic when its homotopy fibers have the integral homology of a point. The plus construction X → X⁺ is the acyclic map that kills the largest perfect subgroup of the fundamental group of X. An E₁-group is a space with a multiplication that is associative up to coherent homotopy and has inverses up to homotopy.

**Problem.** Recognize when a given map is a model of the plus construction. The paper uses this to compare its construction of the group completion with other ones.

**How the definition helps.** An acyclic map X → Y is onto on fundamental groups, and its kernel is perfect (a group equal to its own commutator subgroup). An E₁-group has abelian fundamental group, so the largest perfect subgroup of π₁(X) must go to zero in it. So the kernel is exactly that subgroup, and Y is X⁺. This argument is our own. The corollary also says that an acyclic map between E₁-groups is an equivalence. The main theorem, on a version of Quillen's S⁻¹S construction for n ≥ 2, stays hard.

**Paper or page:** [Group completion via the action ∞-category](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.12118). It says: “Let X → Y be an acyclic map with Y an E₁-group. Then Y is a model for the plus construction of X.”

**Sources:**

- [Georg Lehner, Group completion via the action ∞-category, arXiv:2405.12118 (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.12118)

### Nonconnective K-theory gives Bass–Heller–Swan without idempotent completeness

**Remember:** Nonconnective K-theory cannot see idempotent completion, so idempotent completeness is not needed.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 19D35 (Negative \\(K\\)-theory, NK and Nil), 18F25. arXiv math.KT, math.AT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Nonconnective K-theory K∞ is the spectrum of algebraic K-theory with negative K-groups added, built by a delooping construction. A full subcategory is cofinal when every object of the larger category is a direct summand of an object of the smaller one.

**Problem.** The Bass–Heller–Swan decomposition splits the K-theory of a twisted Laurent extension into a mapping torus and two Nil-terms. For connective K-theory, the paper needs the additive category to be idempotent complete.

**How the definition helps.** Since K∞ does not change under a cofinal inclusion (Lemma 2.2), one can replace any additive category by its idempotent completion. So the decomposition for K∞, Theorem 3.1, holds for all additive categories. The same lemma gives only that the connective K-groups Kₙ agree for n ≥ 1, so K₀ can change. This is why the connective version, Theorem 3.3, needs idempotent completeness. The reduction to the idempotent complete case is our own reading of how the two theorems fit. The hard part is the proof of the decomposition itself (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Vanishing of Nil-terms and negative K-theory for additive categories](https://arxiv.org/abs/2002.03412), [Vanishing of Nil-terms and negative K-theory for additive categories](https://arxiv.org/abs/2002.03412), [Vanishing of Nil-terms and negative K-theory for additive categories](https://arxiv.org/abs/2002.03412). It says: “Let I : 𝒜 → 𝒜′ be the inclusion of a full cofinal additive subcategory. … The induced map K∞(I) : K∞(𝒜) → K∞(𝒜′) is a weak homotopy equivalence.”

**Sources:**

- [Arthur Bartels, Wolfgang Lueck, Vanishing of Nil-terms and negative K-theory for additive categories, Proc. Roy. Soc. Edinburgh Sect. A 154 (2024) 1945–2023, arXiv:2002.03412](https://doi.org/10.1017/prm.2024.103)

### Regular coherent additive categories have no negative K-groups or Nil-terms

**Remember:** Regular coherent categories have K-theory with no negative part and no Nil-terms.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 19D35 (Negative \\(K\\)-theory, NK and Nil), 18F25. arXiv math.KT, math.AT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** An additive category is regular coherent when, roughly, its finitely presented modules form an abelian category. Each such module must also have a finite resolution by finitely generated projective modules. This extends regular coherence for rings to additive categories.

**Problem.** Negative K-groups and Nil-groups are the error terms in the Bass–Heller–Swan formula and in the Farrell–Jones conjecture. One wants simple conditions under which they vanish.

**How the definition helps.** Regular coherence lets the classical resolution argument work for additive categories (our own). So the vanishing follows as it does for regular rings. The precise theorem for negative K-groups, Theorem 11.1, asks that every polynomial extension 𝒜\[t₁, …, tₘ\] is regular coherent, not only 𝒜. For coherent rings this is a real extra condition, because coherence need not pass to polynomial rings (our own). This matters for the Farrell–Jones conjecture, where coefficients are additive categories, not rings (our own). The hard part is the passage from rings to additive categories with twisted polynomial extensions.

**Paper or page:** [Vanishing of Nil-terms and negative K-theory for additive categories](https://arxiv.org/abs/2002.03412). It says: “For instance the negative K-groups and all twisted Nil-groups vanish for an additive category if it is regular coherent.”

**Sources:**

- [Arthur Bartels, Wolfgang Lueck, Vanishing of Nil-terms and negative K-theory for additive categories, Proc. Roy. Soc. Edinburgh Sect. A 154 (2024) 1945–2023, arXiv:2002.03412](https://doi.org/10.1017/prm.2024.103)

### c-categories extend the Dundas–Goodwillie–McCarthy theorem to stacks

**Remember:** Control a category by connective rings, and trace methods still apply.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 19D55 (\\(K\\)-theory and homology; cyclic homology and cohomology), 18N60, 14A30. arXiv math.KT, math.AT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A c-category is a category whose behaviour is controlled by connective ring spectra. Any c-category has a resolution in finitely many steps by categories of compact modules over connective ring spectra. A truncating invariant is one that does not change when a connective ring spectrum is replaced by its zeroth homotopy ring.

**Problem.** The Dundas–Goodwillie–McCarthy theorem says that the fiber of the cyclotomic trace from K-theory to TC is unchanged by nilpotent extensions of connective rings. The aim is to extend it to perfect complexes on stacks.

**How the definition helps.** The finite resolution by compact modules lets the theorem for connective rings pass to every c-category, step by step (our own). The paper shows that perfect complexes on many stacks form a c-category. So the generalization follows from that fact. The hard part is showing that a given category is a c-category.

**Paper or page:** [c-structures and trace methods beyond connective rings](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.14774). It says: “We introduce nilpotent extensions of c-categories, and show that they induce isomorphisms on truncating invariants, such as the fiber of the cyclotomic trace map.”

**Sources:**

- [Ishan Levy, Vladimir Sosnilo, c-structures and trace methods beyond connective rings, arXiv:2509.14774 (2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.14774)

### Perfect complexes instead of vector bundles let K-theory glue along open covers

**Remember:** Use perfect complexes, not vector bundles, and K-theory glues along open covers.

*Rules out counterexamples. Confidence: medium.* MSC 19E08 (\\(K\\)-theory of schemes), 18F25. arXiv math.KT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** The Thomason–Trobaugh K-theory of a scheme X is the Waldhausen K-theory of the category of perfect complexes on X. Waldhausen K-theory is a K-theory construction for categories with cofibrations and weak equivalences. A perfect complex is a complex that is locally quasi-isomorphic to a bounded complex of vector bundles. The weak equivalences are the quasi-isomorphisms, which are the maps that induce isomorphisms on cohomology.

**Problem.** Prove that K-theory of schemes has a localization sequence and a Mayer–Vietoris sequence for open covers (Zariski descent). This should hold for all quasi-compact quasi-separated schemes.

**How the definition helps.** Perfect complexes restrict and extend well along open immersions (inclusions of open subschemes), and descent needs exactly this. Quillen's K-theory of vector bundles is defined on all schemes. But a scheme without an ample family of line bundles may have too few vector bundles, and then the descent and localization theorems are not available. With perfect complexes, Thomason and Trobaugh prove a localization sequence and Mayer–Vietoris for open covers of quasi-compact quasi-separated schemes. The nLab credits them with Zariski descent for finite-dimensional noetherian schemes; the wider statement is from their paper. On schemes with an ample family of line bundles, the two K-theories agree, so nothing is lost. The descent proofs are still long.

**nLab:** [algebraic K-theory](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/algebraic+K-theory), [Waldhausen S-construction](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Waldhausen+S-construction). It says: “Thomason-Trobaugh K-theory coincides with Quillen K-theory for schemes that admit an ample family of line bundles, but has the advantage of better global descent properties.”

**Sources:**

- [R. W. Thomason, Thomas Trobaugh, Higher algebraic K-theory of schemes and of derived categories, The Grothendieck Festschrift vol. III, Progress in Math. 88 (1990) 247–435](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-0-8176-4576-2_10)

### Defining KK and E-theory by universal properties gives the comparison functor

**Remember:** A rule that respects all extensions respects split extensions.

*True by definition.* MSC 19K35 (Kasparov theory (\\(KK\\)-theory)), 46L80. arXiv math.OA, math.KT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** On separable C\*-algebras, Kasparov's KK category is the target of the universal functor that is homotopy invariant, stable and split exact. Stable means that tensoring with the compact operators becomes invertible. Split exact means that split extensions become direct sums. E-theory has the same universal property, but with exactness required for all extensions.

**Problem.** There is a canonical functor from Kasparov's KK category to E-theory that is compatible with the maps from C\*-algebras.

**How the definition helps.** The E-theory functor is homotopy invariant and stable, and it is exact on all extensions, hence on split ones. So the universal property of KK gives the functor at once. The nLab gives exactly this argument. The work moves to Higson's theorems that the analytic definitions have these universal properties (our own). Deducing split exactness from exactness also needs the long exact sequences that homotopy invariance provides (our own).

**nLab:** [E-theory](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/E-theory). It says: “since every split exact sequence is in particular exact, there is a universal functor”

**Sources:**

- [Nigel Higson, A characterization of KK-theory (1987).](https://doi.org/10.2140/pjm.1987.126.253)
- [Nigel Higson, Categories of fractions and excision in KK-theory (1990).](https://doi.org/10.1016/0022-4049(90)90114-w)

### The universal property of KK-theory gives every split-exact stable functor Bott periodicity

**Remember:** A functor that factors through KK inherits its periodicity.

*True by definition.* MSC 19K35 (Kasparov theory (\\(KK\\)-theory)), 46L80. arXiv math.KT, math.OA. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Kasparov's KK-theory gives a category whose objects are separable C\*-algebras. Higson showed that the functor into it is universal among functors to abelian groups that are additive, homotopy invariant, stable and split exact. Stable means that tensoring with the compact operators changes nothing, and split exact means that split short exact sequences go to split short exact sequences. Kasparov's own definition builds the morphisms from operators on Hilbert modules.

**Problem.** Every functor F with these four properties satisfies F(S²A) ≅ F(A), naturally in A. Here the suspension SA is A tensored with the continuous functions on ℝ that vanish at infinity.

**How the definition helps.** By the universal property, F factors through the KK category. So the Bott isomorphism between S²A and A in KK goes to an isomorphism under F. The work is Kasparov's proof of Bott periodicity in KK and Higson's theorem that KK has this universal property. Wikipedia states that such theories inherit Bott periodicity from KK.

**Wikipedia:** [KK-theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/KK-theory). It says: “Any such theory satisfies Bott periodicity in the appropriate sense”

**Sources:**

- [Gennady Kasparov, The operator K-functor and extensions of C\*-algebras (1981, English translation)](https://doi.org/10.1070/IM1981v016n03ABEH001320)
- [Nigel Higson, A characterization of KK-theory (1987)](https://doi.org/10.2140/pjm.1987.126.253)

## 20 Group theory and generalizations

### A left identity and left inverses are enough to make a group

**Remember:** Check only one side, but the same side for identity and inverses.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 20A05 (Axiomatics and elementary properties of groups). arXiv math.GR. Level 1: early undergraduate.

**Definition.** A group is a set with an associative operation, an identity e with ex = xe = x, and two-sided inverses. The weaker scheme asks only for some e with ex = x for all x and, for each x, some y with yx = e.

**Problem.** To show that a structure is a group, it is enough to check associativity, a left identity and left inverses. The left inverses are then two-sided, and so is the identity.

**How the definition helps.** The weaker axioms halve the work of checking a group, and associativity supplies the other side. Our own sketch: if yx = e and zy = e, then xy = (zy)(xy) = z(yx)y = zy = e. So left inverses are right inverses, and then xe = x(yx) = (xy)x = ex = x. ProofWiki shows that a left identity in a semigroup need not be unique. Our own example: on a set with two or more elements, let xy = y. Then every element is a left identity and has a right inverse, but this is not a group. The proof that the two schemes agree is a short computation.

**Paper or page:** [Equivalence of Axiom Schemata for Groups](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Equivalence_of_Axiom_Schemata_for_Groups), [Left Identity in Semigroup may not be Unique](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Left_Identity_in_Semigroup_may_not_be_Unique). It says: “there exists at least one element e ∈ G such that e is a left identity; For any element g in a group G, there exists at least one left inverse of g.”

**Sources:**

- [ProofWiki, Equivalence of Axiom Schemata for Groups](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Equivalence_of_Axiom_Schemata_for_Groups)
- [ProofWiki, Left Identity in Semigroup may not be Unique](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Left_Identity_in_Semigroup_may_not_be_Unique)

### The subgroup test asks for nonempty, since the empty set passes

**Remember:** The empty set is closed under everything, so test for nonempty first.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 20A05 (Axiomatics and elementary properties of groups). arXiv math.GR. Level 1: early undergraduate.

**Definition.** A subgroup of a group G is a subset H that is a group under the operation of G. A group always contains an identity, so it is never empty.

**Problem.** Give a short test for a subset H of a group G to be a subgroup.

**How the definition helps.** Closure under products and inverses holds vacuously for the empty set, so the nonempty clause is what brings the identity into H. Our own sketch: with some a in H, closure gives a⁻¹ in H, and then e = aa⁻¹ is in H. ProofWiki records that the empty set is a submagma of any magma, a set with one operation. So without clause (1), the test would accept ∅, which is not a group. ProofWiki also records that a monoid cannot be empty, which is why groups and their subgroups are nonempty. Nothing hard remains.

**Paper or page:** [Two-Step Subgroup Test](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Two-Step_Subgroup_Test), [Empty Set is Submagma of Magma](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Empty_Set_is_Submagma_of_Magma), [Monoid is not Empty](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Monoid_is_not_Empty). It says: “(1): H ≠ ∅, that is, H is non-empty (2): a, b ∈ H ⟹ a ∘ b ∈ H (3): a ∈ H ⟹ a⁻¹ ∈ H.”

**Sources:**

- [ProofWiki, Two-Step Subgroup Test](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Two-Step_Subgroup_Test)
- [ProofWiki, Empty Set is Submagma of Magma](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Empty_Set_is_Submagma_of_Magma)
- [ProofWiki, Monoid is not Empty](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Monoid_is_not_Empty)

### Transitive actions on inhabited sets are coset spaces

**Remember:** Transitive means one orbit, and one orbit needs at least one point.

*Rules out counterexamples. Confidence: medium.* MSC 20B05 (General theory for finite permutation groups), 20B07, 18B40. arXiv math.GR. Level 1: early undergraduate.

**Definition.** An action of a group G on a set X is transitive when, for all x and y in X, there is g in G with y = g · x. Often one also requires X to be inhabited, that is, nonempty.

**Problem.** Show that every transitive G-set is isomorphic to a coset space G/H. Also show that the transitive G-sets are the connected objects of the category of G-sets. A connected object is not empty and does not split as a coproduct of two nonempty objects.

**How the definition helps.** Asking for at least one point removes the empty set, which is the one case that breaks both statements. By the literal definition, the empty set carries a transitive action. But it is not a coset space G/H, and it is not a connected object. When X is inhabited, pick x in X and let H be its stabilizer, the subgroup of elements that fix x. Transitivity makes the map gH ↦ g · x a bijection G/H → X. Every G-set then splits uniquely as a coproduct of transitive ones.

**nLab:** [transitive action](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/transitive+action). It says: “Let \* : G × X → X be a transitive action and suppose that X is inhabited. Then \* is equivalent to the action of G by multiplication on a coset space G/H”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Counting inversions makes the sign of a permutation well defined

**Remember:** Inversions fix the sign; transpositions only flip it.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 20B30 (Symmetric groups). arXiv math.GR. Level 1: early undergraduate.

**Definition.** An inversion of a permutation σ of {1, …, n} is a pair i &lt; j with σ(i) &gt; σ(j). The sign of σ is +1 if the number of inversions is even and −1 if it is odd.

**Problem.** The sign is a homomorphism from the symmetric group Sₙ to {+1, −1}. Every way of writing σ as a product of transpositions uses a number of transpositions with the same parity. The even permutations form the alternating group Aₙ, the kernel of the sign.

**How the definition helps.** The number of inversions depends on σ alone, so the sign is well defined from the start. The work moves into one lemma: composing with a transposition of two adjacent positions changes the number of inversions by exactly one. Every transposition is a product of an odd number of adjacent ones, so every transposition changes the sign (our own). If the sign were defined by counting transpositions, a separate proof would be needed that the parity does not depend on the decomposition.

**Wikipedia:** [Parity of a permutation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parity_of_a_permutation). It says: “We can thus define the parity of σ to be that of its number of constituent transpositions in any decomposition. And this must agree with the parity of the number of inversions under any ordering, as seen above.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Defining Sylow subgroups as maximal p-subgroups makes every p-subgroup lie in one

**Remember:** Sylow subgroups are the largest p-subgroups, so every p-subgroup grows into one.

*True by definition.* MSC 20D20 (Sylow subgroups, Sylow properties, \\(\\pi\\)-groups, \\(\\pi\\)-structure). arXiv math.GR. Level 1: early undergraduate.

**Definition.** For a prime p, a p-group is a group in which the order of every element is a power of p. A p-subgroup is a subgroup that is a p-group. A Sylow p-subgroup of a group G is a p-subgroup that is not contained in any larger p-subgroup.

**Problem.** In a finite group, every p-subgroup lies in some Sylow p-subgroup. Sylow's theorems add that all Sylow p-subgroups are conjugate and have order pⁿ, the largest power of p that divides the order of G.

**How the definition helps.** With the maximal definition, the containment statement is almost automatic. In a finite group, enlarge a p-subgroup step by step until it cannot grow. The work moves into Sylow's other theorems: a subgroup of order pⁿ exists, and all maximal p-subgroups are conjugate to it. Modern proofs of conjugacy let a p-subgroup act on the cosets of a Sylow subgroup and count fixed points. The page uses the same definition in infinite groups, where there is no order to compare. There, conjugacy can fail (our own). In the infinite dihedral group, each reflection generates a maximal 2-subgroup of order 2, and these subgroups form two conjugacy classes (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Sylow theorems](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sylow_theorems). It says: “A Sylow p-subgroup of a group G is a maximal p-subgroup—that is, a p-subgroup of G not contained in any strictly larger p-subgroup.”

**Sources:**

- [L. Sylow, Théorèmes sur les groupes de substitutions, Mathematische Annalen 5 (1872) 584–594](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01442913)

### Normal subgroups are exactly the kernels, so quotient groups exist

**Remember:** Normal means the cosets can be multiplied.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 20E07 (Subgroup theorems; subgroup growth). arXiv math.GR. Level 1: early undergraduate.

**Definition.** A subgroup N of G is normal if gNg⁻¹ = N for all g ∈ G. Equivalently, the coset g₁g₂N of a product depends only on the cosets g₁N and g₂N.

**Problem.** Give the set G/N of cosets a group structure. Match normal subgroups with congruences, the equivalence relations that respect multiplication.

**How the definition helps.** Normality is exactly the condition that makes coset multiplication well defined. For an arbitrary subgroup, multiplying cosets is not well defined. For a normal subgroup, G/N is a group and N is the kernel of G → G/N; conversely, every kernel is normal. So normal subgroups are the same as kernels and as congruences on G. Congruences on a group commute with each other, because groups form a Mal'cev category. So the normal subgroups of a group form a modular lattice (a lattice where a ≤ c implies a ∨ (b ∧ c) = (a ∨ b) ∧ c). The lattice of all subgroups need not be modular; for the dihedral group of order 8 it contains a pentagon, the five-element lattice that is not modular.

**nLab:** [normal subgroup](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/normal+subgroup). It says: “Thus normal subgroups may also be defined as kernels f⁻¹(e) of group homomorphisms G → H (e ∈ H is the identity), and this is largely the point of normal subgroups: they are equivalent to congruence relations in the category of groups.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### The trivial group is not simple, so composition factors are unique

**Remember:** Simple means exactly two normal subgroups, not at most two.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 20E32 (Simple groups), 20D30, 20D05. arXiv math.GR. Level 1: early undergraduate.

**Definition.** A group G is simple if it has exactly two normal subgroups: the trivial subgroup and G itself. So the trivial group is not simple, because it has only one normal subgroup.

**Problem.** The Jordan–Hölder theorem says that any two composition series of a finite group have the same length and the same simple factors, up to order. A composition series is a chain of subgroups, each normal in the next, whose successive quotients (the factors) are simple. The problem also includes the classification of finite simple groups as the building blocks of all finite groups.

**How the definition helps.** The 'exactly two' rule forbids trivial factors, so the length of a composition series is well defined. If the trivial group counted as simple, one could pad a composition series by repeating a term, which adds a trivial factor. With the 'exactly two' definition, each composition factor is nontrivial, so the Jordan–Hölder theorem holds without exceptions, and the list of finite simple groups has no trivial entry. The nLab calls this example the namer of the principle 'too simple to be simple'. It compares it with 1 not being prime: for cyclic groups, simple groups match prime numbers and composition series match prime factorizations. The padding argument is our own reading; the nLab states the exclusion and the theorem separately. The proof of Jordan–Hölder is still an induction on the order of the group.

**nLab:** [simple group](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/simple+group), [too simple to be simple](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/too+simple+to+be+simple), [Jordan-Hölder theorem](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Jordan-H%C3%B6lder+theorem). It says: “Note that the trivial group does not itself count as simple, on the grounds that it has only \*one\* quotient group (or only one normal subgroup).”

**Sources:**

- [David Speyer, The Jordan–Hölder theorem, course notes for Math 594, University of Michigan (2013)](https://web.archive.org/web/20210926062254/http://www.math.lsa.umich.edu/~speyer/594_2013/JordanHolder.pdf)

### Characteristic subgroups pass normality down, which normal subgroups cannot

**Remember:** Fixed by every automorphism, so fixed by conjugation from above.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 20F28 (Automorphism groups of groups). arXiv math.GR. Level 1: early undergraduate.

**Definition.** A subgroup H of G is characteristic if every automorphism of G maps H onto itself. A normal subgroup needs only to be fixed by the inner automorphisms, the conjugations by elements of G.

**Problem.** If H is characteristic in K and K is normal in G, then H is normal in G. Also, a characteristic subgroup of a characteristic subgroup is characteristic.

**How the definition helps.** A characteristic subgroup is fixed by all automorphisms, so it survives conjugation from a larger group, and the proof is one line (our own). Conjugation by an element of G restricts to an automorphism of the normal subgroup K (our own). That automorphism need not be inner in K, but it still fixes H (our own). Plain normality fails in the dihedral group of order 8 (our own). There a reflection generates a subgroup that is normal in a Klein four-subgroup, which is normal in the whole group (our own). But the subgroup of the reflection is not normal in the whole group (our own). This is why induction proofs often use centers, commutator subgroups and Fitting subgroups, which are characteristic (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Characteristic subgroup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Characteristic_subgroup). It says: “Moreover, while normality is not transitive, it is true that every characteristic subgroup of a normal subgroup is normal.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Setting a⁰ equal to the identity gives index laws for all integers

**Remember:** The empty product is the identity, so a⁰ = e.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 20M10 (General structure theory for semigroups), 20M17. arXiv math.RA. Level 1: early undergraduate.

**Definition.** In a monoid, a⁰ is defined as the identity element e, and aⁿ⁺¹ = aⁿ ∘ a. For an invertible a, a⁻ⁿ is defined as (a⁻¹)ⁿ.

**Problem.** For an invertible element a of a monoid and all integers m and n, a to the power nm equals (aᵐ)ⁿ and (aⁿ)ᵐ.

**How the definition helps.** The value a⁰ = e is the empty product. For an invertible a, it is the only value that keeps aᵐ⁺ⁿ = aᵐ ∘ aⁿ true when m or n is 0. With it, the recursive definition starts at 0 and the laws need no separate cases for zero. In a semigroup without identity, a⁰ has no meaning, and the laws hold only for positive exponents; this remark is our own. The proof for negative exponents still needs the inverse of a.

**Paper or page:** [Index Laws for Monoids/Product of Indices](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Index_Laws_for_Monoids/Product_of_Indices). It says: “Then: ∀ m, n ∈ ℤ: aⁿᵐ = (aᵐ)ⁿ = (aⁿ)ᵐ”

**Sources:**

- [ProofWiki, Index Laws for Monoids/Product of Indices](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Index_Laws_for_Monoids/Product_of_Indices)

### Defining quotients by their maps out makes the third isomorphism theorem automatic

**Remember:** Killing N and then H/N kills exactly the elements of H.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 20A05 (Axiomatics and elementary properties of groups). arXiv math.GR. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** Define the quotient G/N by a homomorphism from G that sends N to the identity. Every other homomorphism from G that sends N to the identity must factor through it in exactly one way. The usual definition builds G/N from the cosets gN, the translates of N.

**Problem.** Let N and H be normal subgroups of G, with N inside H. Then H/N is normal in G/N, and (G/N)/(H/N) is isomorphic to G/H.

**How the definition helps.** With this definition, both sides are defined by the same maps out, so they are isomorphic. A homomorphism from (G/N)/(H/N) is a homomorphism from G/N that sends H/N to the identity. That is the same as a homomorphism from G that sends N and H to the identity. G/H has exactly these maps out, so a uniqueness argument (the Yoneda lemma) gives the isomorphism. This argument is our own; ProofWiki proves the theorem with cosets. The work moves to showing that the coset construction has this mapping property, which needs coset multiplication to be well defined.

**Paper or page:** [Third Isomorphism Theorem/Groups](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Third_Isomorphism_Theorem/Groups). It says: “(G / N) / (H / N) ≅ G / H”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Order as a kernel generator makes image orders divide original orders

**Remember:** A larger subgroup of ℤ has a generator that divides the smaller subgroup’s generator.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 20A05 (Axiomatics and elementary properties of groups). arXiv math.GR. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** For a group element a, take the homomorphism n ↦ aⁿ from ℤ and let K be its kernel. If K is not just {0}, define the order of a as its positive generator. If K = {0}, the order is infinite. The usual definition calls the order the least positive n with aⁿ = e, where e is the identity.

**Problem.** If f is a group homomorphism and a has finite order, then the order of f(a) divides the order of a.

**How the definition helps.** The generator definition makes the divisibility claim a containment of subgroups of ℤ. Whenever aⁿ = e, we have f(a)ⁿ = e. So if m and d are the orders of a and f(a), then mℤ is contained in dℤ. This containment says d divides m. Our own account moves the work from proving a divisibility rule for powers to proving that subgroups of ℤ are cyclic. Division with remainder shows that the least positive member generates such a subgroup.

**Wikipedia:** [Order (group theory)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Order_%28group_theory%29). It says: “Group homomorphisms tend to reduce the orders of elements: if f: G → H is a homomorphism, and a is an element of G of finite order, then ord(f(a)) divides ord(a).”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Powers defined by a group homomorphism obey the exponent law

**Remember:** A homomorphism turns sums into products, so bᵐ⁺ⁿ = bᵐbⁿ is built in.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 20A05 (Axiomatics and elementary properties of groups), 97H20. arXiv math.GR, math.HO. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** Fix an element b of a group G. Let h be the unique homomorphism from the integers under addition to G with h(1) = b. A homomorphism here sends sums of integers to products in G. Define bⁿ = h(n).

**Problem.** For all integers m and n, bᵐ⁺ⁿ = bᵐbⁿ.

**How the definition helps.** The homomorphism definition makes the exponent law the rule that h sends sums to products. The usual definition instead uses repeated multiplication and defines negative powers using inverses. With that definition, the law needs a check that positive and negative powers combine correctly. The work moves into proving that the integers under addition have exactly one such homomorphism for each b. Proving existence from repeated products and inverses does the same check once for all groups (our own framing).

**Wikipedia:** [Exponentiation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exponentiation). It says: “This definition of exponentiation with negative exponents is the only one that allows extending the identity bᵐ⁺ⁿ = bᵐ · bⁿ to negative exponents (consider the case m = −n).”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### The kernel definition makes preimages of normal subgroups normal

**Remember:** The preimage of a kernel is the kernel of the composite.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 20A05 (Axiomatics and elementary properties of groups). arXiv math.GR. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** A subgroup N of G is normal if it is the kernel of a group homomorphism out of G. The kernel is the set of elements sent to the identity. The usual definition instead requires gNg⁻¹ = N for every g in G.

**Problem.** Let φ from G₁ to G₂ be any group homomorphism and H a normal subgroup of G₂. The preimage of H is normal in G₁.

**How the definition helps.** The kernel definition makes the preimage the kernel of one composite homomorphism. If H is the kernel of q, then its preimage under φ is the kernel of q ∘ φ. This argument is our own and does not require φ to be onto, as in the cited statement. The usual proof instead conjugates in G₁ and uses normality of H after applying φ. The work behind the kernel definition is constructing G/N and checking that its quotient map has kernel N.

**Paper or page:** [Preimage of Normal Subgroup under Epimorphism is Normal Subgroup](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Preimage_of_Normal_Subgroup_under_Epimorphism_is_Normal_Subgroup). It says: “φ⁻¹\[H\] is a normal subgroup of (G₁, ∘)”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Primitive actions are exactly the actions on cosets of maximal subgroups

**Remember:** No block to keep means no subgroup in between.

*True by definition.* MSC 20B15 (Primitive groups), 20E28. arXiv math.GR. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** A transitive action of G on a set X is primitive if it preserves no partition of X except the two trivial ones. These are the partition into one block and the partition into single points. Galois introduced the term in his last letter.

**Problem.** A transitive action of G on the cosets G/H is primitive if and only if H is a maximal subgroup of G. So listing the primitive actions of G is the same as listing its maximal subgroups up to conjugacy.

**How the definition helps.** The blocks that contain the base point correspond to the subgroups between H and G, so the equivalence is almost a restatement (our own). A subgroup K with H &lt; K &lt; G gives the block of cosets kH for k in K (our own). Every block that contains the base point arises this way (our own). The transitivity condition in the definition excludes one bad case. The trivial group acting on a two-element set preserves only trivial partitions but is not transitive. The hard work moves to the structure of primitive groups and to the lists of maximal subgroups of the simple groups (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Primitive permutation group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Primitive_permutation_group). It says: “A group action is primitive if it is isomorphic to G/H for a maximal subgroup H of G, and imprimitive otherwise”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### The sign kernel makes the alternating group normal with index two

**Remember:** The two signs give the two cosets of the kernel.

*True by definition.* MSC 20B30 (Symmetric groups), 20B35. arXiv math.GR. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** For n ≥ 2 let Sₙ be the group of permutations of n letters. Take the sign of a permutation to be the determinant of the matrix that permutes the standard basis in the same way. The alternating group Aₙ is the kernel of this sign map. The alternative defines Aₙ as the permutations expressible as a product of an even number of swaps.

**Problem.** For n ≥ 2, the alternating group Aₙ is normal in Sₙ and has index two. That means Sₙ has two cosets of Aₙ, so Aₙ has n!/2 elements.

**How the definition helps.** The kernel definition makes normality automatic and makes the index the number of signs. Determinants multiply, so sign is a homomorphism. The identity has sign 1 and a swap has sign −1, so both occur. This is our own account of the kernel argument. Starting with swaps, one must show that no permutation has both an even and an odd expression. The determinant comparison does that work because a product of k swaps has sign (−1)ᵏ.

**Wikipedia:** [Parity of a permutation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parity_of_a_permutation), [Alternating group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alternating_group). It says: “It is the kernel of the signature group homomorphism sgn : Sₙ → {1, −1} explained under symmetric group.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Defining induction as a tensor product makes Frobenius reciprocity automatic

**Remember:** Induction is a tensor product, so Frobenius reciprocity is the tensor–hom rule.

*True by definition.* MSC 20C05 (Group rings of finite groups and their modules (group-theoretic aspects)), 16D20. arXiv math.RT, math.GR. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** Let H be a subgroup of a group G, and let V be a representation of H. The induced representation Ind V is the tensor product 𝕂\[G\] ⊗ V, taken over the group algebra 𝕂\[H\]. Induction is left adjoint to restriction (it is the best approximation from the left), where restriction takes a representation of G to a representation of H.

**Problem.** Prove Frobenius reciprocity. In words, maps of G-representations from Ind V to W match maps of H-representations from V to the restriction Res W. The same holds for characters: the inner product over G of Ind χ and ψ equals the inner product over H of χ and Res ψ.

**How the definition helps.** With this definition, Frobenius reciprocity is a case of the tensor–hom adjunction for modules, so it holds almost by definition. The tensor–hom adjunction says that maps out of a tensor product M ⊗ V match maps from V into a module of maps out of M. For finite groups over ℂ, the identity for characters follows when you take the dimensions of the two spaces of maps. Two things stay hard. For a subgroup of finite index, you must prove that the left and right induced representations agree (an ambidextrous adjunction, where one functor is both a left and a right adjoint). You must also prove Mackey's formula, which describes the restriction of an induced representation.

**nLab:** [induced representation](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/induced+representation), [Frobenius reciprocity](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Frobenius+reciprocity). It says: “is the statement that the induction functor for representations of groups (or in some other algebraic categories) is left adjoint to the restriction functor.”

**Sources:**

- [George Mackey, Induced representations of locally compact groups I, Annals of Math. 55 (1952) 101–139](https://doi.org/10.2307/1969423)

### Representations as group algebra modules turn Maschke into Wedderburn structure

**Remember:** The complex group algebra is one matrix algebra per irreducible representation.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 20C05 (Group rings of finite groups and their modules (group-theoretic aspects)), 16S34. arXiv math.RT, math.RA. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** The group algebra K\[G\] has the elements of the finite group G as a basis, with multiplication from the group. A representation of G on V is the same as a K\[G\]-module structure on V. By Maschke's theorem, K\[G\] is semisimple when the characteristic of K does not divide the order of G. Semisimple means that every module is a direct sum of simple modules.

**Problem.** Over the complex numbers, ℂ\[G\] is a product of matrix algebras, one for each irreducible representation, of size its dimension. So the squares of the dimensions of the irreducible representations add up to the order of G. The number of irreducible representations equals the number of conjugacy classes.

**How the definition helps.** Viewing representations as modules over one algebra lets ring theory, here the Wedderburn–Artin theorem, do the counting.
