**Problem.** In constructive mathematics (mathematics without the law of excluded middle), a bounded inhabited set of real numbers need not have a supremum. One wants a kind of number in which every inhabited set has a supremum.

**How the definition helps.** For lower reals, the supremum of an inhabited set is simply the union of their sets of rationals, and this union is again a lower real. It is a bounded lower real exactly when the set has a bounded upper bound; otherwise it is +∞. A side benefit concerns the sheaf topos on a space X. There, the internal extended lower reals correspond exactly to the lower semicontinuous functions from X to ℝ ∪ {+∞} (Mulvey, Reichman). The price is that, constructively, the order on lower reals is not total and the comparison law for &lt; fails. The comparison law says that if a &lt; b, then a &lt; c or c &lt; b for every c. So lower reals are less well behaved than the usual located reals, where for any rationals q &lt; r, q is below the number or r is above it.

**nLab:** [one-sided real number](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/one-sided+real+number). It says: “Explicitly, the supremum of any inhabited set of lower reals is a lower real and the infimum of any inhabited set of upper reals is an upper real.”

**Sources:**

- [J. Z. Reichman, Semicontinuous real numbers in a topos, Journal of Pure and Applied Algebra 28 (1983) 81–91](https://doi.org/10.1016/0022-4049(83)90075-0)

### The genuine integral of cogerm forms ignores second-order terms

**Remember:** Sum the form on small steps of the curve, as in a Riemann sum.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 26A39 (Denjoy and Perron integrals, other special integrals), 58A10. arXiv math.CA, math.DG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A cogerm differential 1-form on X gives a number for each germ of a curve in X (the behaviour of the curve near one point). Examples are dx, \|dx\|, dx² and d²x. The genuine integral of a form ω along a curve c is the limit of Riemann sums Σ⟨ω \| Δtᵢ · c at tᵢ\*⟩ over fine tagged partitions: each term applies ω to the germ of c at the tag tᵢ\*, scaled by the step Δtᵢ. The limit is taken in the Henstock style, with gauges (functions that set how fine the partition must be near each point).

**Problem.** Forms such as dx² and d²x are 'second-order', and they should integrate to zero. Then integrands from better approximations give the same integral as f(x) dx. An example is the trapezoid rule integrand f(x) dx + ½ f′(x) dx².

**How the definition helps.** The genuine integral uses Riemann sums of ω itself, so terms that are small on each step add up to something small. Call ω o(dx) if ⟨ω \| h·c⟩/h → 0 as h → 0, that is, if ω on a step of size h is much smaller than h. Then, on a fine enough partition, each term of the sum is smaller than ε·Δtᵢ. So the integral of an o(dx) form is 0, by a short argument from the definition. The naive integral ∫ ⟨ω \| cₜ⟩ dt does not have this property: it gives d²x the integral (x∘c)′(b) − (x∘c)′(a), which is in general not zero. The cost is that the genuine integral satisfies the fundamental theorem of calculus only for differentials of functions. Also, its existence needs extra conditions on the form.

**nLab:** [cogerm differential form](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/cogerm+differential+form). It says: “The answer 0 given by the genuine integral is preferable if we regard dx as a "first-order change in x", so that dx² or d²x are "second-order" quantities and hence ought to be negligible.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### A weak Jacobian for maps with jumps tracks vortices of circle-valued maps

**Remember:** Use the weak Jacobian to keep track of what jumps carry.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 26B30 (Absolutely continuous real functions of several variables, functions of bounded variation), 49Q15, 49J45. arXiv math.AP. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A map u of bounded variation has a derivative that is a finite measure, which can charge jump curves. The paper defines the 2 × 2 minors of its gradient as limits of smooth minors along smooth maps that converge strictly to u. On a jump, the limit averages over the segment between the two one-sided values of u. For smooth maps the weak Jacobian is the usual Jacobian determinant.

**Problem.** Take maps u into the unit circle with energy ∫\|∇u\|² plus 1/ε times the jump length, bounded by C\|log ε\|. Then a subsequence of weak Jacobians tends in the flat norm to π times a finite sum of integer-weighted Dirac masses. The energy divided by \|log ε\| Γ-converges to π times the total mass of that sum.

**How the definition helps.** The weak Jacobian is defined for maps with jumps, so the compactness theorem can track defects in the same terms as for Sobolev maps. Our own observation is that the pointwise Jacobian of an S¹-valued map is zero almost everywhere, so it cannot see the vortices. The work is to prove compactness, identify the point masses and obtain the limiting energy.

**Paper or page:** [A new approach to topological singularities via a weak notion of Jacobian for functions of bounded variation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.14746v1). It says: “such a notion extends the standard definition of Jacobian determinant to non-Sobolev maps.”

**Sources:**

- [Lucia De Luca, Riccardo Scala, Nicolas Van Goethem, A new approach to topological singularities via a weak notion of Jacobian for functions of bounded variation, arXiv:2205.14746 (2022)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.14746v1)

### Convergence at every nonstandard point makes Cauchy's proof correct

**Remember:** Convergence everywhere, nonstandard points included, is uniform convergence.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 26E35 (Nonstandard analysis), 40A30, 26A15. arXiv math.CA, math.HO. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Read 'the sequence fₙ(x) converges for every x' so that x also ranges over hyperreal points. The hyperreals are the numbers of nonstandard analysis, and they include points infinitely close to a real number. Then fₙ(x + h) must be infinitely close to the limit f∞(x + h) for every infinite n, even when h is infinitesimal.

**Problem.** Cauchy's 1821 sum theorem, with his own proof: a convergent sum of continuous functions is continuous.

**How the definition helps.** If 'everywhere' includes nonstandard points, then Cauchy's hypothesis is uniform convergence, and his proof works. In nonstandard analysis, a sequence converges uniformly exactly when it converges at every hyperreal point. So under this reading, his proof with infinitesimals becomes correct. The counterexamples, such as the Fourier series near x = 1/n, fail to converge at some nonstandard point, which fits how Cauchy rejected them. This hyperreal reading is Robinson's. Lakatos held it to be ahistorical and read Cauchy as asking for convergence at 'variable' points, which again amounts to uniform convergence. It is a reading of history, not a new theorem: the mathematical content is the equivalence of the nonstandard and the ε–N forms of uniform convergence.

**nLab:** [Cauchy sum theorem](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Cauchy+sum+theorem). It says: “By this analysis, Cauchy's notion of convergence everywhere is our modern notion of uniform convergence, not pointwise convergence, and his theorem is true”

**Sources:**

- [Abraham Robinson, Non-standard Analysis, North-Holland (1966); revised edition Princeton University Press (1996)](https://doi.org/10.1515/9781400884223)
- [Imre Lakatos, Mathematics, Science and Epistemology (Philosophical Papers vol. 2), Cambridge University Press (1978), chapter 3](https://doi.org/10.1017/CBO9780511624926)

### The HoTT book real numbers are complete because limits are constructors

**Remember:** Every Cauchy approximation has a limit because "limit" is a constructor.

*True by definition.* MSC 26E40 (Constructive real analysis), 03B38. arXiv math.LO, math.CA. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** The HoTT book real numbers are a higher inductive-inductive type. Such a type is generated by constructors for its points and for equalities between them, defined together with a relation. Here the generators are the rationals, a limit lim for every Cauchy approximation, and a rule that identifies two points that are ε-close for every ε &gt; 0. Equivalently, they are the initial sequentially complete Archimedean ordered field.

**Problem.** The real numbers should be sequentially Cauchy complete, even without countable choice. Then analytic functions such as exp, sin and cos are well defined.

**How the definition helps.** In the higher inductive-inductive type, limits are constructors, so completeness holds by definition and you need no choice. Compare the naive quotient of regular Cauchy sequences. It is complete only if you can lift every sequence of real numbers to a sequence of Cauchy sequences that represent them, and this needs countable choice. That is why Bishop's constructive analysis stays with setoids (sets with an explicit equivalence relation) and does not pass to the quotient. The remaining work is to develop the order and the arithmetic on this type, and the HoTT book does this in Section 11.3.

**nLab:** [HoTT book real number](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/HoTT+book+real+number). It says: “The analytic functions, such as the exponential function, the sine function, and the cosine function are well defined in the HoTT book real numbers, since all regular Cauchy sequences converge in the HoTT book real numbers.”

**Sources:**

- [The Univalent Foundations Program, Homotopy Type Theory: Univalent Foundations of Mathematics, Institute for Advanced Study (2013)](https://homotopytypetheory.org/book/)
- [Auke Booij, Analysis in Univalent Type Theory, PhD thesis, University of Birmingham (2020)](http://etheses.bham.ac.uk/id/eprint/10411)

### Time scales prove the discrete and continuous Weyl–Titchmarsh theories at once

**Remember:** One derivative that is a difference on ℤ covers both worlds.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 26E70 (Real analysis on time scales or measure chains), 34N05, 34B24. arXiv math.CA, math.SP. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A time scale is any nonempty closed subset of the real line. The paper uses the nabla derivative, which looks backward. If t has a nearest point ρ(t) &lt; t on its left, the derivative is (f(t) − f(ρ(t)))/(t − ρ(t)). Otherwise it is the usual limit of difference quotients, so on ℝ it is the usual derivative and on ℤ a backward difference.

**Problem.** Weyl–Titchmarsh theory sorts singular linear Hamiltonian systems on a half-line into limit point and limit circle cases, using nested matrix discs. The paper proves this once for systems on a class of time scales. This covers differential and difference equations together.

**How the definition helps.** A single derivative that is a limit on ℝ and a difference on ℤ lets one proof cover both settings. The quote says that the results unify the continuous and the discrete cases. Our own remark is that the two theories had parallel but separate proofs before. Our own remark is that the price is extra terms in product rules, from the gap to the neighbouring point. The Floquet paper uses the same idea to treat discrete, continuous and hybrid periodic systems with one algorithm.

**Paper or page:** [Unifying discrete and continuous Weyl-Titchmarsh theory via a class of linear Hamiltonian systems on Sturmian time scales](https://arxiv.org/abs/1001.4040v1), [Floquet multipliers and the stability of periodic linear differential equations: a unified algorithm and its computer realization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.04447v8). It says: “These results unify and extend certain classic and recent results on the subject in the continuous and discrete cases, respectively, to Sturmian time scales.”

**Sources:**

- [Douglas R. Anderson, Unifying discrete and continuous Weyl-Titchmarsh theory via a class of linear Hamiltonian systems on Sturmian time scales, arXiv:1001.4040 (2010)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1001.4040v1)
- [Mengda Wu, Yonghui Xia, Ziyi Xu, Floquet multipliers and the stability of periodic linear differential equations: a unified algorithm and its computer realization, arXiv:2201.04447 (2022)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.04447v8)
- [Hilger, Analysis on Measure Chains — A Unified Approach to Continuous and Discrete Calculus, Results in Mathematics 18 (1990), 18–56](https://doi.org/10.1007/bf03323153)

## 28 Measure and integration

### Measure zero describes exactly the Riemann integrable functions

**Remember:** Countably many tiny intervals can hide a set of measure zero.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 28A12 (Contents, measures, outer measures, capacities), 26A42. arXiv math.CA. Level 1: early undergraduate.

**Definition.** A set of real numbers has measure zero if, for every ε &gt; 0, countably many intervals with total length less than ε cover it.

**Problem.** Which bounded functions on \[a,b\] are Riemann integrable?

**How the definition helps.** With this definition, the answer fits in one short sentence. The Lebesgue–Vitali theorem says: exactly the functions that are continuous almost everywhere, that is, whose points of discontinuity form a set of measure zero. Vitali and Lebesgue proved it independently in 1907. The theorem uses only the notion of measure zero, not Lebesgue's full measure or integral. It shows at once that monotone functions are integrable, because they have only countably many discontinuities. It also shows that the indicator function of the rationals is not integrable. Countable covers matter: the rationals in \[0,1\] have measure zero, but finitely many intervals of small total length cannot cover them (our own remark).

**Wikipedia:** [Riemann integral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemann_integral). It says: “A bounded function on a compact interval \[a, b\] is Riemann integrable if and only if it is continuous almost everywhere (the set of its points of discontinuity has measure zero, in the sense of Lebesgue measure).”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Dynkin systems make two measures that agree on intervals agree everywhere

**Remember:** Agreement sets form a Dynkin system, so check measures on a π-system.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 28A05 (Classes of sets (Borel fields, \\(\\sigma\\)-rings, etc.), measurable sets, Suslin sets, analytic sets), 28A12. arXiv math.CA, math.PR. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** A Dynkin system (or λ-system) on a set Ω is a family of subsets that contains Ω. It is closed under differences B minus A when A ⊆ B, and under increasing countable unions. A π-system is a family closed under finite intersections. The π-λ theorem says that a Dynkin system containing a π-system contains the σ-algebra it generates.

**Problem.** Two probability measures that agree on a π-system agree on the σ-algebra it generates. So a law on the real line is fixed by its distribution function. Lebesgue measure is the only Borel measure that gives each interval its length.

**How the definition helps.** The family of sets on which two probability measures agree is always a Dynkin system, so the π-λ theorem applies to it at once. This family need not be a σ-algebra, because agreement on A and B does not give agreement on A ∪ B. A direct proof that it contains all Borel sets therefore fails, and the Dynkin system is the right weaker structure. The page also uses the same method to check independence on generating π-systems only. What stays hard is the π-λ theorem itself, a short but careful set-theoretic argument. Standard measure texts prove the same results with monotone classes instead.

**Wikipedia:** [Dynkin system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dynkin_system), [Pi-system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pi-system). It says: “One application of Sierpiński-Dynkin's π-λ theorem is the uniqueness of a measure that evaluates the length of an interval (known as the Lebesgue measure)”

**Sources:**

- [W. Sierpiński, Un théorème général sur les familles d'ensembles, Fundamenta Mathematicae 12 (1928) 206–210](https://doi.org/10.4064/fm-12-1-206-210)

### Intersecting σ-algebras lets generators test measurability

**Remember:** The sets with measurable preimages form a σ-algebra containing the generators.

*True by definition.* MSC 28A05 (Classes of sets (Borel fields, \\(\\sigma\\)-rings, etc.), measurable sets, Suslin sets, analytic sets), 28A20. arXiv math.CA, math.PR. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** A σ-algebra on X contains X and is closed under complements and countable unions. The σ-algebra generated by a family of subsets is the intersection of all σ-algebras containing that family. A map is measurable if the preimage of each set in the target σ-algebra belongs to the source σ-algebra.

**Problem.** Let the σ-algebra on Y be generated by a family 𝒢. A map from a space with a σ-algebra to Y is measurable exactly when each set in 𝒢 has a measurable preimage.

**How the definition helps.** The intersection definition lets us test just the generators instead of describing all the generated sets. The sets whose preimages are measurable form a σ-algebra because preimages preserve complements and countable unions. If it contains the generators, it contains the intersection in the definition. This is our own proof of the criterion. A construction that adds sets in successive stages would instead check that each operation preserves the preimage condition. The work here is just checking that intersections of σ-algebras are σ-algebras.

**Paper or page:** [Mapping Measurable iff Measurable on Generator](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Mapping_Measurable_iff_Measurable_on_Generator). It says: “That is, the preimage of every generator under f is a measurable set.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Keeping signed measures finite makes them a vector space

**Remember:** No infinite values means no ∞ − ∞, so signed measures add.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 28A10 (Real- or complex-valued set functions), 46E27. arXiv math.CA, math.FA. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** A signed measure is a countably additive set function on a σ-algebra that may take negative values. A finite signed measure takes only real values. An extended signed measure may take the value +∞ or the value −∞, but not both.

**Problem.** Finite signed measures form a real vector space, and with the total variation norm a Banach space. So the Riesz representation theorem can identify a dual space with a space of measures. The dual of the continuous functions vanishing at infinity is the space of finite regular signed (or complex) measures.

**How the definition helps.** Finite values make the sum of two signed measures defined on every set, so the space is closed under addition. The definition excludes adding a measure with value +∞ on a set to one with value −∞ on the same set. There the sum would be ∞ − ∞, which is undefined. Even the extended definition forbids both infinite values in one measure for this reason. The Hahn and Jordan decompositions write each signed measure as a difference of two positive measures, which gives the total variation norm. What stays hard is the representation theorem, which needs regularity and the positive case first.

**Wikipedia:** [Signed measure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Signed_measure). It says: “Finite signed measures form a real vector space, while extended signed measures do not because they are not closed under addition.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Carathéodory's measurability condition builds additivity into the definition

**Remember:** A measurable set cuts every other set into two pieces whose sizes add up.

*True by definition.* MSC 28A12 (Contents, measures, outer measures, capacities), 28A05. arXiv math.CA. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** Let μ\* be an outer measure on a set X. An outer measure gives a size to every subset, gives the empty set size 0, and is monotone and countably subadditive (the size of a countable union is at most the sum of the sizes). A set E is measurable when μ\*(A) = μ\*(A ∩ E) + μ\*(A ∖ E) for every subset A of X. In words, E cuts every set A into two pieces whose sizes add up to the size of A.

**Problem.** The measurable sets form a σ-algebra (a family of sets closed under complements and countable unions). On these sets μ\* is countably additive, so it is a measure.

**How the definition helps.** The definition keeps exactly the sets on which additivity holds, so additivity comes almost for free. Some sets must be left out. No length on all subsets of ℝ can give intervals their length and also be translation invariant and countably additive. Carathéodory's definition keeps exactly the sets that split every set additively. So finite additivity is almost the definition, and short arguments give countable additivity and closure under countable unions. What stays hard is to show that the sets you care about, such as intervals and Borel sets, pass the test. This is the work in Carathéodory's extension theorem.

**Wikipedia:** [Outer measure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outer_measure), [Carathéodory's extension theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carath%C3%A9odory%27s_extension_theorem). It says: “The purpose of constructing an outer measure on all subsets of X is to pick out a class of subsets (to be called measurable) in such a way as to satisfy the countable additivity property.”

**Sources:**

- [C. Carathéodory, Vorlesungen über reelle Funktionen, Teubner (1918; 2nd ed. 1927)](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-663-15768-7)

### Completing a product measure makes every subset of a null set measurable

**Remember:** A subset of nothing should also count as nothing.

*Rules out counterexamples. Confidence: medium.* MSC 28A12 (Contents, measures, outer measures, capacities), 28A35. arXiv math.CA. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** A measure space is complete if every subset of a set of measure zero is measurable. The completion of a measure space adds all subsets of null sets and extends the measure, giving them measure zero.

**Problem.** Two-dimensional Lebesgue measure is the completion of the product of one-dimensional Lebesgue measure with itself. In a complete space, any function equal almost everywhere to a measurable function is itself measurable.

**How the definition helps.** Completeness builds the rule that subsets of null sets are null into the measure space. So statements up to null sets become true without extra checks. The page gives the counterexample. In the plain product, {0} × A, with A a Vitali set, lies inside the null set {0} × ℝ but is not measurable. Borel measure on the line is also not complete, since the Cantor set is null and has more subsets than there are Borel sets. The cost is that the completed product is not a product σ-algebra, so Fubini's theorem gives measurable sections only for almost every point (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Complete measure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complete_measure). It says: “So this "two-dimensional Lebesgue measure" as just defined is not complete, and some kind of completion procedure is required.”

**Sources:**

- [H. Lebesgue, Intégrale, Longueur, Aire, Annali di Matematica Pura ed Applicata 7 (1902)](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02420592)

### Countable covers give the rationals measure zero, unlike Jordan content

**Remember:** Countably many points cost nothing when covers may be countable.

*True by definition.* MSC 28A12 (Contents, measures, outer measures, capacities). arXiv math.CA. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** Jordan content measures a bounded set by finite unions of boxes from inside and outside, and a set is Jordan measurable if the two agree. Lebesgue outer measure uses countable covers by intervals instead. Lebesgue measure agrees with Jordan content wherever the latter is defined.

**Problem.** Countable sets have Lebesgue measure zero, and the Lebesgue measurable sets form a σ-algebra on which measure is countably additive. Jordan measurable sets are closed only under finite unions.

**How the definition helps.** Countable covers let the n-th point get an interval of length ε/2ⁿ, so a countable set has outer measure at most ε for every ε (our own). Jordan content fails here. Each point has content zero, but the rationals in \[0, 1\] are not Jordan measurable, as their boundary is all of \[0, 1\]. So a countable union of Jordan measurable sets need not be Jordan measurable. The page says that for this reason Jordan content is not a true measure. What stays hard is to build Lebesgue measure on a σ-algebra, for example with Carathéodory's condition.

**Wikipedia:** [Peano–Jordan measure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peano%E2%80%93Jordan_measure). It says: “Intuitively however, the set of rational numbers is a "small" set, as it is countable, and it should have "size" zero. That is indeed true, but only if one replaces the Jordan measure with the Lebesgue measure.”

**Sources:**

- [H. Lebesgue, Intégrale, Longueur, Aire, Annali di Matematica Pura ed Applicata 7 (1902)](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02420592)

### Measure 0 for the empty set excludes only constant infinite functions

**Remember:** If the empty set is not 0, everything is infinite.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 28A12 (Contents, measures, outer measures, capacities), 28A10. arXiv math.CA. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** A countably additive function on a σ-algebra gives the union of countably many disjoint sets the sum of their values. A measure is a countably additive function with values in \[0, +∞\] that gives the empty set the value 0.

**Problem.** A countably additive function f with extended real values has f(∅) = 0, or f is constant +∞, or f is constant −∞.

**How the definition helps.** The condition μ(∅) = 0 in the definition of a measure removes a single bad case. Writing ∅ as a countable union of copies of ∅ shows that f(∅) is 0 or infinite. Adding ∅ to any set A then shows that an infinite f(∅) makes f(A) infinite. So for nonnegative functions, the only excluded example is the function that is +∞ everywhere; this point is our own. Some books instead ask that one set has finite measure. In our own reading, this dichotomy shows that both choices give the same class.

**Paper or page:** [Countably Additive Function Dichotomy by Empty Set](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Countably_Additive_Function_Dichotomy_by_Empty_Set), [Measure of Empty Set is Zero](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Measure_of_Empty_Set_is_Zero). It says: “Then the exactly one of the following is true: (1): f(∅) = 0 (2): f(∅) = +∞. Moreover, f(A) = +∞ for all A ∈ 𝒜.”

**Sources:**

- [ProofWiki, Countably Additive Function Dichotomy by Empty Set](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Countably_Additive_Function_Dichotomy_by_Empty_Set)
- [ProofWiki, Measure of Empty Set is Zero](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Measure_of_Empty_Set_is_Zero)

### Measuring only some sets keeps length countably additive

**Remember:** Measure theory keeps countable additivity by refusing to measure every set.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 28A12 (Contents, measures, outer measures, capacities), 28A05. arXiv math.CA. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** A measure is defined only on a σ-algebra of measurable sets, not on every subset. (A σ-algebra is a family of sets that is closed under complements and countable unions.) Lebesgue measure λ is countably additive and translation invariant on its measurable sets. Countably additive means that the measure of a countable disjoint union is the sum of the measures.

**Problem.** We want a notion of length on sets of real numbers. It must give b − a for an interval from a to b, stay the same under translation, and be countably additive.

**How the definition helps.** Vitali's set can have no length, so length can only be defined on some sets. Vitali (1905) chose one point in \[0,1\] from each class of reals that differ by a rational number; call this set V. Its translates by the rationals in \[−1,1\] are disjoint, cover \[0,1\] and lie inside \[−1,2\]. If V had a length λ(V), countable additivity would make a sum of infinitely many copies of λ(V) lie between 1 and 3, which is impossible. Restricting the measure to measurable sets leaves V out and keeps countable additivity. Whether the restriction is needed depends on the axiom of choice. Solovay built a model without choice in which every set of reals is Lebesgue measurable, assuming an inaccessible cardinal (a very large infinite cardinal whose existence ZFC cannot prove).

**Wikipedia:** [Vitali set](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vitali_set), [Outer measure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outer_measure). It says: “So V cannot have been measurable after all, i.e., the Lebesgue measure λ must not define any value for λ(V).”

**Sources:**

- [R. M. Solovay, A model of set-theory in which every set of reals is Lebesgue measurable, Ann. of Math. 92 (1970), 1–56, doi:10.2307/1970696](https://doi.org/10.2307/1970696)

### Metric outer measures make every Borel set measurable

**Remember:** Additive on sets far apart gives every Borel set measurable.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 28A12 (Contents, measures, outer measures, capacities), 28A78. arXiv math.CA. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** Two sets in a metric space are positively separated if they are at positive distance from each other. An outer measure μ is a metric outer measure if μ(A ∪ B) = μ(A) + μ(B) for all such pairs. Hausdorff measures are built from covers by small sets and are metric outer measures.

**Problem.** For a metric outer measure, every closed set, and hence every Borel set, satisfies Carathéodory's measurability condition. So each Hausdorff measure restricts to a true measure on the Borel sets.

**How the definition helps.** Additivity for separated sets is the geometric form of Carathéodory's condition, so closed sets pass the condition with a short argument. With covers of one fixed size, the outer measure can fail this additivity (our own). Taking covers by sets of diameter at most δ, and then letting δ go to 0, makes the result a metric outer measure. Then the Borel σ-algebra comes for free from Carathéodory's theorem. What stays hard is computing Hausdorff measures and dimensions of particular sets.

**Wikipedia:** [Metric outer measure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metric_outer_measure). It says: “Consequently, all the Borel subsets of X — those obtainable as countable unions, intersections and set-theoretic differences of open/closed sets — are μ-measurable.”

**Sources:**

- [F. Hausdorff, Dimension und äußeres Maß, Mathematische Annalen 79 (1918)](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01457179)

### The cover definition of Lebesgue measure makes translation invariance immediate

**Remember:** Slide the cover, and its total length stays the same.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 28A12 (Contents, measures, outer measures, capacities). arXiv math.CA. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** Define the Lebesgue outer measure of a set of reals as the infimum of the total lengths of its countable covers by intervals. Another construction extends the length of half-open intervals to a measure on Borel sets by an abstract extension theorem.

**Problem.** Translating a Borel subset of the real line does not change its Lebesgue measure.

**How the definition helps.** Translating a cover by intervals gives a cover of the translated set with the same total length, so the infimum does not change. This argument is our own; the nLab gives only the cover formula. With the abstract extension, one instead needs the theorem that measures agreeing on intervals agree on Borel sets, in our own account. In both constructions, the real work is proving that Borel sets are measurable and that intervals get their length.

**nLab:** [Lebesgue measure](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Lebesgue+measure). It says: “\|B\| = inf {∑ⱼ₌₁∞ \|Iⱼ\| : B ⊆ ⋃ⱼ₌₁∞ Iⱼ}.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Borel sets on the target make measurable functions compose

**Remember:** Pull back only Borel sets, so a Borel map after it is safe.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 28A20 (Measurable and nonmeasurable functions, sequences of measurable functions, modes of convergence), 28A05. arXiv math.CA. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** A Lebesgue measurable function f goes from ℝ with the Lebesgue sets to ℂ with the Borel sets. The preimage of each Borel set must be Lebesgue measurable. So the σ-algebra on the source is large, but the one on the target is only the Borel sets.

**Problem.** If f is Lebesgue measurable and g is Borel measurable, then g ∘ f is Lebesgue measurable. In particular, continuous functions of measurable functions, and sums and products of measurable functions, are measurable.

**How the definition helps.** Composition is measurable when the σ-algebra pulled back by the outer function lies inside the one on which the inner function is measurable. With Borel sets on the target, this holds for every Borel outer function. The page states the general rule: composition needs Σ₃ ⊆ Σ₂. If both functions used Lebesgue sets on the target, the composition could fail to be measurable, as the page says. The standard construction uses the Cantor function to send a non-measurable set onto a null set (our own). The cost is asymmetry: a Lebesgue measurable function cannot always be used as the outer function.

**Wikipedia:** [Measurable function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Measurable_function). It says: “Indeed, two Lebesgue-measurable functions may be constructed in such a way as to make their composition non-Lebesgue-measurable.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### The Lebesgue integral lets limits pass inside the integral

**Remember:** Lebesgue slices the range, not the domain, so limits keep their integrals.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 28A25 (Integration with respect to measures and other set functions), 28A20. arXiv math.CA. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** The Lebesgue integral of a measurable function comes from the measures of the sets where the function takes given values. You build it by approximation with simple functions (functions that take finitely many values, each on a measurable set). A function is measurable when the preimage of every Borel set is measurable. A pointwise limit of measurable functions is measurable.

**Problem.** Under mild conditions, the integral of a limit equals the limit of the integrals. The monotone convergence theorem and the dominated convergence theorem give these conditions.

**How the definition helps.** In Lebesgue's theory, a limit of measurable functions is measurable, so the limit has an integral, and monotone and dominated convergence hold. For the Riemann integral the statement fails in general, because the limit need not be Riemann integrable. Our own example: the indicator functions of the first k rationals in \[0, 1\] increase, and each has Riemann integral 0. Their limit is the Dirichlet function, which the article notes has no Riemann integral. A condition is still needed: let fₙ = n on (0, 1/n\] and 0 elsewhere. Each fₙ has integral 1, but fₙ converges to 0, and no integrable function dominates all the fₙ. The hard work moves into the construction of Lebesgue measure.

**Wikipedia:** [Lebesgue integral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lebesgue_integral), [Dominated convergence theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominated_convergence_theorem). It says: “The main purpose of the Lebesgue integral is to provide an integral notion where limits of integrals hold under mild assumptions.”

**Sources:**

- [H. Lebesgue, Intégrale, longueur, aire, Ann. Mat. Pura Appl. 7 (1902), 231–359, doi:10.1007/BF02420592](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02420592)
- [H. Lebesgue, Leçons sur l'intégration et la recherche des fonctions primitives, Gauthier-Villars, Paris, 1904](https://archive.org/details/leconegrarecher00leberich)

### Requiring σ-finite measures makes Tonelli's theorem true

**Remember:** σ-finite spaces can be cut into countably many finite pieces.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 28A35 (Measures and integrals in product spaces), 28A12. arXiv math.CA. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** A measure space is σ-finite when it is a countable union of sets of finite measure.

**Problem.** Tonelli's theorem is about a non-negative measurable function on a product of two measure spaces. It says that the two iterated integrals are equal, and that they equal the integral for the product measure. (An iterated integral integrates over one factor first and then over the other.)

**How the definition helps.** σ-finiteness rules out examples like the following one, where the two iterated integrals differ. Take \[0,1\] with Lebesgue measure, and \[0,1\] with counting measure on all subsets, which gives each set its number of points and is not σ-finite. Integrate the function that is 1 on the diagonal x = y and 0 elsewhere. Integrating first over the Lebesgue factor gives 0, and integrating first over the counting factor gives 1. The two iterated integrals differ, so no product measure can make Tonelli's theorem hold. Requiring both spaces to be σ-finite excludes this case, and it also makes the product measure unique. Measurability of the function is still needed: assuming the continuum hypothesis, Sierpiński gave a bounded non-negative function on the unit square whose two iterated integrals exist and differ.

**Wikipedia:** [Fubini's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fubini%27s_theorem). It says: “This shows that Tonelli's theorem can fail for spaces that are not σ-finite no matter which product measure is chosen.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Standard Borel spaces always have conditional distributions

**Remember:** Standard Borel spaces are the measurable spaces of Polish spaces.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 28A05 (Classes of sets (Borel fields, \\(\\sigma\\)-rings, etc.), measurable sets, Suslin sets, analytic sets), 60A10, 60B05. arXiv math.PR. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A measurable space is standard Borel if its σ-algebra is the Borel σ-algebra of some Polish topology. A Polish topology is one given by a complete separable metric. Up to isomorphism, the standard Borel spaces are the countable discrete spaces and ℝ.

**Problem.** Conditional probability needs two things. For a probability space and a sub-σ-algebra, there should be a regular conditional distribution (a measurable family of probability measures that gives the conditional probabilities). Also, every Markov kernel (a measurable map from points to probability measures) should have a Bayesian inverse, a kernel in the opposite direction that agrees with Bayes' rule.

**How the definition helps.** On standard Borel spaces, conditional distributions always exist, with no extra hypothesis. On a standard Borel probability space, a regular conditional distribution exists for every sub-σ-algebra, and the sub-σ-algebra does not need to be countably generated. Every Markov kernel between standard Borel spaces has a Bayesian inverse that is unique almost surely. In the language of Markov categories, the category BorelStoch has conditionals. The nLab notes that in the larger category Stoch of all measurable spaces, conditionals can fail to exist, and that is why one restricts to standard Borel spaces. Standard Borel spaces are also closed under countable products and under the Giry monad (which sends a space to its space of probability measures), so the restriction costs little.

**nLab:** [standard Borel space](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/standard+Borel+space), [Markov kernel](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Markov+kernel), [Markov category](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Markov+category). It says: “They provide a setting for many constructions in probability theory, including conditional probability, disintegration, and countable products.”

**Sources:**

- [Chris Preston, Some notes on standard Borel and related spaces (2008), arXiv:0809.3066](https://arxiv.org/abs/0809.3066)

### The partition definition of total variation makes it the least dominating measure

**Remember:** A dominating measure pays for every partition at once.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 28A10 (Real- or complex-valued set functions), 28A25. arXiv math.CA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For a signed or complex measure μ, define its total variation \|μ\|(A) as the supremum of Σ\|μ(Aᵢ)\| over finite measurable partitions of A. Another definition, for signed measures, adds the positive and negative parts of the Jordan decomposition.

**Problem.** Always \|μ(A)\| ≤ \|μ\|(A). Every positive measure ν with \|μ(A)\| ≤ ν(A) for all measurable A satisfies \|μ\|(A) ≤ ν(A).

**How the definition helps.** With the partition definition, both claims take one line, in our own proof. If ν dominates μ, each partition sum Σ\|μ(Aᵢ)\| is at most Σν(Aᵢ) = ν(A). The partition with one part gives \|μ(A)\| ≤ \|μ\|(A). The work moves into proving that the partition supremum is countably additive, in our own account. With the Jordan definition, one would first need the Hahn decomposition, which splits the space into a positive set and a negative set.

**Paper or page:** [Total Variation is Smallest Measure exceeding Modulus of Measure](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Total_Variation_is_Smallest_Measure_exceeding_Modulus_of_Measure). It says: “\|μ(A)\| ≤ ν(A) for each A ∈ Σ.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Localizable measures are exactly where the main measure theorems hold

**Remember:** Localizable means measurable sets modulo null sets form a complete Boolean algebra.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 28A12 (Contents, measures, outer measures, capacities), 28A60, 28A25. arXiv math.FA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A measure is semifinite if every set of infinite measure contains a subset of finite positive measure. A measure is localizable if it is semifinite and every collection of measurable sets has an essential union. An essential union is a smallest measurable set that contains each set of the collection up to null sets. Equivalently, the Boolean algebra of measurable sets modulo null sets is complete (every subset of it has a least upper bound).

**Problem.** Three theorems should hold without the usual σ-finiteness hypothesis. They are the Radon–Nikodym theorem, the Hahn decomposition, and the Riesz representation L∞ ≅ (L¹)\*. The last one says that L∞ is the dual space of L¹.

**How the definition helps.** Localizability is exactly the condition that these theorems need, not just a sufficient one. Textbooks state the theorems for σ-finite measures, but they hold for every localizable measure. The Segal–Kelley theorem gives the converse: for a space with a faithful semifinite measure, each theorem is equivalent to localizability. So the real content is the Segal–Kelley equivalence. The nLab also says that localizability alone does not remove all pathologies. So it adds further conditions, strict localizability and compactness, to get a good category.

**nLab:** [localizable measure](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/localizable+measure), [categories of measure theory](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/categories+of+measure+theory), [Radon–Nikodym derivative](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Radon%E2%80%93Nikodym+derivative). It says: “The takeaway from this result is that without the localizability property much of the measure theory as we know is false, so it is completely reasonable to require it from the start.”

**Sources:**

- [Irving E. Segal, Equivalences of measure spaces, American Journal of Mathematics 73:2 (1951) 275](https://doi.org/10.2307/2372178)
- [John L. Kelley, Decomposition and representation theorems in measure theory, Mathematische Annalen 163:2 (1966) 89–94](https://doi.org/10.1007/bf02052840)

### Truly continuous measures give Radon–Nikodym without σ-finiteness

**Remember:** Truly continuous means absolute continuity controlled by one set of finite measure.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 28A12 (Contents, measures, outer measures, capacities), 28A25. arXiv math.FA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let ν be a finitely additive set function and μ a measure. Then ν is truly continuous with respect to μ if, for every ε &gt; 0, there are a set E of finite μ-measure and a δ &gt; 0 with this property: \|ν(F)\| &lt; ε whenever μ(E ∩ F) &lt; δ. Equivalently, ν is countably additive and absolutely continuous, and every set of positive ν-measure contains a subset of finite μ-measure and positive ν-measure.

**Problem.** Take any measure space (X, Σ, μ). For which ν is there an integrable function f such that ν(E) is the integral of f over E for all E? In words, when does ν have a density f?

**How the definition helps.** With this definition the Radon–Nikodym theorem becomes an exact 'if and only if' on every measure space, with no σ-finiteness hypothesis. Ordinary absolute continuity does not exclude the nLab's counterexample. Take counting measure on the countable–cocountable σ-algebra of an uncountable set (the sets that are countable or have a countable complement). Let ν be 0 on countable sets and 1 on the others. A localizable counterexample of the same kind exists exactly when real-valued-measurable cardinals exist. Such a cardinal κ carries a probability measure on all its subsets that is zero on single points and additive over unions of fewer than κ sets. In the σ-finite case, for countably additive ν, the new condition reduces to the usual absolute continuity.

**nLab:** [Radon–Nikodym derivative](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Radon%E2%80%93Nikodym+derivative). It says: “The following example shows that the condition of being truly continuous is necessary in the non-σ-finite case.”

**Sources:**

- [David H. Fremlin, Measure Theory, Volume 2, Chapter 23](https://www1.essex.ac.uk/maths/people/fremlin/mt.htm)

### Defining convergence in measure by truncated distances makes it metrizable

**Remember:** Cap each pointwise error at one, then integrate.

*True by definition.* MSC 28A20 (Measurable and nonmeasurable functions, sequences of measurable functions, modes of convergence), 46E30. arXiv math.CA, math.FA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Define the topology of convergence in measure by the pseudometrics that integrate min{\|f − g\|, 1} over sets of finite measure. A pseudometric is a distance that may be zero between different functions. The usual definition asks that μ{\|fₙ − f\| &gt; ε} tend to zero for each ε &gt; 0.

**Problem.** On a finite measure space, convergence in measure comes from one metric on measurable functions, once functions equal almost everywhere are identified.

**How the definition helps.** With this definition, on a finite measure space one may integrate over the whole space, so one pseudometric defines the topology. Wikipedia states this. Identifying functions that are equal almost everywhere turns that pseudometric into a metric, in our own account. The work is the equivalence with the usual ε test, in our own account. It splits the integral where \|f − g\| is below or above ε.

**Wikipedia:** [Convergence in measure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convergence_in_measure). It says: “When μ(X) &lt; ∞, we may consider only one metric ρ<sub>X</sub>, so the topology of convergence in finite measure is metrizable.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Defining the Lebesgue integral by horizontal slices gives the layer cake formula

**Remember:** Add up the areas of the horizontal slabs.

*True by definition.* MSC 28A25 (Integration with respect to measures and other set functions), 26A42. arXiv math.CA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For a nonnegative measurable f, let F(t) be the measure of the set where f &gt; t. Define the integral of f as the improper Riemann integral of F over (0, ∞), allowing the value ∞. The usual construction takes the supremum of integrals of simple functions below f. A simple function takes finitely many values, each on a measurable set.

**Problem.** Let f be nonnegative and measurable. Its integral equals the integral over t from 0 to ∞ of μ{f &gt; t}, also when both are infinite.

**How the definition helps.** With the slice definition, this formula is the definition itself, and Wikipedia says the integral may be defined this way. The work is proving that the slice integral agrees with the simple-function integral, in our own account. One checks it for simple functions and then passes to increasing limits with the monotone convergence theorem, in our own account.

**Wikipedia:** [Lebesgue integral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lebesgue_integral). It says: “The Lebesgue integral may then be defined as the improper Riemann integral of f∗:”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Defining product measure by integrating sections makes Tonelli's equality hold by construction

**Remember:** Measure each slice, then integrate the slice measures.

*True by definition.* MSC 28A35 (Measures and integrals in product spaces). arXiv math.CA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For σ-finite measure spaces, define the product measure of a measurable set E as the integral over x of ν(Eₓ). Here Eₓ is the vertical section of E at x. The rectangle construction instead extends the rule that E₁ × E₂ has measure μ(E₁)ν(E₂).

**Problem.** For σ-finite measures, the integral of a nonnegative measurable function on the product equals the iterated integral, first over y and then over x.

**How the definition helps.** For indicator functions of sets, which equal one on the set and zero elsewhere, the equality is the definition itself, in our own account. Sums and the monotone convergence theorem extend it to all nonnegative measurable functions, in our own proof. The work is proving that x ↦ ν(Eₓ) is measurable and that the formula defines a measure. The other order of integration needs the uniqueness of product measures, which uses σ-finiteness.

**Paper or page:** [Existence of Product Measures](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Existence_of_Product_Measures). It says: “ρ₁(E) = ∫<sub>X</sub> ν(E<sub>x</sub>) dμ”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Standard probability spaces make every measure-algebra map come from a point map

**Remember:** Standard spaces have enough points, so set maps come from point maps.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 28A60 (Measures on Boolean rings, measure algebras), 60A10. arXiv math.PR, math.DS. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A probability space is standard if, after removing null sets, it is isomorphic to one of three things. These are an interval with Lebesgue measure, a countable set of atoms, or a disjoint union of both. The measure algebra is the Boolean algebra of measurable sets, with sets that differ by a null set treated as equal.

**Problem.** On standard probability spaces, every homomorphism of measure algebras is induced by a measure-preserving map of points. So on these spaces one can pass between maps of events and maps of points, up to null sets.

**How the definition helps.** A standard space has no missing points, so a map defined on events can be realized by a map on points. The definition excludes spaces such as the perforated interval, a set of inner measure 0 and outer measure 1 with the induced measure. Its events match those of the interval, but conditional measures given the identity map do not exist at missing points. On the perforated circle, rotations act on events but not on points. The definition is due to Rokhlin, after von Neumann. What stays hard is the criterion for standardness, which uses an injective generating map into a standard Borel space.

**Wikipedia:** [Standard probability space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Standard_probability_space). It says: “It may seem that every homomorphism of measure algebras has to correspond to some measure preserving map, but it is not so. However, for standard probability spaces each F corresponds to some f.”

**Sources:**

- [V. A. Rokhlin, On the fundamental ideas of measure theory, Mat. Sbornik 25 (67) (1949), 107–150; English translation, AMS Translations 71 (1952), 1–54](http://ma.huji.ac.il/~matang02/rohlin.pdf)

### Stone's condition lets an abstract Daniell integral come from a measure

**Remember:** Truncate at height one, and the integral finds its measure.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 28C05 (Integration theory via linear functionals (Radon measures, Daniell integrals, etc.), representing set functions and measures), 28A12. arXiv math.FA, math.CA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Daniell starts from a vector lattice T₀ of functions, closed under maximum and minimum, and a positive linear functional I on it. The functional must be continuous under monotone limits: if φₙ decreases to 0, then I(φₙ) tends to 0. Stone's condition asks that min(φ, 1) is in T₀ whenever φ is.

**Problem.** Daniell's method builds an integral, with monotone and dominated convergence, without any measure. When is this integral an ordinary integral against a measure? The Daniell–Stone theorem says: whenever Stone's condition holds.

**How the definition helps.** Stone's condition lets one cut functions off at height one, so indicator functions of sets can be reached as limits. Then the integral gives a measure on those sets. The paper's Theorem 4.4 shows the role of the condition. The measurable sets form a σ-ring, and a σ-algebra if the constant function 1 is measurable. The convergence theorems need no measure at all and are proved first. The paper's Proposition 4.9 checks the continuity condition for the Riemann integral of continuous functions with compact support. This route then gives Lebesgue measure (our own remark).

**Paper or page:** [The Daniell Integral: Integration without measure](https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.14964v1), [The Daniell Integral: Integration without measure](https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.14964v1). It says: “with the property that χX ∧ φ ∈ T₀ whenever φ ∈ T₀. Let I be an I-integral on T₀. Then there is a σ-algebra 𝒜 on X and a measure μ on 𝒜”

**Sources:**

- [Adriaan de Clercq, The Daniell Integral: Integration without measure, arXiv:2211.14964 (2022)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.14964v1)

### Compatible finite quotient averages give Haar measure on profinite groups

**Remember:** On each finite quotient, average with equal weight for every point.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 28C10 (Set functions and measures on topological groups or semigroups, Haar measures, invariant measures), 20E18. arXiv math.FA, math.GR. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A profinite group is an inverse limit of finite groups with the discrete topology. On functions that factor through a finite quotient G/N, define the integral as the ordinary average over that quotient. The usual definition asks for a translation invariant regular Borel probability measure, called Haar probability measure.

**Problem.** These finite averages determine Haar probability measure on any profinite group, without using Haar’s general existence theorem.

**How the definition helps.** The finite averages make translation invariance immediate because translations permute each finite quotient (our own). Passing to a finer quotient does not change the average, since each fibre has the same number of points (our own). Functions from finite quotients uniformly approximate continuous functions, since the cosets form an open basis and the group is compact (our own). The averages therefore extend to a positive linear functional on all continuous functions (our own). The Riesz representation theorem makes it integration against a regular Borel probability measure (our own). The work lies in that theorem and the density argument, not in applying Haar’s general construction (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Compact group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compact_group). It says: “In the profinite case there are many subgroups of finite index, and Haar measure of a coset will be the reciprocal of the index.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Defining Haar measure on Baire sets makes the regularity conditions unnecessary

**Remember:** On Baire sets, invariant measures are regular for free.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 28C10 (Set functions and measures on topological groups or semigroups, Haar measures, invariant measures), 43A05. arXiv math.FA, math.GR. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A left Haar measure on a locally compact group is a nonzero left-invariant measure. On Borel sets it must be finite on compact sets, outer regular on Borel sets and inner regular on open sets. The Baire sets form the σ-algebra generated by compact sets that are countable intersections of open sets.

**Problem.** Every locally compact group has a left Haar measure, unique up to a positive constant. On the Baire sets this can be stated without any regularity condition.

**How the definition helps.** Baire measures that are finite on compact sets are automatically regular, so on Baire sets the regularity part of the statement holds by itself. On Borel sets, regularity must be assumed. The page shows that the Haar measure itself can fail inner regularity on some Borel sets. Take the circle times the real line with the discrete topology, and the closed set {1} × \[0, 1\]. Its compact subsets are finite, so they have measure 0, but the set itself does not. The work moves into existence, built from counting covers by translates. Weil first proved existence and uniqueness in full generality, and Cartan gave a proof without the axiom of choice.

**Wikipedia:** [Haar measure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haar_measure). It says: “Some authors define a Haar measure on Baire sets rather than Borel sets. This makes the regularity conditions unnecessary as Baire measures are automatically regular.”

**Sources:**

- [A. Haar, Der Massbegriff in der Theorie der kontinuierlichen Gruppen, Annals of Mathematics 34 (1933)](https://doi.org/10.2307/1968346)

### Left invariant volume forms give Haar measure on Lie groups

**Remember:** Translate a volume form at the identity to get invariant volume everywhere.

*True by definition.* MSC 28C10 (Set functions and measures on topological groups or semigroups, Haar measures, invariant measures), 22E15. arXiv math.DG, math.GR. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** On an n-dimensional Lie group, choose a nonzero alternating n-linear form on the tangent space at the identity. Move it by left translation to get a smooth volume form ω on the group. Its absolute value defines a measure by integration. The general definition of left Haar measure asks for a nonzero regular Borel measure unchanged by left translation.

**Problem.** Every Lie group has a left Haar measure, given by its left invariant volume form.

**How the definition helps.** The volume form makes invariance automatic because left translation preserves the form. Integrating its absolute value then gives a positive measure on nonempty open sets and a finite measure on compact sets (our own). Standard integration of a smooth density gives regularity, which means approximation by open and compact sets (our own). This replaces Haar’s general existence proof with the construction and integration of a smooth form.

**Wikipedia:** [Haar measure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haar_measure). It says: “On an n-dimensional Lie group, Haar measure can be constructed easily as the measure induced by a left-invariant n-form. This was known before Haar's theorem.”

**Sources:**

- [A. Haar, Der Massbegriff in der Theorie der kontinuierlichen Gruppen, Annals of Mathematics 34 (1933)](https://doi.org/10.2307/1968346)

### The Haar scaling definition makes compact groups unimodular

**Remember:** Left translation cannot rescale the finite mass of the whole group.

*True by definition.* MSC 28C10 (Set functions and measures on topological groups or semigroups, Haar measures, invariant measures), 22C05. arXiv math.FA, math.GR. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let ν be right Haar measure, a nonzero measure on a locally compact Hausdorff group that is unchanged by right translation. Its modular function Δ assigns to g the factor with ν(g⁻¹S) = Δ(g)ν(S). Unimodular means Δ equals 1 everywhere. The equivalent definition asks for a Haar measure that is both left and right invariant.

**Problem.** The modular function is multiplicative. Every compact Hausdorff group is unimodular.

**How the definition helps.** Defining Δ by scaling makes its multiplicativity a composition law and lets us test unimodularity on the whole group. Applying two translations multiplies their scaling factors (our own). For compact G, the whole group has finite positive Haar measure and a translation leaves it unchanged. Thus Δ(g) = 1. The usual argument treats Δ as a continuous homomorphism into the positive reals, which have no nontrivial compact subgroup (our own). The scalar definition shifts the invariance check to uniqueness of right Haar measure up to scale and avoids proving continuity of Δ.

**Wikipedia:** [Haar measure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haar_measure). It says: “Thus, by uniqueness up to a constant scaling factor of the Haar measure, there exists a function Δ from the group to the positive reals, called the Haar modulus, modular function or modular character”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Inner regularity is what Kolmogorov's extension theorem needs beyond Euclidean spaces

**Remember:** Compact sets inside every event let finite laws glue into one process.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 28C15 (Set functions and measures on topological spaces (regularity of measures, etc.)), 60G05, 28A35. arXiv math.PR, math.CA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A measure on a topological space is inner regular if each set has measure equal to the supremum over the compact sets inside it. A consistent family gives a probability measure on each finite product. These measures agree under the projections between products.

**Problem.** A consistent family of finite-dimensional laws extends to a unique probability measure on the infinite product. The page states this for inner regular laws on Hausdorff spaces. Borel probability measures on Polish spaces are automatically inner regular, so the classical Euclidean statement needs no extra condition.

**How the definition helps.** Inner regularity lets the proof use compact sets, and nested compact sets with the finite intersection property have a common point, which gives countable additivity. Without such a condition the extension can fail. A known example on non-regular spaces is due to Andersen and Jessen (our own). The page notes that Borel probability measures on Polish spaces are automatically Radon, which is why the condition is invisible for real-valued processes. The measure lives only on the product σ-algebra, which is coarse. Events that depend on uncountably many times stay outside it, and that problem needs separate work.

**Wikipedia:** [Kolmogorov extension theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kolmogorov_extension_theorem). It says: “In fact, any collection of measurable spaces together with a collection of inner regular measures defined on the finite products of these spaces would suffice, provided that these measures satisfy a certain compatibility relation.”

**Sources:**

- [A. Kolmogoroff, Grundbegriffe der Wahrscheinlichkeitsrechnung, Springer, 1933](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-642-49888-6)

### Measures that respect directed unions of open sets have a support

**Remember:** τ-additive: the measure of a directed union of open sets is the supremum.

*True by definition.* MSC 28C15 (Set functions and measures on topological spaces (regularity of measures, etc.)), 28A12. arXiv math.FA, math.GN. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A Borel measure μ on a topological space is τ-additive if it has this property for every directed family of open sets: the measure of their union is the supremum of their measures. A directed family is one in which any two members are contained in a third member. A valuation gives a measure to open sets only. The same condition on a valuation (Scott continuity) defines a continuous valuation.

**Problem.** Every measure should have a support: a smallest closed set of full measure.

**How the definition helps.** τ-additivity says directly that the union of the null open sets is null. The null open sets form a directed family, so their union has measure zero, and its complement is the support. For a general Borel measure, the union of all null open sets can fail to be null, so the support need not have full measure. Every Radon measure on a Hausdorff space is τ-additive, so the definition covers the usual examples. Fritz, Perrone and Rezagholi show that the support is then a morphism of monads on the category Top of topological spaces.

**nLab:** [tau-additive measure](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/tau-additive+measure), [valuation (measure theory)](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/valuation+%28measure+theory%29), [correspondence between measure and valuation theory](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/correspondence+between+measure+and+valuation+theory). It says: “the union of all null open sets is null”

**Sources:**

- [Tobias Fritz, Paolo Perrone, Sharwin Rezagholi, Probability, valuations, hyperspace: Three monads on Top and the support as a morphism (2019); arXiv:1910.03752](https://arxiv.org/abs/1910.03752)

### Regularity makes the measure in the Riesz representation theorem unique

**Remember:** Regularity picks one measure for each positive functional on continuous functions.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 28C15 (Set functions and measures on topological spaces (regularity of measures, etc.)), 28C05. arXiv math.CA, math.FA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A Borel measure is outer regular when the measure of each Borel set is the infimum of the measures of open sets that contain it. It is inner regular when each open set, and each Borel set of finite measure, has the supremum over compact subsets as its measure. A regular measure has both properties and gives each compact set finite measure.

**Problem.** Let X be a locally compact Hausdorff space. The Riesz–Markov–Kakutani theorem says that each positive linear functional on the compactly supported continuous functions on X is integration against a unique regular Borel measure. It also identifies the dual of C₀(X) with the regular complex Borel measures.

**How the definition helps.** Regularity makes a measure depend only on its values on compact sets, and integrals of continuous functions fix those values (our own summary). The measure of a compact set K is the infimum of ∫f over compactly supported continuous f ≥ 1 on K (our own). The page gives a counterexample on the ordinals up to the first uncountable ordinal Ω, with the order topology. Evaluation at Ω is integration against the point mass at Ω. It is also integration against a non-regular measure, a form of the Dieudonné measure (our own name). That measure gives measure 1 to each Borel set that contains a closed unbounded set, and gives the point Ω measure 0. Existence still takes the whole construction of the measure from the functional through an outer measure.

**Wikipedia:** [Riesz–Markov–Kakutani representation theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riesz%E2%80%93Markov%E2%80%93Kakutani_representation_theorem). It says: “Without the condition of regularity the Borel measure need not be unique.”

**Sources:**

- [S. Kakutani, Concrete representation of abstract (M)-spaces, Annals of Mathematics 42 (1941), 994–1024](https://doi.org/10.2307/1968778)

### Linear functional tests show continuous linear maps preserve Gaussian laws

**Remember:** Compose a linear functional with the operator to test the image law.

*True by definition.* MSC 28C20 (Set functions and measures and integrals in infinite-dimensional spaces (Wiener measure, Gaussian measure, etc.)), 60G15. arXiv math.PR, stat.ML. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A separable Banach space is a complete normed vector space with a countable dense set. A probability law on such a space is Gaussian if every continuous linear functional sends it to a normal law. A linear functional maps vectors to real numbers, and a constant counts as normal with variance zero.

**Problem.** A continuous linear map B between separable Banach spaces sends each Gaussian law to a Gaussian law. The output means and covariances of linear tests come from composing those tests with B.

**How the definition helps.** The functional definition makes preservation a composition rule (our own). If L tests the output, then L∘B is a continuous linear functional on the input, where the Gaussian condition already gives normality (our own). The finite-dimensional density approach cannot work here because infinite-dimensional Banach spaces have no Lebesgue measure. The work shifts to constructing the original Gaussian law and checking that the operator is continuous on the chosen spaces (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Gaussian measure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaussian_measure). It says: “Even so, it is possible to define Gaussian measures on infinite-dimensional spaces, the main example being the abstract Wiener space construction.”

**Paper or page:** [Gaussian Process Priors for Systems of Linear Partial Differential Equations with Constant Coefficients](https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.14319v4). It says: “be a linear continuous map. Then B∗γ is a Gaussian measure”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Sober measurable spaces make measurable Gelfand duality hold by definition

**Remember:** Sober: every zero-one measure is a point, just as every point of a locale is.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 28A05 (Classes of sets (Borel fields, \\(\\sigma\\)-rings, etc.), measurable sets, Suslin sets, analytic sets), 46L05. arXiv math.FA, math.OA. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A zero-one measure is a measure that takes only the values 0 and 1. A measurable space X is sober if every zero-one measure on it is the Dirac measure of exactly one point. Equivalently, the map X → Sp(L∞(X)) that sends x to evaluation at x is an isomorphism. Here L∞(X) is the algebra of all bounded measurable functions on X, and Sp(L∞(X)) is its spectrum.

**Problem.** Which measurable spaces are determined by their algebra of bounded measurable functions, as a σ-C\*-algebra? A σ-C\*-algebra is a C\*-algebra that is closed under countable bounded monotone suprema.

**How the definition helps.** Sober spaces are defined as exactly the spaces on which the duality holds, so the duality is automatic. The functor L∞ and the spectrum functor Sp form an idempotent adjunction between measurable spaces and commutative σ-C\*-algebras. (Idempotent means that going around the adjunction twice gives the same result as going around once.) For an idempotent adjunction, the objects on which the unit is an isomorphism form one side of an equivalence. Sober spaces are exactly these objects, so the duality between sober measurable spaces and spatial σ-C\*-algebras holds by definition. The work is in proving that the adjunction is idempotent, and in examples. Every standard Borel space is sober, while the invariant σ-algebra of an ergodic system is in general not.

**nLab:** [sober measurable space](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/sober+measurable+space), [measurable Gelfand duality](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/measurable+Gelfand+duality). It says: “As usual with idempotent adjunctions, we have that the center is equivalently given by”

**Sources:**

- [Tobias Fritz, Antonio Lorenzin, Categories of abstract and noncommutative measurable spaces, Advances in Mathematics 488 (2026) 110793; arXiv:2504.13708](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.13708)

### Take inclusion-exclusion as an axiom of constructive measures

**Remember:** Use the formula you actually need as the axiom.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 28A10 (Real- or complex-valued set functions), 03F60. arXiv math.CA, math.LO. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Take the two-set inclusion-exclusion law μ(A ∪ B) + μ(A ∩ B) = μ(A) + μ(B) as an axiom of a measure, in place of additivity on disjoint sets. In words, the measure of the union plus the measure of the intersection equals the sum of the two measures. On a Cheng space, a positive measure is defined by this law, absolute continuity and countable subadditivity. A Cheng space is a set with a σ-algebra of complemented pairs (pairs of disjoint subsets that stand for a set and its complement).

**Problem.** In constructive mathematics (mathematics without excluded middle), additivity on disjoint sets does not imply the two-set inclusion-exclusion law. But a usable measure theory needs the inclusion-exclusion principle.

**How the definition helps.** If the law you need is an axiom, its constructive proof is no longer a problem. Classically, the two-set law follows easily from additivity, and the general finite formula follows by induction. Constructively the proof of the two-set law fails, so the nLab proposes to make the two-set law itself a clause of the definition. The general finite formula then follows by the same induction. On Cheng spaces, inclusion-exclusion also follows from finite additivity and the rule that intersection with a full set keeps the measure, so there the choice of axiom makes no difference. The countable version of the law forces countable additivity. Counting measure satisfies the law constructively only on sets with decidable equality (where any two elements are provably equal or not equal).

**nLab:** [inclusion-exclusion](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/inclusion-exclusion), [Cheng space](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Cheng+space). It says: “On the other hand, we may adopt (\*) as the proper clause in the definition of measure.”

**Sources:**

- [Errett Bishop, Henry Cheng, Constructive measure theory, Memoirs of the AMS 116 (1972)](https://doi.org/10.1090/memo/0116)
- [Errett Bishop, Douglas Bridges, Constructive Analysis, Grundlehren 279, Springer (1985)](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-642-61667-9)

### The Carathéodory extension theorem becomes a Kan extension of transformations

**Remember:** Extending a premeasure is a Kan extension.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 28A12 (Contents, measures, outer measures, capacities), 18A40. arXiv math.CT, math.CA. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A premeasure is a countably additive function on a Boolean algebra of sets. An outer measure is a monotone, countably subadditive function on all subsets. The paper treats both as transformations between poset-valued functors. Lax and colax transformations satisfy inequalities where strict transformations satisfy equalities.

**Problem.** The Carathéodory extension theorem says that a premeasure on a generating Boolean algebra extends to a measure on the generated σ-algebra. So, to define a measure, one only needs its values on a generating Boolean algebra.

**How the definition helps.** A Kan extension is the best extension of a map along another map, so the extension of a premeasure becomes a universal construction. The abstract says that the Carathéodory extension corresponds to a Kan extension of strict transformations. The paper develops a general framework for extensions of transformations between poset-valued functors. It then shows that the functors and transformations that come from measures satisfy the conditions of this framework. That step proves the Carathéodory extension theorem. Our own remark: the measure-theoretic estimates do not disappear, but move into this last check.

**Paper or page:** [A categorical proof of the Carathéodory extension theorem](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.01720). It says: “To prove this result categorically, we represent (pre)measures and outer measures by certain (co)lax and strict transformations. The Carathéodory extension then corresponds to a Kan extension of strict transformations.”

**Sources:**

- [Ruben Van Belle, A categorical proof of the Carathéodory extension theorem, arXiv:2210.01720 (2022)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.01720)

### Comparing distribution functions up to constants characterizes vague convergence of signed measures

**Remember:** Compare masses of intervals, not mass accumulated from minus infinity.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 28A33 (Spaces of measures, convergence of measures), 28A20. arXiv math.PR, math.CA. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Finite signed measures μₙ on ℝ converge vaguely to μ when ∫ f dμₙ → ∫ f dμ for every continuous f with compact support. The distribution function of μ is F(x) = μ((−∞, x\]). The abstract's notion is convergence in Lebesgue measure up to constants: Fₙ + cₙ → F in measure for some constants cₙ.

**Problem.** Corollary 3.14 says that μₙ converges vaguely to μ exactly when two things hold. The total variation of μₙ on each bounded interval is bounded uniformly in n. There are constants cₙ with Fₙ + cₙ → F in Lebesgue measure on each bounded interval.

**How the definition helps.** Vague convergence cannot see mass that escapes to infinity, and the free constants cₙ remove this blind spot from the distribution functions (our own). For example, the unit mass at −n converges vaguely to zero (our own). Its distribution function is 1 at each fixed point for large n, while the limit has distribution function 0 (our own). With cₙ = −1 the comparison succeeds (our own). Theorem 3.12 gives equivalent forms through basic and almost basic convergence, which the paper studies. Both directions of the proof use the local bound on total variation (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Vague and basic convergence of signed measures](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.11377v1). It says: “it is locally uniformly bounded in variation and the corresponding sequence of distribution functions either converges in Lebesgue measure up to constants, converges basically, or converges almost basically.”

**Sources:**

- [Michael Staněk, Vague and basic convergence of signed measures, arXiv:2406.11377 (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.11377v1)

### Virtual continuity replaces Luzin's theorem in several variables and gives traces

**Remember:** Delete small sets one coordinate at a time, not in the square.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 28A35 (Measures and integrals in product spaces), 46E35. arXiv math.FA, math.CA. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Let f(x, y) be a measurable function on a product X × Y of two probability spaces. The function f is virtually continuous if it is continuous, for suitable metrics, on a product X′ × Y′ of large subsets. For any ε &gt; 0, each of X′ and Y′ may miss a set of measure ε, as in Theorem 3 of the paper. So what remains is always a product of two large sets, not an arbitrary large subset of X × Y.

**Problem.** Luzin's theorem says that a measurable function of one variable is continuous off a set of small measure.
