Take L = −div A∇ off Γ, with the ellipticity bounds of A comparable to dist(·, Γ) to the power d + 1 − n. Harmonic measure at x is the measure on Γ whose integral of boundary data gives the solution at x.

**Problem.** For such an operator, harmonic measure exists on Γ. It is doubling: doubling the radius of a boundary ball multiplies its mass by at most a fixed factor. It also satisfies change-of-pole formulas and a comparison principle.

**How the definition helps.** Because d + 1 − n &lt; 0, the weight grows near Γ, and this lets solutions feel a boundary of high codimension. Our own comparison is the ordinary Laplacian in ℝ³ outside one point. There, bounded harmonic functions extend across the point, so the point carries no harmonic measure. The paper still proves trace theorems, a maximum principle, Harnack and Hölder estimates, and Green function bounds before it defines harmonic measure.

**Paper or page:** [Elliptic theory for sets with higher co-dimensional boundaries](https://arxiv.org/abs/1702.05503v3). It says: “The aim of this manuscript is to develop a version of elliptic theory, associated to a linear PDE, which ultimately yields a notion analogous to that of the harmonic measure, for sets of codimension higher than 1.”

**Sources:**

- [Guy R. David, Joseph Feneuil, Svitlana Mayboroda, Elliptic theory for sets with higher co-dimensional boundaries, arXiv:1702.05503 (2023)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1702.05503v3)

### Irreducibility makes the ground state of a positive form unique and positive

**Remember:** One connected piece gives one positive ground state.

*Rules out counterexamples. Confidence: medium.* MSC 31C25 (Dirichlet forms), 47A07, 47D07. arXiv math.FA, math.SP. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A closed quadratic form on L² is the energy q(u) = ‖√A u‖² of a self-adjoint operator A ≥ 0, with semigroup e⁻ᵗᴬ. The form satisfies the first Beurling–Deny criterion if q(\|u\|) ≤ q(u) for every u, so the semigroup keeps positive functions positive. The form is irreducible if no measurable set B, with B and its complement both of positive measure, splits it. Splitting means that the semigroup maps all functions on B to functions on B alone.

**Problem.** The kernel of a form is the set of u with q(u) = 0, the ground states. When is it at most one line, spanned by a function that is positive everywhere? The paper shows: whenever the form is irreducible and satisfies the first Beurling–Deny criterion.

**How the definition helps.** Irreducibility excludes the split case, in which the form is a sum of forms on disjoint pieces. In our own example, take the energy ∫\|u′\|² on two disjoint intervals, with no boundary condition. It vanishes on the indicator of each interval, so its kernel is two-dimensional. Positivity preservation lets one replace a ground state u by \|u\|. Irreducibility then forces it to be positive everywhere. So two ground states cannot be orthogonal (our own account of the Perron–Frobenius argument). This is a Perron–Frobenius theorem for forms.

**Paper or page:** [(Weak) Hardy and Poincaré inequalities and criticality theory](https://arxiv.org/abs/2108.11681v1). It says: “let q be an irreducible closed quadratic form on Lᵖ(X,μ) satisfying the first Beurling-Deny criterion. Then ker q is at most one-dimensional and if ker q≠{0}, there exists a strictly positive h∈Lᵖ(X,μ) such that ker q=ℝh.”

**Sources:**

- [Marcel Schmidt, (Weak) Hardy and Poincaré inequalities and criticality theory, arXiv:2108.11681 (2021), Springer Proc. Math. Stat. (2022) 421–459](https://arxiv.org/abs/2108.11681v1)

### Changing exterior data on a capacity-zero set leaves the Perron solution unchanged

**Remember:** Sets of zero capacity are invisible to the solution.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 31C45 (Other generalizations (nonlinear potential theory, etc.)), 35R11, 35J66. arXiv math.AP. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** The paper studies nonlocal equations of fractional p-Laplace type, where data are prescribed on the whole exterior Ωᶜ of the domain Ω. The Sobolev capacity C₍s,p₎(E) measures how large a set E is for the fractional Sobolev space. The upper Perron solution is the infimum of the superharmonic functions that lie above the data outside Ω. The paper's new definition of Perron solutions accepts any exterior data g with values in \[−∞, ∞\].

**Problem.** Let g be continuous on ℝⁿ and lie in the paper's Sobolev-type space for Ω. Let h be zero outside a set E with C₍s,p₎(E) = 0. Then the upper and lower Perron solutions of g + h agree, and P(g + h) = Pg in Ω.

**How the definition helps.** The new Perron definition accepts arbitrary exterior data, so the perturbation h may take any values on E, even ±∞. Without it, P(g + h) would not be defined for such h. For Sobolev solutions the invariance is nearly free: a set of zero capacity has zero volume, so g + h and g are the same Sobolev function. This explanation is our own. The real work is the theorem that Sobolev and Perron solutions coincide, which carries the invariance over to Perron solutions. The quote says that the invariance follows from that coincidence. Theorem 1.4 gives the same result for bounded continuous data with a limit at infinity.

**Paper or page:** [Perron solutions and boundary regularity for nonlocal nonlinear Dirichlet problems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.05994v3). It says: “This also implies invariance of the Perron solutions under perturbations on sets of zero fractional capacity.”

**Sources:**

- [Anders Björn, Jana Björn, Minhyun Kim, Perron solutions and boundary regularity for nonlocal nonlinear Dirichlet problems, arXiv:2406.05994v3 (2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.05994v3)

## 32 Several complex variables and analytic spaces

### Pseudoconvexity turns the domain of holomorphy problem into a local test

**Remember:** Domains of holomorphy are exactly the pseudoconvex domains, a local test.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 32E40 (The Levi problem), 32U05, 32U10. arXiv math.CV. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A function is plurisubharmonic if it is upper semicontinuous and subharmonic on every complex line. Upper semicontinuous means that its value at each point is at least the lim sup of nearby values. A domain G in ℂⁿ is pseudoconvex if it has a continuous plurisubharmonic exhaustion, a function whose sublevel sets are relatively compact in G. For a domain with C² boundary, this is the same as the Levi condition on the boundary.

**Problem.** A domain of holomorphy is a domain with a holomorphic function that cannot be continued beyond it. The Levi problem asks whether every pseudoconvex domain in ℂⁿ is a domain of holomorphy. The answer is yes, so the two classes are the same (Oka, 1942 to 1953, our own dating).

**How the definition helps.** Being a domain of holomorphy is a global property, but pseudoconvexity can be checked near each boundary point. In one variable every open set is a domain of holomorphy, so no such notion is needed. For n ≥ 2, Hartogs's extension theorem shows that U minus a compact set K is not one, when U minus K is connected. So a geometric test was needed, and plurisubharmonic exhaustions give it. The easy direction is that −log of the distance to the boundary is plurisubharmonic on a domain of holomorphy. The hard direction, from pseudoconvex to domain of holomorphy, was proved by Oka, and later by Hörmander's L² methods (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Pseudoconvexity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pseudoconvexity), [Domain of holomorphy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domain_of_holomorphy), [Plurisubharmonic function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plurisubharmonic_function). It says: “Pseudoconvex sets are important, as they allow for classification of domains of holomorphy.”

**Sources:**

- [H. Grauert, On Levi's Problem and the Imbedding of Real-Analytic Manifolds, Annals of Mathematics 68 (1958)](https://doi.org/10.2307/1970257)
- [K. Oka, Sur les fonctions analytiques de plusieurs variables VI. Domaines pseudoconvexes, Tohoku Mathematical Journal 49 (1942)](https://www.nara-wu.ac.jp/aic/gdb/nwugdb/oka/ko_ron/f/n06/p001.html)

### The largest disc-contracting distance makes every holomorphic map distance-decreasing

**Remember:** Define the distance by discs, and holomorphic maps never stretch it.

*True by definition.* MSC 32F45 (Invariant metrics and pseudodistances in several complex variables), 32Q45. arXiv math.CV, math.DG. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** The Kobayashi pseudometric on a complex space X is the largest pseudometric such that every holomorphic map from the unit disc into X is distance-decreasing. Distance on the disc is measured by the Poincaré metric ρ, the hyperbolic distance of the disc. X is Kobayashi hyperbolic if this pseudometric is a true metric.

**Problem.** Every holomorphic map between complex spaces is distance-decreasing for their Kobayashi pseudometrics. So every holomorphic map from ℂ to a hyperbolic space is constant.

**How the definition helps.** A disc mapped into X and then on to Y is a disc mapped into Y, so the distance-decreasing property follows from the definition. Schwarz's lemma says that the Kobayashi metric on the unit disc is the Poincaré metric. The Kobayashi pseudometric of ℂ is zero, because ℂ contains arbitrarily large discs. The work moves to showing that particular spaces are hyperbolic. For example, ℂ minus two points is hyperbolic, and this gives Picard's theorem. Brody's theorem says that a compact space is hyperbolic exactly when every holomorphic map from ℂ into it is constant.

**Wikipedia:** [Kobayashi metric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kobayashi_metric). It says: “the Kobayashi pseudometric dₓ is defined as the largest pseudometric on X such that dₓ(f(x),f(y)) ≤ ρ(x,y), for all holomorphic maps f from the unit disc D to X”

**Sources:**

- [S. Kobayashi, Invariant distances on complex manifolds and holomorphic mappings, Journal of the Mathematical Society of Japan 19 (1967)](https://doi.org/10.2969/jmsj/01940460)

### The exponential sequence makes first Chern classes add under tensor products

**Remember:** Transition functions multiply, and the connecting map turns their products into sums.

*True by definition.* MSC 32L10 (Sheaves and cohomology of sections of holomorphic vector bundles, general results), 55R40. arXiv math.CV, math.AT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** On a complex manifold M, the exponential sends local holomorphic functions to nowhere-zero ones. Every such function has a local logarithm, and logarithms differ by multiples of 2πi. This short exact sequence of sheaves, which track functions and their restrictions, induces a map from line bundles to H²(M, ℤ). Define the first Chern class c₁ to be this map.

**Problem.** Show that the first Chern class turns tensor products of holomorphic line bundles into sums. Determine which bundles have first Chern class zero.

**How the definition helps.** The exponential-sequence definition makes additivity immediate because the connecting map is a group homomorphism. The group law on line bundles is tensor product, which multiplies the functions used to glue their local pieces. Exactness says the kernel is the image of H¹(M, O), where O records local holomorphic functions. In our own comparison, the Euler-class definition needs a separate proof of additivity for complex line bundles. The work shifts to establishing the sequence and proving that its class agrees with the Euler class.

**Wikipedia:** [Exponential sheaf sequence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exponential_sheaf_sequence). It says: “Here H¹(O<sub>M</sub>\*) can be identified with the Picard group of holomorphic line bundles on M. The connecting homomorphism sends a line bundle to its first Chern class.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### The Kähler condition makes the Laplacians agree and gives the Hodge decomposition

**Remember:** A closed Kähler form ties the metric, complex and symplectic structures together.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 32Q15 (Kähler manifolds), 53C55, 58A14. arXiv math.DG, math.CV. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A Kähler manifold is a complex manifold with a Hermitian metric whose associated 2-form ω is closed. Equivalently, the complex structure is parallel for the Levi-Civita connection.

**Problem.** The Hodge decomposition: on a compact Kähler manifold, each cohomology group with complex coefficients splits. The r-th group is the direct sum of the Dolbeault groups of type (p, q) with p + q = r. Dolbeault groups are the cohomology of the complex-differential operator ∂̄.

**How the definition helps.** The Kähler condition gives the Kähler identities, so the de Rham Laplacian is twice each of the two Dolbeault Laplacians. Then a form is harmonic exactly when each of its (p, q) parts is harmonic. Hodge theory gives each cohomology class a unique harmonic representative, so the splitting passes to cohomology. On a general compact complex manifold, the Laplacians differ and the splitting can fail. Our own example is the Hopf surface, which is S¹ × S³ with a complex structure. Its first Betti number is 1, which is odd, so it cannot be Kähler. Every smooth complex projective variety is Kähler, which is why Hodge theory is central to algebraic geometry.

**Wikipedia:** [Kähler manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K%C3%A4hler_manifold). It says: “If X is Kähler, the Kähler identities imply these Laplacians are all the same up to a constant”

**Sources:**

- [E. Kähler, Über eine bemerkenswerte Hermitesche Metrik, Abhandlungen aus dem Mathematischen Seminar der Universität Hamburg 9 (1933) 173–186](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02940642)

### On Stein manifolds sheaf cohomology solves the first Cousin problem

**Remember:** Stein means enough holomorphic functions, so prescribed poles always glue together.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 32Q28 (Stein manifolds), 32E10. arXiv math.CV. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A Stein manifold is a complex manifold with two properties. It is holomorphically convex: the hull of each compact set, defined by bounds on all global holomorphic functions, is compact. It is holomorphically separable: global holomorphic functions separate points.

**Problem.** The first Cousin problem gives meromorphic functions fᵢ on open sets Uᵢ, with each fᵢ − fⱼ holomorphic on the overlap. It asks for one global meromorphic f with f − fᵢ holomorphic on each Uᵢ. On a Stein manifold this problem always has a solution.

**How the definition helps.** Sheaf cohomology rewrites the gluing problem as one obstruction class in H¹(M, O), where O is the sheaf of holomorphic functions. By a long exact sequence, a solution exists as soon as that group is zero. The work moves into Cartan's theorem B. On a Stein manifold, coherent sheaves, which are locally given by finitely many generators and relations, have no cohomology in positive degrees. The Stein conditions exclude compact manifolds, where only constants are holomorphic. On a compact complex torus the problem can fail, since no elliptic function has only one simple pole (our own example).

**Wikipedia:** [Cousin problems](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cousin_problems), [Stein manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stein_manifold). It says: “the first Cousin problem is always solvable provided that the first cohomology group H¹(M,O) vanishes. In particular, by Cartan's theorem B, the Cousin problem is always solvable if M is a Stein manifold.”

**Sources:**

- [K. Stein, Analytische Funktionen mehrerer komplexer Veränderlichen zu vorgegebenen Periodizitätsmoduln und das zweite Cousinsche Problem, Mathematische Annalen 123 (1951)](https://doi.org/10.1007/bf02054949)

### A tensor test for complex structures, by the Newlander–Nirenberg theorem

**Remember:** Zero Nijenhuis tensor means honest holomorphic charts.

*True by definition.* MSC 32Q60 (Almost complex manifolds), 53C15. arXiv math.CV, math.DG. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** An almost complex structure on a manifold is a smooth field J of linear maps on tangent spaces with J² = −1. It is integrable if its Nijenhuis tensor, built from J and Lie brackets of vector fields, is zero. A complex manifold has charts to ℂⁿ whose transition maps are holomorphic.

**Problem.** Decide whether a manifold with an almost complex structure J is a complex manifold with J as its multiplication by i. To find holomorphic charts, one must solve differential equations. A tensor, in contrast, can be computed pointwise.

**How the definition helps.** If 'complex structure' means 'almost complex structure with zero Nijenhuis tensor', checking it is a local computation. The hard analytic work moves into the Newlander–Nirenberg theorem (1957), which builds holomorphic coordinates from the tensor condition. The definition does not make every question easy. The page notes that it is still unknown whether the 6-sphere, which has an almost complex structure from the octonions, has an integrable one.

**Wikipedia:** [Almost complex manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almost_complex_manifold). It says: “Since the existence of an integrable almost complex structure is equivalent to the existence of a complex structure, this is sometimes taken as the definition of a complex structure.”

**Sources:**

- [A. Newlander and L. Nirenberg, Complex analytic coordinates in almost complex manifolds, Annals of Mathematics 65 (1957) 391–404](https://doi.org/10.2307/1970051)

### Hyperfunctions as boundary values form a flabby sheaf

**Remember:** Every hyperfunction on a smaller set extends to the whole line.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 32A45 (Hyperfunctions). arXiv math.CV. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Take an open set U of ℝ and a complex neighbourhood of U. A hyperfunction on U is a pair of holomorphic functions on the upper and lower parts of that neighbourhood. Two pairs are equal when they differ by one holomorphic function on the whole neighbourhood. Sato introduced them in 1958, and the page also writes them as a local cohomology group of holomorphic functions.

**Problem.** A sheaf is flabby when every section on an open set extends to the whole space. One wants generalized functions that can be cut and glued freely, and that include distributions of infinite order.

**How the definition helps.** Defining hyperfunctions by holomorphic functions turns flabbiness into a fact about ℂ, whose open sets have no first cohomology for holomorphic functions (our own summary). Distributions are not flabby. On (0, 1), take the sum of the n-th derivatives of the delta functions at the points 1/n (our own example). This is a distribution, but it has no extension to ℝ, because its order grows without bound near 0 (our own example). The page calls hyperfunctions distributions of infinite order, so this obstruction does not arise. The page also says that distributions embed into hyperfunctions. What stays hard is the theory in several variables, which needs more sheaf cohomology.

**Wikipedia:** [Hyperfunction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyperfunction). It says: “The obvious restriction maps turn ℬ into a sheaf (which is in fact flabby).”

**Sources:**

- [M. Sato, Cyōkansū no riron (Theory of Hyperfunctions), Sūgaku 10 (1958), no. 1, 1–27](https://doi.org/10.11429/sugaku1947.10.1)

### A Berkovich boundary gives a compactification on which GAGA holds

**Remember:** Add a valuative boundary, and analytic sheaves can no longer grow wildly.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 32J05 (Compactification of analytic spaces), 14G22, 14F06. arXiv math.AG, math.CV. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For a complex algebraic variety X, the analytic space X(ℂ) is compact only when X is proper. Poineau adds at infinity a Berkovich space over ℂ with the trivial absolute value. The result is a canonical compact space X⌝, functorial for proper morphisms.

**Problem.** Serre's GAGA says that for a proper variety, coherent analytic sheaves are the same as coherent algebraic sheaves. For a non-proper variety, can a compactification restore this?

**How the definition helps.** The boundary keeps track of growth at infinity, so coherent sheaves on the compactification are algebraic (our own reading). Without it, GAGA fails. On the affine line, the exponential function is analytic but is not a polynomial (our own). Poineau proves that coherent sheaves on X and on X⌝ form equivalent categories, with the same global sections. The construction keeps properties such as normality, regularity and the Cohen–Macaulay property. The paper calls the theorem partial, and it states it for coherent sheaves and global sections only.

**Paper or page:** [Valuative compactifications of analytic varieties](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.18643v2), [Valuative compactifications of analytic varieties](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.18643v2). It says: “We prove a partial GAGA theorem in this setting : there is an equivalence between the categories of coherent sheaves on X and X⌝, and it induces bijections on global sections.”

**Sources:**

- [Jérôme Poineau, Valuative compactifications of analytic varieties, arXiv:2503.18643v2 (2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.18643v2)

### Uniform relative K-polystability is exactly the condition for toric extremal metrics

**Remember:** Measure stability with a norm, and it matches extremal metrics exactly.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 32Q26 (Notions of stability for complex manifolds), 53C55, 14M25. arXiv math.DG, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A polarized manifold is a complex manifold with a chosen positive line bundle L. An extremal Kähler metric is one whose scalar curvature has a holomorphic gradient. K-polystability tests a polarized manifold against degenerations to simpler spaces, using a number called the Donaldson–Futaki invariant. The uniform and relative version asks that this number grow at least like a norm of the degeneration, after removing symmetries.

**Problem.** The Yau–Tian–Donaldson conjecture asks for an algebraic condition that is equivalent to the existence of a canonical Kähler metric. The paper proves a uniform version for polarized toric manifolds, which have a large torus symmetry.

**How the definition helps.** The uniform condition is chosen to match coercivity of the K-energy, so the equivalence can be stated and proved. Coercive means that this energy, whose minima are the metrics, grows at least like a distance. The paper's corollary treats toric Fano manifolds, those whose anticanonical bundle is positive. There, several stability notions are equivalent to the vanishing of the Futaki invariant. All are equivalent to the barycenter of the moment polytope being at the origin. The hardest step, from coercivity to the existence of a metric, rests on earlier existence theorems (our own).

**Paper or page:** [A uniform version of the Yau-Tian-Donaldson correspondence for extremal Kähler metrics on polarized toric manifolds](https://arxiv.org/abs/2110.10386), [A uniform version of the Yau-Tian-Donaldson correspondence for extremal Kähler metrics on polarized toric manifolds](https://arxiv.org/abs/2110.10386). It says: “Then the followings are equivalent. (1) (X, L) admits an S-invariant extremal Kähler metric. (2) (X, L) is uniformly relatively K-polystable. (3) The relative K-energy of (X, L) is T-coercive.”

**Sources:**

- [Y. Nitta and S. Saito, A uniform version of the Yau-Tian-Donaldson correspondence for extremal Kähler metrics on polarized toric manifolds, arXiv:2110.10386 (2021)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2110.10386)

### Weighted projective embeddings give orbifolds a stability condition for constant curvature

**Remember:** Weighted coordinates remember the finite groups at singular points.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 32Q26 (Notions of stability for complex manifolds), 53C55, 14L24. arXiv math.AG, math.DG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** An orbifold looks locally like a smooth space divided by a finite group. It is polarized if it carries an ample line bundle. In weighted projective space, the coordinates scale by different powers of one parameter. Embedding an orbifold there gives a notion of K-semistability that sees its finite groups.

**Problem.** Donaldson proved that a constant scalar curvature Kähler metric on a manifold implies K-semistability. Does this hold for orbifolds with cyclic stabilizer groups?

**How the definition helps.** The weighted embedding gives orbifolds a K-semistability notion, so Donaldson’s theorem has an orbifold statement. The paper proves that an orbifold metric of constant scalar curvature implies this K-semistability. With slope stability for orbifolds, this gives an explicit obstruction to such metrics. The abstract says that results of Troyanov, Ghigi–Kollár, Rollin–Singer and others fit this frame. Our own explanation is that ordinary projective embeddings lose the information of the finite groups.

**Paper or page:** [Weighted projective embeddings, stability of orbifolds and constant scalar curvature Kähler metrics](https://arxiv.org/abs/0907.5214v2). It says: “We then prove an orbifold version of Donaldson's theorem: the existence of an orbifold Kahler metric of constant scalar curvature implies K-semistability.”

**Sources:**

- [J. Ross, R. P. Thomas, Weighted projective embeddings, stability of orbifolds and constant scalar curvature Kähler metrics, arXiv:0907.5214 (2009), J.Diff.Geom.88:109-159,2011](https://arxiv.org/abs/0907.5214v2)

### Visibility gives convex domains the Denjoy–Wolff property

**Remember:** If geodesics must dive inward, orbits cannot drift to two boundary points.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 32Q45 (Hyperbolic and Kobayashi hyperbolic manifolds), 32H50. arXiv math.CV, math.DS. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** The Kobayashi distance is a distance on a complex domain that holomorphic maps never increase. A domain has a visibility property when near-geodesics between two different boundary points all pass through one compact set inside it. So such geodesics bend into the interior, as in the hyperbolic disc. Complex visibility and essential visibility are versions of this idea.

**Problem.** The Denjoy–Wolff property says that for every holomorphic self-map without fixed points, all orbits converge to one boundary point. The theorem in the data gives it for some bounded convex domains in ℂᴺ. Their boundary must contain no non-trivial analytic discs, and they must be complex visible or essentially visible.

**How the definition helps.** Visibility stops an orbit from accumulating at two different boundary points. The theorem says this directly: every other limit point of the orbit is non-visible from the first one. Our own reason is that the Kobayashi geodesic between two such points would have to pass through a fixed compact set. Our own example of the failure is the bidisc, which is convex but has discs in its boundary. Take a parabolic automorphism φ of the disc and the map (z, w) ↦ (φ(z), w). Each orbit tends to a boundary point that depends on w. The 2021 paper notes that the proof needs a form of visibility between two of the notions it compares.

**Paper or page:** [Some open questions and conjectures about visibility and iteration in bounded convex domains in ℂᴺ](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.19967v2), [Notions of Visibility with respect to the Kobayashi distance: Comparison and Applications](https://arxiv.org/abs/2111.00549v2). It says: “In particular, if Ω is complex visible or essentially visible then it enjoys the Denjoy-Wolff property.”

**Sources:**

- [Filippo Bracci, Ahmed Yekta Ökten, Some open questions and conjectures about visibility and iteration in bounded convex domains in ℂᴺ, Complex Anal. Synerg. 11 (2025) Paper No. 23, arXiv:2507.19967](https://doi.org/10.1007/s40627-025-00172-2)
- [Vikramjeet Singh Chandel, Anwoy Maitra, Amar Deep Sarkar, Notions of Visibility with respect to the Kobayashi distance: Comparison and Applications, arXiv:2111.00549 (2021)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2111.00549v2)
- [Bharali, Zimmer, Goldilocks domains, a weak notion of visibility, and applications, Advances in Mathematics 310 (2017), 377–425](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.aim.2017.02.005)

### The convex approximation property gives every form of the Oka principle

**Remember:** Approximate on convex sets, and every Oka principle follows.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 32Q56 (Oka principle and Oka manifolds), 32Q28. arXiv math.CV. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A complex manifold Y has the convex approximation property (CAP) when the following holds for every compact convex set K in ℂⁿ. Every holomorphic map to Y from a neighbourhood of K is a uniform limit on K of holomorphic maps from all of ℂⁿ. Manifolds with this property are called Oka manifolds.

**Problem.** Let X be a Stein space, a complex space with many holomorphic functions, such as a closed complex submanifold of ℂⁿ. For maps from X to a manifold Y with CAP, every continuous map is homotopic to a holomorphic one, also with approximation, interpolation and parameters. All these versions of the Oka principle are equivalent to each other.

**How the definition helps.** CAP is one simple test on convex sets in ℂⁿ, and the quoted theorem derives all the global Oka properties from it. So, in our own words, once Oka manifolds are defined by CAP, a new example needs only this one test. The work moves into that theorem, due to Forstnerič. Our own example of a manifold without CAP is the unit disc. A holomorphic map from ℂⁿ into the disc is constant by Liouville's theorem, so a nonconstant map on a small ball cannot be approximated. The survey also gives a homotopy form. Holomorphic maps from X into an Oka manifold Y form a space weakly homotopy equivalent to the continuous maps.

**Paper or page:** [From Stein manifolds to Oka manifolds: the h-principle in complex analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.21197v1). It says: “A complex manifold Y which enjoys CAP has all Oka properties in Def. for maps X → Y from any Stein space X. Furthermore, all these Oka properties are pairwise equivalent.”

**Sources:**

- [Franc Forstnerič, From Stein manifolds to Oka manifolds: the h-principle in complex analysis, arXiv:2509.21197 (2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.21197v1)
- [Forstnerič, Runge approximation on convex sets implies the Oka property, Annals of Mathematics 163 (2006), 689–707](https://doi.org/10.4007/annals.2006.163.689)

### Paracyclic representations define perverse sheaves on surfaces without derived categories

**Remember:** On a surface, a perverse sheaf is a representation of Milnor disks.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 32S60 (Stratifications; constructible sheaves; intersection cohomology (complex-analytic aspects)), 14F08. arXiv math.AG, math.AT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A perverse sheaf is usually a complex of constructible sheaves with support conditions. Such complexes form the heart of a t-structure, the objects that lie in both halves of a chosen splitting of the derived category. Dyckerhoff, Kapranov and Soibelman describe perverse sheaves on a stratified surface as functors on the Milnor disks of the surface's paracyclic category. A Milnor disk is a pair of a closed disk and a part of its boundary.

**Problem.** Constructible sheaves on a stratified space are exactly the representations of the exit-path category. Is there a similar description of perverse sheaves?

**How the definition helps.** Only functors on Milnor disks with simple gluing conditions are needed, so perverse sheaves form an abelian category with no derived categories. Usually the abelian structure comes from a theorem about the heart of a t-structure (our own). The key step is a purity property. A constructible complex is perverse exactly when its relative cohomology on every Milnor disk is zero outside degree 0. These degree-0 groups are the values of the functor. The method is for stratified surfaces only.

**Paper or page:** [Perverse sheaves on Riemann surfaces as Milnor sheaves](https://arxiv.org/abs/2012.11388v2). It says: “In particular, this perspective yields an intrinsic definition of perverse sheaves as an abelian category without reference to derived categories and t-structures.”

**Sources:**

- [Tobias Dyckerhoff, Mikhail Kapranov, Yan Soibelman, Perverse sheaves on Riemann surfaces as Milnor sheaves, arXiv:2012.11388v2 (2021)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2012.11388v2)

## 33 Special functions

### Defining cosh and sinh by exponentials makes their addition laws algebra

**Remember:** The exponential addition law gives the hyperbolic addition laws.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 33B10 (Exponential and trigonometric functions), 26A09. arXiv math.CA. Level 1: early undergraduate.

**Definition.** Define cosh t = (eᵗ + e⁻ᵗ)/2 and sinh t = (eᵗ − e⁻ᵗ)/2. The geometric definition takes (cosh t, sinh t) as the point on the right branch of x² − y² = 1. There, t is twice the signed area of the sector from (1, 0) to that point.

**Problem.** For real x and y, sinh(x + y) = sinh x cosh y + cosh x sinh y.

**How the definition helps.** With exponential definitions, the identity is a polynomial identity in eˣ and eʸ (our own). Expanding the right side, the terms eˣ⁻ʸ and eʸ⁻ˣ cancel, and only eˣ⁺ʸ and e⁻ˣ⁻ʸ remain (our own). With the geometric definition, one first needs the exponential formulas. The work moves into an area calculation. For a point (p, q) on the hyperbola, twice the sector area equals ln(p + q) (our own). Solving p + q = eᵗ and p² − q² = 1 then gives the exponential formulas (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Hyperbolic functions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyperbolic_functions). It says: “sinh(x + y) = sinh x cosh y + cosh x sinh y”

**Sources:**

- [James McMahon, Hyperbolic Functions, John Wiley and Sons (1896).](https://archive.org/details/hyperbolicfuncti031883mbp)

### Unit-circle coordinates give the Pythagorean identity

**Remember:** The squares of the coordinates of a point on the unit circle sum to one.

*True by definition.* MSC 33B10 (Exponential and trigonometric functions), 97G60. arXiv math.CA, math.HO. Level 1: early undergraduate.

**Definition.** On the unit circle centred at (0, 0), start at (1, 0) and turn through the angle θ in radians. Take counterclockwise turns as positive. Define cos θ as the horizontal coordinate of the endpoint and sin θ as the vertical coordinate. The right-triangle definition instead uses ratios of sides and starts with acute angles.

**Problem.** For every real angle θ, cos²θ + sin²θ = 1.

**How the definition helps.** The coordinate definition makes cos²θ + sin²θ = 1 the equation of the circle. The Pythagorean theorem gives that equation by relating distance from the origin to the two coordinates. For acute angles, the triangle definition gives the same coordinates because the hypotenuse has length 1.

**Wikipedia:** [Trigonometric functions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trigonometric_functions). It says: “And since the equation x²+y²=1 holds for all points P = (x,y) on the unit circle, this definition of cosine and sine also satisfies the Pythagorean identity.”

### Unit-circle coordinates make sine and cosine periodic

**Remember:** One more full turn lands on the same point, so the values repeat.

*True by definition.* MSC 33B10 (Exponential and trigonometric functions), 97G60. arXiv math.CA, math.HO. Level 1: early undergraduate.

**Definition.** Start at (1, 0) and travel a signed distance θ along the unit circle, with positive distance measured counterclockwise. Define cos θ as the horizontal coordinate of the endpoint and sin θ as the vertical coordinate.

**Problem.** For every real θ and every integer k, sin(θ + 2πk) = sin θ and cos(θ + 2πk) = cos θ.

**How the definition helps.** Sine and cosine repeat because travelling one more circumference returns to the same point. The circumference of a unit circle is 2π, so any whole number of extra turns leaves both coordinates unchanged. With power-series definitions, a different proof is needed. One route proves that the series agree with the circle coordinates, using arc length to link the angle to the series (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Trigonometric functions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trigonometric_functions). It says: “the points A, B, C, D, and E are the same for two angles whose difference is an integer multiple of 2π. Thus trigonometric functions are periodic functions with period 2π.”

### Defining π through the exponential gives Euler’s identity

**Remember:** π is where exp(it) first reaches −1, so exp(iπ) = −1 is the definition.

*True by definition.* MSC 33B10 (Exponential and trigonometric functions), 26A09. arXiv math.CA, math.CV. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** For real t, let φ(t) = exp(it), where i² = −1. Define π as the least positive t with φ(t) = −1. The geometric definition uses the ratio of a circle’s circumference to its diameter.

**Problem.** exp(iπ) = −1. Also, exp(z + 2πi) = exp(z) for every complex number z.

**How the definition helps.** Euler’s identity is the condition that defines π. Squaring it gives exp(2πi) = 1, so the addition law for exp gives the stated period. The work is to show that φ reaches −1 and has a first positive time at −1. The nLab proves that φ reaches the whole circle by showing it first covers an arc near 1. Since φ(−t) = 1/φ(t), any negative solution gives a positive one. Continuity keeps solutions away from 0 and ensures that the first positive solution exists (our own). To recover geometric π, show that the curve runs along the unit circle at speed 1 (our own).

**nLab:** [pi](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/pi). It says: “We may define π to be the least positive t such that φ(t) = −1”

### Exponential definitions make the cosine product-to-sum rule algebra

**Remember:** Write everything as exponentials, multiply out, and read off the identity.

*True by definition.* MSC 33B10 (Exponential and trigonometric functions), 30D20. arXiv math.CA, math.CV. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** Define the complex exponential by the series exp(z) = 1 + z + z²/2! + z³/3! + ⋯. For real x, define cos x = (exp(ix) + exp(−ix))/2. Define sin x = (exp(ix) − exp(−ix))/(2i), where i² = −1. The geometric definition instead uses the coordinates of a point on the unit circle.

**Problem.** For all real a and b, 2 cos a cos b = cos(a − b) + cos(a + b).

**How the definition helps.** The exponential definition reduces the product of cosines to four products of exponentials. The law exp(u + v) = exp(u) exp(v) converts each product to a single exponential. Pairing exponents of opposite sign gives the two cosines (our own calculation). With the circle definition, one can instead add the formulas for cos(a + b) and cos(a − b). The work moves into proving the exponential law and showing that these formulas for sine and cosine give the circle coordinates (our own comparison).

Give t a negative sign below the axis and define cosh t = x and sinh t = y. Another definition sets cosh t = (exp(t) + exp(−t))/2 and sinh t = (exp(t) − exp(−t))/2.

**Problem.** For every real t, cosh²t − sinh²t = 1.

**How the definition helps.** The coordinate definition makes the identity the equation of the hyperbola. With the exponential definition, one instead expands and subtracts the two squares. The work moves into showing that the signed area gives the exponential formulas. Our own calculation uses the fact that twice the signed area is the integral of x dy − y dx along the arc. With u = x + y and x − y = 1/u, this becomes the integral of 1/u from 1 to x + y. Thus x + y = exp(t) and x − y = exp(−t).

### Euler’s limit definition gives Γ(x + 1) = xΓ(x) at every non-pole

**Remember:** In Euler’s limit, neighbouring products cancel and leave a factor tending to x.

*True by definition.* MSC 33B15 (Gamma, beta and polygamma functions). arXiv math.CA. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** Let x be complex, other than 0, −1, −2, …. Define Γ(x) as the limit of k!·k raised to x − 1, over x(x + 1)⋯(x + k − 1), as k grows. The usual definition is Euler’s integral of t raised to x − 1 times exp(−t) over the positive half-line. That integral converges only when the real part of x is positive.

**Problem.** For every complex x other than 0, −1, −2, …, Γ(x + 1) = xΓ(x).

**How the definition helps.** With Euler’s limit, the quotient of the finite expressions at x + 1 and at x is kx/(x + k), which tends to x. So the formula holds at once on the whole domain. The integral definition gives the formula by integration by parts, but only where the real part of x is positive. Beyond that region one needs analytic continuation, which itself uses the formula. The work moves to two facts, that the limit exists and that it equals the integral when the real part of x is positive. These proof steps are our own; the nLab page states the definition and the formula.

### Working with 1/Γ gives a gamma product formula with no exceptions

**Remember:** The gamma function has poles; its reciprocal has zeros and no exceptions.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 33B15 (Gamma, beta and polygamma functions). arXiv math.CV. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** The reciprocal gamma function is 1/Γ(z). It is entire of order 1. It has simple zeros at 0, −1, −2, … and no other zeros.

**Problem.** For every complex z, 1/Γ(z) = z exp(γz) ∏ (1 + z/n) exp(−z/n), where γ is the Euler–Mascheroni constant. The reflection formula becomes 1/(Γ(z)Γ(1 − z)) = sin(πz)/π for all z (our own).

**How the definition helps.** Turning the poles of Γ into zeros gives an entire function, so its identities hold at every point (our own explanation). For Γ itself, each formula must exclude the non-positive integers. As an entire function, 1/Γ is a Weierstrass product over its zeros. Weierstrass called it the factorielle and used it in developing his factorization theorem. The page also gives Hankel's contour integral for 1/Γ, valid for all z. The page notes that 1/Γ has order 1 but infinite type, so its growth is not of the simplest kind.

### Poisson arrival times make the regularized incomplete gamma a Poisson probability

**Remember:** The nth arrival is late exactly when fewer than n have arrived.

*True by definition.* MSC 33B20 (Incomplete beta and gamma functions (error functions, probability integral, Fresnel integrals)), 60G55. arXiv math.CA, math.PR. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** Fix a positive integer n and x ≥ 0. Let Q(n, x) be the chance that the nth event of a rate-one Poisson process comes after time x. In such a process the waiting times between events are independent and exponential with mean one. The usual definition is the integral of t raised to n − 1 times exp(−t) from x to infinity, divided by (n − 1)!.

**Problem.** For each positive integer n and x ≥ 0, Q(n, x) equals the probability that a Poisson variable with mean x is less than n.

**How the definition helps.** The nth event comes after time x exactly when fewer than n events have happened by time x. The number of events by time x is a Poisson variable with mean x, so the two probabilities agree. With the integral definition, Wikipedia notes that the formula needs repeated integration by parts. The work moves to showing that the nth arrival time has density t raised to n − 1 times exp(−t), divided by (n − 1)!. Convolving n exponential densities gives this. The first two steps and the convolution are our own.

### Rodrigues’s formula makes Hermite polynomials orthogonal by integration by parts

**Remember:** Integrate by parts n times, and the derivatives kill the lower degree polynomial.

*True by definition.* MSC 33C45 (Orthogonal polynomials and functions of hypergeometric type (Jacobi, Laguerre, Hermite, Askey scheme, etc.)). arXiv math.CA. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Problem.** For the weight exp(−x²/2) on the real line, Hₙ is orthogonal to every polynomial q of degree below n.

**How the definition helps.** With Rodrigues’s formula the weight cancels, so the integral pairs q with an nth derivative of the Gaussian exp(−x²/2). Integration by parts n times moves every derivative onto q. The boundary terms vanish because the Gaussian decays fast. The nth derivative of q is zero, since its degree is below n. From the generating function, the usual proof instead integrates a product of two generating functions. ### Defining spherical harmonics by harmonic polynomials makes each degree rotation invariant

**Remember:** Rotations preserve degree and commute with the Laplacian.

*True by definition.* MSC 33C55 (Spherical harmonics). arXiv math.CA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A degree n spherical harmonic is the restriction to the unit sphere of a harmonic homogeneous polynomial of degree n in x, y, z. Harmonic means that the Laplacian, the sum of the three second partial derivatives, is zero. The usual definition uses explicit formulas in spherical coordinates with associated Legendre functions.

**Problem.** For each n, every rotation of the sphere maps degree n spherical harmonics to degree n spherical harmonics.

**How the definition helps.** Rotations preserve both conditions in the definition, so they preserve the space of degree n harmonics. A homogeneous polynomial of degree n composed with a rotation is again homogeneous of degree n. The Laplacian commutes with rotations, so harmonic polynomials stay harmonic. From the coordinate formulas, the same fact needs the addition theorem or Wigner’s rotation matrices. The work moves to showing that the coordinate formulas give a basis of the polynomial space. Separation of variables and a dimension count of 2n + 1 do this. These proof steps are our own; Wikipedia gives the polynomial description.

**Wikipedia:** [Spherical harmonics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spherical_harmonics). It says: “The spherical harmonics can be expressed as the restriction to the unit sphere of certain polynomial functions”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Subtracting 1/λ² makes the Weierstrass ℘ series converge without a constant

**Remember:** Subtract each pole's value at zero, and ℘ converges with no constant term.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 33E05 (Elliptic functions and integrals), 30D30. arXiv math.CV. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A lattice Λ is the set of all integer combinations of two periods that are independent over ℝ. For such a lattice, ℘(z) = 1/z² + Σ over nonzero λ in Λ of (1/(z − λ)² − 1/λ²). The series converges absolutely, locally uniformly away from the lattice.

**Problem.** ℘ is an even elliptic function with periods in Λ and a double pole at each lattice point. It satisfies (℘′)² = 4℘³ − g₂℘ − g₃, where g₂ and g₃ are Eisenstein sums of the lattice.

**How the definition helps.** Each subtracted term makes the summand small, of size 1/\|λ\|³, so the series converges absolutely and can be rearranged. The plain sum of 1/(z − λ)² does not converge absolutely, because the sum of 1/\|λ\|² over a lattice diverges (our own). The same normalization gives ℘(z) − 1/z² the value 0 at z = 0, so the Laurent series has no constant term. Then a combination of powers of ℘ and ℘′ has no pole and is constant by Liouville's theorem, which gives the differential equation. With a constant term c, the equation would gain a ℘² term (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Weierstrass elliptic function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weierstrass_elliptic_function), [Elliptic function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elliptic_function). It says: “It is constructed in such a way that it has a pole of order two at every lattice point. The term −1/λ² is there to make the series convergent.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Orbital residues decide elliptic summability up to two terms

**Remember:** Zero orbital residues make f summable, apart from two explicit extra terms.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: low.* MSC 33E05 (Elliptic functions and integrals), 39A10, 14K20. arXiv math.NT, math.CV. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** An elliptic function f is summable for a shift by s if f = g(z + s) − g(z) for an elliptic function g. Elliptic orbital residues are numbers computed from the poles of f, grouped by their orbits under the shift. A non-torsion point s is one whose multiples never return to zero on the curve.

**Problem.** The Corollary, for a fixed choice it calls an analytic pinning, states when all orbital residues of f vanish. This happens exactly when f minus a summable function equals a + b(ζ(z + s) − ζ(z)), for constants a and b. Here ζ is the Weierstrass zeta function, whose derivative is minus the Weierstrass ℘ function.

**How the definition helps.** Our own reason: the residues reduce summability to a check that a list of numbers is zero, up to two explicit terms. The abstract calls the residues only a partial obstruction. The paper says it refines them into a complete obstruction. The corollary shows what remains: a constant and one multiple of ζ(z + s) − ζ(z). Our own note: that leftover part needs a separate test.

**Paper or page:** [Summability of Elliptic Functions via Residues](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.22770). It says: “Dreyfus, Hardouin, Roques, and Singer introduced a notion of elliptic orbital residues, which altogether serve as a partial obstruction to summability for elliptic functions with respect to the shift by a non-torsion point over an elliptic curve.”

**Sources:**

- [Matthew Babbitt, Summability of Elliptic Functions via Residues, arXiv:2503.22770 (2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.22770)

## 34 Ordinary differential equations

### A Lipschitz condition makes solutions of differential equations unique

**Remember:** Lipschitz bounds the slope of every chord, so solutions cannot split.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 34A12 (Initial value problems, existence, uniqueness, continuous dependence and continuation of solutions to ordinary differential equations), 26A16. arXiv math.CA. Level 1: early undergraduate.

**Definition.** A function f(t, y) is Lipschitz in y when there is a constant L with \|f(t, y₁) − f(t, y₂)\| ≤ L\|y₁ − y₂\|. The constant L does not depend on t.

**Problem.** For f continuous in t, the initial value problem y′ = f(t, y), y(t₀) = y₀ has exactly one solution near t₀.

**How the definition helps.** The Lipschitz condition makes the Picard iteration a contraction, and a contraction has exactly one fixed point. Without the condition, uniqueness fails. The equation y′ = a y²ᐟ³ with y(0) = 0 has at least two solutions. One is y = 0. The other is (at/3)³ for t &lt; 0 and 0 for t ≥ 0. The function y²ᐟ³ is not Lipschitz near 0, because its derivative is unbounded there. With the Lipschitz condition, the integral operator of Picard iteration is a contraction on a short time interval, and the Banach fixed-point theorem gives existence and uniqueness. The result stays local: for y′ = 1 + y² with y(0) = 0, the solution tan t exists only for \|t\| &lt; π/2 (our own example).

**Wikipedia:** [Picard–Lindelöf theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Picard%E2%80%93Lindel%C3%B6f_theorem). It says: “The uniqueness theorem does not apply because the derivative of the function f(y) = y²ᐟ³ is not bounded in the neighborhood of y = 0 and therefore it is not Lipschitz continuous, violating the hypothesis of the theorem.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Riccati equations have global solutions on the projective line

**Remember:** Let y pass through infinity and the blow-up becomes an ordinary point.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 34A05 (Explicit solutions, first integrals of ordinary differential equations), 34A12. arXiv math.CA. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** A Riccati equation is a first-order equation dy/dt = a₀(t) + a₁(t) y + a₂(t) y². Its solutions may take values in the projective line ℝP¹ or ℂP¹, not only in the line ℝ or ℂ. The projective line is the line with one extra point at infinity.

**Problem.** Solutions should exist for all time. They should depend on the initial value by a fractional linear map y(t) = (f y(0) + g)/(h y(0) + i).

**How the definition helps.** On the projective line, a blow-up only passes through the point at infinity, so the solution does not stop. On the ordinary line a Riccati solution can blow up in finite time; for example, dy/dt = 1 + y² gives y = tan t. On the projective line the point at infinity is an ordinary point. So, when the coefficients are defined and regular for all t, the solutions exist for all time. The flow is then given by the action of PGL(2), the group of fractional linear maps, on the projective line, just as linear equations act by affine maps. The reason is standard but not spelled out on the page. The equation is the projective form of a linear 2 × 2 system, whose solutions always exist for all time.

**nLab:** [Riccati equation](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Riccati+equation). It says: “solutions of Riccati equations can blow up in finite time; however, these solutions become defined for all time if we let y take values in the projective line rather than the affine line”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Regular Sturm–Liouville problems have a full basis of eigenfunctions

**Remember:** Finite interval, positive coefficients, one condition per end: pure eigenvalues.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 34B24 (Sturm-Liouville theory), 34B09. arXiv math.CA, math.SP. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** A Sturm–Liouville problem is the equation (p y′)′ + q y = −λ w y on an interval. It is regular if the interval \[a, b\] is finite, p, p′, q and w are continuous, and p &gt; 0 and w &gt; 0. It also needs one separated boundary condition at each end: α₁ y(a) + α₂ y′(a) = 0 and β₁ y(b) + β₂ y′(b) = 0.

**Problem.** For a regular problem, the eigenvalues are real, simple and increase to infinity. The normalized eigenfunctions form an orthonormal basis of the weighted L² space on \[a, b\].

**How the definition helps.** The regularity conditions make the inverse of the operator a compact self-adjoint operator, so the spectral theorem for compact operators applies (our own). Separated conditions make each eigenvalue simple, because only one solution up to a constant meets the condition at a (our own). The conditions exclude singular problems. For example, −y″ = λy on the half-line \[0, ∞) with y(0) = 0 has no square-integrable eigenfunctions (our own). Its spectrum is the continuous set \[0, ∞). For singular problems, eigenfunction expansions still exist but they use integrals, as the Fourier transform does. The hard part there is Weyl's theory of the endpoints (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Sturm–Liouville theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sturm%E2%80%93Liouville_theory). It says: “If the interval is unbounded, or if the coefficients have singularities at the boundary points, one calls L singular. In this case, the spectrum no longer consists of eigenvalues alone and can contain a continuous component.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Asymptotic stability asks for stability as well as attraction

**Remember:** Attracting is not enough; nearby orbits must also stay nearby.

*Rules out counterexamples. Confidence: medium.* MSC 34D20 (Stability of solutions to ordinary differential equations), 37C75. arXiv math.DS, math.CA. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** An equilibrium is Lyapunov stable if solutions that start near it stay near it for all later time. It is attractive if solutions that start near it converge to it. It is asymptotically stable if it is both stable and attractive.

**Problem.** Lyapunov's direct method says that a strict Lyapunov function near an equilibrium makes it asymptotically stable. Massera's converse theorem says that every asymptotically stable equilibrium of a smooth enough system has such a function (our own).

**How the definition helps.** The stability clause rules out equilibria that attract every orbit only after a large excursion. Hahn's book, which the page cites, gives such examples. In Vinograd's planar system of 1957, all orbits tend to the origin, but some that start very close first go far away (our own). A strict Lyapunov function decreases along orbits, so it traps them in small level sets and forbids this (our own). So without the stability clause, the converse theorem would be false (our own). The hard part is building the Lyapunov function in Massera's theorem.

**Wikipedia:** [Lyapunov stability](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lyapunov_stability). It says: “There are examples showing that attractivity does not imply asymptotic stability.”

**Sources:**

- [W. Hahn, Stability of Motion, Springer (1967), Section 40](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-642-50085-5)
- [J. L. Massera, On Liapounoff's conditions of stability, Annals of Mathematics 50 (1949)](https://doi.org/10.2307/1969558)

### Radially unbounded Lyapunov functions make asymptotic stability global

**Remember:** Level sets must close up, or orbits slide off to infinity.

*Rules out counterexamples. Confidence: medium.* MSC 34D23 (Global stability of solutions to ordinary differential equations), 34D20, 93D30. arXiv math.DS, math.OC. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** A function V on ℝⁿ is radially unbounded if V(x) → ∞ whenever ‖x‖ → ∞. Then every sublevel set {V ≤ c} is bounded, and so compact if V is continuous (our own).

**Problem.** Lyapunov's method alone gives stability only near the equilibrium. The Barbashin–Krasovskii theorem asks that V be positive definite, radially unbounded, and strictly decreasing along solutions away from the equilibrium. Then the equilibrium is globally asymptotically stable, so it attracts every starting point.

**How the definition helps.** Radial unboundedness makes each sublevel set of V compact, so a solution that starts in it stays in a compact set. Then the local argument works everywhere. Without it, V can decrease along an orbit that runs off to infinity, because V stays bounded there (our own). The page's example f₂ = r²/(1 + r²) + (x₁ − x₂)², with r² = x₁² + x₂², is positive definite. But along the line x₁ = x₂ it stays below 1. So each sublevel set {f₂ ≤ c} with c ≥ 1 is unbounded, and a solution can escape inside it (our own). The hard part remains finding a suitable V.

**Wikipedia:** [Radially unbounded function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radially_unbounded_function), [Lyapunov function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lyapunov_function), [LaSalle's invariance principle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LaSalle%27s_invariance_principle). It says: “are not radially unbounded since along the line x₁ = x₂, the condition is not verified even though the second function is globally positive definite.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Carathéodory solutions let differential equations have discontinuous right-hand sides

**Remember:** Ask for the equation almost everywhere, and recover y with the Lebesgue integral.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 34A36 (Discontinuous ordinary differential equations), 34A12. arXiv math.CA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Take the initial value problem y′ = f(t, y), y(t₀) = y₀. A solution in the extended sense is an absolutely continuous function y that satisfies the equation almost everywhere and satisfies the initial condition. An absolutely continuous function is one that is the Lebesgue integral of its own derivative, up to a constant.

**Problem.** Show that solutions exist for an ordinary differential equation whose right-hand side is measurable in t but not continuous in t.

**How the definition helps.** The extended definition asks for the equation only almost everywhere, so f need not be continuous in t. Take y′ = H(t), where H is the Heaviside step function (0 for t &lt; 0 and 1 for t &gt; 0). The natural answer is the ramp function (0 for t &lt; 0 and t for t ≥ 0), but it is not differentiable at 0, so it is not a classical solution. With the extended definition, the ramp is a solution. Carathéodory's theorem gives existence when f is continuous in y, measurable in t, and bounded by an integrable function. Peano's theorem, for continuous f, becomes a special case. Uniqueness again needs a Lipschitz-type bound, now with an integrable constant k(t).

**Wikipedia:** [Carathéodory's existence theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carath%C3%A9odory%27s_existence_theorem). It says: “This suggests that the idea of a solution be extended to allow for solutions that are not everywhere differentiable, thus motivating the following definition.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Filippov solutions let systems slide along a switching surface

**Remember:** On a switching surface, average the two sides and slide.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 34A60 (Ordinary differential inclusions), 34A36. arXiv math.CA, math.DS. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Filippov replaces x′ = f(x), for a locally bounded f, by the inclusion x′ ∈ F(x). Here F(x) is the closed convex hull of the values of f near x, ignoring sets of measure zero (our own). A Filippov solution is an absolutely continuous function that satisfies the inclusion at almost every time.

**Problem.** Take x′ = −1 for x &gt; 0 and x′ = 1 for x ≤ 0, with x(0) = 0 (our own). No solution exists, even in Carathéodory's sense, because x cannot leave 0 in either direction and cannot stay there either. Existence theory for inclusions usually assumes that F has closed convex values and depends upper hemicontinuously on x.

**How the definition helps.** At the switching point, the convex hull contains both side values and every average of them, so it contains 0. Then x ≡ 0 is a solution, and the motion slides along the surface (our own). Filippov's construction gives exactly the closed convex values that the existence theorem for inclusions needs (our own). Convexity is the key condition: existence for non-convex F is still an active research area. Uniqueness is not automatic and needs extra conditions (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Differential inclusion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Differential_inclusion). It says: “Differential inclusions can be used to understand and suitably interpret discontinuous ordinary differential equations, such as arise for Coulomb friction in mechanical systems and ideal switches in power electronics.”

**Sources:**

- [A. F. Filippov, Differential Equations with Discontinuous Righthand Sides, Kluwer (1988)](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-94-015-7793-9)

### Weyl's limit-point case means no boundary condition is needed

**Remember:** Each limit-circle end needs one boundary condition; limit-point ends need none.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 34B24 (Sturm-Liouville theory), 47E05. arXiv math.CA, math.SP. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Take a Sturm–Liouville expression τu = (−(pu′)′ + qu)/r on an interval (a, b) whose endpoints may be singular. At an endpoint in the limit circle case, every solution of τu = λu is square integrable near that endpoint. In the limit point case, for non-real λ, only a one-dimensional space of solutions is. Weyl showed that the case does not depend on λ.

**Problem.** The deficiency indices of the minimal operator are 2, 1 or 0 when both, one or neither endpoint is in the limit circle case. So the operator is self-adjoint with no boundary conditions at all exactly when both endpoints are in the limit point case.

**How the definition helps.** The definition counts the square-integrable solutions at each endpoint, and the theorem shows that this count is the number of boundary conditions needed. Part (i) of the theorem gives the mechanism. In the limit point case, the Wronskian boundary term of any two functions in the maximal domain vanishes. Our own example is τu = −u″ + c x⁻² u on (0, ∞). Its solutions near 0 are powers of x, and 0 is limit point exactly when c ≥ 3/4; this is also our own. Our own remark is that the hard part is Weyl's alternative, that the case is the same for every λ.

**Paper or page:** [The Jacobi operator on (−1,1) and its various m-functions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.12164v1), [On Sesquilinear Forms for Lower Semibounded (Singular) Sturm-Liouville Operators](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.07205v1). It says: “In particular, Tₘᵢₙ = Tₘₐₓ is self-adjoint (i.e., Ṫₘᵢₙ is essentially self-adjoint) if and only if τ is in the limit point case at a and b.”

**Sources:**

- [Fritz Gesztesy, Lance L. Littlejohn, Mateusz Piorkowski, Jonathan Stanfill, The Jacobi operator on (−1,1) and its various m-functions, Complex Anal. Oper. Theory 18 (2024) Paper No. 155, arXiv:2307.12164](https://doi.org/10.1007/s11785-024-01576-4)
- [Jussi Behrndt, Fritz Gesztesy, Seppo Hassi, Roger Nichols, Henk de Snoo, On Sesquilinear Forms for Lower Semibounded (Singular) Sturm-Liouville Operators, arXiv:2509.07205 (2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.07205v1)
- [Weyl, Über gewöhnliche Differentialgleichungen mit Singularitäten und die zugehörigen Entwicklungen willkürlicher Funktionen, Mathematische Annalen 68 (1910), 220–269](https://doi.org/10.1007/bf01474161)

### Defining singular Schrödinger operators by quadratic forms makes them self-adjoint

**Remember:** Define the operator by its energy, and self-adjointness comes free.

*True by definition.* MSC 34L40 (Particular ordinary differential operators (Dirac, one-dimensional Schrödinger, etc.)), 47B25, 47A07. arXiv math.SP, math.FA. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** The potential q is a real 1-periodic distribution in the Sobolev space H⁻¹, such as a periodic sum of Dirac deltas. H⁻¹ is the dual of H¹, the space of functions with a square-integrable derivative. So −u″ + qu has no direct meaning for most u. The form-sum operator is the self-adjoint operator given by the quadratic form ∫\|u′\|² + ⟨q, \|u\|²⟩ on H¹(ℝ).

**Problem.** For a singular potential, which operator is the Schrödinger operator, and is it self-adjoint? Several definitions exist, such as quasi-differential operators, form sums and limits of smooth potentials.

**How the definition helps.** With the form definition, self-adjointness and a lower bound come from the representation theorem for closed forms that are bounded below. The real step is to show that ⟨q, \|u\|²⟩ is small compared with ∫\|u′\|², so the sum stays closed and bounded below (our own). Proposition 17, quoted from earlier work, states that these form-sum operators are well defined and self-adjoint. Theorem 18, the main work, shows that the quasi-differential operators equal the form-sum operators. In our own gloss, quasi-differential operators rewrite the equation as a first-order system. Corollary 15 shows that the minimal operator, the Friedrichs extension and the maximal operator also coincide. So there is only one self-adjoint realization, and the abstract says all five definitions agree.

**Paper or page:** [One-dimensional Schrödinger operators with singular periodic potentials](https://arxiv.org/abs/0805.1000), [One-dimensional Schrödinger operators with singular periodic potentials](https://arxiv.org/abs/0805.1000), [One-dimensional Schrödinger operators with singular periodic potentials](https://arxiv.org/abs/0805.1000), [One-dimensional Schrödinger operators with singular periodic potentials](https://arxiv.org/abs/0805.1000). It says: “with 1-periodic real-valued singular potentials q(x) ∈ H⁻¹per(ℝ,ℝ) on the Hilbert space L₂(ℝ). We show equivalence of five basic definitions of the operators S(q) and prove that they are self-adjoint.”

**Sources:**

- [V. Mikhailets, V. Molyboga, One-dimensional Schrödinger operators with singular periodic potentials, Methods Funct. Anal. Topology 14 (2008), no. 2, 184–200, arXiv:0805.1000](https://arxiv.org/abs/0805.1000)

## 35 Partial differential equations

### Weak solutions let kinked traveling waves satisfy the transport equation

**Remember:** Move derivatives onto the test function and the traveling wave can have kinks.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 35D30 (Weak solutions to PDEs), 35F10. arXiv math.AP. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** A test function φ is smooth and has compact support in the time and space variables. A locally integrable u weakly solves ∂ₜu + ∂ₓu = 0 if the integral of u(∂ₜφ + ∂ₓφ) is zero for every φ. A classical solution instead needs derivatives of u itself.

**Problem.** For every locally integrable g on ℝ, the traveling wave u(t, x) = g(x − t) is a weak solution. In particular, \|x − t\| is a solution even though it has a kink at x = t.

**How the definition helps.** The weak definition lets us state the claim for any locally integrable profile because it differentiates only the test function. In our own proof, substitute y = x − t. The integrand becomes g(y) times the time derivative of φ(t, y + t) with y fixed. The time integral is zero because φ has compact support. The work moves into the integration-by-parts formula that recovers the classical equation for smooth functions.

**Wikipedia:** [Weak solution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weak_solution). It says: “The key to the concept of weak solution is that there exist functions u that satisfy equation (2) for any φ, but such u may not be differentiable and so cannot satisfy equation (1).”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Fundamental solutions solve forced equations by convolution

**Remember:** Solve once for a point source, then convolve with the data.

*True by definition.* MSC 35A08 (Fundamental solutions to PDEs), 46F10. arXiv math.AP. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let P be a nonzero linear differential operator with constant coefficients. A fundamental solution is a distribution E with PE = δ, where δ evaluates a test function at zero. A distribution is a continuous linear functional on smooth test functions of compact support. The classical Newtonian potential for the Laplacian instead starts with an explicit integral kernel.

**Problem.** If f is a distribution with compact support, the convolution u = E ∗ f satisfies Pu = f as distributions.

**How the definition helps.** The defining equation PE = δ gives the convolution identity P(E ∗ f) = (PE) ∗ f = f, in our own proof. Derivatives pass to the first factor, and δ is the identity for convolution. The work moves into proving these rules and into the Malgrange–Ehrenpreis theorem, which supplies E for every such P. Our own comparison is with proving Poisson’s equation by differentiating the Newtonian potential directly near its singularity.

**Wikipedia:** [Fundamental solution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fundamental_solution). It says: “Once the fundamental solution is found, it is straightforward to find a solution of the original equation, through convolution of the fundamental solution and the desired right hand side.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Wave front sets say when two distributions can be multiplied

**Remember:** The wave front set records where a distribution is singular and in which directions.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 35A27 (Microlocal methods and methods of sheaf theory and homological algebra applied to PDEs), 46F10. arXiv math.AP. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** The wave front set WF(u) of a distribution u is the set of points x with covector directions k such that the Fourier transform of u, localized near x, does not decay rapidly in direction k. So it records where u is singular and in which directions. It is a subset of the cotangent bundle minus the zero section.

**Problem.** When is the product u · v of two distributions defined?

**How the definition helps.** The wave front set gives a simple test for when a product of distributions exists. In general, two distributions cannot be multiplied. Hörmander's criterion says that the product exists when WF(u) + WF(v) does not meet the zero section. In words: at no point does a direction in one wave front set have its opposite in the other. The product is then the pullback of the tensor product along the diagonal. Without the wave front set there is no clean general statement. This criterion is the basis of the rigorous treatment of products of propagators in perturbative quantum field theory.

**nLab:** [product of distributions](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/product+of+distributions), [Hörmander's criterion](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/H%C3%B6rmander%27s+criterion). It says: “the condition that the product of two distributions is well defined is that for each wave vector direction in the wave front set of one of the two distributions, the opposite direction must not be an element”

**Sources:**

- [Lars Hörmander, Fourier integral operators. I, Acta Mathematica 127 (1971) 79–183](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02392052)

### Leray's weak solutions give global existence for the Navier–Stokes equations

**Remember:** Ask only what the energy controls, and solutions exist for all time.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 35D30 (Weak solutions to PDEs), 35Q30, 35A01. arXiv math.AP. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A Leray weak solution is a divergence-free velocity field with finite energy and a square-integrable gradient. It satisfies the equations after integration against smooth divergence-free test fields. It also obeys an energy inequality (our own).

**Problem.** Leray proved in 1934 that the three-dimensional Navier–Stokes equations have a weak solution for all time, from every initial velocity of finite energy. Whether smooth solutions exist for all time is open, and it is a Millennium Prize problem.

**How the definition helps.** The weak form asks only for bounds that the energy estimate supplies, so limits of approximate solutions are again solutions (our own). So Leray could prove in 1934 that weak solutions exist for all time and for all finite-energy data. Their uniqueness and smoothness remain open, and that is the hard part. The definition thus splits the problem into an easy global existence and an open regularity question.

**Wikipedia:** [Navier–Stokes existence and smoothness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Navier%E2%80%93Stokes_existence_and_smoothness). It says: “He also proved the existence of so-called weak solutions to the Navier–Stokes equations, which may not satisfy the equations pointwise but do satisfy them in mean value.”

**Sources:**

- [J. Leray, Sur le mouvement d'un liquide visqueux emplissant l'espace, Acta Mathematica 63 (1934) 193–248](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02547354)

### The weak formulation lets Lax–Milgram solve Poisson's equation

**Remember:** Test against every v in the same space where you look for u.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 35D30 (Weak solutions to PDEs), 35J25, 46E35. arXiv math.AP. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** The weak formulation of −Δu = f, with u = 0 on the boundary, asks for u in the Sobolev space H¹₀(Ω) with ∫ ∇u · ∇v = ∫ f v for every v in H¹₀(Ω). H¹₀(Ω) is the space of functions that vanish on the boundary and have square-integrable weak derivatives. A weak derivative is a derivative defined through integration by parts against smooth test functions.

**Problem.** We want existence and uniqueness of a solution of Poisson's equation with zero boundary values. We also want an estimate of the solution in terms of f.

**How the definition helps.** In H¹₀ the problem fits the Lax–Milgram theorem exactly, so the theorem gives the solution at once. In this space the left side is a bounded and coercive bilinear form; coercive means that the form of u with itself is at least c‖u‖² for some c &gt; 0. So the Lax–Milgram theorem (1954) gives a unique solution and the bound ‖u‖ ≤ ‖f‖/c. Our own remark: for a symmetric form, as here, the result is just the Riesz representation theorem for the inner product given by the form. The article shows that the same theorem covers a finite linear system. The choice of space does the work: its elements vanish on the boundary and have square-integrable weak derivatives, which is exactly what the weak equation needs. Showing that the weak solution is a classical solution is a separate regularity question.

**Wikipedia:** [Weak formulation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weak_formulation), [Sobolev space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sobolev_space). It says: “The appropriate space to satisfy these requirements is the Sobolev space H¹₀(Ω) of functions with weak derivatives in L²(Ω) and with zero boundary conditions”
