- [Trevor Clark, Kostiantyn Drach, Oleg Kozlovski, Sebastian van Strien, The dynamics of complex box mappings, arXiv:2105.08654 (2022)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2105.08654v2)

### Diophantine frequencies bound the small divisors, so KAM tori survive

**Remember:** Badly approximable frequencies resist small perturbations.

*Rules out counterexamples. Confidence: medium.* MSC 37J40 (Perturbations of finite-dimensional Hamiltonian systems, normal forms, small divisors, KAM theory, Arnol'd diffusion), 37C55. arXiv math.DS, math.SG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A frequency vector ω in ℝᵈ is Diophantine if there are numbers γ, τ &gt; 0 with this property. For every nonzero integer vector k, \|ω · k\| is at least γ divided by ‖k‖ to the power τ. So ω is badly approximated by rational relations among its entries.

**Problem.** An integrable Hamiltonian system has phase space filled with invariant tori that carry quasiperiodic motion. Under a small perturbation, which tori survive? The KAM theorem says that tori with Diophantine frequencies survive, if a non-degeneracy condition holds and the perturbation is small enough.

**How the definition helps.** The proof divides by the numbers ω · k, the small divisors, and the Diophantine bound keeps them from being too small (our own). They shrink only polynomially in ‖k‖, so a rapidly converging Newton method can beat them (our own). The condition excludes resonant tori, where ω · k = 0 for some k, and the page says these break up under perturbation. When τ &gt; d − 1, almost every frequency vector is Diophantine, in the sense of measure (our own). The hard part is the convergence proof.

**Wikipedia:** [Kolmogorov–Arnold–Moser theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kolmogorov%E2%80%93Arnold%E2%80%93Moser_theorem). It says: “Surviving tori meet the non-resonance condition, i.e., they have sufficiently irrational frequencies.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Observables that vanish on the constraint set have zero Eden bracket

**Remember:** Project onto the allowed states before taking the bracket.

*True by definition.* MSC 37J60 (Nonholonomic dynamical systems), 37J55. arXiv math-ph, math.SG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** The contact Eden bracket combines two observables of a mechanical system with dissipation and velocity constraints. One first pulls both observables back along a projection onto the allowed states, then takes a bracket there.

**Problem.** The paper proves that a function constant on the allowed states has zero Eden bracket with every observable. In particular, a function that vanishes there does. So two extensions of an observable that agree on the allowed states give the same bracket.

**How the definition helps.** The projection turns a function that vanishes on the allowed states into the zero function, so its bracket with anything is zero by bilinearity. In our own words, this is why the bracket depends only on values on the allowed states. The case of nonzero constants also uses the form of the bracket. The work moves to proving that the bracket gives the constrained motion.

**Paper or page:** [The contact Eden bracket and the evolution of observables](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.00997v1). It says: “Any function g on T∗Q × ℝ that is constant on ℳ × ℝ is a Casimir, i.e.,”

**Sources:**

- [V. M. Jiménez, M. De León, The contact Eden bracket and the evolution of observables, arXiv:2504.00997v1 (2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.00997v1)

## 39 Difference and functional equations

### Falling powers make polynomial differences and sums simple

**Remember:** Differences of falling powers copy the power rule, so sums telescope.

*True by definition.* MSC 39A70 (Difference operators), 05A10. arXiv math.CO. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** The falling factorial (x)ₘ is the product x(x − 1)⋯(x − m + 1) for a positive integer m, with (x)₀ = 1. The forward difference of a function f is Δf(x) = f(x + 1) − f(x). Instead of usual powers xᵐ, one can use falling factorials to write polynomials.

**Problem.** For m ≥ 1, Δ(x)ₘ = m(x)ₘ₋₁. The sum of (k)ₘ for k = 0, …, n − 1 is (n)ₘ₊₁/(m + 1) for integers m ≥ 0 and n ≥ 1.

**How the definition helps.** The falling-factorial definition gives the difference rule because the two products share all but one factor. Factoring out (x)ₘ₋₁ leaves the difference (x + 1) − (x − m + 1) = m (our own calculation). Adding consecutive differences cancels the intermediate terms and gives the sum, since (0)ₘ₊₁ = 0. The difference of an ordinary power instead gives several terms by the binomial theorem. For general polynomial sums, the work moves into rewriting the polynomial in falling factorials (our own comparison).

**Wikipedia:** [Falling and rising factorials](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Falling_and_rising_factorials). It says: “In this formula, the falling factorial (x)ₙ in the calculus of finite differences plays the role of xⁿ in differential calculus.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Twisted Mahler residues decide whether a rational function is a twisted difference

**Remember:** Group poles by pth powers before checking for cancellation.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 39A13 (Difference equations, scaling (\\(q\\)-differences)), 12H10. arXiv math.NT, math.CA. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Fix integers p &gt; 1 and λ. Write a rational function f in partial fractions. Group its poles into classes whose members are related by repeated pth powers or pth roots. The λ-twisted Mahler discrete residues are built from the partial-fraction coefficients along these classes.

**Problem.** Let f be a rational function over the paper’s base field 𝕂. The question is whether f(x) equals p to the power λ times g(xᵖ), minus g(x), for some rational function g. Theorem 1.1 says this holds exactly when every λ-twisted Mahler discrete residue of f is zero.

**How the definition helps.** The residues turn an equation with an unknown rational function g into a finite list of tests on f. In our own explanation, the substitution x ↦ xᵖ moves poles only within a class, so g can cancel f only class by class. In our own account, one direction is direct, and the harder direction builds g when all residues vanish. The case λ = 0 is the untwisted Mahler summability problem from the authors’ earlier work.

**Paper or page:** [Twisted Mahler discrete residues](https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.16765v1). It says: “For λ ∈ ℤ, f(x) ∈ 𝕂(x) is λ-Mahler summable if and only if every λ-Mahler discrete residue of f is zero.”

**Sources:**

- [Carlos E. Arreche, Yi Zhang, Twisted Mahler discrete residues, arXiv:2308.16765v1 (2023). International Mathematics Research Notices IMRN 2024(23), 14259-14288, (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.16765v1)

### Mahler discrete residues decide Mahler summability

**Remember:** All Mahler residues vanish exactly when f has the form g(xᵖ) − g(x).

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 39A20 (Multiplicative and other generalized difference equations), 39A45. arXiv math.NT, math.CA. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Fix an integer p &gt; 1. A rational function f(x) is Mahler summable if f(x) = g(xᵖ) − g(x) for some rational function g. Mahler discrete residues are vectors computed from f, one for each group of poles of f and each order k. Our own note: poles α and β share a group when α raised to pʳ equals β raised to pˢ for some r and s.

**Problem.** Decide whether a given rational function is Mahler summable. The paper shows that f is Mahler summable exactly when all its Mahler discrete residues are zero. Proposition 4.18 states this one component at a time.

**How the definition helps.** Our own reason: the residues turn a search for an unknown g into a check that some vectors are zero. Our own analogy: a rational function is the derivative of a rational function exactly when all its ordinary residues are zero. The abstract says that the paper extends known discrete residues to the Mahler case. Our own note: Chen and Singer introduced such residues for the shift case. What stays hard is to find the right grouping of poles, so that the residues are complete (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Mahler discrete residues and summability for rational functions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.09805). It says: “We construct Mahler discrete residues for rational functions and show that they comprise a complete obstruction to the Mahler summability problem”

**Sources:**

- [Carlos E. Arreche, Yi Zhang, Mahler discrete residues and summability for rational functions, Proceedings of ISSAC 2022, pp. 525-533, arXiv:2202.09805](https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.09805)
- [Shaoshi Chen, Michael F. Singer, Residues and telescopers for bivariate rational functions, Advances in Applied Mathematics (2012)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.aam.2012.04.003)

### A radiation condition makes lattice wave problems uniquely solvable

**Remember:** Keep the outgoing wave and rule out waves coming in from infinity.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 39A27 (Boundary value problems for difference equations), 39A14. arXiv math.AP. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** The discrete Helmholtz equation is Δu + k²u = 0, where Δ is the difference Laplacian of the triangular lattice. A radiating solution also satisfies a radiation condition at infinity. This condition is a lattice form of the Sommerfeld condition and allows only outgoing waves far from the sources.

**Problem.** Fix a wave number k with 0 &lt; k &lt; 2√2. Prescribe data on finitely many finite rows or columns of lattice sites. The exterior problem then has exactly one radiating solution.

**How the definition helps.** The radiation condition removes the solutions that the equation and the finite data cannot tell apart. Our own example is a finite sum of lattice plane waves chosen to vanish at the finitely many data sites. It solves the problem with zero data, but it does not decay, so the condition excludes it. The paper proves uniqueness first and then builds the solution from difference potentials.

**Paper or page:** [Propagation of Waves from Finite Sources Arranged in Line Segments within an Infinite Triangular Lattice](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.18806v3). It says: “Consistent with a continuum theory, we employ the notion of radiating solution and establish a unique solvability result and Green's representation formula using difference potentials.”

**Sources:**

- [David Kapanadze, Zurab Vashakidze, Propagation of Waves from Finite Sources Arranged in Line Segments within an Infinite Triangular Lattice, arXiv:2405.18806 (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.18806v3)

## 40 Sequences, series, summability

### Absolute convergence makes rearranging a series safe

**Remember:** If the sizes alone add up to something finite, the order cannot matter.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 40A05 (Convergence and divergence of series and sequences). arXiv math.CA. Level 1: early undergraduate.

**Definition.** A series Σaₙ converges absolutely when the series of absolute values Σ\|aₙ\| converges.

**Problem.** Every rearrangement of a convergent series has the same sum.

**How the definition helps.** Absolute convergence is exactly the condition under which, for real series, the order of the terms does not change the sum. The statement is false for convergent series in general. Cauchy (1833) found that a rearrangement of the alternating harmonic series can have a different sum. Dirichlet saw that absolute convergence rules this out. Riemann showed that the condition is sharp for real series. A convergent real series that does not converge absolutely can be rearranged to give any real sum, or to diverge. In ℝⁿ the picture is harder: Lévy and Steinitz showed that the set of sums of all rearrangements is an affine subspace.

**Wikipedia:** [Riemann series theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemann_series_theorem), [Absolute convergence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Absolute_convergence). It says: “Around the same time, Peter Gustav Lejeune Dirichlet highlighted that such phenomena are ruled out in the context of absolute convergence, and gave further examples of Cauchy's phenomenon for some other series which fail to be absolutely convergent.”

**Sources:**

- [B. Riemann, Über die Darstellbarkeit einer Function durch eine trigonometrische Reihe, Abh. Königl. Ges. Wiss. Göttingen 13 (1868), 87–132](http://resolver.sub.uni-goettingen.de/purl?PPN250442582_0013)
- [E. Steinitz, Bedingt konvergente Reihen und konvexe Systeme, J. reine angew. Math. 143 (1913), 128–176, doi:10.1515/crll.1913.143.128](https://doi.org/10.1515/crll.1913.143.128)

### Convergence of an infinite product excludes the limit zero

**Remember:** A convergent product may not quietly drift to zero.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 40A20 (Convergence and divergence of infinite products). arXiv math.CA. Level 1: early undergraduate.

**Definition.** Take an infinite product ∏ aₖ with at most finitely many zero factors. It converges if the partial products of its non-zero factors have a limit, and this limit is not zero. Its value is 0 if some factor is 0. Otherwise its value is that limit.

**Problem.** Get the analogue of the test for series. If ∑ aₖ converges, then aₖ → 0. The analogue says that if ∏ aₖ converges, then aₖ → 1.

**How the definition helps.** The demand for a non-zero limit removes the two ways in which the naive definition breaks the test. With the naive definition, a product converges if the limit of its partial products exists. First, a single factor 0 then makes each later partial product 0, whatever the aₖ do. Second, factors with \|aₖ\| ≤ M &lt; 1 push the partial products to 0, although aₖ need not tend to 1. The non-zero limit of the non-zero factors rules out both. Then the expected theorems hold. For example, convergence implies aₖ → 1, and a convergent product is zero only if some factor is zero.

**nLab:** [infinite product](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/infinite+product). It says: “To avoid these "pathological" situations, we make the following modified definition.”

**Sources:**

- [Alfred Pringsheim, Ueber die Convergenz unendlicher Producte, Mathematische Annalen 33 (1888) 119–154](https://doi.org/10.1007/bf01444113)

### Uniform convergence repairs Cauchy's sum theorem

**Remember:** Uniform convergence means that one N works for every point at once.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 40A30 (Convergence and divergence of series and sequences of functions), 26A15. arXiv math.CA. Level 1: early undergraduate.

**Definition.** A sequence of functions fₙ converges uniformly to f∞ if, for every ε &gt; 0, there is one N with \|fₙ(x) − f∞(x)\| &lt; ε for all n ≥ N and all x at the same time. Pointwise convergence lets N depend on x.

**Problem.** Cauchy's sum theorem of 1821 says this: if a sequence of continuous functions converges, then its limit is continuous.

**How the definition helps.** Uniform convergence gives one N for all nearby points, and the standard proof needs exactly that. With pointwise convergence the statement is false. For example, fₙ(x) = xⁿ on \[0,1\], the sawtooth Fourier series and exp(−n\|x\|) all have continuous terms and a discontinuous limit. The ε/3 proof fails because the N for the point x + h depends on h, while the δ for continuity depends on n. Uniform convergence makes N independent of h, and then the same ε/3 argument is a valid proof (Seidel 1847). Equicontinuity (one δ for all the functions fₙ at once) is a second repair: it makes δ independent of n.

**nLab:** [Cauchy sum theorem](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Cauchy+sum+theorem). It says: “Analysing this argument, Philipp von Seidel (first, and others afterwards) realised that it could be fixed if f converges to f∞ uniformly, so that n is independent of h.”

**Sources:**

- [Imre Lakatos, Mathematics, Science and Epistemology (Philosophical Papers vol. 2), Cambridge University Press (1978), chapter 3](https://doi.org/10.1017/CBO9780511624926)

### Improper integrals as suprema of partial areas make comparison immediate

**Remember:** If every partial area of f is smaller, so is the supremum.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 40A10 (Convergence and divergence of integrals), 26A42. arXiv math.CA. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** Let f ≥ 0 be Riemann integrable on every closed bounded subinterval of an open interval I. Define its improper integral as the supremum of its integrals over those subintervals. The value may be +∞. The usual definition fixes an interior point and takes separate limits toward the two ends of I.

**Problem.** Let 0 ≤ f ≤ g on I, both Riemann integrable on every closed bounded subinterval. If the improper integral of g is finite, then so is that of f, and it is no larger.

**How the definition helps.** With the supremum definition, the claim is that a pointwise bound passes to suprema (our own). Each partial area of f is at most the matching partial area of g, so at most the supremum for g (our own). The usual definition first needs both one-sided limits to exist (our own). The work moves into showing that the definitions agree for f ≥ 0. Partial areas grow with the subinterval, and a bounded increasing function has a limit (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Comparison Test for Improper Integral](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Comparison_Test_for_Improper_Integral). It says: “If the improper integral of φ over I exists, then so does that of f.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Regular, linear, stable summation methods must give geometric series the value c/(1−r)

**Remember:** Shift the series, scale it, and its value is forced.

*True by definition.* MSC 40A25 (Approximation to limiting values (summation of series, etc.)), 40D05. arXiv math.CA. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** A summation method gives a value to some series. It is regular if it agrees with the ordinary sum on convergent series. It is linear if it respects sums and scalar multiples. It is stable if the value equals the first term plus the value of the rest of the series.

**Problem.** Every stable linear method that sums the geometric series Σ c rᵏ with r ≠ 1 must give c/(1 − r). In particular, Grandi's series 1 − 1 + 1 − ⋯ gets the value 1/2 whenever it is summed.

**How the definition helps.** The axioms turn the value of a series into the solution of an equation. Stability gives G = c + Σ c rᵏ⁺¹, and linearity turns this into G = c + rG. So G = c/(1 − r) whenever the method assigns a finite value. The page says this partly explains why Cesàro, Abel and other methods agree on such series. Whether a given method sums a given series is not given by the axioms; that needs separate work for each method.

**Wikipedia:** [Divergent series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Divergent_series). It says: “Taking regularity, linearity and stability as axioms, it is possible to sum many divergent series by elementary algebraic manipulations. This partly explains why many different summation methods give the same answer for certain series.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Stable linear summation methods cannot give 1+2+3+⋯ a value

**Remember:** A finite value needs a method that is not stable or not linear.

*True by definition.* MSC 40A25 (Approximation to limiting values (summation of series, etc.)), 40D05. arXiv math.CA. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** A summation method is linear if it respects sums and scalar multiples of series. It is stable if putting a term in front of the series raises the value by that term.

**Problem.** Show that the value −1/12 for 1 + 2 + 3 + ⋯ cannot come from any stable linear method.

**How the definition helps.** With the axioms written down, a few lines of algebra settle the question. Suppose a stable linear method gives 1 + 2 + 3 + ⋯ the value s. Putting 0 in front by stability and subtracting by linearity gives 1 + 1 + 1 + ⋯ the value 0. Doing the same again gives 1 + 0 + 0 + ⋯ the value 0, but stability says its value is 1. So zeta function regularization and Ramanujan summation, which give −1/12, must fail linearity or stability. The page notes that zeta regularization is not linear.

**Wikipedia:** [1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + ⋯](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1_%2B_2_%2B_3_%2B_4_%2B_%E2%8B%AF), [Divergent series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Divergent_series). It says: “Most of the more elementary definitions of the sum of a divergent series are stable and linear, and any method that is both stable and linear cannot sum 1 + 2 + 3 + ⋯ to a finite value”

**Sources:**

- [Mario A. Natiello and Hernán Gustavo Solari, On the removal of infinities from divergent series, Philosophy of Mathematics Education Journal 29 (2015) 1–11](https://hdl.handle.net/11336/46148)

### Averaging the partial sums recovers every continuous function (Fejér)

**Remember:** Average the partial sums, and the wobbles of the Fourier series cancel.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 40G05 (Cesàro, Euler, Nörlund and Hausdorff methods), 42A24. arXiv math.CA. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** Let s₀, s₁, s₂, … be the partial sums of a series. The series is Cesàro summable to s when the averages σₙ = (s₀ + s₁ + … + sₙ)/(n + 1) converge to s. In words, σₙ is the mean of the first n + 1 partial sums. If the partial sums converge to s, the averages also converge to s.

**Problem.** Every continuous function with period 2π should be recovered from its Fourier series, uniformly.

**How the definition helps.** Averaging the partial sums smooths out the failures of ordinary convergence, and it loses nothing. With ordinary partial sums the statement is false: some continuous functions have a Fourier series that diverges at a point. The classical example is du Bois-Reymond's from 1873 (our own detail). Fejér (1900) showed that the Cesàro means of the Fourier series of a continuous function converge to it uniformly. Our own remark: a kernel is the function whose convolution with f gives the partial sums or their means; the Dirichlet kernel for the partial sums is not positive and its L¹ norms are unbounded, while the Fejér kernel for the means is positive. Because Cesàro summation gives the ordinary sum whenever that exists, nothing is lost. The question for ordinary partial sums stays hard: Carleson proved in 1966 that the Fourier series of an L² function converges almost everywhere.

**Wikipedia:** [Fejér's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fej%C3%A9r%27s_theorem), [Convergence of Fourier series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convergence_of_Fourier_series). It says: “Sadly however, the theorem does not work in a general sense when we replace the sequence σₙ(f,x) with sₙ(f,x). This is because there exist functions whose Fourier series fails to converge at some point.”

**Sources:**

- [L. Fejér, Untersuchungen über Fouriersche Reihen, Math. Ann. 58 (1904), 51–69, doi:10.1007/BF01447779](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01447779)

### Unordered sums over index sets split over disjoint pieces

**Remember:** Sum over finite subsets, and the order of terms stops mattering.

*True by definition.* MSC 40A05 (Convergence and divergence of series and sequences), 54A20, 54H15. arXiv math.CA, math.GN. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A generalized sum of a family (gₖ) indexed by any set K is a limit of finite partial sums. The limit is taken over the finite subsets of K, ordered by inclusion. It uses no order on K.

**Problem.** Let G be a commutative topological semigroup, which has a continuous addition. Let I and J be disjoint index sets, and let the generalized sums over I and over J converge. Then the sum over I ∪ J converges and equals the sum of the two sums.

**How the definition helps.** Because the definition uses all finite subsets and no ordering, rearranging the terms cannot change the sum. A finite subset of I ∪ J splits into a finite part of I and a finite part of J. So the theorem then needs only the continuity of addition. Our own comparison is with ordinary series in ℝ, where the order of the terms matters. By the Riemann rearrangement theorem, a conditionally convergent series can be rearranged to have any real sum. Our own remark is that in ℝ a family has a generalized sum exactly when it is absolutely summable.

**Paper or page:** [Generalized Sum over Union of Disjoint Index Sets](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Generalized_Sum_over_Union_of_Disjoint_Index_Sets). It says: “the generalized sum ∑ₖ gₖ converges and: ∑ₖ gₖ = (∑ᵢ gᵢ) + (∑ⱼ gⱼ)”

**Sources:**

- [ProofWiki, Generalized Sum over Union of Disjoint Index Sets](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Generalized_Sum_over_Union_of_Disjoint_Index_Sets)

### Ideal convergence frees Olivier's theorem from monotonicity

**Remember:** Ignore a set of indices with finite harmonic sum, and n aₙ → 0.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 40A35 (Ideal and statistical convergence), 26D15. arXiv math.CA. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** An ideal on ℕ is a family of sets of indices that counts as negligible; it is closed under subsets and finite unions. A sequence tends to L along the ideal when, for each ε &gt; 0, the n with \|xₙ − L\| ≥ ε are negligible. The summable ideal holds the sets A for which the sum of 1/n over n in A is finite.

**Problem.** Olivier's theorem says that n aₙ → 0 when (aₙ) is positive and nonincreasing and ∑ aₙ &lt; ∞. Šalát and Toma found when monotonicity can be dropped. Their theorem says when n aₙ → 0 along an ideal for every convergent positive series: exactly when the ideal contains the summable ideal.

**How the definition helps.** Ideal convergence ignores a negligible set of indices, and the set where n aₙ stays large always has a finite harmonic sum. Our own one-line proof follows. If n aₙ ≥ ε on A, then the sum of 1/n over A is at most (1/ε)·∑ aₙ. Our own counterexample to plain convergence takes aₙ = 1/n when n is a square and aₙ = 1/n² otherwise. The series converges, but n aₙ = 1 on the squares, and the squares form a set in the summable ideal. Our own remark: sets with finite harmonic sum have density zero, so n aₙ → 0 in the statistical sense for every convergent positive series.

**Paper or page:** [The ideal test for the divergence of a series](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.01506v1), [The ideal test for the divergence of a series](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.01506v1). It says: “we either drop the monotonicity assumption completely or we relax it to the monotonicity on a large set of indices. In both cases, the convergence of (n aₙ) is replaced by ideal convergence.”

**Sources:**

- [Rafał Filipów, Adam Kwela, Jacek Tryba, The ideal test for the divergence of a series, Rev. R. Acad. Cienc. Exactas Fís. Nat. Ser. A Mat. RACSAM 117 (2023), no. 3, Paper No. 98, arXiv:2307.01506](https://doi.org/10.1007/s13398-023-01430-w)

### Keeping original indices makes subsequences of ideal-convergent sequences converge

**Remember:** Keep the original indices when restricting an ideal.

*True by definition. Confidence: low.* MSC 40A35 (Ideal and statistical convergence), 54A20. arXiv math.GN. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** An ideal on the natural numbers is a family of index sets, closed under subsets and finite unions, whose members count as negligible. A sequence converges to x for the ideal if, for each neighborhood of x, the indices of terms outside it form a negligible set. A set of indices M is nonthin if it is not negligible. On M, the restricted ideal consists of the negligible sets inside M, and the subsequence keeps its original indices.

**Problem.** Our own statement of the result is this. Restrict an ideal-convergent sequence to a nonthin set of indices. Then it converges to the same limit for the restricted ideal.

**How the definition helps.** Keeping the original indices makes the result true by definition, by our own proof. The bad indices of the restricted sequence are the original bad indices inside M, which form a negligible set inside M. Our own example shows what goes wrong after renumbering. Let the sequence be one at the squares and zero elsewhere. The squares have density zero, so the sequence converges to zero for the ideal of density-zero sets. Renumbered, the subsequence at the squares is constantly one, so it converges to one instead. Here the set of squares is not nonthin, so the paper's definition excludes it.

**Paper or page:** [Compactness with ideals](https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.00050v1). It says: “subsequence of an ideal convergent sequence may fail to be ideal convergent with respect to same ideal.”

**Sources:**

- [Manoranjan Singha, Sima Roy, Compactness with ideals, arXiv:2107.00050v1 (2021)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.00050v1)

## 41 Approximations and expansions

### The Hermite–Genocchi integral makes divided differences continuous at repeated nodes

**Remember:** When all nodes meet, the integrand is constant and only the volume remains.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 41A05 (Interpolation in approximation theory), 26A24. arXiv math.CA. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** The usual divided difference f\[x₀, …, xₙ\] is a recursion of difference quotients on distinct nodes. Instead, define it as the integral of f⁽ⁿ⁾(t₀x₀ + … + tₙxₙ) over the simplex of weights tᵢ ≥ 0 with sum 1. Measured in the free weights t₁, …, tₙ, this simplex has volume 1/n!. This is the Hermite–Genocchi formula.

**Problem.** Let f have n continuous derivatives on an interval. Then its order n divided difference extends continuously to repeated nodes. When all n + 1 nodes equal x, its value is f⁽ⁿ⁾(x)/n!.

**How the definition helps.** With the integral definition, both claims follow from continuity of the integrand (our own). The integrand depends continuously on the nodes and the simplex is compact, so the integral is continuous in the nodes (our own). When every node is x, the integrand is the constant f⁽ⁿ⁾(x), so the integral is f⁽ⁿ⁾(x)/n! (our own). The work moves into the proof that the integral satisfies the recursion at distinct nodes (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Divided differences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Divided_differences). It says: “the divided difference can be expressed as an integral over a n-simplex Δₙ:”

### Defining Bernstein polynomials as binomial expectations makes them fix affine functions

**Remember:** The expected success fraction is the success probability x.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 41A36 (Approximation by positive operators), 41A10. arXiv math.CA. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** Let K count the successes in n independent trials, each with success probability x. Define the nth Bernstein polynomial of f at x as the expected value of f(K/n). The usual definition is the sum over k from 0 to n of f(k/n) times C(n, k)xᵏ(1 − x)ⁿ⁻ᵏ.

**Problem.** For n ≥ 1 and all real a and b, the Bernstein polynomial of a + bx is a + bx on \[0, 1\].

**How the definition helps.** Expectation is linear, so the claim reduces to two facts. The expectation of a constant is that constant, and the expected value of K/n is x. With the sum formula, the same claim needs the binomial identities for the total weight and for the mean. The work moves to checking that the expectation equals the sum, which is the formula for the binomial distribution. This fact is the first step of Bernstein’s proof of the Weierstrass approximation theorem. The proof steps are our own; the Wikipedia text notes only that Bernstein polynomials look like binomial expectations.

**Wikipedia:** [Bernstein polynomial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernstein_polynomial). It says: “Here, we take advantage of the fact that Bernstein polynomials look like Binomial expectations.”

### The cosine definition makes monic Chebyshev polynomials minimize the maximum

**Remember:** Equal alternating peaks stop any monic rival from lowering them all.

*True by definition.* MSC 41A50 (Best approximation, Chebyshev systems), 33C45. arXiv math.CA, math.NA. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** Define the Chebyshev polynomial Tₙ by Tₙ(cos θ) = cos(nθ). The algebraic definition uses the recurrence Tₙ₊₁ = 2xTₙ − Tₙ₋₁ with T₀ = 1 and T₁ = x. For n ≥ 1 the leading coefficient of Tₙ is 2ⁿ⁻¹, so 2¹⁻ⁿTₙ is monic.

**Problem.** For n ≥ 1, among monic polynomials of degree n, 2¹⁻ⁿTₙ has the smallest maximum absolute value on \[−1, 1\]. That maximum is 2¹⁻ⁿ.

**How the definition helps.** The cosine definition shows at once that Tₙ takes the values ±1 alternately at the n + 1 points cos(kπ/n). Suppose a monic w of degree n had maximum below 2¹⁻ⁿ. Then 2¹⁻ⁿTₙ − w has degree at most n − 1 and alternates in sign at those n + 1 points. So it has n zeros and must be zero, which is impossible. Wikipedia gives this proof. The work goes into showing that cos(nθ) is a polynomial in cos θ, which gives the recurrence.

**Wikipedia:** [Chebyshev polynomials](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chebyshev_polynomials). It says: “is the one of which the maximal absolute value on the interval \[−1, 1\] is minimal.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Taylor polynomials as best local approximations compose by substitution and truncation

**Remember:** Substitute the inner polynomial into the outer one, then drop high powers.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 41A58 (Series expansions (e.g., Taylor, Lidstone series, but not Fourier series)), 26A24. arXiv math.CA. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** Let P be a polynomial of degree at most n. Call P an order n approximation of f at c if (f(x) − P(x))/\|x − c\|ⁿ → 0 as x → c. At most one such polynomial exists. The usual definition instead matches the derivatives of f at c up to order n.

**Problem.** Let g be smooth near c and f smooth near g(c). Let Q and P be their order n Taylor polynomials at c and at g(c). Then the order n Taylor polynomial of f ∘ g at c is P(Q(x)) with powers of (x − c) above n dropped.

**How the definition helps.** With the approximation definition, one only checks that the truncated P(Q(x)) approximates f(g(x)) to order n (our own). Since g is differentiable at c, \|g(x) − g(c)\| ≤ C\|x − c\| near c (our own). So f(g(x)) − P(g(x)) is negligible against \|x − c\|ⁿ (our own). P has bounded slope near g(c), so P(g(x)) − P(Q(x)) is also negligible (our own). Dropping powers above n changes the result by at most a constant times \|x − c\|ⁿ⁺¹ (our own). The work moves into Taylor's theorem with the Peano remainder. It shows that the derivative polynomial is this unique best approximation.

**nLab:** [Taylor's theorem](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Taylor%27s+theorem). It says: “whose derivatives at c match those of f up to order k.”

**Wikipedia:** [Taylor's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taylor%27s_theorem). It says: “The Taylor polynomial is the unique "asymptotic best fit" polynomial”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Treating Taylor polynomials as classes modulo (x − c)ⁿ⁺¹ makes products truncate

**Remember:** Multiplying then truncating gives the same as truncating then multiplying.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 41A58 (Series expansions (e.g., Taylor, Lidstone series, but not Fourier series)), 26A24. arXiv math.CA. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** Fix a point c and n ≥ 0. Call two smooth functions equal to order n at c if their difference is (x − c)ⁿ⁺¹ times a smooth function. Define the order n Taylor polynomial of f as the one polynomial of degree at most n in the class of f. The usual definition is the sum of f⁽ᵏ⁾(c)(x − c)ᵏ/k! for k ≤ n.

**Problem.** Let f and g be smooth near c. Multiply their order n Taylor polynomials at c and drop the powers above n. The result is the order n Taylor polynomial of fg.

**How the definition helps.** With classes, the claim says that multiplication respects the equivalence, which takes one line (our own). Suppose f − P and g − Q are multiples of (x − c)ⁿ⁺¹ (our own). Then so is fg − PQ = f(g − Q) + Q(f − P) (our own). Dropping powers above n from PQ changes it by another such multiple (our own). The work moves into Hadamard's lemma. It says that the remainder after the usual Taylor polynomial is (x − c)ⁿ⁺¹ times a smooth function. With the usual definition, one instead matches coefficients by the general Leibniz rule (our own).

**nLab:** [Hadamard lemma](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Hadamard+lemma). It says: “the Taylor series of a smooth function on the real line around the origin has a remainder at order n”

### Defining cardinal B-splines by convolution makes their two-scale relation binomial

**Remember:** Split one box into two half boxes, then expand the convolution power.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 41A15 (Spline approximation). arXiv math.CA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let χ be the indicator function of \[0, 1). Define the cardinal B-spline B of degree p as the convolution of p + 1 copies of χ. The usual definition uses the Cox–de Boor recursion on integer knots.

**Problem.** B(x) equals 2 raised to −p times the sum over j from 0 to p + 1 of C(p + 1, j)·B(2x − j).

**How the definition helps.** With the convolution definition, the relation follows from one splitting of the box and the binomial theorem. Write χ(x) = χ(2x) + χ(2x − 1), a sum of two half boxes. Convolution is commutative, so the (p + 1)-fold convolution of this sum expands by the binomial theorem. Each term is a shifted (p + 1)-fold convolution of the half box, which equals 2 raised to −p times B(2x − j). From the Cox–de Boor recursion, the relation needs an induction on the degree. The work moves to showing that the convolution powers satisfy the recursion. These steps are our own; Wikipedia only links cardinal B-splines with convolution.

**Wikipedia:** [B-spline](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/B-spline). It says: “A cardinal B-spline has uniformly spaced knots, therefore interpolation between the knots equals convolution with a smoothing kernel.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Defining the spline by least bending gives zero end curvature for free

**Remember:** Free end slopes force zero end curvature at a minimizer.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 41A15 (Spline approximation), 49K05. arXiv math.NA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Take nodes x₀ &lt; x₁ &lt; ⋯ &lt; xₙ with n ≥ 1 and a data value at each node. Among functions on \[x₀, xₙ\] with square-integrable second derivative and these values, choose the one with the least integral of the squared second derivative. The usual definition asks for a piecewise cubic with two continuous derivatives and zero second derivative at both ends.

**Problem.** The minimizer s has zero second derivative at x₀ and at xₙ.

**How the definition helps.** The data do not fix the end slopes, so a minimizer must not improve when an end slope changes. So the integral of s″h″ is zero for every allowed h that vanishes at the nodes. On each piece between nodes, s is a cubic, and integration by parts leaves only boundary terms. At x₀ the remaining term is s″(x₀)h′(x₀), and h′(x₀) is arbitrary, so s″(x₀) = 0. The usual definition puts this condition in by hand, and the work moves to existence and to proving that the pieces are cubics. Holladay’s 1957 theorem connects the two definitions. These proof steps are our own.

**Wikipedia:** [Spline (mathematics)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spline_%28mathematics%29). It says: “Spline functions for interpolation are normally determined as the minimizers of suitable measures of roughness (for example integral squared curvature) subject to the interpolation constraints.”

**Sources:**

## 42 Harmonic analysis on Euclidean spaces

### Defining the Fejér kernel as a square makes it nonnegative

**Remember:** A squared absolute value cannot be negative.

*True by definition.* MSC 42A24 (Summability and absolute summability of Fourier and trigonometric series). arXiv math.CA. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** Define the nth Fejér kernel as 1/n times \|1 + exp(ix) + ⋯ + exp(i(n − 1)x)\|². The usual definition is the average of the first n Dirichlet kernels. The kth Dirichlet kernel is the sum of exp(ijx) over integers j from −k to k.

**Problem.** Each Fejér kernel is nonnegative everywhere, and its average over one period is one.

**How the definition helps.** As a squared absolute value divided by n, the kernel is nonnegative with no calculation. Its average is one because the exponentials are orthogonal, so the average of the square is n. From the average of Dirichlet kernels, nonnegativity usually needs the closed formula (1/n)(sin(nx/2)/sin(x/2))². The work moves to showing that the square equals that average. Expanding the square gives n − \|j\| pairs of frequencies with difference j, and this matches the average. These proof steps are our own; Wikipedia states only that the kernel is a positive summability kernel.

**Wikipedia:** [Fejér kernel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fej%C3%A9r_kernel). It says: “The Fejér kernel is a positive summability kernel.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Defining the Poisson kernel by Fourier coefficients makes radii multiply

**Remember:** Convolution multiplies Fourier coefficients, so the radii multiply.

*True by definition.* MSC 42A24 (Summability and absolute summability of Fourier and trigonometric series). arXiv math.CA. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** For 0 &lt; r &lt; 1, define the circle Poisson kernel Pᵣ by its Fourier coefficients, r raised to \|k\| at frequency k. The usual definition is the formula (1 − r²)/(1 − 2r cos θ + r²).

**Problem.** For 0 &lt; r, s &lt; 1, the convolution of Pᵣ and Pₛ over the circle, with normalized measure, is the kernel at radius rs.

**How the definition helps.** Convolution turns into multiplication of Fourier coefficients, as the Wikipedia text says. So the coefficients of the convolution are r raised to \|k\| times s raised to \|k\|, which are the coefficients at radius rs. With the rational formula, the same identity needs a hard integral. The work moves to showing that the coefficient definition gives the rational formula. Summing the two geometric series over positive and negative frequencies does this. The last three steps are our own.

**Wikipedia:** [Poisson kernel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poisson_kernel). It says: “After the Fourier transform, convolution with Pᵣ(θ) becomes multiplication by the sequence”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Extending by continuity defines the Fourier transform on all of L²

**Remember:** Define it where the integral converges, check it keeps L² norms, extend by continuity.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 42A38 (Fourier and Fourier-Stieltjes transforms and other transforms of Fourier type), 46E30. arXiv math.CA, math.FA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** The Fourier transform on L²(ℝ) is the unique continuous extension to L² of the Fourier integral defined on L¹ ∩ L².

**Problem.** Plancherel's theorem: the Fourier transform is a unitary map of L²(ℝ) onto itself. This holds even though the Fourier integral of a general L² function need not converge.

**How the definition helps.** The definition never uses the integral where it diverges, so divergence causes no exceptions. For f in L² but not in L¹, the integral ∫ f(x) exp(−2πixξ) dx need not converge. Plancherel showed that on L¹ ∩ L² the transform preserves the L² norm, and L¹ ∩ L² is dense in L². So the transform extends uniquely to an isometry of L², and this extension is unitary; that it is onto needs the inversion formula (our own remark). So the theorem has no exception for functions with a divergent Fourier integral. Pointwise questions remain hard, such as almost-everywhere convergence of the inversion integral (Carleson); our own remark.

**Wikipedia:** [Plancherel theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plancherel_theorem). It says: “In effect, this makes it possible to speak of Fourier transforms of L² functions.”

**Sources:**

- [Plancherel, M. (1910). Contribution à l'étude de la représentation d'une fonction arbitraire par des intégrales définies. Rendiconti del Circolo Matematico di Palermo 30(1), 289–335.](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF03014877)

### The Hilbert transform multiplier squares to minus one

**Remember:** Two quarter turns make a half turn and negate the function.

*True by definition.* MSC 42A50 (Conjugate functions, conjugate series, singular integrals), 42B10. arXiv math.CA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** On square-integrable functions, define the Hilbert transform H by multiplying the Fourier transform by −i at positive frequencies and by i at negative frequencies. The value at frequency zero does not matter because a single point has measure zero. The usual integral definition uses the kernel 1/(πt) and takes a principal value, the limit with a symmetric gap around the singularity.

**Problem.** For every square-integrable u on the real line, H(H(u)) = −u. The inverse of H is therefore −H.

**How the definition helps.** The multiplier definition turns H applied twice into squaring either i or −i, both of which give −1. Our own comparison is with the principal value integral, where a second application brings in two singular kernels. The work moves into computing the Fourier transform of the principal value kernel to show that the two definitions agree.

**Wikipedia:** [Hilbert transform](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert_transform). It says: “The signal is negated; i.e., H(H(u)) = −u”

**Sources:**

- [M. Riesz (1928), Sur les fonctions conjuguées, Mathematische Zeitschrift](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01171098)

### The Bohr compactification turns almost periodic means into Haar integrals

**Remember:** On a compact group, translation invariant integration gives the mean.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 42A75 (Classical almost periodic functions, mean periodic functions), 43A60, 28C10. arXiv math.CA, math.FA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A function on ℝ is uniformly almost periodic if it is a uniform limit of finite sums of waves a·exp(iλx), with real λ. Equivalently, it is the restriction of a continuous function on the Bohr compactification bℝ. This is a compact group with a continuous homomorphism from ℝ whose image is dense.

**Problem.** For a uniformly almost periodic function, the averages over \[−T, T\] converge as T tends to infinity. Their limit is translation invariant and equals the integral of the extension to bℝ.

**How the definition helps.** The compactification lets us define the mean as an integral with respect to Haar probability measure, the translation invariant probability measure on bℝ (our own). Translation invariance then follows from the measure itself (our own). To compare with interval averages, first check a single wave (our own). Both the averages in the limit and the integral give 0 for λ ≠ 0 and 1 for λ = 0 (our own). Both operations have norm at most 1, so uniform approximation gives the equality for all these functions (our own). The work lies in the identification with continuous functions on bℝ and the existence of Haar measure.

**Wikipedia:** [Almost periodic function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almost_periodic_function). It says: “The space of uniform almost periodic functions on G can be identified with the space of all continuous functions on the Bohr compactification of G.”

**Sources:**

- [H. Bohr, Zur Theorie der fast periodischen Funktionen I, Acta Mathematica 45 (1925)](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02395468)

### Uniform trigonometric approximation makes almost periodic functions an algebra

**Remember:** Uniform limits preserve the algebra operations on bounded functions.

*True by definition.* MSC 42A75 (Classical almost periodic functions, mean periodic functions), 43A60. arXiv math.CA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A function on ℝ is uniformly almost periodic when finite sums of waves a·exp(iλx), with real λ, approximate it uniformly. The other definition uses ε-almost periods, shifts T with \|f(t + T) − f(t)\| &lt; ε for every t. For every ε &gt; 0, it requires every interval of some fixed length to contain such a shift.

**Problem.** Sums, products and uniform limits of uniformly almost periodic functions remain uniformly almost periodic.

**How the definition helps.** The approximation definition makes this class the uniform closure of an algebra. Finite sums of waves are closed under sums and products because multiplying two waves adds their frequencies (our own). For bounded functions those operations pass to uniform limits (our own). With the shift definition, even proving closure under sums requires finding common almost periods (our own). The work moved to Bohr’s theorem that the approximation and shift definitions agree.

**Wikipedia:** [Almost periodic function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almost_periodic_function). It says: “Bohr (1925) defined the uniformly almost-periodic functions as the closure of the trigonometric polynomials with respect to the uniform norm”

**Sources:**

- [H. Bohr, Zur Theorie der fast periodischen Funktionen I, Acta Mathematica 45 (1925)](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02395468)

### The Leray multiplier projects vector fields onto divergence-free fields

**Remember:** Remove the part of the vector that points along its frequency.

*True by definition.* MSC 42B15 (Multipliers for harmonic analysis in several variables), 35Q30, 76D05. arXiv math.AP. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Define the Leray map P on square-integrable vector fields on ℝⁿ by multiplying their Fourier transforms by I − ξξᵀ/\|ξ\|² for ξ ≠ 0. Here I is the identity matrix, and ξξᵀ/\|ξ\|² projects onto the line through ξ. The usual Helmholtz description instead takes the divergence-free part of an orthogonal splitting into divergence-free fields and limits of gradients.

**Problem.** The Leray map is the orthogonal projection onto the fields with zero divergence. It sends ∇φ to zero for every smooth φ of compact support.

**How the definition helps.** The multiplier definition reduces this orthogonal splitting to projection in a finite-dimensional vector space, in our own proof. For each nonzero ξ, the matrix projects onto the vectors perpendicular to ξ. Fourier transformation turns divergence into a scalar multiple of the dot product with ξ, so these are exactly the vectors that give zero divergence. Fourier transforms of gradients are parallel to ξ, so the matrix sends gradients to zero. The work moves into Plancherel’s norm identity, which makes the pointwise orthogonal projection an orthogonal projection of square-integrable fields. This identifies the map with the Helmholtz projection.

**Wikipedia:** [Leray projection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leray_projection). It says: “This definition must be understood in the sense of pseudo-differential operators: its matrix valued Fourier multiplier m(ξ) is given by”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Riesz transform multipliers recover second derivatives from the Laplacian

**Remember:** Two Riesz transforms recover a second derivative from the Laplacian, up to sign.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 42B20 (Singular and oscillatory integrals (Calderón-Zygmund, etc.)), 35J05. arXiv math.CA, math.AP. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Define the j-th Riesz transform Rⱼ on square-integrable functions on ℝⁿ by multiplying their Fourier transforms by −iξⱼ/\|ξ\| away from ξ = 0. The usual integral definition uses a kernel proportional to zⱼ divided by \|z\| to the power n + 1. It takes a principal value, the limit that excludes a shrinking ball around the singularity.

**Problem.** For every smooth, rapidly decreasing u, ∂ᵢ∂ⱼu = −RᵢRⱼΔu. The square-integral norm of ∂ᵢ∂ⱼu is at most that of Δu.

**How the definition helps.** The multiplier definition reduces the derivative identity to multiplying three scalar functions of ξ, in our own proof. With the Fourier kernel exp(−ix·ξ), both sides multiply by −ξᵢξⱼ. The multiplier of RᵢRⱼ has absolute value at most one, so Plancherel’s norm identity gives the bound. The work moves into matching the multipliers to the principal value kernels. Bounds with other integrability exponents require separate estimates for these singular integrals.

**Wikipedia:** [Riesz transform](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riesz_transform). It says: “The Riesz transforms are given by a Fourier multiplier.”

### The Muckenhoupt condition is exactly what weighted maximal function bounds need

**Remember:** Test the maximal inequality on one cube and you get Aₚ.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 42B25 (Maximal functions, Littlewood-Paley theory). arXiv math.FA, math.CA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A weight is a positive locally integrable function w. Let a(Q) be the average of w over a cube Q, and let b(Q) be the average of w to the power −1/(p − 1). For 1 &lt; p &lt; ∞, w is in Aₚ if a(Q) times b(Q) to the power p − 1 is bounded over all cubes. The class A₁ asks that a(Q) ≤ C w(x) for almost every x in Q.

**Problem.** The Hardy–Littlewood maximal operator M sends f to the largest average of \|f\| over cubes that contain the point. A weak type (p, p) bound says that the set where Mf &gt; λ has w-measure at most C/λᵖ times ∫\|f\|ᵖ w. The theorem says that M has this bound exactly when w is in Aₚ.

**How the definition helps.** The Aₚ condition comes from testing the maximal inequality on one function that lives on one cube. So it is necessary almost by construction (our own remark). The theorem says that this one-cube test is also enough, so a hard inequality becomes a simple condition on averages. The condition sorts even simple weights. For p &gt; 1, the power weight \|x\|ᵃ on ℝⁿ is in Aₚ exactly when −n &lt; a &lt; n(p − 1) (our own remark). For the weak bound, sufficiency follows from Hölder's inequality and a covering lemma (our own remark). For p &gt; 1, Muckenhoupt also proved the strong bound, which needs more work.

**Paper or page:** [Weighted weak (1,1) estimate for non-commutative square function](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.00987v3). It says: “For 1≤p&lt;∞, the weak type (p,p) inequality … is true if and only if w satisfies the Muckenhoupt's Aₚ condition.”

**Sources:**

- [Weighted weak (1,1) estimate for non-commutative square function, arXiv:2410.00987 (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.00987v3)
- [B. Muckenhoupt, Weighted norm inequalities for the Hardy maximal function, Trans. Amer. Math. Soc. 165 (1972), p. 207](https://doi.org/10.1090/s0002-9947-1972-0293384-6)

### Defining polynomials by orthogonality makes the three-term recurrence a short argument

**Remember:** Move the factor x across the inner product to the lower degree side.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 42C05 (Orthogonal functions and polynomials, general theory of nontrigonometric harmonic analysis). arXiv math.CA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Fix a positive measure on the real line with infinite support and finite moments. Define pₙ as the monic polynomial of degree n that is orthogonal to all polynomials of lower degree. Monic means the leading coefficient is one. The alternative builds pₙ₊₁ as (x − bₙ)pₙ − aₙpₙ₋₁, with constants bₙ and aₙ &gt; 0.

**Problem.** For these monic orthogonal polynomials, x·pₙ = pₙ₊₁ + bₙpₙ + aₙpₙ₋₁ with constants bₙ and aₙ &gt; 0, where p₋₁ = 0.

**How the definition helps.** With orthogonality as the definition, multiplication by x moves across the inner product. So the inner product of x·pₙ with pₖ equals that of pₙ with x·pₖ, which is zero when k + 1 &lt; n. Hence only three terms of the expansion of x·pₙ survive. With the recurrence as the definition, the recurrence is free but orthogonality is hard. That converse is Favard’s theorem, which Wikipedia names; it builds a positive measure from the recurrence. The proof steps are our own.

**Wikipedia:** [Orthogonal polynomials](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orthogonal_polynomials). It says: “These recurrence relations are key for deriving properties of orthogonal polynomials.”

### Defining Walsh functions as group characters makes their orthogonality automatic

**Remember:** Translate by a bit that flips the sign of the product.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 42C10 (Fourier series in special orthogonal functions (Legendre polynomials, Walsh functions, etc.)), 43A40. arXiv math.CA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let 𝔻 be the group of infinite binary sequences under digitwise addition modulo two, with the product of fair coin measures. Define the Walsh functions as the continuous characters of 𝔻. A character is a homomorphism to the complex numbers of absolute value one. The usual definition on \[0, 1) multiplies Rademacher functions, square waves that equal +1 or −1 according to one binary digit.

**Problem.** Distinct Walsh functions are orthogonal for uniform measure on \[0, 1).

**How the definition helps.** Characters of a compact group are orthogonal by a general translation argument. If χ ≠ ψ, then χψ̄ is a nontrivial character, so some translation multiplies it by a number other than one. The measure does not change under translation, so the integral of χψ̄ is zero. On \[0, 1), the usual proof instead uses the independence of binary digits. The work moves to the identification that Wikipedia describes. The binary expansion carries the product measure to the uniform measure, and it fails to be one-to-one only on a set of measure zero. The translation argument is our own.

**Wikipedia:** [Walsh function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walsh_function). It says: “Elements of 𝔻̂ are readily identified with Walsh functions.”

### Real phase retrieval works exactly when every split leaves a spanning part

**Remember:** Split measurements by sign agreement and let the spanning side settle the answer.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 42C15 (General harmonic expansions, frames), 94A12. arXiv cs.LG, math.FA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A real measurement family has the complement property if every split into two parts leaves at least one part spanning the whole space. Phase retrieval asks whether absolute inner products determine a vector up to its overall sign.

**Problem.** A finite real measurement family recovers every vector up to sign exactly when it has the complement property.

**How the definition helps.** The complement property prevents two different vectors from agreeing in magnitude without agreeing up to sign. Our own proof sketch splits measurements by whether the inner products agree or are opposite. If neither part spans, our own counterexample construction adds and subtracts nonzero vectors orthogonal to the two parts.

### Weak porosity is exactly what makes a distance weight an A₁ weight

**Remember:** Enough room in the holes, and the distance weight stays averaged.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 42B25 (Maximal functions, Littlewood-Paley theory), 28A75. arXiv math.CA. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A weight w is in the Muckenhoupt class A₁ when the Hardy–Littlewood maximal function of w is at most a constant times w almost everywhere. A set E is porous when every ball contains a hole, a ball that misses E, with a fixed fraction of its radius. Weak porosity is a weaker condition on the holes of E inside each ball. Our own summary, unchecked in the data, is that holes not much smaller than the largest one must fill a fixed fraction of the ball.

**Problem.** For which nonempty sets E ≠ ℝⁿ is the weight dist(x,E)⁻ᵅ in A₁ for some α &gt; 0? Such weights matter because the maximal operator and singular integrals are bounded on the weighted spaces.

**How the definition helps.** Weak porosity asks for exactly as much empty space as the A₁ averages need, so the answer is one equivalence; this reading is our own. Our own summary of the history is that porous sets were known to give A₁ distance weights, but porosity is not necessary. The paper also measures the best exponent α by a number it calls the Muckenhoupt exponent of E. Our own remark is that the proof still takes real work with cube decompositions. The abstract gives a set E in ℝ that is not weakly porous. For each 0 &lt; α &lt; 1, its weight is in every Aₚ with p &gt; 1 but not in A₁. So for the classes Aₚ with p &gt; 1, weak porosity is not the right condition.

**Paper or page:** [Weakly porous sets and Muckenhoupt Aₚ distance functions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.06284v2). It says: “As our first main result we show that the distance weight w(x)=dist(x,E)⁻ᵅ belongs to the Muckenhoupt class A₁, for some α&gt;0, if and only if E⊂ℝⁿ is weakly porous.”

**Sources:**

- [Theresa C. Anderson, Juha Lehrbäck, Carlos Mudarra, Antti V. Vähäkangas, Weakly porous sets and Muckenhoupt Aₚ distance functions, arXiv:2209.06284 (2022)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.06284v2)

## 43 Abstract harmonic analysis

### Amenability gives invariant measures through its fixed-point definition

**Remember:** An invariant measure is a fixed point for the action on probability measures.

*True by definition.* MSC 43A07 (Means on groups, semigroups, etc.; amenable groups), 37A15. arXiv math.GR, math.DS. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A locally compact group G is amenable if it admits a left-invariant mean on bounded right uniformly continuous functions. These are functions for which small left translations make uniformly small changes. The mean is a positive linear functional that sends the constant one to one and is unchanged by left translation. Equivalently, every continuous action preserving convex combinations on a nonempty compact convex subset of a locally convex space has a fixed point.

**Problem.** If an amenable group acts continuously on a nonempty compact metric space X, then X has an invariant Borel probability measure.

**How the definition helps.** The fixed-point definition gives an invariant measure by making measures the points of a convex set (our own). Probability measures are compact in the topology of convergence of integrals against continuous functions, by the Riesz representation and Banach–Alaoglu theorems. The group acts continuously by transporting measures along its maps on X, and it preserves convex combinations. A fixed point of this action is an invariant measure. The work goes into Day’s theorem, which turns a left-invariant mean into the fixed-point property.

**Wikipedia:** [Amenable group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amenable_group). It says: “Fixed-point property. Any action of the group by continuous affine transformations on a compact convex subset of a (separable) locally convex topological vector space has a fixed point.”

**Sources:**

- [M. M. Day, Fixed-point theorems for compact convex sets, Illinois J. Math. 5 (1961) 585–590](https://doi.org/10.1215/ijm/1255631582)

### Amenable groups explain why Banach–Tarski needs three dimensions

**Remember:** A group with an invariant mean cannot double a ball.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 43A07 (Means on groups, semigroups, etc.; amenable groups), 20F65. arXiv math.GR, math.FA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A discrete group G is amenable if there is a finitely additive probability measure on all subsets of G that is invariant under left translation. Von Neumann introduced the idea in 1929 in response to the Banach–Tarski paradox. Day named it amenable in 1949.

**Problem.** Banach–Tarski: a ball in ℝ³ can be cut into finitely many pieces and moved by rigid motions into two copies of itself. No such paradox exists for a disc in the plane or an interval on the line.

**How the definition helps.** The definition names the property of the group of motions that blocks paradoxes, so the difference between dimensions becomes a statement about groups. The rotation group SO(3) contains a free group on two generators, which is not amenable. The groups of rigid motions of the line and the plane are solvable, so they are amenable (our own). An invariant mean then rules out a paradoxical decomposition (our own). Tarski later proved that an action has a paradoxical decomposition exactly when no invariant finitely additive measure exists (our own). What stays hard: the converse guess of von Neumann, that every nonamenable group contains a free subgroup, is false, as Olshanskii showed in 1980.

**Wikipedia:** [Amenable group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amenable_group), [Paradoxical set](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paradoxical_set). It says: “The critical step in the Banach–Tarski paradox construction is to find inside the rotation group SO(3) a free subgroup on two generators. Amenable groups cannot contain such groups, and do not allow this kind of paradoxical construction.”

**Sources:**

- [J. von Neumann, Zur allgemeinen Theorie des Masses, Fundamenta Mathematicae 13 (1929) 73–116](https://doi.org/10.4064/fm-13-1-73-116)

### Invariant means make quotients of amenable groups amenable

**Remember:** Pull back functions from the quotient to reuse the invariant mean.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 43A07 (Means on groups, semigroups, etc.; amenable groups). arXiv math.GR. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A locally compact Hausdorff group is amenable if it admits a left translation invariant mean on its bounded right uniformly continuous real functions. Here right uniform continuity means that f(gx) approaches f(x) as g approaches the identity, uniformly in x. A mean is a positive linear functional that sends the constant 1 to 1.

**Problem.** Let G be amenable and N a closed normal subgroup. Then the quotient G/N is amenable.

**How the definition helps.** The mean definition lets us use the same functional on functions pulled back from the quotient (our own). Pullback preserves right uniform continuity and commutes with left translations (our own). The composite functional is therefore again a translation invariant mean (our own). For discrete groups, the alternative Følner definition uses finite sets nearly invariant under translations (our own). Their images in a quotient may have unequal fibre sizes, so the same direct argument does not apply to those sets (our own). The work lies in the equivalence of the mean and Følner definitions.

**Wikipedia:** [Amenable group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amenable_group). It says: “Every quotient of an amenable group is amenable.”

**Sources:**

- [M. M. Day, Amenable semigroups, Illinois Journal of Mathematics 1 (1957)](https://doi.org/10.1215/ijm/1255380675)

### The fixed-point definition makes locally compact abelian groups amenable

**Remember:** Commuting affine maps on a compact convex set share a fixed point.

*True by definition.* MSC 43A07 (Means on groups, semigroups, etc.; amenable groups), 47H10. arXiv math.GR, math.FA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A locally compact Hausdorff group is amenable if every continuous affine action on a nonempty compact convex set has a common fixed point. The set lies in a locally convex vector space, such as a normed space, and affine maps preserve convex combinations. The other definition uses a mean, a positive normalized linear functional on essentially bounded measurable functions, unchanged by left translation.

**Problem.** Every locally compact Hausdorff abelian group is amenable.

**How the definition helps.** The fixed-point definition lets us apply the Markov–Kakutani theorem directly, because the maps in an abelian group action commute. That theorem gives a common fixed point for commuting continuous affine maps on a nonempty compact convex set. With the mean definition one must instead produce a translation invariant functional. The work shifted to the fixed-point theorem and the theorem equating the fixed-point and mean definitions.

**Wikipedia:** [Amenable group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amenable_group). It says: “For locally compact abelian groups, this property is satisfied as a result of the Markov–Kakutani fixed-point theorem.”

**Sources:**

- [S. Kakutani, Two fixed-point theorems concerning bicompact convex sets, Proc. Imp. Acad. Tokyo 14 (1938)](https://doi.org/10.3792/pia/1195579652)

### The Følner definition makes the integers and slow-growing groups amenable

**Remember:** Long intervals change little under any fixed shift.

*True by definition.* MSC 43A07 (Means on groups, semigroups, etc.; amenable groups), 20F69. arXiv math.GR. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A discrete group satisfies the Følner condition if every finite set of shifts admits a nonempty finite set changed by arbitrarily small proportions. The change under g is \|gS Δ S\| divided by \|S\|, where Δ collects the elements in exactly one of the two sets. The other definition asks for an invariant mean, a positive normalized linear functional on bounded functions unchanged by translation.

**Problem.** The integers are amenable. So are finitely generated groups of subexponential growth, meaning their balls in a finite generating set grow more slowly than every exponential.

**How the definition helps.** The Følner definition reduces amenability to finding finite sets with small changes under shifts. In ℤ, shifting {1, …, n} by g changes at most 2\|g\| elements, so the relative change tends to zero (our own). In a group of subexponential growth, a suitable subsequence of balls works. For each fixed k, there are arbitrarily large radii r at which the ball of radius r + k is barely larger (our own). Otherwise the sizes would grow exponentially in steps of length k (our own). A shift of length at most k puts the ball in the larger one, making the change at most twice the size difference (our own). The work lies in Følner’s equivalence with invariant means, which a direct proof for ℤ instead constructs by Hahn–Banach.

**Wikipedia:** [Amenable group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amenable_group). It says: “The group of integers is amenable (a sequence of intervals of length tending to infinity is a Følner sequence).”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### The Gelfand transform makes Fourier transforms vanish at infinity

**Remember:** Identify the two transforms and inherit vanishing at infinity.

*True by definition.* MSC 43A25 (Fourier and Fourier-Stieltjes transforms on locally compact and other abelian groups), 46J05. arXiv math.FA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** The spectrum of a commutative complex Banach algebra is the set of its nonzero multiplicative linear functionals, with convergence tested separately at each algebra element. The Gelfand transform of an element evaluates each functional at that element. The Fourier transform of an integrable function uses its integral against the conjugate of each character, a continuous homomorphism to the circle.

**Problem.** For a locally compact Hausdorff abelian group G, the Fourier transform of each integrable function is continuous on the character group and vanishes at infinity. This means that for every ε &gt; 0, the set where its modulus is at least ε is compact. Its modulus is bounded by the integral of the original function’s modulus.

**How the definition helps.** The Gelfand description gives continuity and vanishing at infinity from one theorem for commutative Banach algebras (our own). The same theorem also bounds each transformed value by the norm of the algebra element (our own). Form the group algebra of integrable functions with convolution, which multiplies functions by averaging their translates against one another. Its nonzero multiplicative functionals are exactly the integrals against conjugate characters. The work lies in proving that correspondence and showing that the spectrum topology agrees with uniform convergence on compact subsets of G (our own). The usual integral proof instead establishes decay by direct estimates and approximation (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Pontryagin duality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pontryagin_duality). It says: “This means the Fourier transform is a special case of the Gelfand transform.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Inverse limits make profinite group characters have finite order

**Remember:** A small circle arc cannot contain a nontrivial subgroup.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 43A40 (Character groups and dual objects), 20E18. arXiv math.GR. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A profinite group is an inverse limit of finite discrete groups, or equivalently a compact Hausdorff group with no connected subsets larger than one point. In the limit description, the kernels of the projections to the finite quotients form a neighbourhood basis at the identity. A character is a continuous homomorphism to the circle group ℝ/ℤ.

**Problem.** Every character of a profinite group factors through a finite quotient and has finite order under pointwise addition. Thus the character group of an abelian profinite group is a torsion group, meaning every element has finite order.

**How the definition helps.** The limit definition supplies small open subgroups directly (our own). By continuity, a character sends one of these subgroups into a small arc about 0 (our own). No nontrivial subgroup of the circle fits inside that arc, so the character vanishes on the subgroup and factors through a finite quotient (our own). With only the compact and disconnected definition, the work is to prove that open normal subgroups form a basis (our own). That is the key step in recovering the inverse limit description (our own).

**nLab:** [Pontryagin duality for torsion abelian groups](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Pontryagin+duality+for+torsion+abelian+groups). It says: “Notice that for G a profinite group then hom(G,ℝ/ℤ) ≃ hom(G,ℚ/ℤ)”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### The compact-open topology makes duals of compact abelian groups discrete

**Remember:** Uniform closeness to the constant character forces equality on a compact group.

*True by definition.* MSC 43A40 (Character groups and dual objects), 22B05. arXiv math.FA, math.GR. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A character of a topological abelian group G is a continuous homomorphism into the circle group of complex numbers of modulus 1. Its dual Ĝ is the group of characters under pointwise multiplication. The compact-open topology on Ĝ measures uniform closeness on each compact subset of G.

**Problem.** The dual of a compact Hausdorff abelian group is discrete.

**How the definition helps.** For compact G, the compact-open topology lets one test closeness on the whole group at once. The characters whose values stay within distance 1 of 1 form an open set. No nontrivial subgroup lies in that arc, since a suitable power of any point other than 1 leaves it (our own). Thus the constant character 1 is isolated, and multiplication by other characters isolates them too (our own). Pointwise convergence does not isolate the constant character on the circle group (our own). On any finite set of circle points, some nonzero power is arbitrarily close to 1 simultaneously, by the pigeonhole principle (our own). The work is in the arc argument and the description of the compact-open topology as uniform convergence on compact sets (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Pontryagin duality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pontryagin_duality). It says: “That G being compact implies Ĝ is discrete or that G being discrete implies that Ĝ is compact is an elementary consequence of the definition of the compact-open topology on Ĝ and does not need Pontryagin duality.”

**Sources:**

- [L. Pontrjagin, The theory of topological commutative groups, Annals of Mathematics 35 (1934)](https://doi.org/10.2307/1968438)

### The compact-open topology makes duals of discrete abelian groups compact

**Remember:** Characters of a discrete group form a closed subset of a compact product.

*True by definition.* MSC 43A40 (Character groups and dual objects), 22B05, 54D30. arXiv math.FA, math.GR. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A character of a discrete abelian group G is a homomorphism to the circle group T of complex numbers of modulus 1. The dual Ĝ is the group of characters with the compact-open topology, which tests uniform closeness on compact sets. Compact subsets of G are finite, so this is the topology of pointwise convergence.

**Problem.** Every discrete abelian group has a compact dual.

**How the definition helps.** The compact-open topology identifies Ĝ with a closed subspace of a compact product. The product has one copy of T for each element of G and is compact by Tychonoff’s theorem. Each equation χ(x + y) = χ(x)χ(y) is a closed condition on three coordinates (our own). These equations give precisely the characters, so the dual is compact (our own). Uniform convergence on all of G would isolate every character by the circle arc argument, so an infinite dual would not be compact (our own). The work in this proof lies in Tychonoff’s theorem, not the duality theorem (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Pontryagin duality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pontryagin_duality). It says: “That G being compact implies Ĝ is discrete or that G being discrete implies that Ĝ is compact is an elementary consequence of the definition of the compact-open topology on Ĝ and does not need Pontryagin duality.”

**Sources:**

- [L. Pontrjagin, The theory of topological commutative groups, Annals of Mathematics 35 (1934)](https://doi.org/10.2307/1968438)

### Leptin densities give a geometric proof of the model set density formula

**Remember:** Measure density with compact enlargements, then squeeze between interior and closure.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 43A07 (Means on groups, semigroups, etc.; amenable groups), 52C23. arXiv math.GR, math.DS. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A model set comes from a lattice L in a product G × H of locally compact groups. It keeps the G-coordinates of the lattice points whose H-coordinate lies in a set W, called the window. Leptin densities measure mass per unit of Haar measure. They compare a measure on enlarged sets KA with the volume of A, for compact K and A.

**Problem.** Let G be amenable and let the window W be regular, meaning its boundary has Haar measure zero. Then the model set has density equal to the Haar measure of W divided by the covolume of L. The covolume is the volume of a fundamental domain of L.

**How the definition helps.** In our own reading, Leptin densities need no averaging sequence of sets, so the proof can work directly with fundamental domains of the lattice. The paper bounds both Leptin densities between the Haar measures of the interior and closure of W, divided by the covolume. For a regular window these bounds agree, which gives the formula. On unimodular amenable groups, where left and right Haar measures agree, Leptin densities equal the classical Beurling densities.

**Paper or page:** [Leptin densities in amenable groups](https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.04760v2), [Leptin densities in amenable groups](https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.04760v2). It says: “We use Leptin densities for a geometric proof of the model set density formula, which expresses the density of a uniform regular model set in terms of the volume of its window”

**Sources:**

- [Felix Pogorzelski, Christoph Richard, Nicolae Strungaru, Leptin densities in amenable groups, arXiv:2107.04760v2 (2021)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.04760v2)

## 46 Functional analysis
