**Paper or page:** [Optimal convex $M$-estimation via score matching](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.16688v2). It says: “At the population level, the negative derivative of the optimal convex loss is the best decreasing approximation of the derivative of the log-density of the noise distribution.”

**Sources:**

- [Oliver Y. Feng, Yu-Chun Kao, Min Xu, Richard J. Samworth, Optimal convex $M$-estimation via score matching, arXiv:2403.16688v2 (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.16688v2)

### A maximal invariant turns a composite null hypothesis into a simple one

**Remember:** Keep one label for each set of data that the group links.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 62L10 (Sequential statistical analysis), 62B05. arXiv math.ST. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A group acts on the data. A maximally invariant statistic takes the same value on two data sets exactly when the group maps one to the other. The test uses the likelihood ratio of this statistic.

**Problem.** Under the paper's group assumptions, this likelihood ratio has the best worst-case expected log growth among all e-statistics, invariant or not. It also gives an anytime-valid test.

**How the definition helps.** The law of a maximal invariant ignores the nuisance parameters that the group moves, so all null laws give it one law (our own explanation). The null hypothesis becomes a single law, and a likelihood ratio against a single law is a nonnegative martingale (Proposition 6 in the paper). That martingale gives the anytime-valid test. Proving optimality against tests that are not invariant is harder. The abstract says that this needs amenability, a group property that allows averaging over the group.

**Paper or page:** [E-Statistics, Group Invariance and Anytime Valid Testing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2208.07610v2). It says: “We show that among all e-statistics, invariant or not, the likelihood ratio of the maximally invariant statistic is GROW, both in the absolute and in the relative sense,”

**Sources:**

- [Muriel Felipe Pérez-Ortiz, Tyron Lardy, Rianne de Heide, Peter Grünwald, E-Statistics, Group Invariance and Anytime Valid Testing, arXiv:2208.07610v2 (2022)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2208.07610v2)

### Bounding every loss by one e-value lets the data choose the loss

**Remember:** One pointwise limit protects against every later choice of loss.

*True by definition.* MSC 62L10 (Sequential statistical analysis), 62C05. arXiv stat.TH. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** An e-variable is a nonnegative statistic S whose expectation is at most one under every law in the null hypothesis. A decision rule is compatible with S if, for every decision task, the loss of the rule's decision under the null is at most S.

**Problem.** A decision rule that is compatible with an e-variable is Type-I risk safe (Proposition 1). Type-I risk safe means, in the paper's sense, that the expected loss under the null stays controlled even when the data choose the task.

**How the definition helps.** Compatibility bounds the loss of every task by the same S, so it also bounds the loss of whichever task the data select. Taking expectations under the null then gives the risk bound directly, since the expectation of S is at most one. The paper also proves a converse: every Type-I risk safe rule is compatible with some e-variable. By our own reading, the hard part is finding e-variables that give useful decisions.

**Paper or page:** [Beyond Neyman-Pearson: e-values enable hypothesis testing with a data-driven alpha](https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.00901v3). It says: “With e-values it is straightforward, since they provide Type-I risk control in a generalized Neyman-Pearson setting with the decision task (a general loss function) determined post-hoc, after observation of the data”

**Sources:**

- [Peter Grünwald, Beyond Neyman-Pearson: e-values enable hypothesis testing with a data-driven alpha, arXiv:2205.00901v3 (2022)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.00901v3)

### Correcting predicted bets with randomly sampled true labels keeps e-values valid

**Remember:** Use predictions for speed and random true labels to correct their average.

*True by definition.* MSC 62L10 (Sequential statistical analysis), 62C05, 60G42. arXiv stat.ME, math.ST. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** An e-value is a nonnegative statistic whose expected value is at most one when the hypothesis is true. A prediction-powered bet starts from its value at a predicted label. When the true label is requested at random with probability π, it adds the true bet minus the predicted bet, divided by π.

**Problem.** The corrected product of bets is a valid e-value. If the original bets form a test supermartingale or an e-process, so do the corrected bets.

**How the definition helps.** Averaging over the random request cancels the factor 1/π, so each corrected bet has the same conditional mean as the true bet (our own unpacking). Validity then follows at once from the validity of the original bets. Bad predictions do not break validity, because the correction removes their error on average. The corrected bet must stay nonnegative. If each bet lies between a and b, a request probability of at least 1 − a/b is enough (our own calculation; see Theorem 2.2). Proving that the corrected test keeps most of the original power takes more work.

**Paper or page:** [Prediction-Powered E-Values](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.04294v2). It says: “Eᵖᵖⁱₙ is a valid e-value for the null H₀.”

**Sources:**

- [Daniel Csillag, Claudio José Struchiner, Guilherme Tegoni Goedert, Prediction-Powered E-Values, arXiv:2502.04294v2 (2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.04294v2)

### Forecasts that cannot worsen the track record give all calibration theorems

**Remember:** Choose the next error so that it cannot push past errors further.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 62M20 (Inference from stochastic processes and prediction), 91A26. arXiv econ.TH, stat.ML. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** The track record holds, for each forecast bin, the sum of past errors, where an error is the outcome minus the forecast. A forecast-hedging rule picks each forecast so that the expected new error has a nonpositive inner product with the current track record. So the expected track record can only improve.

**Problem.** If a deterministic rule meets the hedging condition for continuous bins, its calibration score tends to 0 against every outcome sequence. If a randomized rule meets an ε-version of the condition for finitely many bins, its expected calibration score is eventually at most ε.

**How the definition helps.** The hedging condition is chosen so that one short estimate proves calibration. Our own sketch: the new squared norm of the record is the old one, plus twice an inner product, plus the squared new error. Hedging makes the inner product nonpositive in expectation. So the squared record grows at most linearly in time, and the record divided by time tends to 0. The real work moves to showing that hedging forecasts exist. The paper uses fixed-point arguments for deterministic rules and the minimax theorem for randomized rules.

**Paper or page:** [Forecast Hedging and Calibration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.07169v1). It says: “This yields all the calibration results by the same simple basic argument”

**Sources:**

- [Dean P. Foster, Sergiu Hart, Forecast Hedging and Calibration, arXiv:2210.07169v1 (2022); Journal of Political Economy 129, 12 (December 2021), 3447-3490](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.07169v1)

### Replacing each forecast by its running bin average removes the calibration penalty

**Remember:** Keep the forecaster's bins, but forecast each bin's running average outcome.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 62M20 (Inference from stochastic processes and prediction), 91A26. arXiv econ.TH, stat.ML. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** The Brier score is the average squared difference between forecasts and outcomes. Group the days into bins by the forecast given on them. The refinement score is the average squared distance from each outcome to its bin's mean outcome. The calibration score does the same for each forecast, and the Brier score is the sum of the two scores.

**Problem.** Take any forecaster who uses finitely many forecast values. A new rule forecasts, for each bin, the average of past outcomes in that bin. Its Brier score is at most the forecaster's refinement score plus a term of order (log t)/t, for every sequence of outcomes and forecasts.

**How the definition helps.** The split shows that the refinement score is the best Brier score possible while keeping the forecaster's bins. Our own explanation: with all outcomes known, the bin mean minimizes the squared error within each bin. The new rule copies this using only past outcomes, so it pays only a small learning cost. Theorem 3 bounds that cost.

**Paper or page:** ["Calibeating": Beating Forecasters at Their Own Game](https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.04892v2). It says: “The Brier score is the sum of the calibration score and the refinement score”

**Sources:**

- [Dean P. Foster, Sergiu Hart, "Calibeating": Beating Forecasters at Their Own Game, arXiv:2209.04892v2 (2022); Theoretical Economics 18 (2023), 4, 1441-1474](https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.04892v2)

### Smoothed calibration can be guaranteed by deterministic forecasts, even when leaked

**Remember:** Blend nearby forecasts, and a deterministic forecaster can stay calibrated even when watched.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 62M20 (Inference from stochastic processes and prediction), 91A26. arXiv econ.TH, stat.ML. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Calibration asks that, for each forecast value, the average outcome on the days with that forecast is close to the forecast. Smooth calibration replaces the days with exactly that forecast by a weighted average over days with nearby forecasts. The weights change continuously, with a Lipschitz bound L, as the forecasts move apart.

**Problem.** For every tolerance ε &gt; 0 and every Lipschitz bound L, some deterministic rule is (ε, L)-smoothly calibrated against every outcome sequence. This holds even when the forecasts are leaked, that is, known before the outcome is chosen. No deterministic rule can guarantee ordinary calibration.

**How the definition helps.** Smoothing lets nearby forecasts share one average, so one adversarial split of the forecasts no longer forces a large error. Our own example shows why exact bins fail. An adversary who sees the forecast chooses outcome 1 when it is below one-half and 0 otherwise. Then forecasts below one-half see only 1s and the others see only 0s, so the error stays near one-half. Smoothing mixes forecasts just below and just above one-half, so these errors can cancel. The paper still has to build the rule, and it does so through online linear regression and weak calibration.

**Paper or page:** [Smooth Calibration, Leaky Forecasts, Finite Recall, and Nash Dynamics](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.07152v1). It says: “While regular calibration can be guaranteed only by randomized forecasting procedures, we show that smooth calibration can be guaranteed by deterministic procedures.”

**Sources:**

- [Dean P. Foster, Sergiu Hart, Smooth Calibration, Leaky Forecasts, Finite Recall, and Nash Dynamics, arXiv:2210.07152v1 (2022); Games and Economic Behavior 109 (May 2018), 271-293](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.07152v1)

## 65 Numerical analysis

### Romberg estimates as extrapolation to zero cancel the leading error terms

**Remember:** Interpolation at zero removes every fitted power of the spacing.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 65B05 (Extrapolation to the limit, deferred corrections), 65D32. arXiv math.NA. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** Let T(h) be the trapezoidal estimate with spacing h. Define a Romberg estimate as the value at zero of the polynomial in h² that interpolates T at k + 1 spacings. The usual definition is the recursive Romberg table, which combines neighbouring estimates to remove one error term at a time. Neville's algorithm shows that the two agree.

**Problem.** Suppose T(h) = I + c₁h² + … + cₖh²ᵏ + O(h²ᵏ⁺²), where I is the integral. Take spacings h₀, …, hₖ that are fixed distinct multiples of h. Then the Romberg estimate differs from I by O(h²ᵏ⁺²).

**How the definition helps.** With the interpolation definition, the polynomial part of the error disappears at once. Interpolation of degree k in h² reproduces I + c₁h² + … + cₖh²ᵏ exactly, so its value at zero is I. The weights for the value at zero depend only on the ratios of the spacings. So the remainders add only O(h²ᵏ⁺²). The work goes into the Euler–Maclaurin formula, which gives the even-power expansion for smooth integrands, and into Neville's algorithm. Wikipedia describes the method as repeated Richardson extrapolation. The argument is our own.

**Wikipedia:** [Romberg's method](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romberg%27s_method). It says: “by applying Richardson extrapolation repeatedly on the trapezium rule or the rectangle rule”

**Sources:**

- [Lewis Fry Richardson, The approximate arithmetical solution by finite differences of physical problems involving differential equations, with an application to the stresses in a masonry dam (1911).](https://doi.org/10.1098/rsta.1911.0009)

### Divided differences as leading coefficients are symmetric in the nodes

**Remember:** Reordering the data cannot change the unique interpolating polynomial.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 65D05 (Numerical interpolation), 41A05. arXiv math.NA. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** Take distinct nodes x₀, …, xₙ and the polynomial of degree at most n that interpolates f at them. Define f\[x₀, …, xₙ\] as its coefficient of xⁿ. The usual definition is recursive: f\[x₀, …, xₙ\] = (f\[x₁, …, xₙ\] − f\[x₀, …, xₙ₋₁\]) / (xₙ − x₀).

**Problem.** f\[x₀, …, xₙ\] does not change when the nodes are permuted.

**How the definition helps.** With the leading-coefficient definition, symmetry is immediate. The interpolating polynomial depends only on the set of data points, not on their order. So its leading coefficient does not depend on the order either. From the recursive definition, symmetry needs an induction. The work goes into the theorem that the leading coefficients satisfy the recursion. Wikipedia states the symmetry. This argument is our own.

**Wikipedia:** [Divided differences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Divided_differences). It says: “Divided differences are symmetric”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Writing interpolants in Newton’s basis keeps old coefficients when nodes are added

**Remember:** A new Newton term vanishes at every old node.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 65D05 (Numerical interpolation). arXiv math.NA. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** Given distinct nodes x₀, x₁, …, write the interpolating polynomial in Newton’s basis. Its jth basis polynomial is (x − x₀)(x − x₁)⋯(x − xⱼ₋₁), and the 0th is one. The Lagrange form instead uses, for each node, the polynomial equal to one there and zero at the other nodes.

**Problem.** Adding a new distinct node at the end of the list adds one Newton term and leaves the earlier coefficients unchanged.

**How the definition helps.** The new basis polynomial vanishes at every old node, so adding a multiple of it keeps all the old interpolation conditions. Its value at the new node is nonzero, so exactly one multiple fits the new data value. By uniqueness of the interpolating polynomial, this sum is the new interpolant. In the Lagrange form, every basis polynomial changes when a node is added. The new coefficient is the divided difference over all the nodes. These proof steps are our own; Wikipedia names Lagrange polynomials as an alternative basis.

**Wikipedia:** [Newton polynomial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newton_polynomial). It says: “The unique interpolating polynomial can alternatively be constructed using Lagrange polynomials as an alternative basis”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### De Casteljau's definition keeps Bézier curves inside the control points' convex hull

**Remember:** Averages of points in a convex set stay in that set.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 65D17 (Computer-aided design (modeling of curves and surfaces)), 41A10. arXiv cs.GR, math.NA. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** Define the point B(t) of a Bézier curve by de Casteljau's algorithm. Replace each adjacent pair of control points P and Q by (1 − t)P + tQ, and repeat until one point remains. The polynomial definition is B(t) = Σ C(n, i) (1 − t)ⁿ⁻ⁱ tⁱ Pᵢ, with Bernstein polynomial weights.

**Problem.** For 0 ≤ t ≤ 1, the curve point B(t) lies in the convex hull of the control points.

**How the definition helps.** With de Casteljau's definition, each step forms convex combinations, so no step can leave the hull. For 0 ≤ t ≤ 1, the weights 1 − t and t are nonnegative and sum to 1. A convex combination of points in a convex set stays in the set. With the Bernstein definition the proof is also short: the weights are nonnegative and sum to 1 by the binomial theorem. The work goes into the theorem that the two definitions agree. Wikipedia states the convex hull property and the interpolation reading of each step.

**Wikipedia:** [Bézier curve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/B%C3%A9zier_curve). It says: “The convex hull of the Bézier polygon contains the Bézier curve.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Orthogonal-polynomial nodes make Gaussian quadrature exact through degree 2n − 1

**Remember:** The part divisible by the node polynomial vanishes both ways.

*True by definition.* MSC 65D32 (Numerical quadrature and cubature formulas), 41A55. arXiv math.NA. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** Let w be a positive weight on an interval, and let pₙ be the degree-n orthogonal polynomial for w. Take the n roots of pₙ as nodes. Define the weights by integrating the interpolating polynomial of degree at most n − 1 through those nodes. The rival definition solves 2n nonlinear moment equations for the nodes and weights together.

**Problem.** The n-node Gaussian rule integrates every polynomial of degree at most 2n − 1 exactly.

**How the definition helps.** With nodes at the roots, the degree count splits into two easy parts. Divide a polynomial h of degree at most 2n − 1 by pₙ to get h = q pₙ + r. Both q and r have degree at most n − 1. The term q pₙ integrates to zero by orthogonality and vanishes at every node. The rule is exact for r because r equals its own interpolant. Wikipedia gives this proof. The work goes into showing that pₙ has n distinct roots inside the interval.

**Wikipedia:** [Gaussian quadrature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaussian_quadrature). It says: “This proves that for any polynomial h(x) of degree 2n − 1 or less, its integral is given exactly by the Gaussian quadrature sum.”

**Sources:**

- [C. G. J. Jacobi, Ueber Gauß neue Methode, die Werthe der Integrale näherungsweise zu finden (1826).](https://doi.org/10.1515/crll.1826.1.301)

### Derivative-based relative condition numbers are submultiplicative under composition

**Remember:** The intermediate size ‖f(x)‖ cancels between the two relative factors.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 65F35 (Numerical computation of matrix norms, conditioning, scaling), 15A12. arXiv math.NA. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** For a differentiable map f with x and f(x) nonzero, define κ(f, x) = ‖J(x)‖ ‖x‖ / ‖f(x)‖. Here J(x) is the derivative matrix, and ‖J(x)‖ is its induced norm. The perturbation definition takes the worst ratio of relative output change to relative input change, in the limit of small changes. For differentiable f the two definitions agree.

**Problem.** Let x, f(x) and g(f(x)) be nonzero. Then κ(g ∘ f, x) ≤ κ(g, f(x)) κ(f, x).

**How the definition helps.** With the derivative formula, the result is the chain rule plus one norm bound. The derivative of g ∘ f at x is the product of the two derivatives. Bound the norm of the product by the product of the norms. Then multiply and divide by ‖f(x)‖, which makes the two factors appear. The work goes into the proof that the derivative formula equals the limit of worst ratios. Wikipedia gives the limit definition. The argument is our own.

**Wikipedia:** [Condition number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Condition_number). It says: “the maximum ratio of the fractional change in f(x) to any fractional change in x”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Max-min singular values make the best rank-k error equal σₖ₊₁

**Remember:** A low-rank map must kill some direction of the best trial space.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 65F55 (Numerical methods for low-rank matrix approximation; matrix compression), 15A18. arXiv math.NA. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** For an n × n matrix M, define the kth singular value σₖ by a max-min. It is the maximum, over k-dimensional subspaces S, of the minimum of ‖Mx‖ over unit vectors x in S. The usual definition takes square roots of the eigenvalues of M\*M, in decreasing order. The min-max theorem shows that the two agree.

**Problem.** For 0 ≤ k &lt; n, the smallest Euclidean operator-norm distance from M to a matrix of rank at most k is σₖ₊₁.

**How the definition helps.** With the max-min definition, the lower bound needs only a dimension count. Let B have rank at most k, and let S be a (k + 1)-dimensional subspace that attains σₖ₊₁. The kernel of B has dimension at least n − k, so it meets S in some unit vector x. Then ‖(M − B)x‖ = ‖Mx‖ ≥ σₖ₊₁. The truncated singular value decomposition attains the bound. The work goes into the singular value decomposition and the max-min formula. Wikipedia states that formula without a reference, and the argument is our own.

**Wikipedia:** [Min-max theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Min-max_theorem). It says: “The singular values {σₖ} of a square matrix M are the square roots of the eigenvalues of M\*M (equivalently MM\*).”

**Sources:**

- [Leon Mirsky, Symmetric gauge functions and unitarily invariant norms (1960).](https://doi.org/10.1093/qmath/11.1.50)

### Subnormal numbers make the Sterbenz lemma hold without exceptions

**Remember:** With gradual underflow, subtracting close floating-point numbers is always exact.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 65G30 (Interval and finite arithmetic), 65G50. arXiv math.NA, cs.NA. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** A floating-point number is subnormal when it is smaller than the smallest normal number. It uses the lowest exponent with a leading digit 0, so it has fewer significant digits. Gradual underflow is the rule of the IEEE 754 standard that keeps these numbers. They fill the gap between zero and the smallest normal number with even spacing.

**Problem.** Let x and y be floating-point numbers with y/2 ≤ x ≤ 2y. Then x − y is a floating-point number, so the computed difference is exact. This is the Sterbenz lemma.

**How the definition helps.** With subnormal numbers, every small difference of nearby floating-point numbers has a representation, so no rounding is needed. The page gives the counterexample. The difference of the two smallest positive normal numbers is necessarily subnormal. If the system flushes it to zero, the result is wrong. Our own: with gradual underflow, x − y = 0 also implies x = y, which simple tests for division by zero rely on. The lemma does not remove catastrophic cancellation, the loss of accuracy when one subtracts close numbers. The page explains that the subtraction is exact, but inputs that already carry errors can give a difference with a large relative error.

**Wikipedia:** [Sterbenz lemma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sterbenz_lemma). It says: “In floating-point number systems without subnormal numbers, such as CPUs in nonstandard flush-to-zero mode instead of the standard gradual underflow, the Sterbenz lemma does not apply.”

**Sources:**

- [P. H. Sterbenz, Floating-Point Computation, Prentice-Hall (1974), Theorem 4.3.1](https://archive.org/details/SterbenzFloatingPointComputation/page/n153/mode/2up)
- [J.-M. Muller et al., Handbook of Floating-Point Arithmetic, 2nd ed., Birkhäuser (2018), Lemma 4.1](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-319-76526-6)

### Backward error and condition number split numerical error into two parts

**Remember:** Forward error is at most condition number times backward error.

*True by definition.* MSC 65G50 (Roundoff error), 65F35. arXiv math.NA. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** The backward error of a computed answer y\* is the smallest change Δx in the data such that the exact answer for x + Δx is y\*. An algorithm is backward stable when this is small for all inputs. The condition number of the problem is the worst-case ratio of the relative change in output to the relative change in input.

**Problem.** To first order, the relative error of the computed answer is at most the condition number times the relative backward error. So a backward stable algorithm is accurate on every well-conditioned problem.

**How the definition helps.** The two definitions fit together. The backward error moves the rounding into the data, and the condition number says how far a change in the data moves the answer. The bound then follows from the definition of the condition number. The condition number page says that the condition number is a property of the problem. It also says that a backward stable algorithm can be expected to solve well-conditioned problems accurately. So the analysis of the algorithm and the analysis of the problem separate. What stays hard is the rounding analysis that shows a given algorithm, such as Householder QR factorization, is backward stable.

**Wikipedia:** [Numerical stability](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Numerical_stability), [Condition number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Condition_number). It says: “An algorithm is forward stable if its forward error divided by the condition number of the problem is small.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Zero-stability makes consistent multistep methods converge

**Remember:** Check the roots of ρ, and convergence comes for free.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 65L20 (Stability and convergence of numerical methods for ordinary differential equations), 65L06. arXiv math.NA. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** A linear multistep method computes each new value from several earlier values. Its first characteristic polynomial ρ satisfies the root condition when all roots have modulus at most 1 and the roots of modulus 1 are simple. A method is zero-stable if and only if the root condition holds.

**Problem.** Take a consistent linear multistep method whose starting values converge. Its numerical solution converges as the step size goes to 0 if and only if the method is zero-stable. This is the Dahlquist equivalence theorem.

**How the definition helps.** Zero-stability is a condition on one polynomial, so a hard limit statement becomes an algebra check. The definition excludes methods whose errors in the starting values grow without bound. Our own: the explicit two-step method yₙ₊₂ + 4yₙ₊₁ − 5yₙ = h(4fₙ₊₁ + 2fₙ) is consistent, even of order 3. But ρ has the root −5, so small errors grow like 5ⁿ and the method diverges. What stays hard is the proof that zero-stability and consistency are enough. The first Dahlquist barrier also shows that zero-stability limits the order a method can reach.

**Wikipedia:** [Linear multistep method](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_multistep_method). It says: “Then, the numerical solution converges to the exact solution as h → 0 if and only if the method is zero-stable. This result is known as the Dahlquist equivalence theorem”

**Sources:**

- [G. Dahlquist, Convergence and stability in the numerical integration of ordinary differential equations, Mathematica Scandinavica 4 (1956) 33–53](https://doi.org/10.7146/math.scand.a-10454)

### Lebesgue constants as operator norms bound interpolation error by best approximation

**Remember:** Subtract the best polynomial first, then let interpolation amplify only that.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 65D05 (Numerical interpolation), 41A05. arXiv math.NA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let L be polynomial interpolation at fixed nodes, viewed as a map on continuous functions with the supremum norm. Define the Lebesgue constant Λ as the operator norm of L. The formula definition takes the maximum of Σ \|ℓⱼ(x)\|. Here ℓⱼ is the cardinal polynomial, which is 1 at node j and 0 at the other nodes.

**Problem.** For every continuous f, ‖f − Lf‖ ≤ (1 + Λ) E(f). Here E(f) is the supremum-norm distance from f to polynomials of the interpolation degree.

**How the definition helps.** With the operator-norm definition, the bound is Lebesgue's lemma, a three-line proof. L fixes every polynomial p of the interpolation degree. So f − Lf = (f − p) − L(f − p), and the triangle inequality gives (1 + Λ)‖f − p‖. Minimize over p. The cited paper's Lemma 2 is the theorem that the two definitions agree, also for complex nodes. The error bound itself is our own here.

**Paper or page:** [Chebyshev admissible meshes and Lebesgue constants of complex polynomial projections](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.06511v1). It says: “the “Lebesgue constant” of Lₙ, that is its uniform norm”

**Sources:**

### Defining conjugate gradients by energy minimization bounds steps by distinct eigenvalues

**Remember:** One polynomial can invert A on every eigenvalue at once.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 65F10 (Iterative numerical methods for linear systems), 15A18. arXiv math.NA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let A be real symmetric positive definite, and solve Ax = b with exact solution x\*. Start from x₀ with residual r₀ = b − Ax₀, and let K(k) be the span of r₀, Ar₀, …, Aᵏ⁻¹r₀. Define the kth conjugate gradient iterate as the point of x₀ + K(k) that minimizes the energy norm √(eᵀAe) of the error e. The Hestenes–Stiefel algorithm computes these points with short recurrences instead.

**Problem.** If A has d distinct eigenvalues, exact conjugate gradients reach the solution in at most d steps.

**How the definition helps.** With the minimization definition, it is enough to show that the exact correction lies in K(d). Let p be the polynomial of degree at most d − 1 with p(λ) = 1/λ at each distinct eigenvalue λ. Since A is diagonalizable, p(A) = A⁻¹. So x\* − x₀ = A⁻¹r₀ = p(A)r₀ lies in K(d), and the minimizer at step d is x\*. The work goes into the proof that the short recurrences give the minimizers. Wikipedia states only the bound of n steps. The bound by distinct eigenvalues and its proof are our own.

**Wikipedia:** [Conjugate gradient method](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conjugate_gradient_method). It says: “Conjugate gradient, assuming exact arithmetic, converges in at most n steps, where n is the size of the matrix of the system”

**Sources:**

- [Magnus R. Hestenes and Eduard Stiefel, Methods of conjugate gradients for solving linear systems (1952).](https://doi.org/10.6028/jres.049.044)

### Defining GMRES iterates as residual minimizers makes residuals never increase

**Remember:** A larger search space cannot make the best residual worse.

*True by definition.* MSC 65F10 (Iterative numerical methods for linear systems). arXiv math.NA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** GMRES (the generalized minimal residual method) solves Ax = b from a first guess x₀. Let r₀ = b − Ax₀, and let Kₙ be the span of r₀, Ar₀, …, Aⁿ⁻¹r₀. Define the nth GMRES iterate xₙ as the point of x₀ + Kₙ with the smallest Euclidean residual ‖b − Axₙ‖. The algorithm computes this point with the Arnoldi process, which builds an orthonormal basis of Kₙ, and a small least-squares problem.

**Problem.** In exact arithmetic, the GMRES residual norm never increases from one step to the next.

**How the definition helps.** With the minimizer definition, the result is a comparison of two minima. The space Kₙ lies inside Kₙ₊₁, so xₙ is a candidate at step n + 1. Hence the best residual at step n + 1 is no larger. Wikipedia makes this argument. The work goes into the proof that the Arnoldi process and the small least-squares problem give this minimizer.

**Wikipedia:** [Generalized minimal residual method](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generalized_minimal_residual_method). It says: “Since every subspace is contained in the next subspace, the residual does not increase.”

**Sources:**

- [Yousef Saad and Martin H. Schultz, GMRES: A Generalized Minimal Residual Algorithm for Solving Nonsymmetric Linear Systems (1986).](https://doi.org/10.1137/0907058)

### Defining Lanczos vectors by Gram–Schmidt on Krylov vectors makes Q\*AQ tridiagonal

**Remember:** A moves each vector at most one step along, and symmetry gives the rest.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 65F15 (Numerical computation of eigenvalues and eigenvectors of matrices). arXiv math.NA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let A be Hermitian and v a starting vector. The Krylov vectors are v, Av, …, Aᵐ⁻¹v. Define the Lanczos vectors q₁, …, qₘ by applying Gram–Schmidt to them. The algorithm instead computes them by a three-term recurrence that keeps only two previous vectors.

**Problem.** In exact arithmetic, while v, Av, …, Aᵐ⁻¹v stay independent, T = Q\*AQ is tridiagonal, where Q has the Lanczos vectors as columns. Tridiagonal means nonzero only on the main diagonal and the two next to it.

**How the definition helps.** With the Krylov definition, the zero pattern of T follows from two facts. First, Aqⱼ lies in the span of q₁, …, qⱼ₊₁, so qᵢ\*Aqⱼ = 0 when i &gt; j + 1. Second, T is Hermitian, so the entries with j &gt; i + 1 vanish too. The three-term recurrence is then a consequence, not a definition. The work goes into showing that the recurrence gives the Gram–Schmidt vectors. Wikipedia states that T = V\*AV is tridiagonal. The argument is our own.

**Wikipedia:** [Lanczos algorithm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lanczos_algorithm). It says: “a tridiagonal real symmetric matrix T = V∗AV”

**Sources:**

### Defining Ritz values by min-max makes them fall as trial spaces grow

**Remember:** A larger trial space offers more subspaces, so each minimum can only drop.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 65F15 (Numerical computation of eigenvalues and eigenvectors of matrices), 15A42. arXiv math.NA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let A be a Hermitian matrix and V a trial subspace. Define the kth Ritz value θₖ(V) by a min-max. It is the minimum, over k-dimensional subspaces S of V, of the largest Rayleigh quotient x\*Ax / x\*x on S. The usual definition takes the eigenvalues of Q\*AQ, where the columns of Q are an orthonormal basis of V.

**Problem.** If V ⊆ W and k ≤ dim V, then θₖ(W) ≤ θₖ(V).

**How the definition helps.** With the min-max definition, the result is a comparison of two minima. Every k-dimensional subspace of V is also one of W. A minimum over a larger family cannot be larger. The work goes into the min-max theorem for Q\*AQ, which shows that the two definitions agree. With W the whole space, the result is one half of the Cauchy interlacing theorem. Wikipedia states the min-max theorem and the interlacing theorem; the comparison argument is our own.

**Wikipedia:** [Min-max theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Min-max_theorem). It says: “a variational characterization of eigenvalues of compact Hermitian operators on Hilbert spaces”

### Min-max generalized eigenvalues fall when the mass matrix grows

**Remember:** Larger denominators lower the quotient in every trial direction.

*True by definition.* MSC 65F15 (Numerical computation of eigenvalues and eigenvectors of matrices), 15A22. arXiv math.NA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For symmetric positive definite matrices A and B, define the kth generalized eigenvalue λₖ(A, B) by a min-max. It is the minimum, over k-dimensional subspaces, of the largest quotient xᵀAx / xᵀBx. The algebraic definition solves Av = λBv. The two agree by the ordinary min-max theorem, applied after a change of variables by the square root of B.

**Problem.** If B̃ − B is positive semidefinite, then λₖ(A, B̃) ≤ λₖ(A, B) for every k.

**How the definition helps.** With the min-max definition, the inequality holds subspace by subspace. Since xᵀAx &gt; 0 and xᵀB̃x ≥ xᵀBx &gt; 0, each quotient for B̃ is at most the one for B. Taking the maximum and then the minimum keeps the inequality. The paper's Corollary 3.6 states this result. The work goes into the min-max theorem for the pair. The subspace argument is our own.

**Paper or page:** [A mathematical theory for mass lumping and its generalization with applications to isogeometric analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.03614v4). It says: “λₖ(A, B̃) ≤ λₖ(A, B) for all k = 1, …, n.”

### Pseudospectra as perturbed spectra make nearby matrices' pseudospectra nest

**Remember:** Two perturbations fit within the sum of their budgets.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 65F15 (Numerical computation of eigenvalues and eigenvectors of matrices), 15A18. arXiv math.NA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Define the ε-pseudospectrum Λ(A, ε) as the set of eigenvalues of all matrices A + E with ‖E‖ ≤ ε, in the Euclidean operator norm. The resolvent definition takes all z with ‖(zI − A)⁻¹‖ ≥ 1/ε, together with the eigenvalues of A. The two agree because the smallest perturbation that makes z an eigenvalue has norm equal to the smallest singular value of zI − A.

**Problem.** If ‖A − B‖ ≤ δ, then Λ(B, ε) ⊆ Λ(A, ε + δ).

**How the definition helps.** With the perturbation definition, the inclusion is the triangle inequality. Let z be an eigenvalue of B + E with ‖E‖ ≤ ε. Then B + E = A + F with F = (B − A) + E, and ‖F‖ ≤ ε + δ. From the resolvent definition, one would need a bound on how the resolvent norm changes with the matrix. The work goes into the theorem that the definitions agree. Wikipedia gives the perturbation definition. The argument is our own.

**Wikipedia:** [Pseudospectrum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pseudospectrum). It says: “The ε-pseudospectrum of a matrix A consists of all eigenvalues of matrices which are ε-close to A”

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 65G30 (Interval and finite arithmetic), 65G40. arXiv math.NA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For intervals X and Y, define X ∗ Y as the set of all x ∗ y with x in X and y in Y. For the four arithmetic operations this set is again an interval, if division by an interval containing zero is excluded. The computational definition gives endpoint formulas instead, such as the minimum and maximum of the four endpoint products.

**Problem.** If X ⊆ X′ and Y ⊆ Y′, then X ∗ Y ⊆ X′ ∗ Y′. By induction, every expression built from these operations is inclusion monotone wherever it is defined.

**How the definition helps.** With the set definition, inclusion monotonicity is immediate. Larger input intervals allow more operand pairs, so the set of results can only grow. From the endpoint formulas, one would have to compare minima and maxima case by case. ### Generalized colleague matrices have a polynomial’s roots as eigenvalues

**Remember:** Multiplication by x modulo the polynomial has the roots as eigenvalues.

*True by definition.* MSC 65H04 (Numerical computation of roots of polynomial equations), 65F15, 15A18. arXiv math.NA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Expand a degree-n polynomial in a basis that satisfies a three-term recurrence, like the Chebyshev polynomials. The generalized colleague matrix is a tridiagonal matrix from the recurrence plus a rank-one correction from the coefficients. Our own reading is that it is the matrix of multiplication by x modulo the polynomial, up to transposition.

**Problem.** The eigenvalues of the generalized colleague matrix are the roots of the polynomial. So finding the roots of a function, once it is approximated by such a polynomial, becomes an eigenvalue problem.

**How the definition helps.** In the ring of polynomials where p counts as zero, multiplication by x has the roots of p as its eigenvalues (our own). The recurrence gives the tridiagonal part, and reducing the top-degree term by p gives the rank-one correction (our own). So the theorem follows from the definition (our own). The paper’s work is to build well-conditioned bases on complex domains and a stable QR algorithm for these matrices.

### Measuring trial functions by the operator’s output makes operator equations well-posed

**Remember:** Measure a trial function by what the operator does to it.

*True by definition.* MSC 65J10 (Numerical solutions to equations with linear operators), 47A50, 46B04. arXiv math.NA, math.FA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Start from an injective linear operator B from a trial space into the dual V′ of a test space. Give each trial function u the norm of Bu in V′. Complete the trial space in this norm and extend B continuously to the completion.

**Problem.** If the range of B is dense in V′, the extended operator is an isometric isomorphism from the completion onto V′. So the extended equation has exactly one solution for each right-hand side, with norm equal to that of the data.

**How the definition helps.** With the new norm, B preserves norms by definition, so the extension is an isometry (our own). The image of a complete space under an isometry is complete, hence closed (our own). A closed dense subspace is the whole space, so the extension is onto (our own). The real work moves to checking injectivity and density for each equation and to identifying the completed space. The paper treats elliptic, parabolic and hyperbolic equations this way.

**Paper or page:** [A unified framework for the analysis, numerical approximation and model reduction of linear operator equations, Part I: Well-posedness in space and time](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.05407v1). It says: “The main concept is completion and extension of operators starting from the strong form of the problem.”

### A-stability turns stiff solvers into a sharp order barrier

**Remember:** Stable for every decaying mode means order two at most.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 65L20 (Stability and convergence of numerical methods for ordinary differential equations), 65L06, 65L04. arXiv math.NA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Apply a method to the test equation y′ = λy with step h. The method is A-stable when its numerical solution goes to zero for every hλ with negative real part. So it copies the decay of every stable linear equation, however stiff (with very fast decaying parts).

**Problem.** No explicit linear multistep method is A-stable. An A-stable linear multistep method has order at most 2, and among those the trapezoidal rule has the smallest error constant.

**How the definition helps.** A-stability replaces the vague wish to handle stiff equations with a property of one test equation, and a property of one rational function can be proved impossible. The page on stiff equations says that the test equation determines the stability region of a method. With this definition, Dahlquist could prove a sharp barrier. The barrier explains why stiff solvers use implicit Runge–Kutta methods or methods that are stable in a weaker sense. What stays hard is the proof of the barrier itself, which uses complex analysis of the stability function.

**Wikipedia:** [Linear multistep method](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_multistep_method), [Stiff equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stiff_equation). It says: “The second Dahlquist barrier states that no explicit linear multistep methods are A-stable. Further, the maximal order of an (implicit) A-stable linear multistep method is 2.”

**Remember:** Only the Hermitian part controls how fast the length can grow.

*True by definition.* MSC 65L20 (Stability and convergence of numerical methods for ordinary differential equations), 15A60. arXiv math.NA. Level 3: graduate.

Grönwall's inequality then gives the bound. Wikipedia states the bound and says that the two definitions agree for bounded operators. The work goes into that equivalence. ### Lax's equivalence theorem trades convergence for stability

**Remember:** Consistency plus stability equals convergence.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 65M12 (Stability and convergence of numerical methods for initial value and initial-boundary value problems involving PDEs), 65M06. arXiv math.NA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A problem is well-posed in Hadamard's sense when a solution exists, is unique, and depends continuously on the data. A finite difference scheme is consistent when it approximates the right equation as the grid shrinks. It is stable (Lax–Richtmyer stable) when the powers of its update operator stay uniformly bounded in norm.

**Problem.** For a consistent linear scheme for a well-posed linear initial value problem, the scheme converges to the true solution if and only if it is stable.

**How the definition helps.** The definitions split the hard question of convergence into two easier checks. The page says that consistency is straightforward to verify and that stability is much easier to show than convergence. Well-posedness is needed: for an ill-posed problem, such as the backward heat equation that the well-posed page names, no scheme could converge in a useful way. Our own: one direction of the proof uses the uniform boundedness principle. What stays hard is to prove stability for a given scheme. The page notes that von Neumann's Fourier test only implies true stability in certain cases.

### Coercivity makes the Galerkin solution nearly the best approximation

**Remember:** Coercivity on the big space passes to every subspace.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 65N30 (Finite element, Rayleigh-Ritz and Galerkin methods for boundary value problems involving PDEs), 35A15. arXiv math.NA, math.AP. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A bilinear form a on a Hilbert space V is coercive when a(v, v) ≥ α‖v‖² for some α &gt; 0 and all v. It is continuous when \|a(v, w)\| ≤ γ‖v‖‖w‖. The Galerkin method solves the same equation a(uₕ, v) = L(v) only for v in a finite-dimensional subspace Vₕ.

**Problem.** The error of the Galerkin solution is at most γ/α times the error of the best approximation of u from Vₕ. This is Céa's lemma, the basic error bound of the finite element method.

### Pressure spaces containing all velocity divergences make discrete flows exactly divergence-free

**Remember:** Test the divergence against itself to show it vanishes.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 65N30 (Finite element, Rayleigh-Ritz and Galerkin methods for boundary value problems involving PDEs), 76D07. arXiv math.NA. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A mixed finite element method approximates velocity and pressure in separate spaces. Choose the pressure space Qₕ to contain the divergence of every discrete velocity in Vₕ. The velocities must also have continuous normal components across shared faces, so each has a square-integrable divergence. Without the containment, the discrete constraint ∫ q div v = 0 for all q in Qₕ leaves div v nonzero in general.

**Problem.** Assume div Vₕ ⊆ Qₕ. Let a discrete velocity v satisfy ∫ q div v = 0 for all q in Qₕ. Then div v = 0.

**How the definition helps.** With the containment, one test function settles the question. Take q = div v, so ∫ (div v)² = 0 and div v = 0. The paper's Lemma 2 states this result for its method on quadrilateral cells, with the containment on the reference cell. The work goes into building such spaces and mapping them to each cell so that the containment survives. The one-line test argument is our own.

**Paper or page:** [Design and analysis of an exactly divergence-free hybridized discontinuous Galerkin method for incompressible flows on meshes with quadrilateral cells](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.05288v2). It says: “then discretely divergence-free functions are weakly divergence-free”

**Sources:**

- [Design and analysis of an exactly divergence-free hybridized discontinuous Galerkin method for incompressible flows on meshes with quadrilateral cells](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.05288v2)

### Seeking solutions in the range of nodal clipping makes bounds automatic

**Remember:** Clip the node values before calling them the solution.

*True by definition.* MSC 65N30 (Finite element, Rayleigh-Ritz and Galerkin methods for boundary value problems involving PDEs), 65N15. arXiv math.NA. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** At each mesh node, replace a value outside the allowed interval by the nearer endpoint. This map is a nonlinear projection. The method seeks its finite element solution in the range of this projection, with a stabilizing term because the projection is not injective.

**Problem.** The numerical solution satisfies the known bounds at every node, by construction. For linear reaction-diffusion problems, it is also the best approximation in the energy norm among all nodally bound-preserving finite element functions.

**How the definition helps.** Every function in the projection’s range satisfies the nodal bounds, so that part needs no proof. Between nodes, the bounds can fail for elements of higher degree (our own). The real work is to show that the stabilized problem has a unique solution. Its clipped part then solves a variational inequality, as in a discrete obstacle problem. The paper uses this to prove the best-approximation result.

**Paper or page:** [A Nodally Bound-Preserving Finite Element Method](https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.01067v1). It says: “The discrete problem involves a nonlinear projection operator mapping arbitrary nodal values into bound-preserving ones and seeks the numerical solution in the range of this projection.”

**Sources:**

- [Gabriel Barrenechea, Emmanuil Georgoulis, Tristan Pryer, Andreas Veeser, A Nodally Bound-Preserving Finite Element Method, arXiv:2304.01067v1 (2023)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.01067v1)
- [Gabriel Barrenechea, Emmanuil Georgoulis, Tristan Pryer, Andreas Veeser, A nodally bound-preserving finite element method, IMA Journal of Numerical Analysis 44 (2024) 2198–2219](https://doi.org/10.1093/imanum/drad055)

## 68 Computer science

### A read-only input tape makes logarithmic space a meaningful class

**Remember:** Do not charge a machine for merely reading its input.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 68Q15 (Complexity classes (hierarchies, relations among complexity classes, etc.)), 68Q04. arXiv cs.CC. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** The class L contains the decision problems that a deterministic Turing machine solves using a logarithmic amount of writable memory. The machine reads its input from a separate tape that it cannot write on. Only the cells used on the work tape count as space.

**Problem.** One wants space classes below linear space, such as L and NL, and theorems about them, such as L ⊆ P. If the input sat on the work tape, every machine would use at least linear space.

**How the definition helps.** Separating the read-only input from the work tape means that space measures only memory the machine writes, so sublinear bounds make sense. A log-space machine can then hold a fixed number of pointers into the input, as the page says. It has only polynomially many configurations, so it runs in polynomial time. The page gives this argument for L ⊆ P. The same set-up defines log-space reductions, used for P-completeness and NL-completeness (our own). What stays hard is the separation questions, such as whether L equals P, which are open.

**Wikipedia:** [L (complexity)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/L_%28complexity%29). It says: “Formally, the Turing machine has two tapes, one of which encodes the input and can only be read, whereas the other tape has logarithmic size but can be written as well as read.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Short certificates prove closure of NP under Kleene star

**Remember:** Split the word and certify each piece.

*True by definition.* MSC 68Q15 (Complexity classes (hierarchies, relations among complexity classes, etc.)). arXiv cs.CC. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** A language is in NP if a verifier can check short certificates in polynomial time. A word belongs to the language exactly when some certificate makes the verifier accept it. The certificate length is bounded by a polynomial in the word length. The machine definition instead accepts if some branch of a polynomial-time computation accepts.

**Problem.** If L is in NP, then L\* is in NP. Here L\* contains all finite concatenations of words from L, including the empty concatenation.

**How the definition helps.** Certificates let the verifier check each piece independently (our own). For a nonempty input, the certificate gives cuts into nonempty pieces and one certificate per piece (our own). Empty pieces can be omitted, so there are at most as many pieces as input letters (our own). The verifier checks all pieces in polynomial time and accepts the empty input separately (our own). The work moves to proving that certificate verification and acceptance along a machine branch define the same class.

**Wikipedia:** [NP (complexity)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NP_%28complexity%29). It says: “NP is closed under union, intersection, concatenation, Kleene star and reversal.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### One NP-complete problem decides whether P equals NP

**Remember:** An NP-complete problem is as hard as all of NP at once.

*True by definition.* MSC 68Q17 (Computational difficulty of problems (lower bounds, completeness, difficulty of approximation, etc.)), 68Q15. arXiv cs.CC. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** NP is the class of yes-or-no problems whose yes answers can be checked in polynomial time. A problem C is NP-complete if C is in NP and every problem in NP reduces to C by a polynomial-time many-one reduction. Such a reduction is a polynomial-time map that turns each instance of a problem into an instance of C with the same answer.

**Problem.** If one NP-complete problem has a polynomial-time algorithm, then every problem in NP has one. So P = NP exactly when a single NP-complete problem is in P.

**How the definition helps.** The theorem follows at once from the definition, because polynomial-time reductions compose. To solve a problem in NP, reduce it to C and then run the fast algorithm for C. The P versus NP question itself is still open. The hard part is the Cook–Levin theorem, which shows that an NP-complete problem exists at all. That problem is Boolean satisfiability: decide whether some assignment of true and false makes a logical formula true. After the Cook–Levin theorem, each new NP-completeness proof needs only one reduction, as in Karp's list of 21 NP-complete problems.

**Wikipedia:** [NP-completeness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NP-completeness). It says: “Hence, if we could find valid solutions of some NP-complete problem quickly (when they exist), we could quickly find valid solutions for every other problem in which a given solution can be easily verified.”

**Sources:**

- [Cook, S. A. (1971). The complexity of theorem-proving procedures. Proc. 3rd ACM Symposium on Theory of Computing, 151–158.](https://doi.org/10.1145/800157.805047)

### Chomsky normal form forces repeated symbols along long derivation paths

**Remember:** Many leaves in a binary tree force a long path.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 68Q42 (Grammars and rewriting systems), 68Q45. arXiv cs.FL. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** In Chomsky normal form, a rule replaces one placeholder by two placeholders or by a letter. The start symbol may also produce the empty word if it never occurs on a right-hand side. These rules give a derivation tree that branches in two until each branch ends in a letter.

**Problem.** If the grammar has m placeholders, take a word of length greater than 2ᵐ⁻¹. Some placeholder must occur twice along one path in its derivation tree.

**How the definition helps.** The binary form bounds the number of letters a tree of a given height can produce (our own). A path with at most m placeholders has at most m − 1 branching steps before its final letter (our own). If every path is that short, the word has at most 2ᵐ⁻¹ letters (our own). A longer path repeats a placeholder, so the derivation between its two occurrences can be repeated. An unrestricted grammar can have rules with longer right-hand sides, so this binary bound does not apply (our own). The work moves to proving that context-free grammars can be converted to this form.

**Wikipedia:** [Pumping lemma for context-free languages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pumping_lemma_for_context-free_languages), [Chomsky normal form](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chomsky_normal_form). It says: “If s is sufficiently long, its derivation tree w.r.t. a Chomsky normal form grammar must contain some nonterminal N twice on some tree path”

**Sources:**

- [N. Chomsky, On certain formal properties of grammars, Information and Control 2 (1959)](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0019-9958(59)90362-6)

### Context-free grammars show context-free languages admit union, concatenation and star

**Remember:** A fresh start symbol joins grammars without mixing their rules.

*True by definition.* MSC 68Q42 (Grammars and rewriting systems), 68Q45. arXiv cs.FL. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** A context-free grammar replaces one placeholder at a time, regardless of its neighbors. It generates words by starting at a designated placeholder and replacing placeholders until only letters remain. The alternative definition uses a pushdown automaton, a finite-state machine with a stack.

**Problem.** Context-free languages are closed under union, concatenation and Kleene star. The star operation takes all finite concatenations, including the empty word.

**How the definition helps.** The grammar definition lets fresh start rules choose or join derivations (our own). First rename the placeholders so that the two grammars share none (our own). For union, let the new start S produce either old start S₁ or S₂ (our own). For concatenation, use S → S₁S₂ (our own). For star, use S → S₁S or S → ε, where ε is the empty word (our own). With pushdown automata, these constructions must also manage the stack at the boundaries (our own). The work moves into proving that pushdown automata and grammars give the same languages (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Context-free language](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Context-free_language). It says: “the union of two context-free languages is always context-free.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Complete deterministic automata recognize complements by swapping accepting states

**Remember:** Each word has one run, so swap accepting and rejecting states.

*True by definition.* MSC 68Q45 (Formal languages and automata). arXiv cs.FL. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** A complete deterministic finite automaton has exactly one next state for each state and letter. A word is accepted if the resulting run from the start state ends in an accepting state. A nondeterministic automaton can have zero or several next states for a letter.

**Problem.** The complement of a language accepted by a complete deterministic automaton has such an automaton with the same number of states.

**How the definition helps.** Completeness and determinism give every word exactly one run, so the final state decides both acceptance and rejection. Swapping the accepting and rejecting states leaves that run unchanged and reverses its verdict. Starting with a nondeterministic machine, the work moves to determinization, which uses sets of old states as new states (our own). That conversion can increase the number of states exponentially (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Complementation of automata](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complementation_of_automata), [Regular language](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regular_language). It says: “A complete deterministic finite automation can be complemented by switching its accepting and non-accepting states while leaving its transitions and initial state unchanged.”

**Sources:**

- [M. O. Rabin, D. Scott, Finite automata and their decision problems, IBM Journal of Research and Development 3 (1959)](https://doi.org/10.1147/rd.32.0114)

### Deterministic automata keep right quotients regular even by arbitrary languages

**Remember:** Keep the transitions and choose new accepting states.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 68Q45 (Formal languages and automata). arXiv cs.FL. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** The right quotient L / K contains the words u for which uv belongs to L for some v in K. A deterministic finite automaton assigns every input word a unique ending state. Its accepting states determine which words it accepts. The alternative definition of regular languages uses regular expressions.

**Problem.** If L is regular and K is any language over the same alphabet, then L / K is regular.

**How the definition helps.** In the automaton definition, the existence of an allowed suffix depends only on the state reached so far (our own). Keep the machine and accept from states that can reach an old accepting state by reading some word of K (our own). This proves existence even if K has no algorithm to decide membership (our own). An expression does not directly record the state after a prefix (our own). The work moves into Kleene’s theorem equating finite automata with regular expressions (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Regular language](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regular_language). It says: “Even more, regular languages are closed under quotients with arbitrary languages: If L is regular then L / K is regular for any K.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Nondeterministic automata recognize reversed regular languages by reversing transitions

**Remember:** Reverse every arrow and swap the start and accepting states.

*True by definition.* MSC 68Q45 (Formal languages and automata). arXiv cs.FL. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** A nondeterministic finite automaton allows zero or several moves for a given state and letter. It may also have several start states. A word is accepted if at least one run from a start state ends in an accepting state. The deterministic definition uses one start state and exactly one move for each state and letter.

**Problem.** If L is regular, the language of its words written backwards is also regular.

**How the definition helps.** The nondeterministic definition allows the several starts and moves that reversal can produce. Reverse every transition and exchange the sets of start and accepting states. Each accepting run now reads its word backwards (our own). The work moves to determinization, which proves that the nondeterministic and deterministic definitions agree (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Regular language](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regular_language). It says: “Given a nondeterministic finite automaton to recognize L, an automaton for Lᴿ can be obtained by reversing all transitions and interchanging starting and finishing states.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Pushdown automata keep intersections with regular languages context-free

**Remember:** Put the finite automaton in the control and keep the stack.

*True by definition.* MSC 68Q45 (Formal languages and automata). arXiv cs.FL. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** A pushdown automaton is a finite-state machine with a stack, whose top symbol can affect each move. A machine can also make a move without reading a letter. It can have several possible moves, and it accepts if some run accepts. Such machines and context-free grammars define the same languages.

**Problem.** The intersection of a context-free language and a regular language is context-free.

**How the definition helps.** The automaton definition leaves room for a second machine in the finite control without adding a stack (our own). Pair each pushdown state with a state of a deterministic finite automaton for the regular language (our own). Update both states on a letter, but keep the finite automaton still on moves that read nothing (our own). Accept if both machines accept (our own). The grammar proof instead tracks the start and end automaton states for each placeholder’s output (our own). The work moves to proving that the two definitions of context-free language agree (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Context-free language](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Context-free_language). It says: “However, if L is a context-free language and D is a regular language then both their intersection L∩D and their difference L∖D are context-free languages.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Regular expressions make regular languages closed under Kleene star

**Remember:** Star is one of the rules for building expressions.

*True by definition.* MSC 68Q45 (Formal languages and automata). arXiv cs.FL. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** Regular expressions start with the empty language and a language for each single letter. They build new languages by union, concatenation and Kleene star, which takes all finite concatenations. A language is regular if an expression describes it. The alternative definition uses a finite automaton, a machine with finitely many states.

**Problem.** Regular languages are closed under union, concatenation and Kleene star.

**How the definition helps.** The expression definition builds in all three closure rules. For a finite automaton, star instead takes a construction that can restart the machine after an accepting run (our own). To apply the expression proof to automata, use Kleene’s theorem, which proves that both definitions give the same languages.

**Wikipedia:** [Regular language](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regular_language). It says: “If A is a regular language, A\* (Kleene star) is a regular language. Due to this, the empty string language {ε} is also regular.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### The Nerode relation makes regularity a finite-index condition

**Remember:** States of the minimal automaton are what the future can still distinguish.

*True by definition.* MSC 68Q45 (Formal languages and automata), 68Q70. arXiv cs.FL. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** Fix a language L, a set of strings. Two strings x and y are Nerode equivalent if, for every string z, xz is in L exactly when yz is in L. This is an equivalence relation defined from L alone, with no automaton in sight.

**Problem.** The theorem says L is regular exactly when the Nerode relation has finitely many classes. The number of classes is the number of states of the minimal deterministic automaton, which is unique up to isomorphism.

**How the definition helps.** The classes are built to remember exactly what matters for the rest of the input, so they are the states of an automaton by definition. Reading a letter a moves the class of x to the class of xa, and the class of the empty string is the start state. Any deterministic automaton for L only puts strings with the same future in the same state, so it has at least as many states. This gives minimality and uniqueness. The theorem also gives a clean way to show a language is not regular: find infinitely many strings that are pairwise not equivalent (our own). Computing the classes fast still needs an algorithm such as Hopcroft's partition refinement (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Myhill–Nerode theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Myhill%E2%80%93Nerode_theorem). It says: “The Myhill–Nerode theorem shows that finiteness is necessary and sufficient for language regularity.”

**Sources:**

- [A. Nerode, Linear automaton transformations, Proceedings of the American Mathematical Society 9 (1958) 541–544](https://doi.org/10.1090/S0002-9939-1958-0135681-9)

### The semantic Brzozowski derivative makes derivatives along words compose

**Remember:** Removing u and then v removes uv.

*True by definition.* MSC 68Q45 (Formal languages and automata), 68Q70. arXiv cs.FL. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** For a language L and a word u, the derivative of L after u is the set of words w with uw in L. Brzozowski also gives syntax rules that compute derivatives of regular expressions symbol by symbol, for union, concatenation and repetition.

**Problem.** The derivative of L after uv equals the derivative after v of the derivative after u.

**How the definition helps.** With the semantic definition, both sides contain w exactly when uvw lies in L. Wikipedia states that the derivative after a word reduces to successive derivatives after its symbols. The work moves to the syntax rules. One must prove that they compute the same language as the semantic definition.

**Wikipedia:** [Brzozowski derivative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brzozowski_derivative). It says: “The derivative with respect to an arbitrary string reduces to successive derivatives over the symbols of that string”

**Sources:**

- [Janusz A. Brzozowski, Derivatives of Regular Expressions](https://doi.org/10.1145/321239.321249)

### Mechanical Sturmian words are balanced because their block sums telescope

**Remember:** Add consecutive differences to count the ones in any block.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 68R15 (Combinatorics on words), 37B10. arXiv math.CO, math.DS. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** A Sturmian word is an infinite binary sequence with exactly n + 1 distinct length-n blocks for each n ≥ 1. The mechanical definition writes its letters as successive differences of ⌊nθ + x⌋ or successive differences of ⌈nθ + x⌉. Here θ is irrational in (0, 1) and x is real.

**Problem.** Every Sturmian word is balanced, meaning that any two blocks of equal length differ in their counts of ones by at most one. The frequency of ones is θ.

**How the definition helps.** The mechanical definition gives balance and frequency by cancellation when adjacent differences are added (our own). For floors, the sum of the n letters after position m is ⌊(m + n)θ + x⌋ − ⌊mθ + x⌋. This is ⌊nθ⌋ or ⌊nθ⌋ + 1, and the same two bounds hold for ceilings. Dividing the initial block count by n gives the frequency θ in the limit. The work goes into the equivalence between counting distinct blocks and constructing the letters by floor or ceiling differences.

**Wikipedia:** [Sturmian word](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sturmian_word). It says: “The sequence w is Sturmian if it is the difference of non-homogeneous Beatty sequences, that is, for some x∈\[0,1) and some irrational θ∈(0,1)”

**Sources:**

- [M. Morse, G. A. Hedlund, Symbolic dynamics II. Sturmian trajectories, Amer. J. Math. 62 (1940) 1–42](https://doi.org/10.2307/2371431)

### Precise definitions turned Brewer's CAP conjecture into a theorem

**Remember:** During a partition, a store must choose between answering and staying consistent.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 68M14 (Distributed systems), 68P15. arXiv cs.DC, cs.DB. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Gilbert and Lynch model a distributed data store as a shared object that clients read and write. Consistency means that every read receives the most recent write or an error. Availability means that every request to a non-failing node gets a response. Partition tolerance means that the system keeps working when the network drops or delays any number of messages between nodes.

**Problem.** Brewer conjectured that a distributed store cannot be consistent, available and partition tolerant at once. Stated only in words, the claim was too vague to prove.

**How the definition helps.** With these definitions the proof is short (our own summary of the proof). Split the nodes into two groups and drop every message between them. A write in one group must complete, by availability. A later read in the other group must also answer, but it cannot have heard of the write, so it breaks consistency. The strength of the theorem comes from the definitions, and so does its limit. The page notes that this consistency is not the consistency of ACID database transactions. It also says that the choice between consistency and availability arises when a partition happens.

**Wikipedia:** [CAP theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CAP_theorem). It says: “In 2002, Seth Gilbert and Nancy Lynch of MIT published a formal proof of Brewer's conjecture, elevating it to a theorem.”

**Sources:**

- [S. Gilbert and N. Lynch, Brewer's conjecture and the feasibility of consistent, available, partition-tolerant web services, ACM SIGACT News 33 (2002) 51–59](https://doi.org/10.1145/564585.564601)

### Intrinsically typed terms make type preservation hold by construction

**Remember:** A reduction step cannot leave its type.

*True by definition.* MSC 68N15 (Theory of programming languages), 03B38. arXiv cs.PL, cs.LO. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Define terms so that each term carries its type and its context of variables. A reduction step then always goes between terms with the same context and type. The extrinsic alternative defines reduction on untyped raw terms and assigns types by a separate relation.

**Problem.** Every reduction step preserves the type of the term.

**How the definition helps.** The type is part of the definition of a reduction step, so no preservation proof is needed. The PLFA chapter on de Bruijn terms says this directly. For the step that applies a function, preservation rests on substitution. That chapter builds type preservation into its definition of substitution. So the work moves into defining substitution on typed terms. Relating typed steps to raw steps needs a separate theorem, and that remark is our own.

**nLab:** [intrinsic and extrinsic views of typing](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/intrinsic+and+extrinsic+views+of+typing). It says: “Like the syntactician's parts of speech, as a way of defining the grammar of well-formed expressions.”

**Sources:**

- [Philip Wadler, Wen Kokke and Jeremy G. Siek, Programming Language Foundations in Agda, DeBruijn chapter](https://plfa.github.io/DeBruijn/#reduction)

### Polymorphism only at let keeps type inference decidable

**Remember:** Polymorphism only at let keeps type inference decidable.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 68N15 (Theory of programming languages), 03B38. arXiv cs.PL, cs.LO. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** In the Hindley–Milner type system, types may contain type variables, as in α → α. Only names bound by let may get a polymorphic type such as ∀α. α → α. Parameters of λ-abstractions must get a type without ∀.

**Problem.** A compiler should infer the types of programs with no annotations. Hindley–Milner gives every typable program a principal type, a most general type of which all its other types are instances, and Algorithm W finds it.

**How the definition helps.** Allowing ∀ only for let-bound names means inference only has to solve first-order unification problems, which have most general solutions. If λ-bound parameters could also be polymorphic, the system would be System F, the polymorphic lambda calculus. Wells proved that type inference in System F is undecidable, as the page notes. So the restriction removes the hard cases but keeps the useful idiom let id = λx.x in (id true, id 0). What stays hard is the worst case, because Hindley–Milner inference takes exponential time on some programs, as the page notes.

**Wikipedia:** [Hindley–Milner type system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hindley%E2%80%93Milner_type_system). It says: “the type system to allow only let-bound variable to have polymorphic types, while the parameters in lambda-abstractions must get a monomorphic type, type inference becomes decidable.”

**Sources:**

- [R. Hindley, The principal type-scheme of an object in combinatory logic, Transactions of the AMS 146 (1969) 29–60](https://doi.org/10.2307/1995158)
- [L. Damas and R. Milner, Principal type-schemes for functional programs, POPL 1982](https://doi.org/10.1145/582153.582176)

### Progress and preservation turn type safety into two inductive lemmas

**Remember:** Never stuck now, and still well typed after each step.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 68N15 (Theory of programming languages), 03B38. arXiv cs.PL, cs.LO. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Wright and Felleisen define type soundness for a language given by step-by-step reduction rules. Progress says that a well-typed term is a value or can take a step. Preservation, also called subject reduction, says that a step keeps the type of a well-typed term.

**Problem.** Type safety says a well-typed program never reaches a stuck state, such as using a number as a function. One wants a proof method that scales to real languages with references, exceptions and polymorphism.

**How the definition helps.** Safety speaks about whole runs, but progress and preservation each speak about one step, so each is proved by induction on typing derivations. Chaining them shows that every reachable term is well typed and so not stuck. Earlier proofs often went through denotational models, which had to be rebuilt for each new feature (our own). The syntactic method needs no model, so it extends one feature at a time. What stays hard is the lemma for each feature, such as substitution lemmas and typing of the store (our own). The method proves only safety, not termination or correctness.

**Wikipedia:** [Type safety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Type_safety). It says: “Computer scientists Andrew K Wright and Matthias Felleisen formulate a definition and proof technique for type safety in languages defined by operational semantics.”

**Sources:**

- [A. K. Wright and M. Felleisen, A syntactic approach to type soundness, Information and Computation 115 (1994) 38–94](https://doi.org/10.1006/inco.1994.1093)

### The value restriction keeps polymorphic references from breaking type safety

**Remember:** Only values, which run no effects, may get polymorphic types.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 68N15 (Theory of programming languages), 03B38. arXiv cs.PL, cs.LO. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** In ML-style type inference, a name bound by let can get a polymorphic type ∀α. τ, usable at many types. Under the value restriction, the type is generalized only when the bound expression is a syntactic value. Syntactic values are constants, variables, λ-abstractions and constructors applied to values. Applications, such as ref (fn x =&gt; x), are not generalized.

**Problem.** Type safety says that a well-typed program never applies an operation to a value of the wrong type. With mutable references and unrestricted let-polymorphism this fails.

**How the definition helps.** Evaluating a syntactic value cannot create a reference cell, so giving it many types cannot let one cell be used at two types. The page gives the counterexample. The binding c = ref (fn x =&gt; x) gets the type ∀α. (α → α) ref. Then c := (fn x =&gt; x + 1) stores an integer function, and !c true applies it to a Boolean.
