- [Michael Dütsch, Klaus Fredenhagen, Algebraic Quantum Field Theory, Perturbation Theory, and the Loop Expansion, Commun. Math. Phys. 219 (2001) 5–30, arXiv:hep-th/0001129](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-th/0001129)

### Perturbative AQFT uses power series and local nets, not a global C\*-algebra

**Remember:** Allow formal power series, and keep only the local algebras.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 81T05 (Axiomatic quantum field theory; operator algebras), 81T15, 81T20. arXiv math-ph, hep-th. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Algebraic quantum field theory (AQFT) assigns an algebra of observables to each region of spacetime, and the Haag–Kastler axioms say how. Locally covariant perturbative AQFT uses these axioms, but it assigns to each causal region a formal power series star-algebra instead of a C\*-algebra. The power series are in Planck's constant and the coupling constant. The theory keeps the local net of algebras and does not ask for one global algebra.

**Problem.** Give a rigorous perturbative algebraic quantum field theory for realistic interacting theories. It should work in 4 dimensions, on curved spacetimes, and when infrared divergences are present.

**How the definition helps.** Formal power series and local nets ask for less, and causal perturbation theory can supply that much. As general background, not from the nLab page: with C\*-algebras, no interacting quantum field theory in dimension 4 is known, and constructing Yang–Mills theory is a Millennium Prize problem. With formal power series algebras, Epstein–Glaser causal perturbation theory produces causally local nets automatically. Only the local nets are asked for, not their would-be colimit. So the 'algebraic adiabatic limit', in which the interaction is switched on over all of spacetime, defines the observables even with infrared divergences. This does not construct a vacuum state (the weak adiabatic limit). It also does not solve the non-perturbative problem.

**nLab:** [perturbative algebraic quantum field theory](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/perturbative+algebraic+quantum+field+theory). It says: “considering these local nets instead of their would-be colimiting global algebra serves to define the perturbation theory even in the presence of infrared divergences”

**Sources:**

- [Romeo Brunetti, Klaus Fredenhagen, Microlocal Analysis and Interacting Quantum Field Theories: Renormalization on Physical Backgrounds, Commun. Math. Phys. 208 (2000) 623–661, arXiv:math-ph/9903028](https://arxiv.org/abs/math-ph/9903028)

### Causal perturbation theory makes causal factorization an axiom of the S-matrix

**Remember:** Interactions in separate regions give S-matrix factors that multiply in causal order.

*True by definition.* MSC 81T15 (Perturbative methods of renormalization applied to problems in quantum field theory). arXiv math-ph, hep-th. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** In causal perturbation theory, a perturbative S-matrix is a map S that satisfies a list of axioms. It sends local interaction terms to formal power series of observables. The key axiom is causal factorization: if the support of O₁ is not in the past of the support of O₂, then S(O₁ + O₂) = S(O₁) S(O₂). In words, the S-matrix of the sum is the product of the two S-matrices, in causal order.

**Problem.** Give a rigorous meaning to the perturbative S-matrix, which informal physics writes as a path integral. Prove that it factorizes over causally ordered regions.

**How the definition helps.** Causal perturbation theory puts causal factorization into the definition, so you do not have to derive it from a path integral. In the path integral picture, causal factorization would follow from properties of integrals and exponentials. But the path integral is not well defined. So causal perturbation theory takes causal factorization (equivalently, causal additivity) as an axiom. The real work then moves to an existence theorem: Epstein and Glaser construct solutions by induction. At each order they must extend a distribution, defined away from a point, to that point. This step is where renormalization happens, and the freedom in the extension is a finite-dimensional space of distributions supported at the point.

**nLab:** [A first idea of quantum field theory -- Interacting quantum fields](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/A+first+idea+of+quantum+field+theory+--+Interacting+quantum+fields), [causal perturbation theory](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/causal+perturbation+theory), [S-matrix](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/S-matrix). It says: “the axioms of causal perturbation theory directly prescribe the desired factorization property, without insisting that it derives from an actual integration.”

**Sources:**

- [Henri Epstein, Vladimir Glaser, The role of locality in perturbation theory, Annales de l'Institut Henri Poincaré A 19 (1973) 211](https://www.numdam.org/item/AIHPA_1973__19_3_211_0/)

### Switching the interaction off far away avoids infrared divergences

**Remember:** Switch the coupling off far away, then look only near the region you measure.

*Rules out counterexamples. Confidence: medium.* MSC 81T15 (Perturbative methods of renormalization applied to problems in quantum field theory), 81T05. arXiv math-ph. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Causal perturbation theory builds the perturbation series of a quantum field theory from causality conditions. In it, the interaction term is multiplied by a smooth function g with compact support in spacetime, called the adiabatic switching function. So the interaction is switched off smoothly outside a compact region.

**Problem.** Construct the interacting quantum observables of a perturbative field theory in every bounded region of spacetime.

**How the definition helps.** The observables of a bounded region do not depend on g far away, so you never need to remove g. The original plan was to take the limit g → 1 at the end. In general this limit does not exist, because of infrared divergences (divergences that come from long distances). Il'in and Slavnov observed that you can compute the algebra of observables of a bounded region with a switching function g whose support contains the causal closure of that region. If you change g away from the region, you get an isomorphic algebra, so no limit is needed. Brunetti and Fredenhagen made this precise and showed that causal perturbation theory gives a causally local net of observables, as in algebraic quantum field theory. This 'algebraic adiabatic limit' does not yet give the interacting vacuum state; that needs a weak adiabatic limit, which is a separate problem.

**nLab:** [causal perturbation theory](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/causal+perturbation+theory), [S-matrix](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/S-matrix), [A first idea of quantum field theory -- Interacting quantum fields](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/A+first+idea+of+quantum+field+theory+--+Interacting+quantum+fields). It says: “it was observed that in fact the algebra of observables on any bounded region may be computed with a g whose compact support contains the causal closure of that region.”

**Sources:**

- [V. A. Il'in, D. S. Slavnov, Algebras of observables in the S-matrix approach, Theoretical and Mathematical Physics 36 (1978) 578–585](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01035870)
- [Romeo Brunetti, Klaus Fredenhagen, Microlocal analysis and interacting quantum field theories: renormalization on physical backgrounds, Communications in Mathematical Physics 208 (2000) 623–661, arXiv:math-ph/9903028](https://arxiv.org/abs/math-ph/9903028)

### The main theorem of perturbative renormalization says S-matrix schemes form a torsor

**Remember:** Two renormalizations always differ by exactly one change of the interaction.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 81T15 (Perturbative methods of renormalization applied to problems in quantum field theory). arXiv math-ph, hep-th. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** The S-matrix is the operator that gives scattering amplitudes. Causal perturbation theory defines a perturbative S-matrix by axioms, not by a path integral, and calls it an S-matrix scheme. The main axiom is causal factorization: if one interaction lies in the future of another, the S-matrix of their sum is the product of their S-matrices. A vertex redefinition changes the interaction by adding higher-order point interactions, called counterterms.

**Problem.** Describe all the freedom in the renormalization of a perturbative quantum field theory.

**How the definition helps.** Because the axioms define the S-matrix, renormalization becomes a choice, and no infinite quantities appear. The choice is how to extend the time-ordered products (the terms of the S-matrix) to the diagonal, where points coincide. Vertex redefinitions form a group, the Stückelberg–Petermann renormalization group. The main theorem says that the S-matrix schemes that satisfy the renormalization condition 'field independence' form a torsor over this group. That is, such schemes exist, and a unique vertex redefinition relates any two of them. Existence is the separate Epstein–Glaser construction, which uses the theory of extension of distributions.

**nLab:** [renormalization](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/renormalization). It says: “states that any two choices of such (re-)normalizations are uniquely related by a re-definition of the interaction Lagrangian density which introduces further point interactions of higher order ("counter terms")”

**Sources:**

- [G. Popineau, Raymond Stora, A pedagogical remark on the main theorem of perturbative renormalization theory, Nuclear Physics B 912 (2016) 70–78](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.nuclphysb.2016.04.046)
- [Henri Epstein, Vladimir Glaser, The role of locality in perturbation theory, Annales de l'Institut Henri Poincaré A 19 (1973) 211](http://www.numdam.org/item/AIHPA_1973__19_3_211_0/)
- [Romeo Brunetti, Klaus Fredenhagen, Microlocal Analysis and Interacting Quantum Field Theories: Renormalization on Physical Backgrounds, Communications in Mathematical Physics 208 (2000) 623–661, arXiv:math-ph/9903028](https://arxiv.org/abs/math-ph/9903028)

### Spin-statistics for topological field theories follows from a sign-twisted duality structure

**Remember:** Put the fermion sign into the rule for duals and adjoints.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 81T45 (Topological field theories in quantum mechanics), 18M05. arXiv math-ph, math.CT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A dagger reverses maps and acts like an adjoint. A fermionically dagger compact category also has dual objects, which describe reversed boundaries or dual vector spaces in the examples. Its compatibility rule between adjoints and duals includes a parity operation, which gives a minus sign on odd states.

**Problem.** In the paper's unitary topological field theories on spin bordisms, a full spin rotation acts by fermion parity. These theories assign linear maps to spin spacetimes viewed as ways to connect their boundaries.

**How the definition helps.** The modified duality rule puts the sign into the structure that a theory must preserve. In our own words, one can then apply a general functor theorem rather than proving a separate sign identity for each theory. The work moves to checking this structure on spin bordisms and on Hilbert spaces graded by parity.

**Paper or page:** [The spin-statistics theorem for topological quantum field theories](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.02282v2). It says: “The spin-statistics theorem for TQFTs emerges as a specific case of a more general result concerning symmetric monoidal dagger functors between fermionically dagger compact categories.”

**Sources:**

- [Luuk Stehouwer, The spin-statistics theorem for topological quantum field theories, arXiv:2403.02282v2 (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.02282v2)

## 82 Statistical mechanics, structure of matter

### Counting swapped identical particles once resolves the Gibbs paradox

**Remember:** Swapping two identical atoms does not make a new state.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 82B03 (Foundations of equilibrium statistical mechanics), 82B05. arXiv cond-mat.stat-mech. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** In correct Boltzmann counting, states of identical particles that differ only by a permutation of the particles count as one state. For N particles, this divides the phase-space volume by N!.

**Problem.** Entropy should be extensive, that is, proportional to the amount of gas. Two identical boxes of gas should have twice the entropy of one box, and opening a door between them should not change the entropy.

**How the definition helps.** Dividing by N! removes an extra term from the entropy, so the entropy becomes extensive. Without the factor 1/N!, the classical entropy of an ideal gas has an extra N ln N term. Then mixing two identical gases raises the entropy, and closing the partition again lowers it, against the second law. Dividing by N! and using Stirling's formula gives the extensive Sackur–Tetrode entropy. Jaynes argues that a definition of entropy depends on what an experiment can distinguish. So, for Jaynes, the factor follows from the choice of macroscopic description, and quantum indistinguishability is a guarantee. What stays debated is whether the classical reason or the quantum reason is the right one.

**Wikipedia:** [Gibbs paradox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gibbs_paradox). It says: “The paradox is averted by assuming the indistinguishability (at least effective indistinguishability) of the particles in the volume.”

**Sources:**

- [Jaynes, E. T. (1992). The Gibbs paradox. In Smith, Erickson and Neudorfer (eds.), Maximum Entropy and Bayesian Methods, Kluwer, 1–22.](https://bayes.wustl.edu/etj/articles/gibbs.paradox.pdf)

### Gibbs measures turn a phase transition into non-uniqueness

**Remember:** A Gibbs measure looks like the Boltzmann distribution in every finite window.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 82B20 (Lattice systems (Ising, dimer, Potts, etc.) and systems on graphs arising in equilibrium statistical mechanics), 82B26, 60K35. arXiv cond-mat.stat-mech, math.PR. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A Gibbs measure on an infinite lattice is a probability measure on configurations with one property. Inside every finite region, given the configuration outside, its conditional distribution is the finite-volume Boltzmann distribution. These are the Dobrushin–Lanford–Ruelle conditions. (The Boltzmann distribution gives a configuration of energy E the probability exp(−βE)/Z, where β is the inverse temperature and Z makes the total equal to 1.)

**Problem.** We want to state what a phase transition is for an infinite system. There the total energy is infinite, and the usual Boltzmann formula has no meaning.

**How the definition helps.** The definition uses only energies of finite regions, so it applies directly to the infinite system. The finite-volume formula exp(−βE)/Z cannot be used when E is infinite. A phase transition can then be stated as the existence of more than one Gibbs measure for the same interaction. For a finite system, there is always exactly one. Proving non-uniqueness for a given model remains hard.

**Wikipedia:** [Gibbs measure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gibbs_measure). It says: “The existence of more than one Gibbs measure is associated with statistical phenomena such as symmetry breaking and phase coexistence.”

**Sources:**

- [Dobrushin, R. L. (1968). The description of a random field by means of conditional probabilities and conditions of its regularity. Theory of Probability and Its Applications 13, 197–224.](https://doi.org/10.1137/1113026)
- [Lanford, O. E.; Ruelle, D. (1969). Observables at infinity and states with short range correlations in statistical mechanics. Communications in Mathematical Physics 13, 194–215.](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01645487)

### Phase transitions defined as non-analytic points need infinitely many particles

**Remember:** No sharp transition without infinitely many particles.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 82B26 (Phase transitions (general) in equilibrium statistical mechanics), 82B30. arXiv cond-mat.stat-mech, math-ph. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A phase transition is a point where the thermodynamic free energy is not an analytic function of the thermodynamic variables, such as temperature. (An analytic function is one that is given near each point by a convergent power series.)

**Problem.** Statistical mechanics should explain sharp phase transitions. But for a finite system, the partition function (the sum of the Boltzmann weights over all states) is smooth.

**How the definition helps.** The definition makes clear that sharp transitions can appear only in the limit of infinitely many particles. Our own step: for a finite system, the partition function is a finite sum of exponentials. So the free energy is analytic and has no sharp transition. Lee and Yang made this precise. The zeros of the partition function in the complex plane can approach the real axis only in that limit. What stays hard is to prove that a given model has such a point, as Onsager did for the two-dimensional Ising model (a grid of spins that each point up or down).

**Wikipedia:** [Phase transition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phase_transition). It says: “Phase transitions occur when the thermodynamic free energy of a system is non-analytic for some choice of thermodynamic variables”

**Sources:**

- [Yang, C. N.; Lee, T. D. (1952). Statistical theory of equations of state and phase transitions. I. Theory of condensation. Physical Review 87(3), 404–409.](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.87.404)

### The one-line projection of the Ising model has continuous one-sided predictions

**Remember:** A continuous prediction from the past need not extend to both sides.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 82B20 (Lattice systems (Ising, dimer, Potts, etc.) and systems on graphs arising in equilibrium statistical mechanics), 60K35, 37D35. arXiv math.PR, cond-mat.stat-mech. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A g-measure is a measure on spin sequences whose conditional probability for the next spin depends continuously on the past spins. The Schonmann projection is the restriction of an extremal Gibbs measure of the two-dimensional Ising model to the spins on one line.

**Problem.** At sufficiently low temperature, the Schonmann projection is a regular g-measure. At low temperature it is also non-Gibbsian, because its conditional probabilities given both sides are discontinuous.

**How the definition helps.** The definition asks only how predictions depend on one side, so a weaker continuity can hold where two-sided continuity fails. The two-sided Gibbs condition would miss that regularity. In our own words, the theorem still needs a proof, which in the paper uses contour estimates at low temperature.

**Paper or page:** [The Schonmann projection as a g-measure-, how Gibbsian is it?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2102.10622v2). It says: “We prove that they are g-measures, which means that their conditional probabilities have a continuous dependence on one-sided boundary condition.”

**Sources:**

- [Aernout van Enter, Senya Shlosman, The Schonmann projection as a g-measure-, how Gibbsian is it?, arXiv:2102.10622v2 (2022)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2102.10622v2)

## 83 Relativity and gravitational theory

### Einstein synchronisation makes equal one-way light speeds a convention

**Remember:** Light takes equal time out and back because we set the clocks that way.

*True by definition.* MSC 83A05 (Special relativity). arXiv physics.class-ph. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** Clock 1 sends a light signal at time τ₁ to clock 2. Clock 2 reflects the signal back, and clock 1 receives it at time τ₂. Set clock 2 so that it shows (τ₁ + τ₂)/2 at the reflection. In words, the reflection happens halfway between sending and receiving.

**Problem.** Show that the one-way speed of light is the same in both directions.

**How the definition helps.** The rule builds the claim into the clocks, so there is nothing left to prove. You cannot measure a one-way speed before you synchronise distant clocks. Einstein's rule synchronises them by assuming that the two one-way times are equal. So the equality of the one-way speeds is a convention, as Poincaré noted. You can reread experiments on the one-way speed of light as tests of a round-trip condition. Some parts are not conventional. The rule is consistent (symmetric and transitive) only under physical conditions such as Reichenbach's round-trip condition, and in rotating frames the rule depends on the path.

**Wikipedia:** [Einstein synchronisation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Einstein_synchronisation). It says: “Since it is meaningless to measure a one-way velocity prior to the synchronisation of distant clocks, experiments claiming a measure of the one-way speed of light can often be reinterpreted as verifying the Laue–Weyl's round-trip condition.”

**Sources:**

- [Einstein, A. (1905). Zur Elektrodynamik bewegter Körper. Annalen der Physik 322(10), 891–921.](https://doi.org/10.1002/andp.19053221004)

### Invariant mass, built from energy and momentum, is the same for everyone

**Remember:** Energy squared minus momentum squared is the same in every frame.

*True by definition.* MSC 83A05 (Special relativity). arXiv physics.class-ph, math-ph. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** The invariant mass m of a body or a system is given by m²c⁴ = E² − \|p\|²c². Here E is the total energy and p the total momentum. The older relativistic mass is E/c², which depends on the observer.

**Problem.** The invariant mass of a system is the same in all inertial frames, and it is conserved. So the invariant mass of the decay products of a particle equals the rest mass of the parent particle.

**How the definition helps.** E² − \|p\|²c² is the Minkowski square of the four-momentum, the spacetime vector (E/c, p) (our own wording). Lorentz transformations preserve it, so frame independence is built into the definition. Relativistic mass changes with speed, so every statement about it needs a chosen frame. The page says that particle physicists tend to avoid it. The work moves into conservation of total four-momentum. The page notes that the invariant mass of widely separated decay products gives the rest mass of the parent. One surprise remains: invariant mass is not additive, since a system of moving parts has more mass than the sum of the parts' masses.

**Wikipedia:** [Mass in special relativity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mass_in_special_relativity). It says: “The term "relativistic mass" tends not to be used in particle and nuclear physics and is often avoided by writers on special relativity, in favor of referring to the body's relativistic energy.”

**Sources:**

- [L. B. Okun, The Concept of Mass, Physics Today 42 (1989), 31–36](https://doi.org/10.1063/1.881171)

### Proper time as spacetime length makes the inertial twin older

**Remember:** For a timelike trip in flat spacetime, the straight path takes the most proper time.

*True by definition.* MSC 83A05 (Special relativity), 53B30. arXiv gr-qc, physics.class-ph. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** Define proper time as the length of a timelike path divided by the speed of light. This length uses the Minkowski metric, which measures time and space displacements with opposite signs. In a frame-based calculation, one instead adjusts each leg’s elapsed time by its speed relative to that frame.

**Problem.** In flat spacetime, compare one inertial leg with two future-directed timelike inertial legs between the same events. The single leg gives at least as much proper time, with equality only if all legs have the same velocity.

**How the definition helps.** Spacetime length turns the comparison into the reversed triangle inequality because the straight displacement is the sum of the two legs. The work is in proving that inequality. Square both sides and use the reversed Cauchy–Schwarz inequality, which says that the spacetime inner product is at least the product of the two lengths. The frame-based proof instead calculates the time dilation on each leg (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Proper time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proper_time), [Minkowski spacetime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minkowski_spacetime), [Twin paradox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twin_paradox). It says: “For two similarly directed time-like vectors u and w, the inequality is ‖u + w‖ ≥ ‖u‖ + ‖w‖, where the equality holds when the vectors are linearly dependent.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Proper time makes four-acceleration perpendicular to four-velocity

**Remember:** Differentiating a vector of constant length gives a perpendicular vector.

*True by definition.* MSC 83A05 (Special relativity), 70H40. arXiv physics.class-ph, gr-qc. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** Proper time τ is the time shown by a clock carried along a timelike path, a path moving below light speed. Define four-velocity U = dx/dτ and four-acceleration A = dU/dτ for the spacetime position x. The coordinate-time description instead differentiates with respect to the time in a chosen frame.

**Problem.** Along any twice differentiable timelike path in flat spacetime, four-velocity and four-acceleration are perpendicular. Perpendicularity uses the Minkowski scalar product, the spacetime version of a dot product.

**How the definition helps.** Proper time makes perpendicularity immediate because it gives U constant squared length. In the convention with positive time sign, U·U = c², where c is the speed of light (our own). Differentiation gives 2U·A = 0. The work lies in normalizing the tangent, which follows from the spacetime length formula for τ (our own). A general coordinate-time tangent need not have constant length (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Four-acceleration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Four-acceleration). It says: “The scalar product of a particle's four-velocity and its four-acceleration is always 0.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Rapidity makes relativistic velocities along one line simply add

**Remember:** Boosts along one line compose by adding their rapidities.

*True by definition.* MSC 83A05 (Special relativity). arXiv physics.class-ph, math-ph. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** The rapidity w of a speed v along a line is the number with tanh w = v/c, where c is the speed of light. It is the hyperbolic angle of the Lorentz boost, the change of frame to a moving observer. For small speeds w is about v/c, and light has infinite rapidity.

**Problem.** Suppose frame B moves relative to frame A with rapidity w₁, and frame C moves relative to B with rapidity w₂, along the same line. Then C moves relative to A with rapidity w₁ + w₂. In terms of speeds, the same law is Einstein's formula (u + v)/(1 + uv/c²).

**How the definition helps.** The definition tanh w = v/c picks exactly the parameter in which composing boosts is addition, so additivity is built in. Boosts along one line form a one-parameter group, with Λ(w₁ + w₂) = Λ(w₁)Λ(w₂). The work moves to showing that boosts are hyperbolic rotations, which Minkowski explained in 1908. The page says that Varićak introduced rapidity as a parameter in 1910. Einstein's velocity formula is then the addition formula for tanh. Additivity fails for boosts in different directions, which do not commute and produce an extra rotation, the Thomas–Wigner rotation (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Rapidity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rapidity). It says: “The simplicity of this formula contrasts with the complexity of the corresponding velocity-addition formula.”

**Sources:**

- [H. Minkowski, Die Grundgleichungen für die elektromagnetischen Vorgänge in bewegten Körpern, Nachrichten von der Gesellschaft der Wissenschaften zu Göttingen (1908), 53–111](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Translation:The_Fundamental_Equations_for_Electromagnetic_Processes_in_Moving_Bodies)

### The Einstein tensor makes Einstein’s equations conserve stress–energy

**Remember:** A divergence-free left side forces a divergence-free right side.

*True by definition.* MSC 83C05 (Einstein's equations (general structure, canonical formalism, Cauchy problems)), 83C40. arXiv gr-qc, math.DG. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Define the Einstein tensor as G = Ric − ½Rg. Here Ric measures curvature, R is its trace, and g is the spacetime metric. Einstein’s equations set G proportional to T, the tensor that measures the density and flow of energy and momentum.

**Problem.** Einstein’s equations with a nonzero constant of proportionality force T to have zero covariant divergence. This is the local conservation law for energy and momentum in curved spacetime.

**How the definition helps.** The Einstein tensor makes conservation immediate because its divergence vanishes for every spacetime metric. The work is in the contracted Bianchi identity, which says the divergence of Ric equals half the gradient of R. The trace correction subtracts exactly that gradient (our own). Using Ric alone on the left would instead force R to be constant if T were conserved (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Einstein tensor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Einstein_tensor). It says: “The (contracted) Bianchi identities automatically ensure the covariant conservation of the stress–energy tensor in curved spacetimes:”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Timelike geodesics give all test bodies the same free fall

**Remember:** The geodesic equation uses the initial position and velocity, not the mass.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 83C10 (Equations of motion in general relativity and gravitational theory), 53C22. arXiv gr-qc, math.DG. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** In general relativity, model a freely falling massive test body by a timelike geodesic, a straightest possible path for the spacetime metric. A test body is one whose own gravity and internal structure are neglected. Newtonian gravity instead treats gravity as a force on a body with separate gravitational and inertial masses.

**Problem.** Two freely falling test bodies at the same event with the same initial velocity follow the same path as long as the geodesic exists.

**How the definition helps.** The geodesic law gives identical paths because it uses the same equation and initial data for both bodies (our own). The equation for a smooth metric has a unique solution for those data (our own). The Newtonian description instead needs the ratio of gravitational mass to inertial mass to be the same for all bodies (our own). The physical work is in justifying the geodesic law as a model for test bodies (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Geodesics in general relativity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geodesics_in_general_relativity). It says: “Importantly, the world line of a particle free from all external, non-gravitational forces is a particular type of geodesic. In other words, a freely moving or falling particle always moves along a geodesic.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Choosing the right time flow makes Kerr–de Sitter wave expansions provable

**Remember:** Choose the time flow before splitting the wave into modes.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 83C57 (Black holes), 58J45. arXiv math.AP, gr-qc. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A Kerr–de Sitter spacetime models a rotating black hole in a universe with a positive cosmological constant. A stationary Killing field is a vector field whose flow preserves the metric and acts as a time direction. A quasinormal mode is a smooth wave that changes by a factor exp(−iσt) along the flow of a chosen stationary Killing field. The paper allows several such fields, among them the fields that generate the horizons.

**Problem.** In a subextremal Kerr–de Sitter spacetime, the mode frequencies form a discrete set of complex numbers. Waves then have an expansion in quasinormal modes up to a decay rate set by the trapped light rays.

**How the definition helps.** A suitable choice of time flow gives a family of operators that are Fredholm, so the standard Fredholm theory applies. Fredholm means that the kernel and cokernel have finite dimension and the range is closed. The earlier paper by the same authors proved the expansion with one such choice. This paper shows that many other choices work too. The control of the trapped light rays is still separate work.

**Paper or page:** [Stationarity and Fredholm Theory in Subextremal Kerr-de Sitter Spacetimes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.09213v2). It says: “One central ingredient in the argument was a new definition of quasinormal modes, where a non-standard choice of stationary Killing vector field had to be used in order for the Fredholm theory to be applicable.”

**Sources:**

- [Oliver Petersen, András Vasy, Stationarity and Fredholm Theory in Subextremal Kerr-de Sitter Spacetimes, arXiv:2306.09213 (2024), SIGMA 20 (2024), 052, 11 pages](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.09213v2)
- [Oliver Petersen, András Vasy, Wave equations in the Kerr–de Sitter spacetime: the full subextremal range, Journal of the European Mathematical Society 27 (2025)](https://doi.org/10.4171/jems/1448)

## 90 Operations research, mathematical programming

### Basic feasible solutions are vertices, so linear programs need finite search

**Remember:** Some optimum always sits at a vertex, and vertices are finitely many.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 90C05 (Linear programming), 90C49. arXiv math.OC. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** A linear program in standard form minimizes cᵀx subject to Ax = b and x ≥ 0. A basic feasible solution is a feasible x whose nonzero entries belong to linearly independent columns of A. With n variables and m equations there are at most 'n choose m' of them.

**Problem.** If a linear program in standard form has an optimal solution, then it has an optimal basic feasible solution. Each basic feasible solution is a vertex of the feasible polyhedron.

**How the definition helps.** The algebraic definition can be checked with linear algebra, and its geometric meaning, a vertex, is where optima lie. Together they turn optimization into a finite search. A linear objective on a convex polyhedron with vertices reaches its best value at a vertex, if it reaches it at all. The page says that the simplex method travels from one basic feasible solution to another until it finds an optimum. What stays hard is that there can be exponentially many vertices (our own). At degenerate vertices the simplex method can also cycle, unless a pivoting rule such as Bland's rule is used (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Basic feasible solution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basic_feasible_solution), [Linear programming](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_programming). It says: “Geometrically, each BFS corresponds to a vertex of the polyhedron of feasible solutions. If there exists an optimal solution, then there exists an optimal BFS.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Total unimodularity makes every vertex of a linear program integral

**Remember:** Determinants ±1 mean Cramer's rule never divides, so vertices are integers.

*True by definition.* MSC 90C10 (Integer programming), 90C57, 05B20. arXiv math.OC, math.CO. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** A matrix is totally unimodular if every square submatrix has determinant 0, +1 or −1. Examples are the incidence matrix of a bipartite graph and the incidence matrix of a directed graph.

**Problem.** If A is totally unimodular and b is an integer vector, every vertex of {x : Ax ≤ b} has integer entries. So the linear program 'maximize cᵀx subject to Ax ≤ b' has an integer optimum whenever it has an optimum, for every c.

**How the definition helps.** The definition asks exactly for the determinants that Cramer's rule divides by, so vertices come out integral. A vertex solves a square subsystem Bx = b′ taken from the rows of A, with B invertible (our own explanation). Cramer's rule writes each entry of x as a determinant divided by det B = ±1, so x is integral. Hoffman and Kruskal proved a converse in 1956 for the polyhedra {x ≥ 0 : Ax ≤ b} (our own; not on the page). If these are integral for every integer b, then the integer matrix A is totally unimodular. So integer problems with such matrices, like bipartite matching, can be solved as linear programs. What stays hard is recognizing total unimodularity efficiently, which uses Seymour's decomposition of regular matroids (our own link).

**Wikipedia:** [Unimodular matrix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unimodular_matrix). It says: “Hence if A is totally unimodular and b is integral, every extreme point of the feasible region (e.g. {x \| Ax ≥ b}) is integral and thus the feasible region is an integral polyhedron.”

**Sources:**

- [A. J. Hoffman and J. B. Kruskal, Integral boundary points of convex polyhedra, in Linear Inequalities and Related Systems, Annals of Mathematics Studies 38 (1956), 223–246](https://doi.org/10.1515/9781400881987-014)

### Negative entropy turns mirror descent into multiplicative exponential weights

**Remember:** Exponentiate the negative gradient, multiply by the old probabilities, then normalize.

*True by definition.* MSC 90C25 (Convex programming), 65K05. arXiv cs.LG, math.OC. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Mirror descent steps against a gradient estimate, with a penalty for moving far from the current point. The penalty is the Bregman divergence of a convex function Ψ, the gap between Ψ and its tangent-plane approximation. For negative entropy Ψ(p) = ∑ p(x) log p(x) on probability vectors, this penalty is the relative entropy.

**Problem.** Take a step size η and a gradient estimate g. With negative entropy, the mirror descent step makes the new p(x) proportional to p(x) exp(−η g(x)). Dividing by the sum over x makes the result a probability vector.

**How the definition helps.** Negative entropy makes the penalty a sum of one-variable terms, so the minimization splits by coordinate. Our own proof sketch sets the derivative of each term to zero. This makes the new log-probability equal to the old one minus η g(x), plus a constant. The constant comes from the constraint that the probabilities sum to one. Exponentiating gives the multiplicative update, which is the classical exponential weights algorithm.

**Paper or page:** [Distances for Markov chains from sample streams](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.18005v1). It says: “When 𝒵 = Δ\_𝒳 is the probability simplex on a finite set 𝒳 and Ψ is the negative entropy defined as Ψ(p) = ∑ₓ p(x) log p(x), p ∈ Δ\_𝒳, the OSMD update reduces to”

**Sources:**

- [Sergio Calo, Anders Jonsson, Gergely Neu, Ludovic Schwartz, Javier Segovia-Aguas, Distances for Markov chains from sample streams, arXiv:2505.18005v1 (2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.18005v1)

### The subgradient definition makes proximal fixed points minimizers

**Remember:** A proximal step stays put exactly when zero is a subgradient.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 90C25 (Convex programming), 65K10, 47H09. arXiv math.OC. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Take a convex function f on a real Hilbert space with a closed epigraph, at least one finite value, and no value of −∞. A subgradient q at x with finite f(x) satisfies f(z) ≥ f(x) + ⟨q, z − x⟩ for all z. Define p = prox(v) by requiring v − p to be a subgradient of f at p. The usual definition instead minimizes f(x) + ½‖x − v‖² over x.

**Problem.** A point x satisfies prox(x) = x exactly when x minimizes f.

**How the definition helps.** The subgradient definition turns a fixed point directly into the condition that zero is a subgradient at x. That condition says f(x) is a global minimum. Our own comparison is that the minimization definition first needs an optimality argument to remove the quadratic penalty. To relate the definitions, first prove that the quadratic problem has a unique answer. Then show that its optimality condition is the subgradient test.

**Wikipedia:** [Proximal operator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proximal_operator). It says: “Fixed points of prox<sub>f</sub> are minimizers of f”

**Sources:**

- [Neal Parikh and Stephen Boyd, Proximal Algorithms, Foundations and Trends in Optimization 1 (2014)](https://doi.org/10.1561/2400000003)

### A strictly feasible point closes the duality gap in convex programs

**Remember:** One strictly feasible point makes the primal and dual optimal values agree.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 90C46 (Optimality conditions and duality in mathematical programming), 90C25. arXiv math.OC. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A convex program minimizes a convex function under convex inequality constraints and linear equations. Slater's condition holds when some point satisfies every nonlinear inequality strictly and every linear constraint exactly. The dual problem maximizes the lowest value of the Lagrangian, which is the objective plus the weighted constraints. The weights on the inequalities must be nonnegative.

**Problem.** Strong duality says that the optimal value of a convex program equals the optimal value of its dual. It can fail for convex programs in general. Under Slater's condition it holds, and a finite dual value is attained.

**How the definition helps.** A strictly feasible point leaves room inside the feasible set, and that room makes Lagrange multipliers exist (our own explanation). In the proof, a hyperplane separates the attainable values from better ones, and the interior point stops it from being vertical. Our own example: minimize x subject to x² ≤ 0. The only feasible point is 0, so no point is strictly feasible. The dual values −1/(4λ) approach 0, but no multiplier λ reaches it, so the dual optimum is not attained. Boyd and Vandenberghe give a convex program with primal value 1 and dual value 0, where Slater's condition also fails (our own). What stays hard is to find a strictly feasible point, which is itself an optimization problem.

**Wikipedia:** [Slater's condition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slater%27s_condition), [Strong duality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strong_duality). It says: “In particular, if Slater's condition holds for the primal problem, then the duality gap is zero, and if the dual value is finite then it is attained.”

**Sources:**

- [M. Slater, Lagrange Multipliers Revisited, Cowles Commission Discussion Paper No. 403 (1950)](https://cowles.yale.edu/sites/default/files/files/pub/d00/d0080.pdf)
- [S. Boyd and L. Vandenberghe, Convex Optimization, Cambridge University Press (2004)](https://web.stanford.edu/~boyd/cvxbook/)

### Constraint qualifications make the KKT conditions necessary at a minimizer

**Remember:** Good constraint gradients guarantee Lagrange multipliers at every constrained minimum.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 90C46 (Optimality conditions and duality in mathematical programming), 90C30. arXiv math.OC. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A constraint qualification is a condition on the constraints at a feasible point. The most used one, the linear independence constraint qualification, asks that the gradients of the active constraints be linearly independent. A constraint is active at a point if it holds with equality there.

**Problem.** Suppose a point minimizes a smooth function under smooth inequality and equality constraints, and a constraint qualification holds there. Then Lagrange multipliers exist, nonnegative for the inequalities and zero for the inactive ones. These are the Karush–Kuhn–Tucker (KKT) conditions.

**How the definition helps.** The qualification makes the linear approximation of the constraints describe the true feasible directions, and then Farkas's lemma gives the multipliers (our own summary). Without it the linear picture can be wrong. Our own example: minimize x subject to x² ≤ 0. The minimizer is 0, but the constraint gradient there is 0, so the KKT equation 1 + 2λ·0 = 0 has no solution. The Fritz John conditions need no qualification, because they put a weight on the objective too, but that weight may be zero. What stays hard is to choose a qualification weak enough for the problem at hand; the page lists a chain of weaker and weaker ones.

**Wikipedia:** [Karush–Kuhn–Tucker conditions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karush%E2%80%93Kuhn%E2%80%93Tucker_conditions). It says: “For the constrained case, the situation is more complicated, and one can state a variety of (increasingly complicated) "regularity" conditions under which a constrained minimizer also satisfies the KKT conditions.”

**Sources:**

- [H. W. Kuhn and A. W. Tucker, Nonlinear programming, Proceedings of the Second Berkeley Symposium on Mathematical Statistics and Probability (1951), 481–492](https://doi.org/10.1525/9780520411586-036)

### The margin turns many random feasibility problems into one concentration theorem

**Remember:** Measure how far you miss the constraints, not just whether you miss.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 90C15 (Stochastic programming), 60F20, 60B20. arXiv math.PR, math.OC. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Let Q be a bounded set in ℝᴺ, E a set in ℝᴹ and A a random M × N matrix. The ℓq-margin is the smallest ℓq distance between a point of AQ and a point of E. The problem 'is there x in Q with Ax in E' is feasible when the margin is zero.

**Problem.** Let Q lie in the Euclidean unit ball and let E be unchanged by permuting coordinates. For 2 ≤ q ≤ ∞, the margin has variance at most C/(1 + (1/2 − 1/q) log M), with C universal. This gives sharp thresholds for random integer feasibility, discrepancy, perceptron and matrix balancing problems.

**How the definition helps.** The margin is one real number that encodes each yes-or-no feasibility problem, so one concentration theorem covers all of them. The paper says that concentration of the margin gives new sharp thresholds and simplifies known results. Our own explanation is that a near miss has a small positive margin, which a yes-or-no test cannot see. The real work is the variance bound in Theorem 1. For q = ∞ it needs permutation symmetry, because classical concentration tools do not reach that case.

**Paper or page:** [Zero-One Laws for Random Feasibility Problems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.13133v3). It says: “Concentration of the margin implies a host of new sharp threshold results in these models, and also greatly simplifies and extends some key known results.”

**Sources:**

- [Dylan J. Altschuler, Zero-One Laws for Random Feasibility Problems, arXiv:2309.13133 (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.13133v3)

### Hidden hyperplane convexity makes aggregated inequalities give the convex hull

**Remember:** Look for convexity in the image of the quadratic map, not in the feasible set.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 90C20 (Quadratic programming), 52A41. arXiv math.OC. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Write each quadratic inequality fᵢ(x) &lt; 0 as a quadratic form in (x, xₙ₊₁) by homogenizing. Hidden hyperplane convexity (HHC) asks that the vector of these forms has a convex image on every linear hyperplane. An aggregation is a nonnegative weighted sum of the original inequalities.

**Problem.** Let n ≥ 3 and let S be the set where finitely many quadratics are all negative. Suppose S is nonempty and its convex hull is not all of ℝⁿ. Under HHC, the convex hull of S is the intersection of the sets given by suitable aggregations.

**How the definition helps.** HHC puts convexity where the proof must separate, which is in the space of constraint values on a hyperplane. A valid linear inequality for the hull gives a hyperplane that misses the homogenized set, by Lemma 5.4 of the paper. On that hyperplane the image is convex and misses the negative orthant. So a separating weight vector exists, and it gives the aggregation, by our own reading. In our own reading, the two-form case of Corollary 2.6 matches Dines' classical convexity theorem.

**Paper or page:** [Aggregations of quadratic inequalities and hidden hyperplane convexity](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.01722v2), [Aggregations of quadratic inequalities and hidden hyperplane convexity](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.01722v2), [Aggregations of quadratic inequalities and hidden hyperplane convexity](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.01722v2). It says: “We show that if the quadratic map associated with S satisfies HHC, then the convex hull of S is defined by special aggregations.”

**Sources:**

- [Grigoriy Blekherman, Santanu S. Dey, Shengding Sun, Aggregations of quadratic inequalities and hidden hyperplane convexity, arXiv:2210.01722v2 (2022)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.01722v2)
- [Grigoriy Blekherman, Santanu S. Dey, Shengding Sun, Aggregations of Quadratic Inequalities and Hidden Hyperplane Convexity, SIAM Journal on Optimization (2024)](https://doi.org/10.1137/22m1528215)

### Mirror descent is a flow with frozen gradient in the Hessian metric

**Remember:** Freeze the objective gradient, not the metric, to get mirror descent.

*True by definition.* MSC 90C25 (Convex programming), 65K05. arXiv cs.LG, math.OC. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Mirror descent with a strictly convex potential ψ subtracts η∇L(wₖ) from ∇ψ(wₖ), where L is the objective. The paper instead follows the flow dw/dt = −H(w)⁻¹∇L(wₖ) for time η, where H is the Hessian of ψ. The objective gradient stays frozen at the start of the step, but the metric H(w) changes along the path.

**Problem.** When the metric is the Hessian of ψ, the end points of these steps are exactly the mirror descent iterates. The flow also makes sense for a Riemannian metric that is not a Hessian, where no dual coordinates exist.

**How the definition helps.** With the gradient frozen, ∇ψ(w) moves at constant velocity, so the equality has a one-line proof. In our own explanation, the chain rule gives d∇ψ(w)/dt = H(w)dw/dt = −∇L(wₖ). After time η, ∇ψ has changed by −η∇L(wₖ), which is the mirror descent update. The definition uses only the metric, so it extends to metrics without a potential. For such metrics one must still solve the flow.

**Paper or page:** [Mirrorless Mirror Descent: A Natural Derivation of Mirror Descent](https://arxiv.org/abs/2004.01025v3). It says: “Let ψ:𝒲→ℝ be strictly convex and twice differentiable and let H(𝐰)=∇²ψ(𝐰) be invertible everywhere. … Then 𝐰⁽ᵏ⁾ are the same as the Mirror Descent updates 𝐰<sub>MD</sub>⁽ᵏ⁾ … obtained with ψ as the potential function and the same initialization and stepsize.”

**Sources:**

- [Suriya Gunasekar, Blake Woodworth, Nathan Srebro, Mirrorless Mirror Descent: A Natural Derivation of Mirror Descent, arXiv:2004.01025v3 (2021)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2004.01025v3)

### Concave tents keep the minimum value when the feasible set is convexified

**Remember:** A concave function cannot dip below all the points holding it up.

*True by definition.* MSC 90C26 (Nonconvex programming, global optimization), 52A41. arXiv math.OC. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Let 𝒳 be a feasible set and f an objective on it. A concave tent is a concave function g on the convex hull of 𝒳 that equals f on 𝒳. The convex hull is the set of finite convex combinations of points of 𝒳.

**Problem.** Let 𝒳 be compact and suppose f has a concave tent g. Then the infimum of f over 𝒳 equals the infimum of g over the convex hull of 𝒳. The two problems also have the same global minimizers.

**How the definition helps.** Concavity gives the inequality directly, so the equality of infima follows from the definition. If x = Σλᵢxᵢ with xᵢ in 𝒳, then g(x) ≥ Σλᵢ f(xᵢ) ≥ inf f, by our own calculation. Points of 𝒳 give the reverse bound because g equals f there. Finding a usable tent is the hard part, and minimizing a concave function can itself be hard.

**Paper or page:** [Concave tents: a new tool for constructing concave reformulations of a large class of nonconvex optimization problems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.18451v2). It says: “We have infₓ∈𝒳 { f(x) } = infₓ∈conv(𝒳) { g(x) }”

**Sources:**

- [Markus Gabl, Concave tents: a new tool for constructing concave reformulations of a large class of nonconvex optimization problems, arXiv:2409.18451v2 (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.18451v2)

### Bi-local solutions turn bilevel programs into one-level problems locally

**Remember:** Follow the nearby inner solution instead of every possible inner solution.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 90C30 (Nonlinear programming), 90C46. arXiv math.OC. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** In a bilevel program, the outer decision x is chosen first. An inner variable y then solves an inner optimization problem that depends on x. A bi-local solution needs inner optimality only among y near the reference inner choice, as x varies near the reference outer choice.

**Problem.** Assume the inner problem satisfies the Jacobian uniqueness conditions, a strong local regularity condition. Then a bi-local solution is a local minimizer of a one-level problem. Its second-order optimality conditions use only second derivatives of the functions that define the bilevel program.

**How the definition helps.** Because only nearby inner solutions count, one smooth branch y(x) of inner solutions can stand in for the whole inner problem. Substituting y(x) into the outer problem gives a one-level problem, by our own explanation. The implicit function theorem gives this branch under the Jacobian uniqueness conditions, by our own account. Deriving the second-order conditions from the branch is still the paper's work.

**Paper or page:** [Second-order optimality conditions for bilevel programs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.11427v1). It says: “Under the Jacobian uniqueness conditions for the lower level problem, we prove that the bi-local solution is a local minimizer of some one-level minimization problem.”

**Sources:**

- [Xiang Liu, Mengwei Xu, Liwei Zhang, Second-order optimality conditions for bilevel programs, arXiv:2307.11427v1 (2023)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.11427v1)

### Pricing an infeasible point at its projection plus distance keeps all minima

**Remember:** Project first, then charge for the distance.

*True by definition.* MSC 90C30 (Nonlinear programming), 90C46. arXiv math.OC. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Let C be the feasible set and f the cost on C. Fix M &gt; 0. Outside C, the penalty at x is the cost at a nearest point p of C plus M times ‖x − p‖.

**Problem.** Let f be lower semicontinuous on a nonempty closed set C in Euclidean space, and let M &gt; 0. Then each local or global minimum of the constrained problem is one of the penalized problem, and conversely, with the same values.

**How the definition helps.** By definition, an infeasible point costs more than its nearest feasible point, so no minimum can lie outside C (our own comparison). Points between x and p have p as their only nearest point, so moving toward p lowers only the distance charge (our own proof). Near a feasible point, nearby points have nearby projections, so local minima carry over. Unlike classical exact penalties, no large enough M is needed, as the abstract says.

**Paper or page:** [The Exact Projective Penalty Method for Constrained Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.02094v1). It says: “each local (global) minimum of one problem is a local (global) minimum of the other, and the optimal values of the problems in the corresponding minima coincide.”

**Sources:**

- [Vladimir Norkin, The Exact Projective Penalty Method for Constrained Optimization, arXiv:2312.02094v1 (2023)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.02094v1)

### Lifting a Markov decision process to distributions keeps its optimal values

**Remember:** The state is now a distribution, so the next state is not random.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 90C40 (Markov and semi-Markov decision processes), 90C39. arXiv math.OC. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** In a measurized Markov decision process, a state is a probability distribution on the original states. An action is a stochastic kernel, which gives a distribution over actions for each original state. The next distribution then follows deterministically from the original transition law.

**Problem.** Consider the discounted problem under the paper's assumptions. Let V\* be the original optimal value and V̄\* the lifted one. Then V̄\*(δₛ) = V\*(s) for every state s, and V̄\*(ν) is the integral of V\* against ν.

**How the definition helps.** The lifted state makes the evolution of laws deterministic, so the value at ν can be compared directly with the average of V\*. A point mass δₛ is a known original state, so the first identity is the natural special case, by our own account. The paper still has to prove that the two optimization problems have matching values.

**Paper or page:** [Measurized Markov Decision Processes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.03888v4), [Measurized Markov Decision Processes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.03888v4). It says: “states are probability measures on the original state space, and actions are stochastic kernels on the original action space.”

**Sources:**

- [Daniel Adelman, Alba V. Olivares-Nadal, Measurized Markov Decision Processes, arXiv:2405.03888v4 (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.03888v4)

### Maximizing a reward quantile becomes a search over probability-minimizing thresholds

**Remember:** Replace the quantile with a search over reward thresholds.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 90C40 (Markov and semi-Markov decision processes), 90C39. arXiv math.OC. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** The α-quantile, or value-at-risk, of a reward R is the least threshold λ with P(R ≤ λ) ≥ α. It is not additive over time, so ordinary dynamic programming does not apply to it directly.

**Problem.** Take a finite-horizon finite Markov decision process. Its optimal value-at-risk is the least λ at which the minimal probability of total reward at most λ reaches α. Each such minimization is an ordinary Markov decision problem on states augmented with the remaining threshold.

**How the definition helps.** The quantile definition places a single threshold outside a probability, so the problem splits into an outer search and an inner probability minimization. At a fixed threshold, the probability is the expected value of a 0-or-1 payoff, by our own observation. So the inner problem has an additive form that dynamic programming can handle. For accumulated rewards, the paper adds the remaining threshold to the state.

**Paper or page:** [Markov Decision Processes with Value-at-Risk Criterion](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.22355v1), [Markov Decision Processes with Value-at-Risk Criterion](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.22355v1). It says: “By establishing the equivalence between the VaR maximization MDP and a series of probabilistic minimization MDPs, we transform the VaR maximization MDP into a constrained bilevel optimization problem.”

**Sources:**

- [Li Xia, Jinyan Pan, Markov Decision Processes with Value-at-Risk Criterion, arXiv:2507.22355v1 (2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.22355v1)

### Robust Bellman evaluation works exactly when worst cases are simultaneously solvable

**Remember:** Independent uncertainty choices let separate worst cases fit together.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 90C40 (Markov and semi-Markov decision processes), 90C17. arXiv math.OC. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A robust Markov decision process has a set 𝒫 of possible transition models. Simultaneous solvability says that for any choice of one linear cost per state, a single model in 𝒫 minimizes all these costs at once. Each state's cost looks only at that state's row of transition probabilities. 𝒫 is s-rectangular when it is the product of its state-by-state parts.

**Problem.** Let 𝒫 be compact. State-by-state worst-case Bellman evaluation gives the true robust value for every stationary policy, reward and discount exactly when simultaneous solvability holds. If 𝒫 is also convex, this happens exactly when 𝒫 is s-rectangular.

**How the definition helps.** Simultaneous solvability states exactly what state-by-state evaluation needs: the separate worst cases fit together into one model. That is Theorem 1. For a product set this is clear, because each state's worst row can be chosen independently, by our own explanation. When rows are coupled, two states can prefer incompatible models, by our own example of one shared parameter. The hard direction of Theorem 2 uses convexity to turn the property back into a product structure.

**Paper or page:** [Tractable Robust Markov Decision Processes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.08435v1), [Tractable Robust Markov Decision Processes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.08435v1), [Tractable Robust Markov Decision Processes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.08435v1). It says: “our proof techniques rely on identifying a novel simultaneous solvability property, which we show is at the heart of several important properties of RMDPs, including the existence of stationary optimal policies and dynamic programming-based formulations.”

**Sources:**

- [Julien Grand-Clément, Nian Si, Shengbo Wang, Tractable Robust Markov Decision Processes, arXiv:2411.08435v1 (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.08435v1)

### White's vector Bellman equations hold once policies may depend on history

**Remember:** Keep the history so separate branches can choose separate continuations.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 90C40 (Markov and semi-Markov decision processes), 90C29. arXiv math.OC. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** In a Markov decision process with vector rewards, a history-dependent policy may choose different actions after different sequences of visited states. A return vector is Pareto efficient if no other return is at least as large in every component and different. White's equations compute sets of efficient returns by backward recursion.

**Problem.** In a finite-horizon model, White's backward recursion gives exactly the Pareto efficient expected returns of the history-dependent policies. For policies that see only the current state, this can fail.

**How the definition helps.** Allowing history lets a policy combine independently chosen continuations after different past paths, which the recursion needs, in our own reading. Proposition 4 of the paper builds such a combined policy. A policy that sees only the current state must make the same later choice after two different histories, by our own account. The paper gives a counterexample for that case and proves the corrected statement.

**Paper or page:** [A Counterexample and a Corrective to the Vector Extension of the Bellman Equations of a Markov Decision Process](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.16937v3), [A Counterexample and a Corrective to the Vector Extension of the Bellman Equations of a Markov Decision Process](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.16937v3). It says: “For all t ≤ N, for all hₜ = (s₁, ..., sₜ) ∈ Hₜ, Uₜ(sₜ) = e(V′ₜ(hₜ)).”

**Sources:**

- [Anas Mifrani, A Counterexample and a Corrective to the Vector Extension of the Bellman Equations of a Markov Decision Process, arXiv:2306.16937v3 (2023)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.16937v3)

### Every local minimizer is asymptotically stationary without any constraint qualification

**Remember:** Let the errors vanish without requiring the multipliers to settle.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 90C46 (Optimality conditions and duality in mathematical programming), 49J52. arXiv math.OC. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Mordukhovich stationarity (M-stationarity) asks for a multiplier that solves a generalized first-order equation at the point. Asymptotic M-stationarity (AM-stationarity) asks instead for points xₖ → x̄ and multipliers λₖ whose residual in this equation tends to 0. The multipliers need not converge or stay bounded.

**Problem.** Every local minimizer of the paper's nonsmooth problem is AM-stationary, with no constraint qualification. A constraint qualification is an extra regularity condition on the constraints. Under the paper's AM-regularity condition, the minimizer is also M-stationary.

**How the definition helps.** Because the multipliers may diverge, the definition removes the usual obstacle to a necessary condition, so it holds at every local minimizer. The theorem still has to construct the approximating points and multipliers. Lemma 3.4 shows what the definition gives back. Bounded multipliers give M-stationarity, and unbounded ones give a degenerate multiplier.

**Paper or page:** [Asymptotic stationarity and regularity for nonsmooth optimization problems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.09734v3), [Asymptotic stationarity and regularity for nonsmooth optimization problems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.09734v3). It says: “Let x̄ ∈ M be a local minimizer of (basic problem). Then x̄ is an AM-stationary point of (basic problem).”

**Sources:**

- [Patrick Mehlitz, Asymptotic stationarity and regularity for nonsmooth optimization problems, Journal of Nonsmooth Analysis and Optimization, Volume 1, Original research articles (December 15, 2020) jnsao:6575 \[arXiv:2006.09734v3\]](https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.09734v3)

### Calm local minimax points admit first- and second-order optimality conditions

**Remember:** Keep the maximizing response within a fixed multiple of the minimizing move.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 90C47 (Minimax problems in mathematical programming), 49K35. arXiv math.OC. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** At a local minimax point (x̄, ȳ), no small move of y raises f(x̄, ·) above f(x̄, ȳ). Also, for each x near x̄, the maximum of f(x, ·) over a small ball around ȳ is at least f(x̄, ȳ). The point is calm when some constant κ works as follows. For x within δ of x̄, a ball of radius κδ around ȳ is large enough.

**Problem.** For calm local minimax points of nonsmooth constrained problems, the paper proves first- and second-order necessary and sufficient conditions. In the smooth unconstrained case, calmness gives this: for every direction u there is h with ∇²f(x̄, ȳ)((u,h),(u,h)) ≥ 0. Under a weak second-order condition on the inner maximization, calm and ordinary local minimax points coincide.

**How the definition helps.** The calm radius bounds the maximizer's response by a multiple of the minimizer's move, so both moves expand in one small parameter. The response to x̄ + tu then has a limiting direction h after scaling by t, by our own explanation. That pair (u, h) enters the second-order condition. The paper still has to prove when an ordinary local minimax point is calm.

**Paper or page:** [Calm local optimality for nonconvex-nonconcave minimax problems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.17443v1), [Calm local optimality for nonconvex-nonconcave minimax problems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.17443v1), [Calm local optimality for nonconvex-nonconcave minimax problems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.17443v1). It says: “Moreover we show that the calm local minimax optimality and the local minimax optimality coincide under a weak sufficient optimality condition for the maximization problem.”

**Sources:**

- [Xiaoxiao Ma, Wei Yao, Jane J. Ye, Jin Zhang, Calm local optimality for nonconvex-nonconcave minimax problems, arXiv:2306.17443v1 (2023)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.17443v1)

### The Hessian makes self-concordance invariant under affine substitution

**Remember:** Measure each direction using the function’s own curvature.

*True by definition.* MSC 90C51 (Interior-point methods), 90C25, 65K10. arXiv math.OC. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Let f be a three-times continuously differentiable convex function on an open convex set, and let M ≥ 0. Self-concordance bounds the absolute third directional derivative by M times the second directional derivative raised to the 3/2 power. The derivatives are those of f restricted to a line. This uses the Hessian, the matrix of second derivatives, rather than a fixed Euclidean norm to measure direction.

**Problem.** Substituting Ax + b for the argument of a self-concordant function preserves the same constant on the nonempty domain of the new function.

**How the definition helps.** The Hessian-based bound is unchanged because both directional derivatives after substitution are the old derivatives along the same transformed direction. This is the chain rule along a line. A bound on changes of the Hessian in a fixed Euclidean norm can instead change its constant under a rescaling. The work in the theory is not invariance. It is using the new bound to control Newton steps, which use first and second derivatives to move toward a minimum.

**Wikipedia:** [Self-concordant function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Self-concordant_function). It says: “The authors note that the right hand side can be made also invariant if we replace the Euclidean metric by the scalar product defined by the Hessian of f”

**Sources:**

- [Yurii Nesterov and Arkadii Nemirovskii, Interior-Point Polynomial Algorithms in Convex Programming, SIAM (1994)](https://doi.org/10.1137/1.9781611970791)

## 91 Game theory, economics, finance, and other social and behavioral sciences

### Mixed strategies give every finite zero-sum game a value

**Remember:** Randomizing makes the best guaranteed gain equal the least guaranteed loss.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 91A05 (2-person games), 90C47. arXiv econ.TH, math.OC. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** In a finite two-player zero-sum game with payoff matrix A, a mixed strategy is a probability vector over a player's actions. If the players use mixed strategies x and y, player one's expected payoff is xᵀAy and player two loses that amount.

**Problem.** Von Neumann's minimax theorem (1928): max over x of min over y of xᵀAy equals min over y of max over x. This common number is the value of the game. With pure strategies only, the two sides can differ.

**How the definition helps.** Mixed strategies make the strategy sets compact convex simplices and the payoff bilinear, and those are exactly the conditions a minimax theorem needs. Our own example: in matching pennies, with payoffs ±1, the pure max-min is −1 and the pure min-max is +1. With fifty-fifty mixing both equal 0. The page states the theorem in general, for compact convex sets and continuous concave-convex functions. The theorem is equivalent to linear programming duality (our own). What stays hard is infinite games, where the theorem can fail without compactness or continuity (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Minimax theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minimax_theorem). It says: “In the context of two-player zero-sum games, the sets X and Y correspond to the strategy sets of the first and second player, respectively, which consist of lotteries over their actions (so-called mixed strategies)”

**Sources:**

- [J. v. Neumann, Zur Theorie der Gesellschaftsspiele, Mathematische Annalen 100 (1928), 295–320](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01448847)

### Letting players randomize makes Nash equilibria exist

**Remember:** Allow players to randomize, and every finite game has an equilibrium.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 91A10 (Noncooperative games). arXiv econ.TH, cs.GT. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** A mixed strategy is a probability distribution over a player's pure strategies. A Nash equilibrium is a choice of one mixed strategy for each player with this property: if the strategies of the others stay fixed, no player can raise their own expected payoff by a change of strategy.

**Problem.** Every finite game in normal form (a game given by a table of payoffs) has at least one Nash equilibrium.

**How the definition helps.** Mixed strategies make the set of strategies compact and convex, so a fixed-point theorem applies. With pure strategies only, some finite games have no equilibrium. The article shows a 2×2 game in which, in each of the 4 cells, some player gains by a change of strategy. With mixed strategies, each player's set of strategies is a simplex, which is compact and convex. Expected payoffs are continuous, so the Kakutani or Brouwer fixed-point theorem applies. Von Neumann and Morgenstern had used mixed strategies only for zero-sum games; Nash defined the equilibrium for every finite game. What stays hard: the fixed-point proof does not say how to find an equilibrium.

**Wikipedia:** [Nash equilibrium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nash_equilibrium). It says: “The key to Nash's ability to prove existence far more generally than von Neumann lay in his definition of equilibrium.”

**Sources:**

- [Nash, J. F. (1950). Equilibrium points in n-person games. PNAS 36(1), 48–49.](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.36.1.48)

### Subgame perfection removes non-credible threats, so backward induction finds equilibria

**Remember:** An equilibrium must stay an equilibrium wherever the game happens to go.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 91A11 (Equilibrium refinements), 91A18. arXiv econ.TH, cs.GT. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** A subgame is the part of a game tree that starts at one decision point and contains everything after it. A strategy profile is a subgame perfect equilibrium if it is a Nash equilibrium in every subgame. Reinhard Selten introduced the idea in 1965.

**Problem.** Every finite game with perfect information has a subgame perfect equilibrium, and backward induction computes it. Plain Nash equilibrium does not give this result, because some Nash equilibria rest on threats that a player would never carry out.

**How the definition helps.** Subgame perfection tests a plan in every subgame, so a threat that a player would not carry out fails the test. Nash equilibrium tests a plan only along the path that is played, so such a threat costs nothing. Our own example: an incumbent firm threatens a price war if a rival enters. The profile 'rival stays out, incumbent fights after entry' is a Nash equilibrium, but fighting is worse for the incumbent once entry has happened. Subgame perfection excludes it, and backward induction then fixes the last mover's best choice first and works backwards. The page notes that backward induction does not apply to infinite horizons or imperfect information. For infinite horizons it names the one-shot deviation principle instead.

**Wikipedia:** [Subgame perfect equilibrium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subgame_perfect_equilibrium). It says: “This ensures that strategies are credible and rational throughout the entire game, eliminating non-credible threats.”

**Sources:**

- [R. Selten, Spieltheoretische Behandlung eines Oligopolmodells mit Nachfrageträgheit, Zeitschrift für die gesamte Staatswissenschaft 121 (1965), 301–324 and 667–689](https://www.jstor.org/stable/40748884)
- [R. Selten, Reexamination of the perfectness concept for equilibrium points in extensive games, International Journal of Game Theory 4 (1975), 25–55](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01766400)

### Gibbard–Satterthwaite counts possible outcomes, so two-outcome rules escape

**Remember:** Three possible winners force a dictator or a chance to lie.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 91B12 (Voting theory), 91B14. arXiv econ.TH, cs.GT. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** A voting rule maps each list of voters' strict rankings of the candidates to one winner. The possible outcomes of the rule are the candidates that win for at least one list of rankings. A rule is manipulable if some voter can get a winner she prefers by reporting a false ranking.

**Problem.** Gibbard–Satterthwaite theorem: every voting rule with at least three possible outcomes is dictatorial or manipulable. A rule is dictatorial if it always picks the top choice of one fixed voter.

**How the definition helps.** With only two possible outcomes, majority vote between them, with a fixed rule for ties, is neither dictatorial nor manipulable (our own). A false ranking can only help the candidate the voter likes less. So the theorem must exclude rules with two outcomes. The page stresses that the condition is on possible outcomes, not on the number of candidates. Candidates who can never win do not matter, so the theorem applies whenever at least three can win. Some books assume instead at least three candidates and that every candidate can win; that version is less general. What stays hard is the proof, which goes through Arrow's theorem or a direct pivotal-voter argument.

**Wikipedia:** [Gibbard–Satterthwaite theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gibbard%E2%80%93Satterthwaite_theorem). It says: “It is only assumed that at least three of them can win, i.e. are possible outcomes of the voting rule.”

**Sources:**

- [A. Gibbard, Manipulation of Voting Schemes: A General Result, Econometrica 41 (1973), 587–601](https://doi.org/10.2307/1914083)
- [M. A. Satterthwaite, Strategy-proofness and Arrow's conditions, Journal of Economic Theory 10 (1975), 187–217](https://doi.org/10.1016/0022-0531(75)90050-2)

### Single-peaked preferences escape Arrow's theorem

**Remember:** One peak per voter on one line means no majority cycles.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 91B12 (Voting theory), 91B14. arXiv econ.TH. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** A group of voters has single-peaked preferences if the alternatives can be put in one order, like points on a line, with this property. Each voter has an ideal point. Between two alternatives on the same side of that point, the voter prefers the closer one.

**Problem.** Majority rule can produce cycles, where A beats B, B beats C and C beats A (Condorcet's paradox). Arrow's theorem says that no ranked voting rule meets all of his conditions on the unrestricted domain. On that domain, every profile (one ranking for each voter) is allowed.

**How the definition helps.** Arrow's theorem needs every profile to be allowed, and single-peaked preferences remove the profiles that cause cycles. The standard bad profile is the Condorcet cycle, with voters ranking A-B-C, B-C-A and C-A-B. It is not single-peaked on any line, because each alternative is ranked last by some voter. When preferences are single-peaked, majority preferences have no cycles. The ideal point of the median voter is then the Condorcet winner, the alternative that beats every other alternative in a majority vote. With an odd number of voters, majority rule meets all of Arrow's conditions (Black). What stays hard: in two or more dimensions a Condorcet winner usually does not exist and cycles come back (the McKelvey–Schofield chaos theorem).

**Wikipedia:** [Single peaked preferences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Single_peaked_preferences), [Arrow's impossibility theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arrow%27s_impossibility_theorem), [Median voter theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Median_voter_theorem). It says: “If the domain is restricted to profiles where every individual has a single-peaked preference with respect to the linear ordering, then social preferences are acyclic.”

**Sources:**

- [Black, D. (1948). On the rationale of group decision-making. Journal of Political Economy 56(1), 23–34.](https://doi.org/10.1086/256633)
- [Arrow, K. J. (1950). A difficulty in the concept of social welfare. Journal of Political Economy 58(4), 328–346.](https://doi.org/10.1086/256963)

### With two alternatives Arrow's conditions hold, and May picks majority rule

**Remember:** Two options give majority rule; three options give Arrow's impossibility.
